teachingStrategy:
══ Pattern A – newest FBISE model paper (“50% MCQs & 50% Descriptive”)
FBISE calls this the “Final conceptual pattern of SSC-I & II” for Physics, Chemistry, Biology and Computer Science. It is the most likely pattern for 2027–28, but confirm with FBISE.
- Theory paper: 60 marks.
- Section A (1 h 20 min): 60 MCQs × 0.5 = 30 marks: 40 straight MCQs + 20 scenario/stimulus MCQs.
- Section B: 6 short questions × 3 = 18 marks, each with an internal choice (OR).
- Section C: 2 long questions × 6 = 12 marks, each with an internal choice.
- Sections B and C together: 1 h 40 min.
- Only summative SLOs are examined. Cognitive levels: about 30% Knowledge, 50% Understanding, 20% Application (±5%).
══ Pattern B – used in the Annual 2026 exam (Inclusive Scheme of Studies 2024)
- Section A: 12 MCQs × 1 = 12 marks (20 min).
- Section B: 10 short questions × 3 = 30 marks, each with an OR choice.
- Section C: 3 long questions × 6 = 18 marks, each with an OR choice (2 h 40 min for B + C).
- Total theory 60 marks. Practical work is assessed separately (PBA).
══ Older papers in your files
- Annual 2025, 2nd Annual 2025 and the Annual 2026 “Curriculum 2022-23 (Old)” paper used 12 MCQs + 11 short (33) + 4 long (20) = 65 marks. Their content is the same curriculum, so their questions are included here as past-paper practice.
- The 2023 and 2024 papers and the “Curriculum 2006 (OLD)” papers follow the old 2006 syllabus and are not used for practice in this app.

chapters.title: Nature of Science in Chemistry
chapters.introduction:
Chemistry is everywhere: in the food you cook, the medicines you take, the battery in your phone and the water you drink. This first unit explains what chemistry is, introduces its main branches, shows the kind of essential questions each branch tries to answer, and explains how science, technology and engineering work together.
It is a short, mostly theory chapter, but FBISE asks 1–3 MCQs and short questions from it every year (for example: “identify the branch of chemistry involved”).

Exam focus: “Identify the branch of chemistry” questions appear in almost every paper (Annual 2025, 2nd Annual 2025, Annual 2026). Learn one clear example for each branch.

══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
Exam focus: “Identify the branch of chemistry” questions appear in almost every paper (Annual 2025, 2nd Annual 2025, Annual 2026). Learn one clear example for each branch.

══ 1.1 Definition of chemistry and its interaction with matter and energy (pp. 6) ══
Chemistry is the science that investigates the materials of the universe and the changes that these materials undergo. It deals with the composition, structure, properties, behaviour and changes of matter, and the energy that goes with those changes.
The FBISE SLO also describes chemistry as the study of the Earth (solids), Air (gases), Sea (liquids) and Sky (plasma) and how they interact with each other.
Why study chemistry?
- It explains natural events (rusting, burning, digestion, photosynthesis).
- It lets us make new substances: medicines, fertilizers, plastics, fuels.
- It helps us protect the environment (green chemistry, water treatment).
Green chemistry is the design of chemical products and processes that reduce or remove the use of hazardous substances. It helps us understand and reduce pollution.
Key Point: - Chemistry = study of matter + its changes + the energy involved.
- Matter interacts with other matter (reactions) and with energy (heat, light, electricity).
- Green chemistry reduces hazardous substances.
Exam Tip: For a 1-mark definition write: “Chemistry is the branch of science that deals with the composition, structure, properties of matter and the changes matter undergoes, along with the energy changes involved.”
کیمیا سائنس کی وہ شاخ ہے جس میں مادّے کی ترکیب، ساخت، خصوصیات اور اس میں ہونے والی تبدیلیوں کا مطالعہ کیا جاتا ہے، اور ان تبدیلیوں کے ساتھ توانائی کی تبدیلی کا بھی۔ گرین کیمسٹری ایسے کیمیائی طریقے بناتی ہے جن میں نقصان دہ مادّوں کا استعمال کم سے کم ہو۔

══ 1.2 Branches of chemistry (pp. 6–7) ══
Chemistry is a very large subject, so it is divided into branches (sub-fields). Many branches overlap with other sciences; these are interdisciplinary fields (e.g. biochemistry = biology + chemistry, geochemistry = geology + chemistry).
1. Organic chemistry – study of carbon compounds (except carbonates, bicarbonates, oxides of carbon and carbides). Example: making medicines, plastics, petrol products.
2. Inorganic chemistry – study of elements and their compounds except organic compounds. Example: metals, salts, minerals, cement, glass.
3. Physical chemistry – laws and theories that explain the structure and changes of matter (energy, rates, equilibrium, electrochemistry). Example: car batteries work on electrochemistry; Boyle’s law; a gas liquefying when cooled.
4. Analytical chemistry – methods and instruments for finding the composition (what and how much) of matter. Example: titration to find concentration; forensic tests.
5. Biochemistry – chemical changes in living organisms. Example: breakdown of glucose to give energy; enzymes; proteins like keratin in hair.
6. Environmental chemistry – chemicals and toxic substances that pollute air, water and soil, and their effects. Example: acid rain from SO₂; CFCs and the ozone layer; rising CO₂.
7. Industrial chemistry – large-scale production of chemicals. Example: ammonia by the Haber process; sulphuric acid by the Contact process.
8. Medicinal chemistry – interaction between drugs and biological targets, and development of new medicines.
9. Polymer chemistry – polymers, their types, properties, uses and polymerisation. Example: nylon, polythene bags, polyester, Teflon, epoxy glue.
10. Geochemistry – composition and changes of elements in the Earth’s crust: rocks, minerals, soil, water, atmosphere.
11. Nuclear chemistry – changes in atomic nuclei: radioactivity, nuclear energy, radioisotopes in medicine (cancer treatment).
12. Astrochemistry – chemical processes in space: stars, planets, comets, interstellar clouds.
[Table: Quick identification table (very common in exams)]
Situation in the question | Branch
• Haber process makes NH₃ on a large scale | Industrial chemistry
• Contact process makes H₂SO₄ on a large scale | Industrial chemistry
• Glucose is broken down to give energy in our body | Biochemistry
• Hair protein keratin; enzymes in digestion | Biochemistry
• CFCs destroy the ozone layer; SO₂ causes acid rain; CO₂ warms the Earth | Environmental chemistry
• Boyle’s law; gas liquefies on cooling; batteries/electrochemistry | Physical chemistry
• Titration to find concentration; testing purity of a drug | Analytical chemistry
• Synthesis of a new medicine | Organic / Medicinal chemistry
• Composition of rocks, minerals and soil | Geochemistry
• Radioisotopes for cancer treatment; nuclear reactor | Nuclear chemistry
• Molecules found in comets or interstellar clouds | Astrochemistry
• Nylon, polythene, Teflon | Polymer chemistry
Key Point: - Organic: carbon compounds (not CO, CO₂, carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides).
- Inorganic: everything else (elements, salts, minerals).
- Biochemistry: living things. Environmental: pollution. Industrial: large scale.
Exam Tip: In “identify the branch” questions, look for the key word: living body → biochemistry; large scale → industrial; pollution/ozone/acid rain → environmental; law/energy/battery → physical; how much/composition/titration → analytical.
کیمیا کو کئی شاخوں میں تقسیم کیا جاتا ہے: نامیاتی کیمیا کاربن کے مرکبات، غیر نامیاتی کیمیا باقی عناصر اور ان کے مرکبات، طبیعی کیمیا قوانین اور نظریات، تجزیاتی کیمیا کسی چیز کی ترکیب معلوم کرنا، حیاتیاتی کیمیا جانداروں میں کیمیائی تبدیلیاں، ماحولیاتی کیمیا آلودگی، صنعتی کیمیا بڑے پیمانے پر کیمیکلز کی تیاری، جیو کیمسٹری زمین کی چٹانیں اور معدنیات، نیوکلیئر کیمسٹری ایٹم کے مرکزے کی تبدیلیاں اور آسٹرو کیمسٹری خلا میں ہونے والے کیمیائی عمل۔

══ 1.3 Essential questions for the branches of chemistry (pp. 7–8) ══
An essential question is a big, open question that a branch of chemistry tries to answer. Writing such questions shows you understand what each branch is about (SLO C-09-A-03).
- Physical chemistry: What is the structure of an atom and how does it affect chemical behaviour? How do ionic, covalent and metallic bonds form?
- Organic chemistry: Why is carbon the backbone of organic compounds? What are functional groups and how do they affect properties?
- Inorganic chemistry: What distinguishes inorganic from organic compounds? How does the periodic table organise elements?
- Analytical chemistry: How can we accurately identify and measure the amount of a substance in a sample?
- Biochemistry: How do carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids build and run living organisms?
- Environmental chemistry: How do human activities pollute the air? How can we reduce the effect of greenhouse gases?
- Medicinal chemistry: How are drugs designed for a specific disease?
- Polymer chemistry: What are polymers and how does their structure affect their properties?
- Geochemistry: How do geological processes control where elements are found in the Earth’s crust?
- Nuclear chemistry: How do nuclear reactions differ from chemical reactions? What is the role of radioisotopes in medicine and industry?
- Astrochemistry: What reactions take place in stars and interstellar space?
Exam Tip: If asked to “formulate” an essential question, start with How/Why/What and link it clearly to the branch. One good question per branch is enough.
ہر شاخ کچھ بنیادی سوالات کا جواب تلاش کرتی ہے، مثلاً تجزیاتی کیمیا: “کسی نمونے میں کون سا مادّہ کتنی مقدار میں ہے؟” ماحولیاتی کیمیا: “انسانی سرگرمیاں ہوا کو کیسے آلودہ کرتی ہیں؟”

══ 1.4 Daily life applications of chemistry (pp. 8–9) ══
- Organic chemistry in action: organic chemists synthesise new medicines that act on specific targets such as proteins or enzymes.
- Inorganic chemistry: lithium-ion (Li-ion) batteries power phones, toys, wireless headphones, power tools and electric vehicles.
- Analytical chemistry: forensic chemistry examines body fluids, bones, fibres and drugs; coloured powders are analysed to find which drug they contain.
- Physical chemistry: batteries in vehicles work on the principle of electrochemistry.
- Environmental chemistry: water contaminated by soil and dust is treated by sedimentation, filtration and disinfection.
- Industrial chemistry: fertilizers, cement, paper, soaps and detergents are made on a large scale.
کیمیا کے روزمرہ استعمال: نئی دوائیں (نامیاتی کیمیا)، موبائل اور گاڑیوں کی لیتھیم آئن بیٹریاں (غیر نامیاتی کیمیا)، جرائم کی تفتیش میں فارنزک ٹیسٹ (تجزیاتی کیمیا)، اور گندے پانی کی صفائی (ماحولیاتی کیمیا)۔

══ 1.5 Science, technology and engineering (pp. 9–12) ══
- Science is the systematic study of the natural world through observation and experiment to discover facts, laws and principles. Example: chemists study why iron rusts.
- Technology is the application of scientific knowledge for practical purposes, giving tools, machines, techniques and materials. Example: paint or galvanising to stop rusting; solar panels.
- Engineering is the application of science and mathematics to design, build and maintain systems, structures, machines and processes that solve problems. Example: designing a solar power plant or a water-filtration plant.
They work together:
- Rusting of iron: scientists find that iron + water + oxygen form rust; technologists develop coatings; engineers design rust-proof bridges and cars.
- Solar energy: scientists study photovoltaic cells → technologists make solar panels → engineers design large solar power plants (wiring by electrical engineers, structures by civil engineers).
- Water filtration: chemical engineers design the purification process; mechanical engineers design the pumps and filters.
- French fries: scientists study carbohydrates and oils → food technologists extract oil from seeds → chemical engineers design oil-production plants.
- Plastic bags: scientists study monomers joining into polymers (polyethylene) → engineers and technicians make strong, flexible bags.
Note: in the FBISE framework this SLO (C-09-A-04) is formative: taught in class but not asked in the annual exam. It is still useful for understanding.
[Table: Science vs technology vs engineering]
 | Science | Technology | Engineering
• Main aim | Understand nature | Apply knowledge to make useful tools | Design and build solutions
• Question asked | Why/how does it happen? | How can we use it? | How can we build it at scale, safely?
• Rust example | Iron + O₂ + H₂O form rust | Paint, galvanising, alloys | Rust-resistant bridges and car bodies
Key Point: Science = knowing; Technology = using; Engineering = designing and building.
سائنس قدرت کو سمجھنے کا منظم مطالعہ ہے، ٹیکنالوجی سائنسی علم کو عملی کاموں میں استعمال کرنا ہے، اور انجینئرنگ سائنس اور ریاضی کی مدد سے نظام، مشینیں اور ڈھانچے ڈیزائن کر کے بنانا ہے۔ مثال: سائنسدان زنگ لگنے کی وجہ معلوم کرتے ہیں، ٹیکنالوجی رنگ اور گیلوانائزنگ دیتی ہے، اور انجینئر زنگ سے محفوظ پل بناتے ہیں۔

══ Chapter 1 in one page
- Chemistry: study of composition, structure, properties and changes of matter, and the energy involved. Earth (solids), sea (liquids), air (gases), sky (plasma).
- Green chemistry: reduce hazardous substances.
- Branches: organic (carbon compounds, not CO, CO₂, carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides) · inorganic (all others) · physical (laws, energy, batteries) · analytical (composition, titration, forensics) · biochemistry (living organisms) · environmental (pollution) · industrial (large scale: Haber, Contact) · medicinal (drugs) · polymer (nylon, polythene, Teflon) · geochemistry (rocks, minerals) · nuclear (nucleus, radioisotopes) · astrochemistry (space).

chapters.definitions:
• Chemistry (کیمیا) [p. 6]: The branch of science that deals with the composition, structure and properties of matter, the changes it undergoes and the energy involved in those changes.
• Green chemistry (گرین کیمسٹری) [p. 6]: The design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use and production of hazardous substances.
• Organic chemistry (نامیاتی کیمیا) [p. 6]: The branch of chemistry that deals with carbon compounds, except carbonates, bicarbonates, oxides of carbon and carbides.
• Inorganic chemistry (غیر نامیاتی کیمیا) [p. 6]: The branch of chemistry that deals with elements and their compounds except organic compounds.
• Physical chemistry (طبیعی کیمیا) [p. 6]: The branch of chemistry that deals with the laws and theories used to understand the structure and changes of matter.
• Analytical chemistry (تجزیاتی کیمیا) [p. 6]: The branch of chemistry that deals with methods and instruments for determining the composition and properties of matter.
• Biochemistry (حیاتیاتی کیمیا) [p. 6]: The branch of chemistry that deals with the physical and chemical changes that occur in living organisms.
• Environmental chemistry (ماحولیاتی کیمیا) [p. 6]: The branch of chemistry that studies chemical and toxic substances that pollute the environment and their harmful effects on living things.
• Industrial chemistry (صنعتی کیمیا) [p. 7]: The branch of chemistry that deals with the large-scale production of chemical substances.
• Medicinal chemistry (ادویاتی کیمیا) [p. 7]: The branch of chemistry that studies the interaction between drugs and biological targets and develops new medicines.
• Polymer chemistry (پولیمر کیمسٹری) [p. 7]: The branch of chemistry that studies polymers, their types, properties, uses and polymerisation.
• Geochemistry (جیو کیمسٹری) [p. 7]: The branch of chemistry that studies the composition, distribution and changes of elements and compounds in the Earth’s crust.
• Nuclear chemistry (نیوکلیئر کیمسٹری) [p. 7]: The branch of chemistry that deals with changes that occur in atomic nuclei.
• Astrochemistry (آسٹرو کیمسٹری) [p. 7]: The branch of chemistry that studies chemical processes and reactions in stars, planets, comets and interstellar space.
• Science (سائنس) [p. 9]: The systematic process of building and organising knowledge about the natural world through observation and experiment.
• Technology (ٹیکنالوجی) [p. 10]: The application of scientific knowledge for practical purposes, producing tools, machines, techniques and materials.
• Engineering (انجینئرنگ) [p. 10]: The application of scientific and mathematical principles to design, build and improve systems, structures and machines.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Matter (مادّہ): Anything that has mass and occupies space
• Composition (ترکیب): What a substance is made of
• Property (خاصیت): A feature of a substance
• Branch (شاخ): A sub-field of a subject
• Interdisciplinary (بین الشعبہ): Combining two or more subjects
• Pollutant (آلودگی پیدا کرنے والا مادّہ): A harmful substance in the environment
• Polymer (پولیمر): A very large molecule made of repeating units
• Radioisotope (تابکار ہم جا): A radioactive isotope
• Technology (ٹیکنالوجی): Application of science
• Engineering (انجینئرنگ): Designing and building systems
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• N₂(g) + 3H₂(g)  2NH₃(g) — Haber process (industrial chemistry example).
• 4Fe(s) + 3O₂(g) + 2xH₂O(l) -> 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂O(s) — Rusting of iron (example used for science–technology–engineering).
• C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ -> 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy — Breakdown of glucose in the body (biochemistry example).

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. A student says, “Carbon dioxide contains carbon, so it is an organic compound.” Is the student correct?
   Answer: No. CO₂ is an oxide of carbon, which is studied in inorganic chemistry. Organic compounds are carbon compounds (usually with C–H bonds), excluding carbonates, bicarbonates, carbon oxides and carbides.
2. Why is biochemistry called an interdisciplinary field?
   Answer: Because it combines biology (living organisms) and chemistry (molecules and reactions) to explain life processes such as digestion and respiration.
3. Is “making a new type of battery for electric cars” science, technology or engineering?
   Answer: Mostly technology (applying electrochemistry to make a product), built on science (understanding the reactions), and engineering is needed to design the battery pack and car systems.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. A factory near a river releases coloured waste water. Which two branches of chemistry would help, and how?
   Answer: Analytical chemistry identifies which chemicals and how much are present; environmental chemistry studies their harmful effects and suggests treatment (neutralisation, filtration, removal of heavy metals).
2. Police find a white powder at a crime scene. Which branch of chemistry is used to identify it?
   Answer: Analytical (forensic) chemistry: tests and instruments identify the substance and its amount.
3. Which branch of chemistry would study why a meteorite contains amino acids?
   Answer: Astrochemistry (chemistry of space), with help from biochemistry.

══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Identify the branch of chemistry involved: (a) Large-scale production of NH₃ by Haber’s process (b) Breakdown of glucose gives energy to our body (c) Use of CFCs in refrigerators linked to depletion of the ozone layer. [FBISE Annual 2026]
   Solution: (a) Industrial chemistry – large-scale production.
(b) Biochemistry – chemical change inside a living body.
(c) Environmental chemistry – a pollutant damaging the environment.

2. Show how science, technology and engineering work together using the example of rusting.
   Solution: - Science: experiments show that iron rusts only when both water and oxygen are present.
- Technology: this knowledge gives paints, oiling, galvanising (zinc coating) and stainless-steel alloys.
- Engineering: engineers choose and apply these methods to design long-lasting bridges, ships and car bodies.
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 1 Exercises (13–14):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. Which branch of chemistry is the study of elements and their compounds except for organic compounds? → C (Inorganic chemistry) | Inorganic chemistry covers all elements and their compounds except organic (carbon) compounds.
ii. Which branch of chemistry helps to protect water that has been poisoned by soil? → A (Environmental chemistry) | Treating polluted water (sedimentation, filtration, disinfection) is environmental chemistry (textbook p. 9).
iii. Which area of chemistry helps to gauge the behaviour of pollutants and develop techniques for pollution control? → C (Environmental chemistry) | Studying pollutants and their control is environmental chemistry.
iv. The branch of chemistry that helps to synthesize new medicines: → B (Organic) | The textbook (p. 8) says organic chemists synthesise new medicines.
v. The branch of science that helps to understand chemical products and processes that reduce the use of hazardous substances: → C (Green chemistry) | Green chemistry designs products and processes that reduce hazardous substances.
vi. To identify the concentration of a particular solution through titration is an application of: → B (Analytical chemistry) | Finding “how much” of a substance (concentration) is analytical chemistry.
vii. The batteries in our vehicles are built on the principle of electrochemistry. It is the application of: → D (Physical chemistry) | Electrochemistry is part of physical chemistry (textbook p. 9).
viii. The branch of chemistry that is concerned with the large-scale production of chemical substances is: → A (Industrial chemistry) | Large-scale production = industrial chemistry.
ix. The branch of chemistry that focuses on the study of polymers, their types, properties and uses is called: → B (Polymer chemistry) | By definition this is polymer chemistry.
x. The study of the interaction between drugs and biological targets, as well as the development of new medicinal agents: → B (Medicinal chemistry) | This is the textbook definition of medicinal chemistry (p. 7).

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) How does chemistry help a doctor to know about the chemical nature of medicine?
   Answer: Chemistry tells the doctor what a medicine is made of and how it acts in the body. Medicinal and organic chemistry explain how a drug molecule binds to a target (an enzyme or protein) to treat a disease, and biochemistry explains how the body breaks the drug down. Analytical chemistry checks the purity and correct dose. With this knowledge the doctor can choose the right medicine, avoid harmful interactions and understand side effects.
(ii) In what ways does technological innovation help to understand the development of new materials?
   Answer: Technology gives chemists tools, machines and techniques (modern microscopes, spectrometers, computers, chromatography). These let them:
- see the structure of materials at the atomic level,
- analyse and identify substances quickly and accurately,
- test new materials (strength, conductivity, heat resistance) and improve them.
So technology makes research faster and helps create better materials, e.g. stronger alloys, new polymers and better battery materials.
(iii) Differentiate between geochemistry and astrochemistry.
   Answer: 
(iv) With the help of an example, correlate the use of science, technology and engineering.
   Answer: Example – solar energy.
- Science: scientists study photovoltaic cells and learn how sunlight is converted into electricity.
- Technology: this knowledge is used to make solar panels and storage batteries.
- Engineering: engineers design and build a solar power plant (electrical engineers do the wiring, civil engineers build the structure).
Together they give a clean, sustainable energy source.
(v) With the help of a Venn diagram, compare and contrast organic and inorganic chemistry.
   Answer: Draw two overlapping circles.
- Organic only: compounds of carbon (with hydrogen), e.g. methane, glucose, ethanol; mostly covalent, low melting points, many burn.
- Inorganic only: all other elements and compounds, e.g. NaCl, H₂SO₄, metals, minerals; many ionic, high melting points.
- Overlap (both): both are branches of chemistry; both study structure, properties and reactions; some carbon compounds such as CO₂, carbonates and carbides are studied in inorganic chemistry; organometallic compounds link both.
(vi) What are the uses of nuclear chemistry?
   Answer: - Medicine: radioisotopes for diagnosis (medical imaging) and cancer treatment (radiotherapy, e.g. cobalt-60).
- Energy: nuclear power plants generate electricity.
- Dating: carbon-14 dating finds the age of ancient objects.
- Industry and agriculture: tracers to detect leaks, sterilise equipment and improve crops.

— Q3–Q8. Descriptive questions —
3. Define chemistry and its interactions with other matter and energy.
   Answer: Chemistry is the branch of science that deals with the composition, structure and properties of matter, the changes matter undergoes and the energy changes that accompany them.
Interaction with matter: substances react with each other to form new substances, e.g. iron + oxygen + water → rust; hydrogen + oxygen → water.
Interaction with energy: chemical changes either release or absorb energy, e.g. burning fuel releases heat and light (exothermic); photosynthesis absorbs light energy (endothermic); a battery changes chemical energy into electrical energy.
The SLO also describes chemistry as the study of the Earth (solids), air (gases), sea (liquids) and sky (plasma) and the interactions among them.
4. Describe the applications of inorganic chemistry and its importance in our daily lives.
   Answer: - Batteries: Li-ion batteries in phones, laptops and electric vehicles.
- Construction: cement, glass, steel and other metals.
- Agriculture: inorganic fertilizers such as ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulphate and NPK salts (urea, by contrast, is an organic compound).
- Water treatment: alum and chlorine purify drinking water.
- Medicine: antacids (Mg(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃), iron supplements, platinum-based anticancer drugs.
- Industry: acids (H₂SO₄, HCl), bases (NaOH) and catalysts (iron, nickel, platinum).
Inorganic chemistry therefore supports housing, food production, health, energy storage and clean water.
5. With the help of a few examples, highlight the relation between science, technology and engineering.
   Answer: Science explains, technology applies, engineering designs and builds.
1. Rusting: science finds iron rusts with O₂ and H₂O → technology gives paints and galvanising → engineering designs rust-resistant bridges.
2. Solar energy: photovoltaic principle → solar panels → solar power plants.
3. Water filtration: chemistry of purification → filters and chlorinators → water-treatment plants designed by chemical and mechanical engineers.
4. Plastic bags: science of monomers forming polymers → polyethylene production → machines that make strong, flexible bags.
6. Evaluate the role of chemistry in environmental science.
   Answer: Chemistry is central to environmental science:
- Identifies pollutants and their sources (CO, SO₂, NOₓ, CFCs, heavy metals, pesticides) using analytical methods.
- Explains their effects: acid rain, smog, ozone depletion, global warming, water-borne diseases.
- Gives solutions: catalytic converters, flue-gas desulphurisation, water treatment (sedimentation, filtration, chlorination), biodegradable plastics and green chemistry.
- Monitoring: measuring air and water quality to make laws and policies.
Without chemistry we could neither detect nor reduce pollution.
7. How does geochemistry help us to solve problems such as pollution and climate change?
   Answer: - It studies how elements and compounds move between rocks, soil, water and air, so it can trace pollutants (e.g. arsenic or lead in groundwater) back to their source.
- It explains the carbon cycle: how CO₂ is stored in rocks, oceans and soil, and how this changes the climate.
- It helps in carbon capture and storage: locking CO₂ into rock formations.
- Ice cores and sediments analysed by geochemists show past climates, which helps predict future change.
- It guides safe mining and the clean-up of contaminated land.
8. How is organic chemistry applied in medicines, biochemistry and industrial science?
   Answer: - Medicines: almost all drugs (paracetamol, aspirin, antibiotics) are organic compounds synthesised by organic chemists.
- Biochemistry: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, enzymes and DNA are organic molecules; organic chemistry explains their structures and reactions.
- Industry: plastics and polymers (polythene, nylon, PVC), fuels (petrol, natural gas), dyes, detergents, paints, cosmetics and pesticides are organic products.

══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Identify the branch of chemistry for each: (a) Boyle’s law – pressure on a gas reduces its volume (b) Industries produce SO₂ which causes acid rain (c) Hair has a protein called keratin.
   Answer: (a) Physical chemistry (laws of matter).
(b) Environmental chemistry (pollution).
(c) Biochemistry (molecules of living things).

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Identify the branch: (a) Earth’s temperature rising due to CO₂ (b) Contact process makes sulphuric acid on a large scale (c) A gas liquefies when cooled to −273 °C.
   Answer: (a) Environmental chemistry (b) Industrial chemistry (c) Physical chemistry.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] Briefly describe nuclear chemistry, biochemistry and geochemistry.
   Answer: - Nuclear chemistry: changes in atomic nuclei, radioactivity and radioisotopes (e.g. cancer treatment, nuclear power).
- Biochemistry: chemical changes in living organisms (e.g. digestion, respiration).
- Geochemistry: composition and changes of rocks, minerals, soil and water of the Earth.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Differentiate between organic chemistry and inorganic chemistry.
   Answer: 

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Briefly describe (a) analytical chemistry (b) medicinal chemistry (c) inorganic chemistry.
   Answer: (a) Analytical chemistry: methods and instruments to find the composition of matter, e.g. titration.
(b) Medicinal chemistry: how drugs act on biological targets and how new medicines are designed.
(c) Inorganic chemistry: elements and their compounds other than organic compounds, e.g. metals, salts, minerals.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Briefly describe (a) nuclear chemistry (b) environmental chemistry (c) astrochemistry.
   Answer: (a) Nuclear: changes in atomic nuclei; radioactivity, nuclear energy.
(b) Environmental: pollutants in air, water and soil and their effects.
(c) Astrochemistry: chemical processes in stars, planets, comets and interstellar space.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Define the following branches of chemistry: (a) astrochemistry (b) geochemistry (c) physical chemistry.
   Answer: (a) Chemical processes in astronomical environments. (b) Composition and changes of elements in the Earth’s crust. (c) Laws and theories explaining the structure and changes of matter.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Define chemistry. How are different states of matter (solids, liquids, gases and plasma) involved in chemical interactions?
   Answer: Chemistry studies the composition, structure and properties of matter and its changes with energy.
The SLO links chemistry to the Earth (solids), sea (liquids), air (gases) and sky (plasma). Chemical interactions happen between these: e.g. CO₂ from the air dissolves in the sea; rocks (solids) are weathered by rain water and acid rain; lightning (plasma) in the sky makes nitrogen oxides from N₂ and O₂ of the air.

9. Write one essential question each for analytical chemistry and environmental chemistry.
   Answer: - Analytical: How can we accurately determine the chemical composition of a sample?
- Environmental: How do human activities pollute the air, and how can we reduce it?

10. Why are carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides and oxides of carbon not studied in organic chemistry?
   Answer: They contain carbon but their properties are like those of inorganic compounds (they are mostly ionic or simple molecules, have no C–H bonds forming chains), so they are studied in inorganic chemistry.

11. What is green chemistry? Give one benefit.
   Answer: Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate hazardous substances. Benefit: less pollution and safer factories, e.g. using water instead of toxic solvents.

12. Give two examples each of polymers and their uses.
   Answer: Polythene – plastic bags; nylon – ropes and clothes; Teflon – non-stick cookware; polyester – fabrics; epoxy – glue.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. Explain with examples that chemistry has many sub-fields and interdisciplinary fields. Describe any six branches.
   Answer: Chemistry is too large to study as one subject, so it has sub-fields. Some overlap with other sciences and are called interdisciplinary (biochemistry = biology + chemistry; geochemistry = geology + chemistry; astrochemistry = astronomy + chemistry).
1. Organic: carbon compounds – medicines, plastics, fuels.
2. Inorganic: other elements and compounds – metals, salts, Li-ion batteries.
3. Physical: laws and theories – gas laws, energy changes, electrochemistry in car batteries.
4. Analytical: composition – titration, forensic analysis.
5. Biochemistry: reactions in living things – digestion, respiration.
6. Environmental: pollution – acid rain, ozone depletion, water treatment.
(Also: industrial, medicinal, polymer, geochemistry, nuclear, astrochemistry.)

2. Differentiate between science, technology and engineering. Explain how they work together to provide clean drinking water.
   Answer: - Science: systematic study of nature by observation and experiment.
- Technology: applying science to make tools, techniques and materials.
- Engineering: using science and mathematics to design and build systems and structures.
Clean water: scientists study which impurities and microbes are present and how coagulation, filtration and chlorine remove them; technology produces filters, chlorinators and testing kits; chemical engineers design the purification process and mechanical/civil engineers build the pumps, tanks and pipelines of a water-treatment plant.

chapters.title: Matter
chapters.introduction:
Everything around you – air, water, rocks, your own body – is matter. In this unit you learn the states of matter (including plasma, liquid crystals and Bose–Einstein condensates), the macroscopic properties that separate solids, liquids and gases, how matter is classified into elements, compounds and mixtures, the allotropes of carbon, and the three kinds of mixtures: solutions, colloids and suspensions, with the effect of temperature on solubility.

Exam focus: compound vs mixture, solution/colloid/suspension, allotropes of carbon, BEC and liquid crystals, effect of temperature on solubility (KCl vs Ca(OH)₂). These appeared in every 2025–2026 paper.

══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
Exam focus: compound vs mixture, solution/colloid/suspension, allotropes of carbon, BEC and liquid crystals, effect of temperature on solubility (KCl vs Ca(OH)₂). These appeared in every 2025–2026 paper.
Note: Textbook Table 2.2 prints the solubility of NaCl at 100 °C as “539.2 g”. This is a misprint; the correct value is about 39.2 g per 100 g water. The app uses 39.2 g.

══ 2.1 Matter and its states (pp. 16) ══
Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space (has volume). Air, water, rocks, plants and people are all matter. Atoms are the building blocks of all matter.
Matter exists in different states – distinct forms decided by how the particles are arranged, how they move and how strong the forces between them are. There are four common states: solid, liquid, gas and plasma.
- Energy changes the state: heating turns solids into liquids and gases; at very high temperatures or in a strong electric field a gas becomes plasma.
- Plasma is an electrically charged (ionised) gas made of ions and free electrons; it is affected by electric and magnetic fields. Examples: lightning, the Sun and stars, neon signs. Ordinary temperatures on Earth are not high enough to ionise atoms, so natural plasma on Earth is rare.
Intermediate state – liquid crystals: some crystalline solids on heating first turn into a cloudy liquid (liquid crystal) that has some properties of liquids (flow) and some of solids (ordered molecules). On further heating it becomes a clear liquid. Used in LCD screens of watches, calculators and mobiles.
Exotic state – Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC): formed when separate atoms are cooled to very close to absolute zero (0 K = −273 °C). The atoms lose their individual identity and behave like one “super atom”. BEC is seen only under extreme cold; superfluids and superconductors are linked to it.
Key Point: - Matter: mass + volume.
- States: solid, liquid, gas, plasma (+ liquid crystal, BEC).
- Plasma = ionised gas (very hot). BEC = atoms near absolute zero (very cold).
Exam Tip: “What is BEC and how is it formed?” came in the 2nd Annual 2025 paper. Answer: a state of matter formed when atoms are cooled to temperatures very close to absolute zero, so they merge into a single quantum state.
مادّہ ہر وہ چیز ہے جس کا وزن (کمیت) ہو اور جو جگہ گھیرے۔ مادّے کی چار عام حالتیں ہیں: ٹھوس، مائع، گیس اور پلازمہ۔ پلازمہ بہت گرم آئنائزڈ گیس ہے جیسے آسمانی بجلی اور سورج۔ مائع قلمیں (لیکوئیڈ کرسٹل) ٹھوس اور مائع کے بیچ کی حالت ہیں جو LCD اسکرینوں میں استعمال ہوتی ہیں۔ BEC اس وقت بنتی ہے جب ایٹموں کو مطلق صفر کے بہت قریب ٹھنڈا کیا جائے۔

══ 2.2 Macroscopic properties: density, compressibility, fluidity (pp. 17) ══
Macroscopic properties can be seen with the naked eye and measured easily. The three key ones for states of matter are:
- Density (mass per unit volume): solids and liquids have high density because their particles are close together; gases have very low density because of large spaces between molecules.
- Compressibility (how much the volume decreases under pressure): gases are highly compressible (large empty spaces); liquids only slightly; solids are almost incompressible (particles already touching).
- Fluidity (ability to flow): liquids and gases can flow because their particles can move past each other; solids cannot flow because particles are fixed in position.
A state can be changed by physical techniques (changing temperature or pressure) without changing the chemical composition, e.g. boiling water gives steam, which is still H₂O.
[Table: Table 2.1 – Properties of the three common states]
Property | Gas | Liquid | Solid
• Density | Low (large spaces between molecules) | High | High
• Compressibility | Very compressible | Slightly compressible | Not compressible
• Fluidity | Flows | Flows | Does not flow
• Shape / volume | No fixed shape or volume | Fixed volume, takes shape of container | Fixed shape and volume
• Particle arrangement | Far apart, random, fast-moving | Close, random, sliding | Close, regular, vibrating
Exam Tip: For “why are solids dense and incompressible while gases are not?” always link the property to the spaces between particles and forces of attraction.
کثافت: ٹھوس اور مائع میں ذرات قریب ہونے کی وجہ سے زیادہ، گیس میں بہت کم۔ دباؤ پذیری: گیس بہت زیادہ دب جاتی ہے کیونکہ ذرات کے درمیان خالی جگہ زیادہ ہے، ٹھوس تقریباً نہیں دبتا۔ بہاؤ: مائع اور گیس بہہ سکتے ہیں، ٹھوس نہیں۔

══ 2.3 Classification of matter: elements, compounds and mixtures (pp. 18) ══
Matter is classified as pure substances (elements and compounds) and mixtures (homogeneous and heterogeneous).
- Element: the simplest form of matter, made up of the same type of atoms (same atomic/proton number). It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means. Examples: H, O, C, Fe, Na.
- Compound: a substance formed when two or more different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio. It is a new substance with properties different from its elements and can only be separated by chemical methods. Examples: H₂O, CO₂, NaCl.
- Mixture: two or more substances combined physically in any ratio. Each component keeps its own properties and can be separated by physical methods (filtration, evaporation, distillation). Example: tea (milk, water, tea leaves, sugar), air, brass.
- Homogeneous mixture: uniform composition throughout (solutions, e.g. salt water, air).
- Heterogeneous mixture: non-uniform; parts can be distinguished (colloids and suspensions, e.g. milk, muddy water).
Physical change alters physical properties only (e.g. melting ice); a chemical change forms a new substance (e.g. burning paper).
[Table: Compound vs mixture (frequently asked)]
Compound | Mixture
• Elements combine chemically | Substances mix physically
• Fixed composition (ratio by mass) | Variable composition
• Properties differ from its elements | Components keep their own properties
• Separated only by chemical methods | Separated by physical methods
• Energy usually given out or taken in when formed | No significant energy change
• Has a fixed melting/boiling point | Melts/boils over a range
• Example: water H₂O, NaCl | Example: air, sea water, tea, brass
Key Point: Element → one kind of atom. Compound → different atoms chemically joined in a fixed ratio. Mixture → physically mixed, any ratio, separable by physical means.
عنصر ایک ہی قسم کے ایٹموں سے بنا سادہ ترین مادّہ ہے۔ مرکب دو یا زیادہ عناصر کے کیمیائی طور پر مقررہ تناسب میں ملنے سے بنتا ہے اور اس کی خصوصیات عناصر سے مختلف ہوتی ہیں۔ آمیزہ میں اجزا صرف طبعی طور پر ملے ہوتے ہیں، کسی بھی تناسب میں، اور انہیں طبعی طریقوں سے الگ کیا جا سکتا ہے۔

══ 2.4 Allotropy: allotropes of carbon (pp. 18–19) ══
Allotropy is the property of an element to exist in different physical forms in the same physical state. These forms are called allotropes. The atoms are the same; only their arrangement differs, so physical properties differ.
Carbon has three important solid allotropes:
1. Diamond
- Each C atom is covalently bonded to four other C atoms in a tetrahedral, rigid 3-D network.
- Hardest natural substance, very high melting point, transparent and sparkling.
- No free electrons → does not conduct electricity.
- Uses: cutting and drilling tools, glass cutters, jewellery.
2. Graphite
- Flat 2-D layers of hexagonal rings; each C atom bonded to three others in its layer.
- Weak forces between layers → layers slide over each other → soft and slippery, used as a lubricant and in pencil “lead”.
- One electron per C atom is delocalised (free) → good conductor of electricity → used for electrodes.
3. Buckminsterfullerene (buckyballs, C₆₀)
- Hollow, football-shaped cage of 60 carbon atoms: 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons; each C bonded to three others.
- Used in research on drug delivery, lubricants and nanotechnology.
Other elements also show allotropy, e.g. oxygen (O₂ and ozone O₃), sulphur (rhombic and monoclinic), phosphorus (white and red).
[Table: Diamond vs graphite]
Property | Diamond | Graphite
• Bonding of each C | 4 other C (tetrahedral, 3-D) | 3 other C (flat hexagonal layers)
• Hardness | Hardest natural substance | Soft, slippery
• Electrical conductivity | Non-conductor (no free electrons) | Good conductor (delocalised electrons)
• Appearance | Transparent, sparkling | Black, shiny, opaque
• Uses | Cutting tools, jewellery | Lubricant, pencils, electrodes
Exam Tip: Diamond is used in cutting tools because of its strong three-dimensional covalent network (FBISE model paper MCQ).
ایلوٹروپی کسی عنصر کا ایک ہی طبعی حالت میں مختلف شکلوں میں پایا جانا ہے۔ کاربن کی تین اہم شکلیں: ہیرا (ہر کاربن چار سے جڑا، بہت سخت، بجلی نہیں گزارتا)، گریفائٹ (تہوں والی ساخت، نرم، بجلی گزارتا ہے، چکنائی کے طور پر استعمال)، اور فلرین C₆₀ (فٹ بال جیسی کھوکھلی ساخت)۔

══ 2.5 Solutions and their types (pp. 19–20) ══
A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances in which one substance is dissolved in another.
- Solute: the substance that dissolves (usually smaller amount).
- Solvent: the substance in which it dissolves (usually larger amount).
- Particles are less than 1 nm; invisible, do not settle, pass through filter paper, do not scatter light. A solution is stable.
- A solution may contain more than one solute, e.g. soft drink: solvent water; solutes sugar, salts and CO₂. In air, N₂ is the solvent and O₂, CO₂ etc. are solutes.
Types by state of the solvent:
- Gaseous solutions: air; N₂ + H₂ mixture for the Haber process. (The textbook also lists fog, clouds and mist (liquid in gas) and smoke (solid in gas); strictly these are colloids.)
- Liquid solutions: CO₂ in water (soft drinks, gas in liquid); vinegar and rectified spirit (liquid in liquid); brine and sugar syrup (solid in liquid).
- Solid solutions: alloys (brass, bronze, steel – solid in solid); amalgam (mercury in a metal – liquid in solid); hydrogen on nickel in the ghee industry (gas in solid).
An aqueous solution has water as the solvent. Water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves most substances.
[Table: Types of solutions]
Solute | Solvent | Example
• Gas | Gas | Air (O₂ in N₂)
• Gas | Liquid | Soda water (CO₂ in water)
• Liquid | Liquid | Vinegar (acetic acid in water), alcohol in water
• Solid | Liquid | Brine, sugar syrup
• Gas | Solid | Hydrogen on nickel (ghee industry)
• Liquid | Solid | Amalgam (mercury in silver/tin)
• Solid | Solid | Brass (Zn in Cu), bronze, steel
محلول دو یا زیادہ چیزوں کا یکساں آمیزہ ہے۔ جو چیز گھلتی ہے وہ منحل (solute) اور جس میں گھلتی ہے وہ محلل (solvent) کہلاتی ہے۔ پانی کو عالمی محلل کہتے ہیں۔ مثالیں: ہوا (گیس)، نمکین پانی (مائع)، پیتل (ٹھوس محلول)۔

══ 2.6 Saturated, unsaturated, supersaturated; dilute and concentrated (pp. 21–22) ══
- Saturated solution: contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature. Extra solute stays undissolved at the bottom. Undissolved and dissolved solute are in dynamic equilibrium (dissolving and crystallising happen at equal rates).
- Unsaturated solution: contains less solute than needed to saturate it at that temperature; it can dissolve more.
- Supersaturated solution: contains more solute than a saturated solution at that temperature. Made by saturating a solution at high temperature and cooling it carefully. It is unstable: adding a small crystal (e.g. of sodium thiosulphate) makes the extra solute crystallise out at once, leaving a saturated solution.
- Dilute solution: relatively small amount of solute. Concentrated solution: relatively large amount of solute (e.g. brine). Adding solvent dilutes a solution.
Test: add a crystal of solute. Unsaturated – it dissolves. Saturated – it stays at the bottom unchanged. Supersaturated – crystals grow rapidly.
[Table: Concentrated vs dilute]
Concentrated solution | Dilute solution
• Large amount of solute in a given amount of solvent | Small amount of solute in a given amount of solvent
• e.g. brine, syrup | e.g. a pinch of salt in a glass of water
• Becomes dilute when solvent is added | Becomes concentrated when solute is added or solvent evaporates
سیر شدہ محلول میں کسی خاص درجہ حرارت پر زیادہ سے زیادہ منحل گھلا ہوتا ہے۔ غیر سیر شدہ میں مزید گھل سکتا ہے۔ فوق سیر شدہ میں سیر شدہ سے بھی زیادہ منحل ہوتا ہے اور یہ غیر مستحکم ہوتا ہے۔ ہلکا محلول میں منحل کم اور گاڑھے محلول میں زیادہ ہوتا ہے۔

══ 2.7 Solubility and the effect of temperature (pp. 22–23) ══
Solubility is the maximum amount of solute (in grams) that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a specific temperature to form a saturated solution. It depends on the nature of solute and solvent, temperature and (for gases) pressure.
Effect of temperature:
- For most solids, dissolving is endothermic (absorbs heat), so solubility increases with temperature: e.g. KCl, NH₄Cl, KNO₃, sugar.
- For some solids, dissolving is exothermic (releases heat), so solubility decreases with temperature: e.g. Ca(OH)₂, Na₂SO₄ (above about 32 °C).
- NaCl’s solubility increases only slightly with temperature.
- Gases are less soluble in hot water (fizzy drinks go flat when warm; fish need cool, oxygen-rich water).
A solubility curve is a graph of solubility against temperature. A point on the curve is saturated; below the curve is unsaturated; above it is supersaturated.
[Table: Table 2.2 – Solubility (g per 100 g water)]
Solute | At 20 °C | At 100 °C | Trend
• NaCl | 36.5 g | 39.2 g (book misprints 539.2) | Small increase
• KCl | 34.7 g | 56 g | Increases
• NH₄Cl | 37.5 g | 77 g | Increases strongly
• Ca(OH)₂ | 0.173 g | 0.066 g | Decreases
Exam Tip: FBISE Annual 2026 asked: how is solubility affected by increasing temperature for (a) KCl (endothermic solution) and (b) Ca(OH)₂ (exothermic solution)? Answer: (a) increases (b) decreases, with Le Chatelier-type reasoning: heat favours the process that absorbs heat.
حل پذیری وہ زیادہ سے زیادہ مقدار ہے جو 100 گرام محلل میں کسی خاص درجہ حرارت پر گھل سکے۔ اکثر ٹھوس اشیا (جیسے KCl) کی حل پذیری درجہ حرارت بڑھنے سے بڑھتی ہے کیونکہ ان کا گھلنا حرارت جذب کرتا ہے، جبکہ Ca(OH)₂ کی حل پذیری کم ہوتی ہے کیونکہ اس کا گھلنا حرارت خارج کرتا ہے۔ گیسیں گرم پانی میں کم گھلتی ہیں۔

══ 2.8 Colloids and suspensions (pp. 24) ══
Colloids are heterogeneous mixtures whose particles (1–1000 nm) are bigger than those of true solutions but too small to see. They stay evenly dispersed and do not settle (also called colloidal dispersions or false solutions).
- Particles pass through ordinary filter paper but not through ultra-filter paper.
- They scatter a beam of light – the Tyndall effect – which distinguishes colloids from true solutions.
- Examples: milk, blood, starch solution, albumin (egg white), soap solution, ink, jelly, toothpaste, fog, smoke.
Suspensions are heterogeneous mixtures in which solid particles are spread through a liquid without dissolving.
- Particles are larger than 1000 nm, visible to the naked eye, and settle on standing.
- They do not pass through filter paper (they can be filtered).
- Examples: chalk in water, muddy water, paints, milk of magnesia (Mg(OH)₂ in water).
How to test a colloid vs a solution: shine a torch or laser beam through each in a dark room. The beam path is visible in a colloid (Tyndall effect) but not in a true solution.
[Table: Table 2.3 – Solution vs colloid vs suspension]
Property | Solution | Colloid | Suspension
• Type of mixture | Homogeneous | Heterogeneous (appears uniform) | Heterogeneous
• Particle size | < 1 nm | 1–1000 nm | > 1000 nm
• Visibility of particles | Invisible | Invisible to naked eye | Visible
• Filtration | Passes through filter and ultra-filter paper | Passes filter paper, not ultra-filter paper | Does not pass filter paper
• Light (Tyndall effect) | Does not scatter | Scatters light | Scatters light
• Settling | Never settles | Does not settle | Settles on standing
• Examples | Sea water, sugar solution | Milk, blood, jelly | Muddy water, chalk in water
کولائیڈ میں ذرات کا سائز 1 سے 1000 نینو میٹر ہوتا ہے، یہ نیچے نہیں بیٹھتے اور روشنی کو بکھیرتے ہیں جسے ٹنڈل اثر کہتے ہیں (مثال: دودھ، خون، جیلی)۔ سسپنشن میں ذرات 1000 نینو میٹر سے بڑے ہوتے ہیں، نظر آتے ہیں اور کچھ دیر بعد نیچے بیٹھ جاتے ہیں (مثال: مٹی والا پانی، چاک اور پانی)۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Particle arrangement in solid, liquid and gas: Solids: close and regular. Liquids: close but random. Gases: far apart and random.

chapters.definitions:
• Matter (مادّہ) [p. 16]: Anything that has mass and occupies space.
• State of matter (مادّے کی حالت) [p. 16]: A distinct form in which matter exists, decided by the arrangement, movement and forces between its particles.
• Plasma (پلازمہ) [p. 16]: An electrically charged (ionised) gas containing ions and free electrons, affected by electric and magnetic fields.
• Liquid crystal (مائع قلم) [p. 16]: An intermediate state between solid and liquid that flows like a liquid but has some ordered arrangement like a solid.
• Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC) (بوس آئن سٹائن کنڈینسیٹ) [p. 16]: A state of matter formed when atoms are cooled to temperatures very close to absolute zero, so they behave as a single quantum entity.
• Macroscopic properties (ظاہری خصوصیات) [p. 17]: Properties that can be seen with the naked eye and measured easily, such as density, fluidity and compressibility.
• Element (عنصر) [p. 18]: The simplest form of matter made up of the same type of atoms; it cannot be broken down by chemical means.
• Compound (مرکب) [p. 18]: A substance formed when two or more different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio.
• Mixture (آمیزہ) [p. 18]: A substance formed when two or more substances combine physically in any ratio.
• Allotropy (ایلوٹروپی) [p. 18]: The property of an element to exist in different physical forms in the same physical state; the forms are called allotropes.
• Solution (محلول) [p. 19]: A homogeneous mixture of two or more substances in which one substance is dissolved in another.
• Solute (منحل) [p. 19]: The substance that dissolves in a solution.
• Solvent (محلل) [p. 19]: The substance in which the solute dissolves.
• Aqueous solution (آبی محلول) [p. 20]: A solution in which water is the solvent.
• Saturated solution (سیر شدہ محلول) [p. 21]: A solution containing the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature.
• Unsaturated solution (غیر سیر شدہ محلول) [p. 21]: A solution containing less solute than is needed to saturate it at a given temperature.
• Supersaturated solution (فوق سیر شدہ محلول) [p. 21]: A solution containing more solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature; it is unstable.
• Dilute solution (ہلکا محلول) [p. 22]: A solution containing a relatively small amount of solute.
• Concentrated solution (گاڑھا محلول) [p. 22]: A solution containing a relatively large amount of solute.
• Solubility (حل پذیری) [p. 22]: The maximum amount of solute in grams that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a specific temperature.
• Colloid (کولائیڈ) [p. 24]: A heterogeneous mixture with particles 1–1000 nm in diameter that remain dispersed and scatter light.
• Tyndall effect (ٹنڈل اثر) [p. 24]: The scattering of a beam of light by colloidal particles, making the beam path visible.
• Suspension (سسپنشن) [p. 24]: A heterogeneous mixture in which solid particles larger than 1000 nm are spread through a liquid without dissolving and settle on standing.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Density (کثافت): Mass per unit volume
• Compressibility (دباؤ پذیری): Decrease in volume under pressure
• Fluidity (روانی / بہاؤ): Ability to flow
• Plasma (پلازمہ): Ionised gas
• Element (عنصر): One kind of atom
• Compound (مرکب): Elements chemically combined
• Mixture (آمیزہ): Substances physically mixed
• Homogeneous (یکساں): Same throughout
• Heterogeneous (غیر یکساں): Not the same throughout
• Allotrope (ایلوٹروپ): Different form of the same element
• Solute (منحل): Substance that dissolves
• Solvent (محلل): Substance that dissolves the solute
• Saturated (سیر شدہ): Cannot dissolve more solute
• Solubility (حل پذیری): Maximum solute in 100 g solvent
• Suspension (معلق آمیزہ): Mixture with settling particles
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Density: density = mass ÷ volume (g cm⁻³) (Gases have very low density.)
• Solubility: g of solute per 100 g of solvent at a stated temperature (Always state the temperature.)
• Buckminsterfullerene: C₆₀ (20 hexagons + 12 pentagons.)
• Ozone (allotrope of oxygen): O₃ (Oxygen gas is O₂.)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• H₂O(s)  H₂O(l)  H₂O(g) — Change of state by heating/cooling: physical change, composition unchanged.
• Fe(s) + S(s) --heat--> FeS(s) — A mixture of iron and sulphur becomes a compound on heating.
• CuSO₄·5H₂O(s)  CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(g) — Hydrated vs anhydrous salt (links to Chapter 9).

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Ice, water and steam are three different states. Are they three different substances?
   Answer: No. All are H₂O. Changing state is a physical change; the chemical composition stays the same.
2. Brass is made of copper and zinc but looks uniform. Is it a compound?
   Answer: No. Brass is a homogeneous mixture (solid solution, alloy); the ratio of Cu to Zn can vary and no fixed formula exists.
3. Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not, although both are carbon?
   Answer: In graphite each C uses only 3 electrons for bonding, leaving one delocalised electron free to move. In diamond all 4 electrons are used in bonds, so there are no free charge carriers.
4. A clear liquid shows a visible beam of light. Is it a true solution?
   Answer: No. A visible beam means light is scattered (Tyndall effect), so it is a colloid, even if it looks clear.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Why are fish in danger when factories release hot water into rivers?
   Answer: Oxygen is less soluble in warm water, so dissolved oxygen falls and fish cannot breathe properly.
2. You are given a beaker of salt solution. How can you check whether it is saturated?
   Answer: Add a small crystal of salt at the same temperature. If it dissolves the solution was unsaturated; if it stays unchanged the solution is saturated.
3. Why is “shake well before use” written on a bottle of milk of magnesia?
   Answer: It is a suspension; the particles settle on standing, so shaking spreads them evenly to give the correct dose.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Identify each as solution, suspension or colloid: (a) air (b) sand in water (c) jelly. [FBISE Annual 2026]
   Solution: (a) Solution (homogeneous gaseous mixture). (b) Suspension (sand is visible and settles). (c) Colloid (particles 1–1000 nm; shows Tyndall effect).

2. Use Table 2.2: How many grams of KCl will crystallise out if a saturated solution in 100 g water is cooled from 100 °C to 20 °C?
   Given: Solubility of KCl: 56 g at 100 °C; 34.7 g at 20 °C (per 100 g water)
   Required: Mass of KCl crystallising
   Formula: mass crystallising = solubility at high T − solubility at low T
   Substitution: = 56 g − 34.7 g
   Calculation: = 21.3 g
   Final Answer: 21.3 g of KCl crystallises out.
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 2 Exercises (25–26):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. Anything that has mass and occupies space is called: → D (Matter) | Definition of matter.
ii. Following are states of matter: → D (All of these) | Gas, liquid and solid (and plasma) are all states of matter.
iii. Macroscopic properties are properties that can be visualized by: → A (the naked eye) | Macroscopic = visible to the naked eye.
iv. Matter can be described by both its: → A (physical properties and chemical properties) | Matter is described by physical and chemical properties.
v. A substance formed when two or more different elements combine chemically: → B (compound) | Definition of a compound.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) Can you write the formula of the carbon dioxide gas that we exhale?
   Answer: Yes: CO₂ – one carbon atom bonded to two oxygen atoms (O=C=O).
(ii) Define element, compound and mixture.
   Answer: - Element: simplest form of matter made of only one type of atom; cannot be broken down chemically (e.g. O₂, Fe).
- Compound: substance formed when two or more different elements combine chemically in a fixed ratio (e.g. H₂O, NaCl).
- Mixture: two or more substances combined physically in any ratio; components keep their properties (e.g. air, tea).
(iii) Differentiate between compound and mixture.
   Answer: 
(iv) Differentiate between concentrated and dilute solution.
   Answer: A concentrated solution has a relatively large amount of solute in a given amount of solvent (e.g. brine). A dilute solution has a relatively small amount of solute (e.g. a pinch of salt in a glass of water). Adding solvent makes a solution more dilute.

— Q3–Q11. Descriptive questions —
3. Define the term allotropes. Explain the allotropes of carbon.
   Answer: Allotropes are different physical forms of the same element in the same physical state, due to different arrangements of atoms (property = allotropy).
Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others in a rigid 3-D tetrahedral network → hardest substance, high melting point, no free electrons so non-conductor; used in cutting tools and jewellery.
Graphite: flat layers of hexagonal rings; each C bonded to 3 others; weak forces between layers let them slide → soft, slippery lubricant; delocalised electrons → conducts electricity; used in pencils and electrodes.
Fullerene (C₆₀, buckyball): hollow football-shaped cage of 60 C atoms (20 hexagons, 12 pentagons); each C bonded to 3 others; used in nanotechnology research.
4. What is the difference between homogeneous and heterogeneous solution (mixture)?
   Answer: A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout; its components cannot be seen separately (e.g. salt water, air, brass). True solutions are homogeneous.
A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition; different parts can be distinguished or will separate (e.g. sand in water, oil in water, milk under a microscope). Colloids and suspensions are heterogeneous.
5. Differentiate between colloids, suspensions and solutions.
   Answer: See Table 2.3: solutions (homogeneous,  1000 nm, visible, settle, filterable, e.g. muddy water).
6. If there are 18 protons in the argon atom, what is the atomic number of argon?
   Answer: Atomic number = number of protons, so the atomic number of argon is 18.
7. Describe states of matter with examples.
   Answer: - Solid: fixed shape and volume; particles close, regular, vibrating; e.g. ice, iron.
- Liquid: fixed volume, takes the shape of container, flows; e.g. water, oil.
- Gas: no fixed shape or volume, highly compressible, low density; e.g. air, steam.
- Plasma: ionised gas of ions and free electrons at very high temperature; e.g. lightning, Sun.
- Also: liquid crystals (LCD screens) and BEC (atoms near absolute zero).
8. Differentiate between: (a) colloids and suspensions (b) elements and compounds (c) concentrated and dilute solutions.
   Answer: (a) Colloids: 1–1000 nm, do not settle, pass filter paper, e.g. milk. Suspensions: > 1000 nm, settle, can be filtered, e.g. chalk in water.
(b) Elements: one kind of atom, cannot be broken down chemically, e.g. Na. Compounds: two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio, can be broken down chemically, e.g. NaCl.
(c) Concentrated: large amount of solute. Dilute: small amount of solute.
9. Examine the concept of solubility.
   Answer: Solubility is the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a given temperature to make a saturated solution.
It depends on (i) the nature of solute and solvent (“like dissolves like”: ionic salts dissolve in water, not in petrol), (ii) temperature – solubility of most solids (KCl, NH₄Cl) increases with temperature, but Ca(OH)₂ decreases; gases become less soluble when hot, and (iii) pressure for gases (more CO₂ dissolves under pressure in soft drinks). Solubility curves show these changes.
10. Why is a solution considered a mixture?
   Answer: Because its components (solute and solvent) are combined physically, not chemically: the ratio can vary, each keeps its own properties, and they can be separated by physical methods such as evaporation or distillation (e.g. salt is recovered from salt water by evaporation).
11. How will you test whether a given solution is a colloid or a true solution?
   Answer: Pass a narrow beam of light (torch or laser) through the liquid in a dark room. If the path of the beam is visible, the particles scatter light – it is a colloid (Tyndall effect). If the beam path is not visible, it is a true solution. (Ultra-filtration also works: colloid particles are held back by ultra-filter paper.)
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Why do solids have high density and very low compressibility whereas gases show the opposite behaviour?
   Answer: In solids particles are packed closely with strong forces of attraction and almost no empty space, so a given volume has a large mass (high density) and there is no space to push particles closer (very low compressibility).
In gases particles are far apart with weak forces and large empty spaces, so the mass per volume is small (low density) and pressure can push the particles closer (highly compressible).

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] What is meant by “element”? State one distinguishing feature that separates it from mixtures.
   Answer: An element is the simplest form of matter, made of only one type of atom, which cannot be broken down by chemical means. Distinguishing feature: an element is a pure substance with a fixed composition and a fixed melting point, while a mixture has variable composition, contains more than one substance and can be separated by physical methods.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] How is solubility affected by increasing temperature for (a) KCl in water (endothermic) (b) Ca(OH)₂ in water (exothermic)?
   Answer: (a) Dissolving KCl absorbs heat, so raising the temperature favours dissolving: solubility increases (34.7 g at 20 °C → 56 g at 100 °C).
(b) Dissolving Ca(OH)₂ releases heat, so raising the temperature works against dissolving: solubility decreases (0.173 g → 0.066 g).

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Differentiate between a suspension and a colloid with one suitable example each.
   Answer: Suspension: particles > 1000 nm, visible, settle on standing, can be filtered – e.g. muddy water. Colloid: particles 1–1000 nm, not visible, do not settle, cannot be separated by ordinary filtration, show Tyndall effect – e.g. milk.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Briefly describe the compressibility of solids, liquids and gases with reason.
   Answer: Solids: almost incompressible – particles already touching. Liquids: slightly compressible – particles close with little space. Gases: highly compressible – large spaces between particles.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] What is fluidity? Why are liquids and gases considered fluids while solids are not?
   Answer: Fluidity is the ability of a substance to flow. In liquids and gases the particles are not fixed and can move past one another, so they flow and take the shape of their container. In solids the particles are held in fixed positions by strong forces and can only vibrate, so solids cannot flow.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] What is meant by BEC? How are BECs formed?
   Answer: A Bose–Einstein condensate is an exotic state of matter in which atoms behave as one single quantum unit. It is formed by cooling a dilute gas of atoms to temperatures very close to absolute zero (0 K, −273 °C), when the atoms lose their separate identities and occupy the same lowest energy state.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Briefly describe the following properties of a gas: (a) density (b) fluidity.
   Answer: (a) Density: very low, because gas molecules are far apart with large empty spaces. (b) Fluidity: gases flow easily in all directions because their molecules move freely and rapidly.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Briefly describe the following properties of solids: (a) compressibility (b) density.
   Answer: (a) Solids are not compressible because the particles are closely packed with no free space. (b) Solids have high density because many particles are packed in a small volume.

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Compare the following properties of liquid crystals with liquids: (a) molecular arrangement (b) fluidity.
   Answer: (a) Liquid crystals have molecules partly ordered (lined up in one direction); ordinary liquids have a completely random arrangement. (b) Both can flow, but liquid crystals usually flow less freely (more viscous) than ordinary liquids.

11. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] State the difference between a compound and a mixture. Briefly describe the composition of each.
   Answer: A compound has a fixed composition – its elements are chemically combined in a definite ratio (water is always 2 H : 1 O). A mixture has a variable composition – its components are physically mixed in any proportion (air, tea).

12. Why does a fizzy drink go flat faster when it is warm?
   Answer: The solubility of gases decreases as temperature increases, so CO₂ escapes from warm water more quickly.

13. What are liquid crystals? Give one use.
   Answer: An intermediate state between solid and liquid: they flow like liquids but have partly ordered molecules like solids. Used in LCD screens of watches, calculators and mobiles.

14. Give two examples of solid solutions.
   Answer: Brass (zinc in copper), bronze (tin in copper), steel (carbon in iron), amalgam (mercury in a metal).


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Differentiate between compounds and mixtures with respect to (a) composition (b) chemical bonding (c) separation methods.
   Answer: (a) Composition: compound – fixed ratio by mass (H₂O always 1:8 H:O by mass); mixture – variable ratio.
(b) Chemical bonding: compound – atoms held by chemical bonds (ionic or covalent), formed by a chemical reaction with energy change; mixture – no chemical bonds between components, only physical mixing.
(c) Separation: compound – only by chemical methods (e.g. electrolysis of water); mixture – by physical methods such as filtration, evaporation, distillation, magnet, chromatography.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Compare diamond and graphite in terms of their structure and properties.
   Answer: Structure: diamond – each C covalently bonded to 4 others, 3-D tetrahedral network, no free electrons. Graphite – each C bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers; weak forces between layers; one delocalised electron per C.
Properties: diamond – hardest natural substance, very high melting point, non-conductor, transparent; used for cutting tools and jewellery. Graphite – soft and slippery, conducts electricity, black and opaque; used as lubricant, pencil lead and electrodes.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] Write four differences between colloids and suspensions.
   Answer: 1. Particle size: colloid 1–1000 nm; suspension > 1000 nm.
2. Settling: colloid particles do not settle; suspension particles settle on standing.
3. Filtration: colloids pass through filter paper; suspensions are retained.
4. Visibility: colloid particles are invisible to the naked eye; suspension particles are visible.
(Examples: colloid – milk, blood; suspension – muddy water, chalk in water.)

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What is meant by allotropy? Discuss any two allotropes of carbon.
   Answer: Allotropy is the existence of an element in different physical forms in the same state. Diamond: 3-D tetrahedral network, hardest, non-conductor, cutting tools. Graphite: layers of hexagons, slippery, conductor, lubricant and electrodes.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Define solubility. How can it be affected by a change in temperature? Explain with a graph.
   Answer: Solubility: maximum grams of solute dissolving in 100 g solvent at a given temperature.
Effect of temperature: draw axes – solubility (g/100 g water) vs temperature (°C). Draw rising curves for KCl and NH₄Cl (endothermic dissolving: solubility increases), an almost flat curve for NaCl (slight increase), and a falling curve for Ca(OH)₂ (exothermic dissolving: solubility decreases). Points on a curve = saturated; below = unsaturated; above = supersaturated.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Compare solutions and colloids (any three points) with one example of each.
   Answer: Solution: < 1 nm, no Tyndall effect, passes ultra-filter paper; e.g. sugar solution. Colloid: 1–1000 nm, shows Tyndall effect, retained by ultra-filter paper; e.g. milk. Both do not settle on standing.
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 2 in one page
- Matter: has mass and occupies space. States: solid, liquid, gas, plasma; intermediate: liquid crystals (LCDs); exotic: BEC (atoms near 0 K).
- Macroscopic properties: density (solid, liquid high; gas low), compressibility (gas high, solid ~0), fluidity (liquids and gases flow).
- Classification: pure substances (elements, compounds) and mixtures (homogeneous = solutions; heterogeneous = colloids, suspensions).
- Compound vs mixture: chemical vs physical combination; fixed vs variable ratio; new vs retained properties; chemical vs physical separation.
- Allotropes of carbon: diamond (4 bonds, 3-D, hardest, non-conductor), graphite (3 bonds, layers, slippery, conductor), fullerene C₆₀ (football cage, 20 hexagons + 12 pentagons).
- Solution: homogeneous,  1000 nm, visible, settles (muddy water, chalk, milk of magnesia).

chapters.title: Atomic Structure
chapters.introduction:
What is inside an atom? This unit follows the story of atomic models from Dalton to Rutherford, Bohr and the modern quantum mechanical model, then looks closely at the nucleus (protons and neutrons held by the strong nuclear force) and electrons in shells. You will learn atomic number, mass number, isotopes and their uses (carbon dating, medical imaging), how to calculate relative atomic mass, how cations and anions form, and how to write electronic configurations.

Exam focus (20 summative SLOs – the largest chapter): protons/neutrons in isotopes, relative atomic mass calculation, carbon-14 dating, path of charged particles in an electric field, relative charge and mass of subatomic particles, ion formation. Asked in every paper.
