══ 3.1 Atomic models: Dalton, Rutherford, Bohr and the quantum model (pp. 28–31) ══
An atomic model is not a physical object; it is a conceptual picture that helps explain experimental observations about atoms. Models are improved as new evidence appears.
══ Dalton’s atomic theory (1803)
1. All elements are made of tiny indivisible particles called atoms.
2. Atoms of an element are identical (same mass and volume).
3. In chemical reactions atoms combine, separate or rearrange in simple whole-number ratios.
4. Atoms can neither be created nor destroyed.
Dalton explained the laws of chemical combination. Later experiments showed atoms are divisible (electrons, protons, neutrons), and the discovery of isotopes showed that atoms of the same element can have different masses – contradicting postulates 1 and 2.
══ Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment (1911)
Rutherford bombarded a very thin gold foil (about 0.00004 cm) with alpha particles (He²⁺, from polonium).
- Most α-particles passed straight through → most of the atom is empty space.
- A few were deflected slightly, and about 1 in a million bounced back by more than 90° → a small, dense, positively charged nucleus repels them.
- Massive α-particles are not deflected by electrons.
Planetary model: the mass and positive charge are concentrated in a tiny nucleus; electrons revolve around it in circular orbits (like planets around the Sun); the atom is neutral.
Defects: (1) by classical physics a revolving charged electron should continuously lose energy and spiral into the nucleus, so the atom would collapse; (2) continuous loss of energy would give a continuous spectrum, but atoms give line spectra.
══ Bohr’s model (1913)
1. Electrons revolve in certain circular orbits of fixed energy called shells or energy levels (K, L, M, N for n = 1, 2, 3, 4).
2. The farther the orbit from the nucleus, the higher its energy.
3. Only orbits with angular momentum = nh/2π are allowed (h = Planck’s constant, 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s).
4. An electron in an orbit does not radiate energy. It absorbs light to jump to a higher orbit and emits light when it falls to a lower orbit.
5. Energy of light = difference between orbit energies: ΔE = E₂ − E₁.
Bohr explained the line spectrum of hydrogen, but his model is flat (2-D) and works well only for hydrogen.
══ Quantum mechanical (modern) model
- Electrons have a dual (wave–particle) nature – proposed by de Broglie (1924) and confirmed by Davisson and Germer (1927).
- Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle (1927): it is impossible to know both the exact position and the exact path (momentum) of an electron at the same time. So exact orbits cannot be drawn.
- Instead we speak of orbitals: 3-D regions around the nucleus where there is a high probability (e.g. 95%) of finding the electron.
[Table: Comparing atomic models]
Model | Main idea | Limitation
• Dalton (1803) | Indivisible solid atoms; atoms of one element identical | Atoms are divisible; isotopes exist
• Rutherford (1911) | Tiny dense positive nucleus; electrons orbit; mostly empty space | Cannot explain stability or line spectra
• Bohr (1913) | Electrons in fixed-energy shells; light absorbed/emitted when they jump | 2-D; explains only hydrogen well
• Quantum mechanical | Electrons are wave–particles found in orbitals (probability regions) | —
Key Point: - Rutherford: nucleus discovered; atom mostly empty.
- Bohr: shells = energy levels; larger shell → higher energy, farther from nucleus.
- Modern: uncertainty principle → orbitals, not fixed orbits.
Exam Tip: C-09-B-10 (uncertainty principle) and C-09-B-12 (atomic models as aids) are formative SLOs: learn them for understanding, but exam questions focus on structure, particles, isotopes and ions.
ڈالٹن نے کہا ایٹم ناقابلِ تقسیم ہیں۔ ردرفورڈ نے سونے کے ورق پر الفا ذرات پھینک کر ثابت کیا کہ ایٹم کا زیادہ حصہ خالی ہے اور درمیان میں چھوٹا، بھاری اور مثبت نیوکلیئس ہے۔ بوہر نے بتایا کہ الیکٹران مخصوص توانائی والے شیلز میں گھومتے ہیں؛ نیوکلیئس سے دور شیل کی توانائی زیادہ ہوتی ہے۔ جدید ماڈل کے مطابق ہائزن برگ کے اصولِ غیر یقینیت کی وجہ سے الیکٹران کا ٹھیک مقام اور راستہ ایک ساتھ معلوم نہیں ہو سکتا، اس لیے ہم آربیٹلز (امکانی علاقے) کی بات کرتے ہیں۔

══ 3.2 Structure of the atom and the strong nuclear force (pp. 31) ══
- The nucleus is at the centre and contains protons and neutrons, together called nucleons. Almost all the mass of the atom is in the nucleus.
- Electrons move around the nucleus in shells (energy levels). A larger shell number means higher energy and greater average distance from the nucleus.
- The atom is electrically neutral because the number of protons (+) equals the number of electrons (−).
Strong nuclear force: protons are all positive and repel each other strongly at such tiny distances, so why does the nucleus not fly apart? A very strong attractive force acts between nucleons – the strong nuclear force. It acts between proton–proton, neutron–neutron and proton–neutron, is much stronger than electrostatic repulsion, but acts only over very short distances (inside the nucleus).
Key Point: Nucleus = protons + neutrons (nucleons) held by the strong nuclear force. Electrons in shells. Neutral atom: protons = electrons.
نیوکلیئس میں پروٹون اور نیوٹران ہوتے ہیں جنہیں مل کر نیوکلیونز کہتے ہیں۔ پروٹون ایک دوسرے کو دھکیلتے ہیں مگر ایک بہت طاقتور کشش کی قوت، مضبوط نیوکلیائی قوت، انہیں جوڑے رکھتی ہے۔ یہ قوت صرف بہت کم فاصلے پر کام کرتی ہے۔

══ 3.3 Subatomic particles: charge, mass and behaviour in an electric field (pp. 32) ══
Protons and neutrons have nearly the same mass (≈ 1 amu); the electron is about 1/1836 of a proton’s mass, so electrons add almost nothing to the mass of an atom.
When a beam of particles passes between two oppositely charged plates (a uniform electric field):
- Protons (+) bend on a curved path towards the negative plate.
- Electrons (−) bend towards the positive plate.
- Neutrons (0) go straight, undeflected.
- If they travel at the same speed, electrons are deflected much more strongly than protons because they are much lighter (same size of charge, about 1836 times smaller mass).
[Table: Subatomic particles]
Particle | Symbol | Location | Relative charge | Relative mass | Actual mass
• Proton | p | Nucleus | +1 | 1 amu | 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
• Neutron | n | Nucleus | 0 | 1 amu | 1.6749 × 10⁻²⁷ kg
• Electron | e⁻ | Shells around nucleus | −1 | 1/1836 amu | 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg
Exam Tip: For the electric-field question, draw two plates (+ top, − bottom), a straight line for neutrons, a gentle curve towards − for protons and a sharp curve towards + for electrons. Label all three.
پروٹون (+1) اور نیوٹران (0) کی کمیت تقریباً ایک amu ہے جبکہ الیکٹران (−1) کی کمیت اس کا 1/1836 حصہ ہے۔ برقی میدان میں پروٹون منفی پلیٹ کی طرف، الیکٹران مثبت پلیٹ کی طرف مڑتے ہیں اور نیوٹران سیدھے جاتے ہیں۔ الیکٹران ہلکے ہونے کی وجہ سے زیادہ مڑتے ہیں۔

══ 3.4 Atomic number, mass number and radioactivity (pp. 33–34) ══
- Proton number / atomic number (Z): the number of protons in the nucleus. In a neutral atom it also equals the number of electrons.
- Z is unique to each element – it decides the element’s identity, its properties and its position in the periodic table (elements are arranged in order of increasing Z). Z = 6 is always carbon; Z = 11 is always sodium.
- Nucleon number / mass number (A): total number of protons + neutrons.
- Number of neutrons = A − Z.
Radioactivity: in some nuclei the forces are not balanced; the nucleus decays by giving out radiation until it becomes stable. If decay changes the number of protons, the atom becomes a different element – radioactivity can change the proton number and the identity of an atom. Examples:
- Carbon-14 decays to nitrogen-14 (a neutron changes into a proton).
- Uranium-238 gives out an alpha particle (He nucleus, 2 protons + 2 neutrons) and becomes thorium-234; uranium finally ends up as stable lead.
ایٹمی نمبر (Z) نیوکلیئس میں پروٹونز کی تعداد ہے اور ہر عنصر کا اپنا منفرد ایٹمی نمبر ہوتا ہے؛ اسی کی بنیاد پر عناصر پیریاڈک ٹیبل میں ترتیب دیے جاتے ہیں۔ ماس نمبر (A) پروٹون اور نیوٹران کا مجموعہ ہے۔ نیوٹران = A − Z۔ تابکاری میں نیوکلیئس ٹوٹ کر پروٹونز کی تعداد بدل سکتا ہے اور ایٹم دوسرا عنصر بن جاتا ہے، جیسے کاربن-14 نائٹروجن-14 میں بدل جاتا ہے۔

══ 3.5 Relative atomic mass and the atomic mass unit (pp. 34–35) ══
A single atom is too small to weigh, so masses are measured relative to a standard. Since 1961 the standard is carbon-12, given a mass of exactly 12 amu.
- Atomic mass unit (amu): exactly 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom (≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
- Relative atomic mass (Aᵣ): the average mass of the atoms (isotopes) of an element compared with 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom. Because it is a weighted average of isotopes, it is usually not a whole number (Cl = 35.5).
Example: a hydrogen atom is 0.0840 times as massive as a C-12 atom, so Aᵣ(H) = 0.0840 × 12 = 1.008.
[Table: Table 3.1 – Relative atomic masses]
Element | Aᵣ | Element | Aᵣ
• H | 1.008 | Al | 26.9815
• N | 14.0067 | S | 32.06
• O | 15.9994 | Cl | 35.453
• Na | 22.9898 | Fe | 55.847
ایک ایٹم کا وزن ناپنا ممکن نہیں، اس لیے کاربن-12 کو معیار بنایا گیا ہے جس کی کمیت ٹھیک 12 amu ہے۔ نسبتی ایٹمی کمیت کسی عنصر کے آئسوٹوپس کی اوسط کمیت ہے جو کاربن-12 کے بارہویں حصے سے موازنہ کی جاتی ہے۔

══ 3.6 Isotopes: hydrogen, carbon, chlorine, uranium (pp. 35–38) ══
Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number (protons) but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons). Word from Greek: isos = same, topos = place (same place in the periodic table); first used by Soddy.
- Isotopes have the same chemical properties (same electrons) but different physical properties (mass, density, melting/boiling point).
- Isotopes affect molecular mass (e.g. heavy water D₂O is heavier than H₂O) but not chemical behaviour.
- Some isotopes are unstable and radioactive (e.g. tritium, carbon-14, uranium-235/238).
Hydrogen: protium ^1₁H (0 neutrons, 99.99%), deuterium ^2₁H or D (1 neutron, 0.0015%), tritium ^3₁H (2 neutrons, radioactive, very rare). Water made with deuterium is heavy water: m.p. 3.81 °C, b.p. 101.4 °C, density 1.104 g cm⁻³ (ordinary water: 0 °C, 100 °C, 0.997 g cm⁻³).
Carbon: ¹²_6C (6 n, 98.8%), ¹³_6C (7 n, 1.1%), ¹⁴_6C (8 n, 0.009%, radioactive).
Chlorine: ³⁵₁₇Cl (18 n, ≈ 75%), ³⁷₁₇Cl (20 n, ≈ 25%).
Uranium: ²³⁴U (0.006%), ²³⁵U (0.72%), ²³⁸U (99.27%). U-235 is used in nuclear reactors and atomic bombs; fission of 1 kg of U-235 gives as much energy as burning more than 17 000 kg of coal.
[Table: Protons, electrons and neutrons in isotopes]
Isotope | Protons | Electrons | Neutrons
• ^1₁H protium | 1 | 1 | 0
• ^2₁H deuterium | 1 | 1 | 1
• ^3₁H tritium | 1 | 1 | 2
• ¹²_6C | 6 | 6 | 6
• ¹³_6C | 6 | 6 | 7
• ¹⁴_6C | 6 | 6 | 8
• ³⁵₁₇Cl | 17 | 17 | 18
• ³⁷₁₇Cl | 17 | 17 | 20
• ²³⁴₉₂U | 92 | 92 | 142
• ²³⁵₉₂U | 92 | 92 | 143
• ²³⁸₉₂U | 92 | 92 | 146
Exam Tip: Isotopes question pattern: “Determine the number of protons and neutrons in ²³₁₁Na, ³⁷₁₇Cl, ¹³_6C” → p = lower number; n = upper − lower.
آئسوٹوپس ایک ہی عنصر کے ایسے ایٹم ہیں جن میں پروٹون برابر مگر نیوٹران مختلف ہوں، اس لیے ان کا ماس نمبر مختلف ہوتا ہے۔ ان کی کیمیائی خصوصیات ایک جیسی (الیکٹران برابر) مگر طبعی خصوصیات مختلف ہوتی ہیں۔ ہائیڈروجن کے تین آئسوٹوپس: پروٹیم، ڈیوٹیریم اور ٹریٹیم۔

══ 3.7 Calculating relative atomic mass from isotopic abundance (pp. 38) ══
Relative atomic mass is the weighted average of the masses of the naturally occurring isotopes:
Aᵣ = (mass₁ × %_1 + mass₂ × %_2 + …) ÷ 100
Carbon: Aᵣ = (12 × 98.8 + 13 × 1.1 + 14 × 0.009) ÷ 100 = (1185.6 + 14.3 + 0.126) ÷ 100 = 12.00
Chlorine: Aᵣ = (35 × 75 + 37 × 25) ÷ 100 = (2625 + 925) ÷ 100 = 35.5
Reverse problem (finding the mass of one isotope): rearrange the same formula. If Aᵣ = 35.5, isotope A = 35 (75.77%), isotope B (24.23%):
35.5 × 100 = 35 × 75.77 + x × 24.23 → 3550 = 2651.95 + 24.23x → x = 898.05 ÷ 24.23 = 37.06 ≈ 37.
Exam Tip: Always check that your answer lies between the smallest and largest isotope masses and is closer to the more abundant isotope.
اوسط ایٹمی کمیت = (ہر آئسوٹوپ کی کمیت × اس کی فیصد مقدار کا مجموعہ) ÷ 100۔ جواب ہمیشہ زیادہ پائے جانے والے آئسوٹوپ کے قریب ہوتا ہے۔

══ 3.8 Uses of isotopes: medicine, carbon dating and more (pp. 38–39) ══
Medicine (diagnosis and treatment):
- Iodine-131: tracer to diagnose thyroid problems (and treat thyroid cancer).
- Iodine-123: imaging the brain.
- Sodium-24: traces the flow of blood and detects obstructions in the circulatory system.
- Cobalt-60: irradiates cancer cells to shrink tumours (radiotherapy).
- Medical imaging: a radioisotope is injected; it collects in an organ and its radiation is detected by a camera to produce an image (e.g. technetium-99m in bone and heart scans).
Research: carbon-14 traces the path of carbon in photosynthesis; sulphur-35 helped find the structure of the thiosulphate ion; radioisotopes show the mechanism of reactions.
Carbon dating: living things take in carbon (including a tiny fixed proportion of radioactive C-14) from CO₂ in air and food. After death, no new C-14 is taken in and the C-14 already present decays at a known rate (half of it in about 5730 years). Comparing the C-14 activity of an old bone, wood or cloth with that of living tissue tells how long ago the organism died. Radioisotopes are also used to date rocks, soils, mummies and archaeological objects.
Energy: U-235 fuels nuclear power plants.
آئسوٹوپس کے استعمال: آیوڈین-131 تھائیرائیڈ کی تشخیص، آیوڈین-123 دماغ کی تصویر، سوڈیم-24 خون کی گردش، کوبالٹ-60 کینسر کا علاج۔ کاربن ڈیٹنگ میں مردہ جاندار کے کاربن-14 کی باقی ماندہ مقدار سے اس کی عمر معلوم کی جاتی ہے کیونکہ مرنے کے بعد نیا C-14 جسم میں داخل نہیں ہوتا اور پرانا ایک مقررہ رفتار سے ختم ہوتا رہتا ہے۔

══ 3.9 Formation of cations and anions; symbols for atoms and ions (pp. 39–42) ══
An ion is a charged atom (or group of atoms) formed when an atom loses or gains electrons. Atoms do this to reach the stable electronic configuration of the nearest noble gas (octet, or duplet for 2 electrons).
Cations (positive ions): formed when an atom loses electrons – usually metals with 1–3 valence electrons. Protons then outnumber electrons.
- Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8) + e⁻ ; 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ → 1s² 2s² 2p⁶
- Mg (2,8,2) → Mg²⁺ (2,8) + 2e⁻
- Li (2,1) → Li⁺ (2); Al (2,8,3) → Al³⁺ (2,8)
Anions (negative ions): formed when an atom gains electrons – usually non-metals with 5–7 valence electrons (high electron affinity). Electrons then outnumber protons.
- O (2,6) + 2e⁻ → O²⁻ (2,8)
- F (2,7) + e⁻ → F⁻ (2,8)
- S (2,8,6) + 2e⁻ → S²⁻ (2,8,8); Cl (2,8,7) + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (2,8,8)
The charge on the ion usually equals the number of electrons lost or gained, which links to the group number (Group I → +1, Group II → +2, Group VI → −2, Group VII → −1).
Symbols: ²⁴₁₂Mg²⁺ – mass number (top left) 24, atomic number (bottom left) 12, charge (top right) 2+. Protons = 12, neutrons = 12, electrons = 12 − 2 = 10.
For an ion: electrons = Z − charge (for a negative ion, subtracting a negative adds electrons: Cl⁻ has 17 + 1 = 18 electrons).
[Table: Cation vs anion]
Cation | Anion
• Positive ion | Negative ion
• Formed by losing electrons | Formed by gaining electrons
• Usually from metals | Usually from non-metals
• Protons > electrons | Electrons > protons
• Smaller than its atom | Larger than its atom
• e.g. Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ | e.g. Cl⁻, O²⁻, F⁻
جب ایٹم الیکٹران کھوتا ہے تو مثبت آئن (کیٹائن) بنتا ہے، جیسے Na سے Na⁺؛ یہ زیادہ تر دھاتیں کرتی ہیں۔ جب ایٹم الیکٹران حاصل کرتا ہے تو منفی آئن (اینائن) بنتا ہے، جیسے Cl سے Cl⁻؛ یہ زیادہ تر غیر دھاتیں کرتی ہیں۔ مقصد نوبل گیس جیسی مستحکم ترتیب (اوکٹیٹ) حاصل کرنا ہے۔

══ 3.10 Shells, sub-shells and electronic configuration (pp. 41) ══
Shells (energy levels) are numbered n = 1, 2, 3, 4 … and named K, L, M, N. As n increases, the distance from the nucleus and the energy increase. Maximum electrons in a shell = 2n² (K 2, L 8, M 18, N 32).
Each shell is divided into sub-shells (s, p, d, f):
- K (n = 1): 1s
- L (n = 2): 2s, 2p
- M (n = 3): 3s, 3p, 3d
- N (n = 4): 4s, 4p, 4d, 4f
Maximum electrons: s = 2, p = 6, d = 10, f = 14.
Aufbau principle: electrons fill the lowest-energy sub-shell first. Order: 1s < 2s < 2p < 3s < 3p < 4s < 3d …
(Notice 4s fills before 3d.)
Electronic configuration is the arrangement of electrons in sub-shells, e.g.
- ¹¹Na: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ (2,8,1)
- ¹⁴Si: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p² (2,8,4)
- ¹⁷Cl: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵ (2,8,7)
- ¹⁹K: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹ (2,8,8,1)
- ²⁰Ca: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² (2,8,8,2)

chapters.shortNotes:
══ Chapter 3 in one page
- Models: Dalton (indivisible atoms) → Rutherford (nucleus, empty space; defects: collapse, continuous spectrum) → Bohr (fixed-energy shells; ΔE = E₂ − E₁; explains H spectrum) → quantum model (wave–particle electrons, uncertainty principle, orbitals).
- Nucleus: protons + neutrons (nucleons) held by the strong nuclear force. Electrons in shells K, L, M, N; higher n → higher energy, farther away.
- Particles: p (+1, 1 amu), n (0, 1 amu), e (−1, 1/1836 amu). Electric field: p → − plate, e → + plate (bends more), n straight.
- Z = protons (unique, orders the periodic table). A = p + n. n = A − Z. Radioactivity can change Z → new element (C-14 → N-14; U-238 → Th-234 + α).
- amu = 1/12 of C-12. Aᵣ = weighted average of isotopes = Σ(mass × %) ÷ 100 (C = 12.00, Cl = 35.5).
- Isotopes: same Z, different A; same chemical, different physical properties; may be radioactive. H: protium, deuterium (heavy water), tritium. C-12, 13, 14. Cl-35, 37. U-234, 235 (reactors), 238.
- Uses: I-131 thyroid, I-123 brain, Na-24 blood flow, Co-60 cancer, C-14 dating and photosynthesis, S-35 structures, U-235 energy.
- Ions: metals lose e⁻ → cations (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺); non-metals gain e⁻ → anions (F⁻, Cl⁻, O²⁻, S²⁻).
- Configuration: 2n² per shell; s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14; Aufbau order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d.

chapters.definitions:
• Atomic model (ایٹمی ماڈل) [p. 31]: A conceptual picture that helps explain the structure and behaviour of atoms; it is improved as new evidence appears.
• Nucleus (نیوکلیئس / مرکزہ) [p. 29]: The tiny, dense, positively charged centre of an atom containing protons and neutrons.
• Nucleons (نیوکلیونز) [p. 31]: Protons and neutrons together.
• Strong nuclear force (مضبوط نیوکلیائی قوت) [p. 31]: The very strong, short-range attractive force that holds protons and neutrons together in the nucleus.
• Shell / energy level (شیل / توانائی کی سطح) [p. 30]: A fixed-energy path around the nucleus in which electrons move; higher shells have higher energy and are farther from the nucleus.
• Heisenberg uncertainty principle (اصولِ غیر یقینیت) [p. 30]: It is impossible to determine both the exact position and the exact path (momentum) of an electron at the same time.
• Orbital (آربیٹل) [p. 31]: A three-dimensional region around the nucleus where there is a high probability of finding an electron.
• Atomic number (proton number), Z (ایٹمی نمبر) [p. 33]: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
• Mass number (nucleon number), A (ماس نمبر) [p. 33]: The total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.
• Radioactivity (تابکاری) [p. 34]: The spontaneous decay of an unstable nucleus with emission of radiation, which can change the proton number and identity of an atom.
• Atomic mass unit (amu) (ایٹمی کمیتی اکائی) [p. 34]: Exactly one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
• Relative atomic mass (نسبتی ایٹمی کمیت) [p. 34]: The average mass of the atoms (isotopes) of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of one carbon-12 atom.
• Isotopes (آئسوٹوپس / ہم جا) [p. 35]: Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers because of different numbers of neutrons.
• Heavy water (بھاری پانی) [p. 36]: Water (D₂O) in which ordinary hydrogen is replaced by deuterium.
• Carbon dating (کاربن ڈیٹنگ) [p. 39]: Finding the age of a once-living object by measuring how much of its carbon-14 has decayed.
• Cation (کیٹائن / مثبت آئن) [p. 39]: A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses one or more electrons.
• Anion (اینائن / منفی آئن) [p. 40]: A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains one or more electrons.
• Electronic configuration (الیکٹرانی ترتیب) [p. 41]: The arrangement of electrons in the shells and sub-shells of an atom.
• Aufbau principle (آف باؤ اصول) [p. 41]: Electrons occupy the lowest-energy sub-shell available first.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Atom (ایٹم): Smallest particle of an element
• Nucleus (مرکزہ): Centre of the atom
• Proton (پروٹون): Positive particle in nucleus
• Neutron (نیوٹران): Neutral particle in nucleus
• Electron (الیکٹران): Negative particle in shells
• Shell (شیل / مدار): Energy level
• Atomic number (ایٹمی نمبر): Number of protons
• Mass number (ماس نمبر): Protons + neutrons
• Isotope (ہم جا): Same element, different mass
• Radioactivity (تابکاری): Decay of unstable nuclei
• Abundance (کثرت / فیصد مقدار): How common an isotope is
• Cation (مثبت آئن): Positive ion
• Anion (منفی آئن): Negative ion
• Configuration (ترتیب): Arrangement of electrons
• Uncertainty (غیر یقینیت): Cannot know exactly
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Number of neutrons: n = A − Z (A = mass number, Z = atomic number)
• Electrons in a neutral atom: e⁻ = Z
• Electrons in an ion: e⁻ = Z − (charge) (Mg²⁺: 12 − 2 = 10; Cl⁻: 17 + 1 = 18)
• Relative atomic mass: Aᵣ = Σ(isotopic mass × % abundance) ÷ 100 (Weighted average)
• Maximum electrons in shell n: 2n² (K = 2, L = 8, M = 18, N = 32)
• Bohr energy jump: ΔE = E₂ − E₁ (Energy of light absorbed or emitted)
• Planck’s constant: h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s
• Atom symbol: ^A_ZXcharge (e.g. ²⁴₁₂Mg²⁺)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• Na -> Na⁺ + e⁻ — Formation of a cation (sodium).
• Mg -> Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ — Formation of a cation (magnesium).
• Al -> Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ — Formation of a cation (aluminium).
• O + 2e⁻ -> O²⁻ — Formation of an anion (oxide).
• Cl + e⁻ -> Cl⁻ — Formation of an anion (chloride).
• ²³⁸₉₂U -> ²³⁴₉₀Th + ^4₂He — Alpha decay: radioactivity changes the element.
• ¹⁴_6C -> ¹⁴_7N + e⁻ — Beta decay of carbon-14 (basis of carbon dating).

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. If an atom of an element gains a proton, does it remain the same element?
   Answer: No. The number of protons decides the element. Gaining a proton increases Z by 1, so it becomes the next element.
2. Why is the mass of an atom concentrated in the nucleus?
   Answer: Protons and neutrons (each ≈ 1 amu) are in the nucleus; electrons are about 1/1836 amu, so they add almost no mass.
3. Why is the relative atomic mass of chlorine 35.5 and not a whole number?
   Answer: It is a weighted average of Cl-35 (≈75%) and Cl-37 (≈25%).
4. Why do Na⁺ and Ne have the same electronic configuration but different properties?
   Answer: Both have 2,8 electrons, but Na⁺ has 11 protons (a +1 charge) while Ne has 10 protons (neutral), so their chemistry is different.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. A doctor suspects a patient’s thyroid is not working properly. Which isotope may be used and why?
   Answer: Iodine-131: the thyroid absorbs iodine, so the radiation from I-131 shows how well the gland takes it up.
2. A wooden tool from an old village contains one-quarter of the C-14 activity of living wood. Estimate its age (half-life ≈ 5730 years).
   Answer: 1 → ½ → ¼ means two half-lives: 2 × 5730 ≈ 11 460 years.
3. Why is heavy water used in some nuclear reactors? (Link to isotopes)
   Answer: Deuterium nuclei slow down fast neutrons without absorbing many of them, helping the fission chain reaction continue.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. The atomic number of an element is 17 and its mass number is 35. How many protons and neutrons are in its nucleus? (Textbook p. 34)
   Given: Z = 17, A = 35
   Required: Protons and neutrons
   Formula: protons = Z; neutrons = A − Z
   Substitution: neutrons = 35 − 17
   Calculation: = 18
   Final Answer: 17 protons and 18 neutrons

2. Calculate the relative atomic mass of carbon. Abundances: C-12 = 98.8%, C-13 = 1.1%, C-14 = 0.009%. (Textbook p. 38)
   Given: Masses 12, 13, 14; abundances 98.8%, 1.1%, 0.009%
   Required: Aᵣ of carbon
   Formula: Aᵣ = Σ(mass × %) ÷ 100
   Substitution: = (12 × 98.8 + 13 × 1.1 + 14 × 0.009) ÷ 100
   Calculation: = (1185.6 + 14.3 + 0.126) ÷ 100 = 1200.026 ÷ 100
   Final Answer: Aᵣ(C) = 12.00 amu

3. Concept Assessment 3.1: An element has two isotopes A and B. Aᵣ = 35.5. Isotope A: mass 35, abundance 75.77%. Find the mass of B (abundance 24.23%).
   Given: Aᵣ = 35.5; A = 35 (75.77%); B = ? (24.23%)
   Required: Isotopic mass of B
   Formula: Aᵣ × 100 = m_A × %A + m_B × %B
   Substitution: 35.5 × 100 = 35 × 75.77 + m_B × 24.23
   Calculation: 3550 = 2651.95 + 24.23 m_B → m_B = 898.05 ÷ 24.23 = 37.06
   Final Answer: Isotopic mass of B ≈ 37 (chlorine-37)

4. An element exists as two isotopes: ⁶⁴X (30%) and ⁶⁶X (70%). Calculate its average relative atomic mass. [FBISE Annual 2026]
   Given: 64 (30%), 66 (70%)
   Required: Aᵣ
   Formula: Aᵣ = Σ(mass × %) ÷ 100
   Substitution: = (64 × 30 + 66 × 70) ÷ 100
   Calculation: = (1920 + 4620) ÷ 100 = 6540 ÷ 100
   Final Answer: Aᵣ = 65.4

5. Describe the formation of cations from Li (Z = 3) and Al (Z = 13). (Concept Assessment 3.2)
   Solution: - Li: 1s² 2s¹ (2,1). It loses its single valence electron: Li → Li⁺ + e⁻. Li⁺ = 1s² (2), like helium (duplet).
- Al: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹ (2,8,3). It loses three valence electrons: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻. Al³⁺ = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (2,8), like neon.

6. Describe the formation of anions from S (Z = 16) and Cl (Z = 17). (Concept Assessment 3.3)
   Solution: - S: 2,8,6 (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴). Gains 2 electrons: S + 2e⁻ → S²⁻ (2,8,8), like argon.
- Cl: 2,8,7 (… 3s² 3p⁵). Gains 1 electron: Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (2,8,8), like argon.


══ ADDITIONAL SLO NUMERICAL PRACTICE ══

1. Gallium has isotopes Ga-69 (60.1%) and Ga-71 (39.9%). Find Aᵣ.
   Given: 69 (60.1%), 71 (39.9%)
   Required: Aᵣ
   Formula: Aᵣ = Σ(mass × %) ÷ 100
   Substitution: = (69 × 60.1 + 71 × 39.9) ÷ 100
   Calculation: = (4146.9 + 2832.9) ÷ 100 = 6979.8 ÷ 100
   Final Answer: Aᵣ ≈ 69.8

2. Copper has Aᵣ = 63.55. Cu-63 has abundance 69.2%. Find the mass of the other isotope (30.8%).
   Given: Aᵣ = 63.55; 63 (69.2%); m (30.8%)
   Required: m
   Formula: Aᵣ × 100 = 63 × 69.2 + m × 30.8
   Substitution: 6355 = 4359.6 + 30.8 m
   Calculation: m = 1995.4 ÷ 30.8 = 64.8
   Final Answer: ≈ 65 (copper-65)

3. How many protons, neutrons and electrons are in ⁵⁶₂₆Fe³⁺?
   Given: Z = 26, A = 56, charge +3
   Required: p, n, e
   Formula: p = Z; n = A − Z; e = Z − charge
   Substitution: n = 56 − 26; e = 26 − 3
   Calculation: n = 30; e = 23
   Final Answer: 26 p, 30 n, 23 e

— Exercise MCQs —
i. Chlorine has two isotopes, both of which have: → D (same number of electrons) | Isotopes have the same protons and (as neutral atoms) the same electrons; they differ in neutrons and mass number.
ii. Number of neutrons in ²⁷₁₂M are: → D (15) | n = A − Z = 27 − 12 = 15.
iii. Which isotope is commonly used to irradiate cancer cells? → C (Cobalt-60) | Cobalt-60 is used in radiotherapy (p. 38).
iv. M shell has sub-shells: → C (3s, 3p, 3d) | n = 3 has 3s, 3p and 3d.
v. A sub-shell that can accommodate 6 electrons is: → C (p) | p holds 6; s 2, d 10, f 14.
vi. ₁₁Na has electronic configuration: → D (1s², 2s², 2p⁶, 3s¹) | 11 electrons fill 1s, 2s, 2p then one in 3s.
vii. Which of the following statements is not correct about isotopes? → D (they have same physical properties) | Different masses give different physical properties.
viii. Which isotope is used in nuclear reactors? → C (U-235) | U-235 undergoes fission (p. 37).

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) Distinguish between shell and sub-shell.
   Answer: 
(ii) Why is an atom electrically neutral?
   Answer: Because the number of positively charged protons in its nucleus is equal to the number of negatively charged electrons around it, so the charges cancel. (Neutrons have no charge.)
(iii) How many sub-shells are there in the N shell?
   Answer: Four: 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f.
(iv) Give notation for sub-shells of the M shell.
   Answer: 3s, 3p, 3d.
(v) List the sub-shells of the M shell in order of increasing energy.
   Answer: 3s < 3p < 3d.
(vi) Can you identify an atom without knowing the number of neutrons in it?
   Answer: Yes. An atom is identified by its atomic number (number of protons), which is unique to each element. Neutrons only decide which isotope it is.

— Q3–Q13. Descriptive questions —
3–4. The electronic configurations listed are incorrect. Explain the mistake in each and write the correct configuration: x = 1s², 2s², 2p⁴, 3p²; y = 1s², 2s¹, 2p¹; z = 1s¹, 2s², 2p⁶, 3s¹.
   Answer: - x (10 electrons): 3p is filled while 2p is not full (and 3s is skipped). Correct: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (neon).
- y (4 electrons): an electron is put in 2p before 2s is full. Correct: 1s² 2s² (beryllium).
- z (10 electrons): 1s has only one electron although it is the lowest sub-shell, and 3s is used before lower sub-shells are full. Correct: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (neon).
Rule broken in all three: the Aufbau principle – lower-energy sub-shells must be filled first.
5–6. Which orbital in each pair is lower in energy? (a) 2s, 2p (b) 3p, 2p (c) 3s, 4s
   Answer: (a) 2s (b) 2p (c) 3s. Lower n, and within the same shell s < p.
7–8. Draw Bohr’s model for (a) potassium (Z = 19, A = 39) (b) silicon (Z = 14, A = 28) (c) argon (Z = 18, A = 39), showing electrons, protons and neutrons.
   Answer: Draw a nucleus with protons and neutrons written inside and concentric circles for shells with electrons as dots.
(a) K: nucleus 19 p, 20 n; shells 2, 8, 8, 1.
(b) Si: nucleus 14 p, 14 n; shells 2, 8, 4.
(c) Ar (book’s A = 39): nucleus 18 p, 21 n; shells 2, 8, 8. (Common argon-40 has 22 n.)
9–10. Write electronic configurations for (a) ²⁸₁₄Si (b) ²⁴₁₂Mg (c) ²⁷₁₃Al (d) ⁴⁰₁₈Ar.
   Answer: (a) Si: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p²
(b) Mg: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s²
(c) Al: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹
(d) Ar: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
11. State the importance and uses of isotopes in various fields of life.
   Answer: - Medicine: I-131 (thyroid), I-123 (brain imaging), Na-24 (blood flow, blockages), Co-60 (killing cancer cells), radioisotope imaging of organs.
- Archaeology/geology: carbon-14 dating of bones, wood, mummies; dating of rocks and soils.
- Research: C-14 traces carbon in photosynthesis; S-35 used to find the structure of the thiosulphate ion; tracers reveal reaction mechanisms.
- Energy: U-235 in nuclear reactors produces electricity.
- Industry/agriculture: tracers to detect leaks; radiation to sterilise equipment and food.

   Answer: - Symbol Al = aluminium.

══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Show the following conversions by drawing electron dot structures: (a) Na → Na⁺ (b) Cl → Cl⁻.
   Answer: (a) Na has one dot (valence electron) in its outer shell: Na• → loses it → [Na]⁺ + e⁻. Na⁺ now has the neon configuration 2,8.
(b) Cl has seven dots around it → gains one electron → [:Cl:]⁻ with eight dots (2,8,8).

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Determine the number of protons and neutrons in the isotopes: (a) ²³₁₁Na (b) ³⁷₁₇Cl (c) ¹³_6C.
   Answer: (a) Na: 11 p, 23 − 11 = 12 n. (b) Cl: 17 p, 37 − 17 = 20 n. (c) C: 6 p, 13 − 6 = 7 n.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] How do energy and distance from the nucleus change as the shell number increases?
   Answer: As n increases (K → L → M → N), the average distance of the electron from the nucleus increases and the energy of the shell increases. Outer electrons are less strongly attracted by the nucleus.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Which sub-atomic particle determines the atomic number of an element? What is the significance of atomic number?
   Answer: The proton determines it (Z = number of protons). Significance: it is unique for each element, so it identifies the element; it gives the number of electrons in a neutral atom and hence chemical properties; elements are arranged in the periodic table in order of increasing atomic number.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Justify: (a) an atom is electrically neutral (b) an atom converts into a positive ion when it loses an electron.
   Answer: (a) Number of protons (+) = number of electrons (−), so the charges cancel. (b) After losing an electron, protons outnumber electrons by one, leaving a net +1 charge.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] How do the paths of positive and negative charges differ in the same uniform electric field? Make a sketch.
   Answer: Positive particles (protons) bend towards the negative plate; negative particles (electrons) bend towards the positive plate; neutral particles go straight. Electrons bend more because they are much lighter. (See the diagram in Tables & Diagrams.)

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] How is carbon-14 used to determine the age of ancient objects?
   Answer: Living organisms keep a constant level of C-14 by taking in carbon from air and food. After death no new C-14 enters and the existing C-14 decays at a known rate (half in about 5730 years). Measuring the remaining C-14 activity and comparing with living tissue gives the time since death.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22); 2nd Annual 2025] State the relative charge and relative mass of the electron, proton and neutron.
   Answer: Electron: charge −1, mass 1/1836 amu. Proton: +1, 1 amu. Neutron: 0, 1 amu.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Determine the number of protons and neutrons in C-12, C-13 and C-14.
   Answer: All have 6 protons. Neutrons: C-12 → 6, C-13 → 7, C-14 → 8.

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Determine the number of protons and neutrons in ²⁴₁₂Mg, ²⁵₁₂Mg, ²⁶₁₂Mg.
   Answer: All have 12 protons. Neutrons: 12, 13 and 14.

11. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What is meant by isotopes of an element? Give an example.
   Answer: Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers (different numbers of neutrons). Example: ^1₁H, ^2₁H, ^3₁H or ³⁵₁₇Cl and ³⁷₁₇Cl.

12. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element X having three isotopes: ¹²_6A 98.8%, ¹³_6B 1.1%, ¹⁴_6C 0.009%.
   Answer: 

13. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Define isotopes of an element. Write the isotopes of hydrogen with their atomic and mass numbers.
   Answer: Isotopes: same Z, different A. Hydrogen: protium ^1₁H (Z 1, A 1), deuterium ^2₁H (Z 1, A 2), tritium ^3₁H (Z 1, A 3).

14. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] An element has two atoms: one with 17 protons and 18 neutrons, the other with 17 protons and 20 neutrons. (a) Are they isotopes? (b) Will their chemical properties be similar? Justify.
   Answer: (a) Yes – same number of protons (17, chlorine) but different neutrons (Cl-35 and Cl-37). (b) Similar chemical properties, because chemical behaviour depends on electrons, and both have 17 electrons with the same configuration (2,8,7). Only their masses and physical properties differ.

15. Why are electrons deflected more than protons in an electric field?
   Answer: They carry the same size of charge but an electron is about 1836 times lighter, so the same force gives it a much larger deflection.

16. What is the strong nuclear force?
   Answer: The very strong, short-range attractive force between nucleons (p–p, n–n, p–n) that holds the nucleus together against the repulsion between protons.

17. How did the discovery of isotopes contradict Dalton’s atomic theory?
   Answer: Dalton said all atoms of an element are identical in mass. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different masses.

18. Give two defects of Rutherford’s model.
   Answer: (1) A revolving electron should lose energy continuously and fall into the nucleus, so atoms would collapse. (2) It predicts a continuous spectrum, but atoms give line spectra.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. Describe Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment, its observations and conclusions. Give the main defects of his model.
   Answer: Experiment: a beam of α-particles (He²⁺) from polonium was directed at a very thin gold foil; a fluorescent screen recorded where they went.
Observations and conclusions:
1. Most α-particles passed straight through → most of the atom is empty space.
2. A few were deflected at small angles, and about 1 in a million bounced back by more than 90° → a small, dense, positively charged nucleus repels them.
3. Electrons do not deflect heavy α-particles.
Model: nucleus at centre with almost all the mass; electrons revolve in orbits; atom neutral.
Defects: a revolving charged electron should radiate energy, spiral into the nucleus and collapse the atom; it would give a continuous spectrum, but atoms give line spectra.

2. State the postulates of Bohr’s atomic model. How did it improve on Rutherford’s model?
   Answer: 1. Electrons revolve in fixed circular orbits (shells) of definite energy.
2. Energy increases with distance from the nucleus.
3. Only orbits with angular momentum nh/2π are allowed.
4. An electron in an orbit does not radiate; it absorbs energy to jump up and emits energy to fall down.
5. ΔE = E₂ − E₁.
Improvement: it explained the stability of the atom (electrons in allowed orbits don’t lose energy) and the line spectrum of hydrogen.

3. What are isotopes? Describe the isotopes of hydrogen and carbon. Why do isotopes have the same chemical but different physical properties?
   Answer: Isotopes: same Z, different A.
Hydrogen: protium (0 n, 99.99%), deuterium (1 n, forms heavy water), tritium (2 n, radioactive).
Carbon: C-12 (6 n, 98.8%), C-13 (7 n, 1.1%), C-14 (8 n, 0.009%, radioactive, used in dating).
Reason: chemical properties depend on the number and arrangement of electrons, which is the same for all isotopes; physical properties such as mass, density, melting and boiling points depend on mass, which differs because of the different numbers of neutrons.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Electronic configuration of element X is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. Identify its group, period and likely name. Compare its properties with the element below it in the same group.
   Answer: 11 electrons → sodium; 1 valence electron → Group I (IA); 3 shells → Period 3.
Element below it: potassium (2,8,8,1). Compared with Na, K has a larger atomic radius, lower ionisation energy, is more reactive (reacts more violently with water), has lower melting point and is more metallic. Both form +1 ions and similar compounds (NaCl, KCl).
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 3 in one page
- Models: Dalton (indivisible atoms) → Rutherford (nucleus, empty space; defects: collapse, continuous spectrum) → Bohr (fixed-energy shells; ΔE = E₂ − E₁; explains H spectrum) → quantum model (wave–particle electrons, uncertainty principle, orbitals).
- Nucleus: protons + neutrons (nucleons) held by the strong nuclear force. Electrons in shells K, L, M, N; higher n → higher energy, farther away.
- Particles: p (+1, 1 amu), n (0, 1 amu), e (−1, 1/1836 amu). Electric field: p → − plate, e → + plate (bends more), n straight.
- Z = protons (unique, orders the periodic table). A = p + n. n = A − Z. Radioactivity can change Z → new element (C-14 → N-14; U-238 → Th-234 + α).
- amu = 1/12 of C-12. Aᵣ = weighted average of isotopes = Σ(mass × %) ÷ 100 (C = 12.00, Cl = 35.5).
- Isotopes: same Z, different A; same chemical, different physical properties; may be radioactive. H: protium, deuterium (heavy water), tritium. C-12, 13, 14. Cl-35, 37. U-234, 235 (reactors), 238.
- Uses: I-131 thyroid, I-123 brain, Na-24 blood flow, Co-60 cancer, C-14 dating and photosynthesis, S-35 structures, U-235 energy.
- Ions: metals lose e⁻ → cations (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺); non-metals gain e⁻ → anions (F⁻, Cl⁻, O²⁻, S²⁻).
- Configuration: 2n² per shell; s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14; Aufbau order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d.

chapters.introduction:
The periodic table organises all 118 elements so that we can predict their behaviour. In this unit you learn how elements are arranged in periods and groups by atomic number, how to find an element’s period, group and block from its electronic configuration, how group number relates to ion charge, and the periodic trends in atomic radius, shielding, ionisation energy, electron affinity, electronegativity, metallic character, reactivity and density. Then you study alkali metals (Group 1), halogens (Group 17), transition elements, noble gases, and compare metals and non-metals.

Exam focus (20 summative SLOs, joint largest): trends down Group 1 and Group 17, halogen displacement reactions, thermal stability of HX, transition-metal properties and catalysts, identifying group/period from configuration, metals vs non-metals. Expect 2–4 MCQs and at least one short and one long question.

The intended question is probably “left to right”, answer: shielding effect. Review Q8 prints oxygen as “^8₆O”; oxygen’s atomic number is 8. Q15(iii) refers to a small figure; positions were read from a zoomed scan.

══ 4.1 The modern periodic table: periodic law, periods and groups (pp. 46–49) ══
After Moseley (1913) showed that atomic number is the basic property of an element, elements were arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
Periodic law: when elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, their properties repeat periodically.
Periods (horizontal rows): there are 7 periods. Period 1 has 2 elements; periods 2 and 3 have 8 each (short periods); periods 4 and 5 have 18; periods 6 and 7 have 32 (long periods). Across a period properties change gradually; the pattern repeats in the next period.
Groups (vertical columns, also called families): 18 groups (IUPAC numbering 1–18). In the older system: A groups IA–VIIIA (8 groups of main-group / representative / normal elements) and B groups (transition elements). Elements in a group have the same number of valence electrons, so they have similar chemical properties.
Group names:
- Group 1 (IA): alkali metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr)
- Group 2 (IIA): alkaline earth metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra)
- Group 16 (VIA): chalcogens (O, S, Se)
- Group 17 (VIIA): halogens (F, Cl, Br, I, At)
- Group 18 (VIIIA): noble gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn)
- Groups 3–12: transition metals (d-block)
- Lanthanides (Z = 57–71) and actinides (Z = 89–103): two rows of f-block elements placed below the main table.
[Table: Number of elements in each period]
Period | Elements | Type | Sub-shells filled
• 1 | 2 (H, He) | Very short | 1s
• 2 | 8 (Li–Ne) | Short | 2s 2p
• 3 | 8 (Na–Ar) | Short | 3s 3p
• 4 | 18 (K–Kr) | Long | 4s 3d 4p
• 5 | 18 (Rb–Xe) | Long | 5s 4d 5p
• 6 | 32 (Cs–Rn) | Very long | 6s 4f 5d 6p
• 7 | 32 (Fr–Og) | Very long | 7s 5f 6d 7p
Key Point: - Arranged by increasing Z.
- 7 periods, 18 groups.
- Same group → same valence electrons → similar chemistry.

══ 4.2 Finding period, group and block from electronic configuration (pp. 49–52) ══
Write the configuration using the Aufbau order: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p.
- Block: the sub-shell (s, p, d or f) that receives the last electron.
- Period: the highest principal quantum number (n) of the valence shell.
- Group: s-block → group = number of valence electrons (1 or 2). p-block → group = valence electrons + 10 (IUPAC 13–18), or simply the number of valence electrons in the A-system (IIIA–VIIIA).
Blocks: s-block = Groups 1–2 (and He); p-block = Groups 13–18; d-block = Groups 3–12 (transition metals); f-block = lanthanides and actinides.
Worked: Na (Z = 11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ → s-block, period 3, group 1.
Al (Z = 13): … 3s² 3p¹ → p-block, period 3, 3 valence electrons → group 13 (IIIA).
K (Z = 19): … 4s¹ → s-block, period 4, group 1.
N (Z = 7): 1s² 2s² 2p³ → p-block, period 2, 5 valence e → group 15 (VA).
O (Z = 8): 1s² 2s² 2p⁴ → period 2, group 16 (VIA).
Exam Tip: Remember: n of the outermost shell = period; outer electrons = group (A-system). Cl 2,8,7 → period 3, group VIIA (17), 7 valence electrons.
آخری الیکٹران جس ذیلی شیل (s، p، d، f) میں جائے وہ بلاک ہے۔ سب سے بیرونی شیل کا نمبر n پیریڈ ہے۔ s بلاک میں گروپ نمبر = ویلنس الیکٹران، p بلاک میں IUPAC گروپ = ویلنس الیکٹران + 10۔

══ 4.3 Group number and the charge on ions (pp. 52–54) ══
Atoms gain or lose valence electrons to reach a stable noble-gas configuration (octet, or duplet for He).
- Elements with 1, 2, 3 valence electrons (Groups 1, 2, 13) lose them → +1, +2, +3 ions. Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺; Be²⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺; Al³⁺.
- Elements with 5, 6, 7 valence electrons (Groups 15, 16, 17) gain 3, 2, 1 electrons → −3, −2, −1 ions. N³⁻; O²⁻, S²⁻; F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻.
- Group 14 (4 valence electrons) can lose or gain 4 (C usually shares electrons instead).
- Group 18 noble gases already have full shells and do not form ions normally.
Examples: Na 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ → Na⁺ 1s² 2s² 2p⁶; Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻; F 1s² 2s² 2p⁵ + e⁻ → F⁻ 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.
[Table: Group and ion charge]
Group | Valence e⁻ | Ion charge | Examples
• 1 (IA) | 1 | +1 | Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺
• 2 (IIA) | 2 | +2 | Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺
• 13 (IIIA) | 3 | +3 | Al³⁺
• 15 (VA) | 5 | −3 | N³⁻, P³⁻
• 16 (VIA) | 6 | −2 | O²⁻, S²⁻
• 17 (VIIA) | 7 | −1 | F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻
• 18 (VIIIA) | 8 (He 2) | none | —
1، 2 یا 3 ویلنس الیکٹران والے عناصر انہیں کھو کر +1، +2، +3 آئن بناتے ہیں۔ 5، 6 یا 7 ویلنس الیکٹران والے عناصر 3، 2 یا 1 الیکٹران لے کر −3، −2، −1 آئن بناتے ہیں۔ نوبل گیسیں آئن نہیں بناتیں۔

══ 4.4 Shielding effect and atomic size (pp. 55–57) ══
Shielding effect: the reduction in the attraction between the nucleus and the valence electrons caused by electrons in the inner shells.
- Down a group: more inner shells → shielding increases (Mg > Be; Na > Li).
- Across a period: inner shells stay the same → shielding stays roughly constant.
Atomic size (atomic radius): the average distance between the nucleus and the outermost shell.
- Across a period (left → right): decreases. Electrons are added to the same shell while nuclear charge increases, so the nucleus pulls the shell in more tightly (Li > Be > B … > F).
- Down a group: increases. Each element has one more shell (Li < Na < K < Rb).
Largest atoms: bottom-left (Cs, Fr). Smallest: top-right (F, He).
Exam Tip: For any pair: the larger atom is further left in a period or further down a group. Mg > Al; S > C; O > F; S > O.
شیلڈنگ اثر: اندرونی شیلز کے الیکٹران نیوکلیئس اور بیرونی الیکٹران کے درمیان کشش کو کم کر دیتے ہیں۔ یہ گروپ میں نیچے جاتے ہوئے بڑھتا ہے اور پیریڈ میں تقریباً یکساں رہتا ہے۔ ایٹمی سائز پیریڈ میں بائیں سے دائیں کم ہوتا ہے (نیوکلیائی چارج بڑھتا ہے) اور گروپ میں نیچے بڑھتا ہے (نئے شیلز)۔

══ 4.5 Ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity (pp. 57–61) ══
Ionisation energy (IE): the minimum energy needed to remove the outermost electron from an isolated gaseous atom. M(g) + IE → M⁺(g) + e⁻. Unit: kJ mol⁻¹. It explains cation formation.
- Down a group: decreases (more shielding, larger atom, weaker hold). Li > Na > K.
- Across a period: increases (greater nuclear charge, smaller atom). Li < Be … < Ne.
- Highest IE: noble gases (He 2372 kJ/mol). Lowest: alkali metals (Na 496 kJ/mol; K 419).
Electron affinity (EA): the energy released when an electron is added to the valence shell of an isolated gaseous atom to form a uni-negative ion. X(g) + e⁻ → X⁻(g) + EA. It explains anion formation.
- Across a period: generally increases (alkali metals lowest, halogens highest).
- Down a group: generally decreases (larger size, more shielding). There are exceptions (e.g. Cl has a higher EA than F) explained in higher classes.
Electronegativity (EN): the ability of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a chemical bond. Pauling scale: F = 4.0 (highest), O 3.5, N 3.0, Cl 3.0, C 2.5, H 2.1, Na 0.9, Cs 0.7.
- Across a period: increases. Down a group: decreases.
[Table: Trend summary]
Property | Left → right in a period | Top → bottom in a group
• Atomic radius | Decreases | Increases
• Shielding effect | Constant | Increases
• Ionisation energy | Increases | Decreases
• Electron affinity | Increases (generally) | Decreases (generally)
• Electronegativity | Increases | Decreases
• Metallic character | Decreases | Increases
• Non-metallic character | Increases | Decreases
• Reactivity of metals | Decreases | Increases
• Reactivity of halogens | — | Decreases
Exam Tip: IE and EA compared: IE is energy absorbed to remove an electron (cation formation); EA is energy released when an electron is added (anion formation). Both increase across a period and decrease down a group.
آئنائزیشن انرجی: گیسی ایٹم سے سب سے بیرونی الیکٹران نکالنے کے لیے کم از کم توانائی؛ پیریڈ میں بڑھتی اور گروپ میں گھٹتی ہے۔ الیکٹران افینیٹی: گیسی ایٹم میں ایک الیکٹران شامل ہونے پر خارج ہونے والی توانائی۔ الیکٹرونیگیٹیویٹی: بانڈ میں مشترک الیکٹرانوں کو اپنی طرف کھینچنے کی صلاحیت؛ فلورین سب سے زیادہ (4.0)۔

══ 4.6 Metallic character, reactivity and density (pp. 61–62) ══
Metallic character: how easily an element loses electrons to form positive ions.
- Increases down a group (outer electrons farther and more shielded → lost easily): K > Na; Ca > Mg.
- Decreases across a period (nuclear charge increases, same shells): Na > Mg > Al > Si.
Reactivity:
- Metals (Groups 1, 2): reactivity increases down the group (easier to lose electrons). Cs is more reactive than Na.
- Non-metals (Group 17): reactivity decreases down the group (harder to gain electrons). F is the most reactive.
- Across a period: very reactive at both ends (Groups 1, 17), less in the middle; Group 18 unreactive.
Density: generally increases down a group (mass increases faster than volume). Across a period density rises to a maximum in the middle (transition metals) then falls.
Group 2 elements are less reactive than Group 1 elements in the same period because they have higher ionisation energies (two electrons to remove, smaller atoms).
دھاتی خاصیت (الیکٹران کھونے کی صلاحیت) گروپ میں نیچے بڑھتی ہے اور پیریڈ میں بائیں سے دائیں گھٹتی ہے۔ دھاتوں کی ری ایکٹیویٹی گروپ میں نیچے بڑھتی ہے جبکہ ہیلوجنز کی کم ہوتی ہے۔ کثافت عموماً گروپ میں نیچے بڑھتی ہے۔

══ 4.7 Group 1: alkali metals (pp. 62–64) ══
Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr. General valence configuration ns¹; form +1 ions.
Properties:
- Very reactive metals (stored under oil); reactivity increases down the group.
- Soft (can be cut with a knife) and have low densities (Li, Na, K float on water). Softness increases down the group.
- Low melting and boiling points, which decrease down the group.
- Density generally increases down the group (K is an exception, lighter than Na).
- Good conductors of heat and electricity.
- React with water to give a metal hydroxide (alkali) and hydrogen: metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen. Li reacts steadily, Na vigorously, K catches fire with a lilac flame.
Predicting: rubidium (below K) will react even more violently with water, have a lower melting point and a higher density than K, and still form RbOH + H₂.
[Table: Trends in Group 1]
Element | Melting point / °C | Density / g cm⁻³ | Reaction with water
• Li | 181 | 0.53 | Steady fizzing
• Na | 98 | 0.97 | Vigorous, melts into a ball
• K | 63 | 0.86 | Very vigorous, lilac flame
• Rb | 39 | 1.53 | Violent (predicted)
• Cs | 28 | 1.88 | Explosive (predicted)
الکلی دھاتیں (گروپ 1) بہت فعال، نرم اور ہلکی ہوتی ہیں۔ گروپ میں نیچے جاتے ہوئے ان کی فعالیت اور کثافت بڑھتی جبکہ نقطہ پگھلاؤ کم ہوتا ہے۔ پانی سے مل کر ہائیڈرو آکسائیڈ اور ہائیڈروجن گیس بناتی ہیں۔

══ 4.8 Group 17: halogens (pp. 65–66) ══
F, Cl, Br, I, At (and Ts). Name from Greek: halos = salt, gen = producer. Reactive non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules (F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂). Valence configuration ns² np⁵: they gain one electron to form X⁻ ions.
Appearance at r.t.p. (colour darkens down the group): fluorine – pale yellow gas; chlorine – yellow-green gas; bromine – red-brown liquid; iodine – grey-black solid (gives purple vapour on warming).
Trends down the group: melting and boiling points increase (gas → liquid → solid); density increases (F₂ 0.0017, Cl₂ 0.0032, Br₂ 3.10, I₂ 4.93 g cm⁻³); electronegativity and reactivity decrease; oxidising power decreases: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
Displacement reactions: a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its halide solution. The halogen acts as an oxidising agent (gains electrons); the halide ion acts as a reducing agent (loses electrons).
- F₂ displaces Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻. Cl₂ displaces Br⁻ and I⁻. Br₂ displaces I⁻. I₂ displaces none.
Hydrogen halides: H₂ + X₂ → 2HX. Thermal stability decreases HF > HCl > HBr > HI because the H–X bond becomes longer and weaker (smaller electronegativity difference, larger atom). HI decomposes on heating most easily.
Predicting astatine: solid, very dark (black), highest melting point, least reactive halogen.
[Table: Halogens at a glance]
Halogen | State and colour at r.t.p. | Density / g cm⁻³ | H–X bond energy / kJ mol⁻¹
• F₂ | Pale yellow gas | 0.0017 | HF 567
• Cl₂ | Yellow-green gas | 0.0032 | HCl 431
• Br₂ | Red-brown liquid | 3.10 | HBr 366
• I₂ | Grey-black solid | 4.93 | HI 299
Exam Tip: Displacement rule: halogen higher in the group displaces the one below it. “Will Br₂ + KCl react?” No – Br is below Cl.
ہیلوجنز (گروپ 17) دو ایٹمی غیر دھاتیں ہیں۔ فلورین ہلکی پیلی گیس، کلورین پیلی سبز گیس، برومین سرخی مائل بھورا مائع اور آیوڈین سیاہی مائل ٹھوس ہے۔ نیچے جاتے ہوئے کثافت اور نقطہ ابال بڑھتا جبکہ فعالیت کم ہوتی ہے۔ زیادہ فعال ہیلوجن کم فعال ہیلوجن کو اس کے نمک سے ہٹا دیتی ہے۔ HF سب سے زیادہ اور HI سب سے کم مستحکم ہے۔

══ 4.9 Transition elements, lanthanides and actinides (pp. 64) ══
Transition elements are the d-block metals (Groups 3–12). Characteristic properties:
1. High density (closely packed, heavy atoms): Fe 7.87 g cm⁻³, W 19.3 g cm⁻³.
2. High melting points (strong metallic bonding involving d electrons): W 3422 °C, Pt 1768 °C.
3. Variable oxidation states (both s and d electrons can be used): Fe +2/+3, Cu +1/+2.
4. Coloured compounds: copper(II) compounds blue/green, chromium compounds red/green, iron(III) yellow-brown.
5. Catalysts in industry:
- Iron – Haber process (NH₃).
- Platinum/palladium/rhodium – catalytic converters in cars.
- Nickel – hydrogenation of vegetable oil to make margarine (banaspati ghee).
- Platinum (or V₂O₅) – Contact process for H₂SO₄.
Lanthanides (rare earth elements, Z = 57–71) and actinides (Z = 89–103) are the two f-block series placed at the bottom of the table.
ٹرانزیشن عناصر (گروپ 3 تا 12، d بلاک) کی خصوصیات: زیادہ کثافت، بلند نقطہ پگھلاؤ، متغیر آکسیڈیشن حالتیں، رنگین مرکبات اور صنعت میں عمل انگیز کے طور پر استعمال (ہیبر عمل میں لوہا، مارجرین میں نکل، کیٹالیٹک کنورٹر میں پلاٹینم)۔

══ 4.10 Group 18: noble gases (pp. 67) ══
He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn, Og. Colourless, odourless, monatomic gases with very low reactivity (also called inert gases).
Reason: they have a complete valence shell – ns² np⁶ (octet), or 1s² (duplet) for helium – so they have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons. They have the highest ionisation energies in their periods and almost zero electron affinity.
Uses: neon in advertising signs; argon in light bulbs and as a shielding gas in welding; helium in balloons and (liquid He) cooling; krypton/xenon in special lamps.
[Table: Table 4.1 – Noble gas configurations]
Element | Z | Configuration
• He | 2 | 1s²
• Ne | 10 | 1s² 2s² 2p⁶
• Ar | 18 | 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶
• Kr | 36 | [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁶
• Xe | 54 | [Kr] 4d¹⁰ 5s² 5p⁶
نوبل گیسیں (گروپ 18) بے رنگ، بے بو، یک ایٹمی گیسیں ہیں جو تقریباً کوئی کیمیائی عمل نہیں کرتیں کیونکہ ان کا بیرونی شیل مکمل (اوکٹیٹ، ہیلیم میں ڈوپلیٹ) ہوتا ہے۔

══ 4.11 Metals and non-metals: physical properties (pp. 67–68) ══
- Thermal conductivity: metals conduct heat well; non-metals are poor conductors (insulators).
- Electrical conductivity: metals are good conductors because they have free (delocalised) electrons; non-metals are poor conductors (exception: graphite).
- Malleability and ductility: metals can be hammered into sheets and drawn into wires because layers of metal ions can slide without breaking the metallic bond; non-metals are brittle.
- Melting and boiling points: metals generally high (strong metallic bonds); non-metals generally low (weak forces between molecules). Exceptions: mercury (liquid metal), diamond (very high m.p. non-metal).
- Other: metals are shiny (lustrous), sonorous, mostly solids; non-metals dull, solids/liquids/gases.
- Chemically: metals lose electrons (electropositive), form basic oxides; non-metals gain/share electrons (electronegative), form acidic oxides.
[Table: Metals vs non-metals]
Property | Metals | Non-metals
• Thermal conductivity | High | Low
• Electrical conductivity | Good (free electrons) | Poor (except graphite)
• Malleability/ductility | Malleable and ductile | Brittle
• Melting/boiling points | Usually high | Usually low
• Lustre | Shiny | Dull (except iodine, graphite)
• Ions formed | Cations (lose e⁻) | Anions (gain e⁻)
• Oxides | Basic | Acidic
دھاتیں حرارت اور بجلی کی اچھی موصل ہیں (آزاد الیکٹران)، ان کی چادریں اور تاریں بن سکتی ہیں اور نقطہ پگھلاؤ زیادہ ہوتا ہے۔ غیر دھاتیں حرارت و بجلی کی کمزور موصل، بھربھری اور کم نقطہ پگھلاؤ والی ہوتی ہیں (گریفائٹ مستثنیٰ ہے)۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Blocks of the periodic table: s-block (Groups 1–2), d-block (3–12), p-block (13–18), f-block below.
2. Trends across the periodic table: Arrows point in the direction of increase.
chapters.shortNotes:
══ Chapter 4 in one page
- Periodic law: properties repeat when elements are arranged by increasing Z. 7 periods (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32), 18 groups.
- Position from configuration: block = last sub-shell; period = highest n; group = valence e⁻ (s-block) or valence e⁻ + 10 (p-block).
- Ion charge: Groups 1, 2, 13 → +1, +2, +3; Groups 15, 16, 17 → −3, −2, −1; noble gases none.
- Trends → (across): radius ↓, IE ↑, EA ↑, EN ↑, metallic ↓, shielding constant. ↓ (down): radius ↑, shielding ↑, IE ↓, EA ↓, EN ↓, metallic ↑, density ↑.
- Group 1: ns¹; soft, low density, low m.p. (↓ down), reactivity ↑ down; metal + water → MOH + H₂.
- Group 17: diatomic; F₂ pale yellow gas, Cl₂ yellow-green gas, Br₂ red-brown liquid, I₂ grey-black solid; density ↑, reactivity ↓; displacement: higher displaces lower; HF > HCl > HBr > HI stability.
- Transition metals: high density and m.p., variable oxidation states, coloured compounds, catalysts (Fe Haber; Ni margarine; Pt converters/Contact).
- Noble gases: monatomic, unreactive, full shells.
- Metals vs non-metals: conductivity, malleability/ductility, m.p./b.p.

پیریاڈک ٹیبل ایٹمی نمبر کی ترتیب پر ہے۔ پیریڈ میں دائیں جانب ایٹمی سائز کم اور آئنائزیشن انرجی، الیکٹرونیگیٹیویٹی بڑھتی ہے؛ گروپ میں نیچے اس کے الٹ۔ الکلی دھاتیں نیچے جاتے ہوئے زیادہ فعال، ہیلوجنز کم فعال۔ ٹرانزیشن عناصر عمل انگیز ہیں اور نوبل گیسیں غیر فعال۔

Exam Focus: Exam focus (20 summative SLOs, joint largest): trends down Group 1 and Group 17, halogen displacement reactions, thermal stability of HX, transition-metal properties and catalysts, identifying group/period from configuration, metals vs non-metals. Expect 2–4 MCQs and at least one short and one long question.
chapters.definitions:
• Periodic law (پیریاڈک قانون) [p. 47]: When elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number, their properties repeat in a periodic manner.
• Periodic table (پیریاڈک ٹیبل) [p. 47]: A table showing the systematic arrangement of elements in periods and groups in order of increasing atomic number.
• Period (پیریڈ) [p. 47]: A horizontal row of elements in the periodic table.
• Group (family) (گروپ) [p. 49]: A vertical column of elements in the periodic table; its members have similar properties.
• Representative (main-group) elements (نمائندہ عناصر) [p. 49]: Elements of the A groups (s- and p-blocks).
• s-block elements (s بلاک عناصر) [p. 52]: Elements of Groups 1 and 2 whose last electron enters an s sub-shell.
• p-block elements (p بلاک عناصر) [p. 52]: Elements of Groups 13–18 (except He) whose last electron enters a p sub-shell.
• Transition elements (ٹرانزیشن عناصر) [p. 64]: d-block elements of Groups 3–12.
• Shielding effect (شیلڈنگ اثر) [p. 55]: The reduction in the force of attraction between the nucleus and valence electrons caused by electrons in the inner shells.
• Atomic size (radius) (ایٹمی سائز) [p. 56]: The average distance between the nucleus and the outermost electron shell of an atom.
• Ionisation energy (آئنائزیشن انرجی) [p. 57]: The minimum energy required to remove the outermost electron from an isolated gaseous atom.
• Electron affinity (الیکٹران افینیٹی) [p. 59]: The energy released when an electron is added to the valence shell of an isolated gaseous atom to form a uni-negative ion.
• Electronegativity (الیکٹرونیگیٹیویٹی) [p. 60]: The ability of an atom to attract the shared pair of electrons towards itself in a chemical bond.
• Metallic character (دھاتی خاصیت) [p. 61]: The tendency of an element to lose electrons and form positive ions.
• Reactivity (فعالیت) [p. 62]: The capability of an element to react with other substances to form new compounds.
• Alkali metals (الکلی دھاتیں) [p. 62]: The soft, highly reactive metals of Group 1 (ns¹) that form alkaline hydroxides with water.
• Halogens (ہیلوجنز) [p. 65]: The reactive diatomic non-metals of Group 17 (ns² np⁵); “salt formers”.
• Displacement reaction (halogens) (ہٹانے کا تعامل) [p. 66]: A reaction in which a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halogen from its halide.
• Noble gases (نوبل گیسیں) [p. 67]: Unreactive, monatomic gases of Group 18 with complete valence shells.
• Lanthanides (لینتھینائیڈز) [p. 64]: The 14 f-block elements following lanthanum (Z = 57–71), also called rare earth elements.
• Actinides (ایکٹینائیڈز) [p. 64]: The f-block series of elements with Z = 89–103.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Periodic table (دوری جدول): Arrangement of elements
• Period (دور / پیریڈ): Horizontal row
• Group (گروہ / گروپ): Vertical column
• Valence electrons (گرفتی الیکٹران): Electrons in the outer shell
• Shielding (حجاب / شیلڈنگ): Blocking of nuclear pull
• Ionisation energy (آئن سازی کی توانائی): Energy to remove an electron
• Electron affinity (الیکٹرانی رغبت): Energy released on gaining an electron
• Electronegativity (برقی منفیت): Pull on shared electrons
• Alkali metals (الکلی دھاتیں): Group 1
• Halogens (ہیلوجنز / نمک ساز): Group 17
• Noble gases (نجیب گیسیں): Group 18
• Transition elements (عبوری عناصر): d-block
• Displacement (ہٹانا / بے دخلی): One element replaces another
• Malleable (چادر پذیر): Can be hammered into sheets
• Ductile (تار پذیر): Can be drawn into wires
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Group (s-block): group = number of valence electrons (Groups 1–2)
• Group (p-block, IUPAC): group = valence electrons + 10 (e.g. Cl: 7 + 10 = 17)
• Period: period = n of outermost shell
• Ionisation: M(g) + IE -> M⁺(g) + e⁻ (Energy absorbed)
• Electron affinity: X(g) + e⁻ -> X⁻(g) + EA (Energy released)
• Alkali metal valence shell: ns¹
• Alkaline earth valence shell: ns²
• Halogen valence shell: ns² np⁵
• Noble gas valence shell: ns² np⁶ (He: 1s²)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g) — Alkali metal + water → alkali + hydrogen.
• 2K(s) + 2H₂O(l) -> 2KOH(aq) + H₂(g) — More vigorous than sodium.
• Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq) — Chlorine displaces bromine (solution turns orange).
• Cl₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> 2KCl(aq) + I₂(aq) — Chlorine displaces iodine (brown).
• Br₂(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> 2KBr(aq) + I₂(aq) — Bromine displaces iodine.
• F₂(g) + 2NaCl(aq) -> 2NaF(aq) + Cl₂(g) — Fluorine displaces all other halogens.
• I₂ + 2KBr -> no reaction — Iodine is less reactive than bromine.
• H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) -> 2HCl(g) — Formation of a hydrogen halide.
• 2HI(g) -> H₂(g) + I₂(g) — HI is least thermally stable: decomposes on heating.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why does atomic size decrease across a period even though electrons are being added?
   Answer: The electrons go into the same shell while the nuclear charge increases by one each time, so the stronger pull draws the shell closer.
2. Why are noble gases unreactive?
   Answer: They have completely filled valence shells (octet; duplet for He), so they have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons.
3. Why is fluorine the most reactive halogen?
   Answer: It is the smallest halogen with the highest electronegativity, so it attracts an extra electron most strongly.
4. Why do Group 1 metals become more reactive down the group while Group 17 elements become less reactive?
   Answer: Metals react by losing electrons, which gets easier down the group; halogens react by gaining electrons, which gets harder down the group as atoms get larger.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. A new element X is soft, can be cut with a knife and reacts violently with water to give an alkaline solution and hydrogen. Where is it in the periodic table?
   Answer: Group 1 (alkali metals), probably low in the group (like Rb or Cs).
2. Why are platinum and palladium used in car exhausts?
   Answer: They are transition-metal catalysts in catalytic converters that change CO and NO into CO₂ and N₂.
3. Why is argon filled in electric bulbs instead of air?
   Answer: Argon is an unreactive noble gas, so the hot filament does not react (oxidise) and lasts longer.
4. A student adds chlorine water to a colourless solution and it turns brown. What could the solution contain?
   Answer: Iodide ions (e.g. KI): Cl₂ displaces iodine, which is brown in solution.

3. Which atom has the smaller ionisation energy? (a) B or N (b) Be or Mg (c) C or Si. (Concept Assessment 4.7)
   Solution: (a) B (further left in period 2). (b) Mg (lower in Group 2). (c) Si (lower in Group 14).

4. Which displacement reactions will occur? (Concept Assessment 4.9) 1. Cl₂ + 2NaF 2. Br₂ + 2KI 3. I₂ + 2KBr 4. Cl₂ + 2KBr 5. Cl₂ + 2NaI

3. No – I is less reactive than Br.

5. Yes – Cl₂ + 2NaI → 2NaCl + I₂.

5. An unknown element has Z = 19. Find its position and predict its properties. (Example 4.7)

— Exercise MCQs —
i. Number of periods in the periodic table are: → B (7) | There are 7 periods.
ii. Which of the following groups contain alkaline earth metals? → B (IIA) | Group IIA (2).
iii. Which of the following elements belongs to VIIIA? → D (Xe) | Xenon is a noble gas (Group VIIIA/18).
iv. Main group elements are arranged in ______ groups. → C (8) | IA–VIIIA = 8 groups.
v. Period number of ²⁷₁₃Al is: → C (3) | 2,8,3 → three shells → period 3.
vi. Valence shell electronic configuration of an element M (atomic no. 14) is: → D (3s², 3p²) | Si: 2,8,4 → 3s² 3p².
vii. Which of the following elements do you expect to have greater shielding effect? → D (Rb) | Shielding increases down the group; Rb has the most inner shells.
viii. As you move from right to left across a period, which of the following does not increase? → D (shielding effect) | Intended answer: shielding effect (stays constant across a period).
ix. All the elements of Group IIA are less reactive than alkali metals. This is because these elements have: → A (high ionisation energies) | Removing two electrons from smaller atoms needs more energy.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) Write the valence shell electronic configuration of an element present in the 3rd period and Group IIIA.
   Answer: 3s² 3p¹ (aluminium).
(ii) Define halogens.
   Answer: Halogens are the elements of Group 17 (VIIA) – F, Cl, Br, I, At – reactive non-metals that exist as diatomic molecules, have 7 valence electrons (ns² np⁵) and form salts with metals (“salt formers”).
(iii) Which atom has higher shielding effect, Li or Na?
   Answer: Na – it has more inner shells (2,8,1) than Li (2,1).
(iv) Explain why Na has higher ionisation energy than K.
   Answer: Na is smaller (3 shells) and its valence electron is closer to the nucleus with less shielding. K has an extra shell, so its 4s electron is farther away and more shielded, making it easier to remove. Hence IE(Na) 496 > IE(K) 419 kJ/mol.
(v) Alkali metals belong to the s-block of the periodic table. Why?
   Answer: Their last (valence) electron enters an s sub-shell (configuration ns¹).

— Q3–Q17. Descriptive questions —
3. Arrange in order of increasing ionisation energy: (a) Li, Na, K (b) Cl, Br, I
   Answer: (a) K < Na < Li (b) I < Br < Cl. IE decreases down a group.
4. Arrange in order of decreasing shielding effect: (a) Li, Na, K (b) Cl, Br, I (c) Cl, Br
   Answer: (a) K > Na > Li (b) I > Br > Cl (c) Br > Cl. Shielding increases down a group.
5. Which of S, P, Cl would you expect to have the greatest electron affinity?
   Answer: Cl – it is furthest right in period 3, with the highest nuclear charge and smallest radius, and needs only one electron to complete its octet.
6. Group the following in pairs with similar chemical properties: A = 1s² 2s²; B = 1s² 2s² 2p⁴; C = 1s² 2s² 2p¹; D = 1s²; E = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴; F = 1s² 2s¹; G = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹; H = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s².
   Answer: Same valence configuration = same group = similar properties:
- A and H (ns²: Be and Mg, Group 2)
- B and E (ns² np⁴: O and S, Group 16)
- F and G (ns¹: Li and Na, Group 1)
- C (B, Group 13) and D (He, noble gas) have no partner in this list.
7. Arrange the elements of Q6 in groups and periods.
   Answer: 
8. Find the group number of ²⁷₁₃Al, ³²₁₆S, ³⁹₁₉K and oxygen (printed as ^8₆O).
   Answer: Al 2,8,3 → IIIA (13); S 2,8,6 → VIA (16); K 2,8,8,1 → IA (1); O (Z = 8) 2,6 → VIA (16).
9. Write the valence shell configuration for (a) alkali metals (b) alkaline earth metals (c) halogens (d) noble gases.
   Answer: (a) ns¹ (b) ns² (c) ns² np⁵ (d) ns² np⁶ (He: 1s²).
10. Write electron dot symbols for (a) Be (b) K (c) N (d) I.
   Answer: Show only valence electrons as dots around the symbol: (a) Be with 2 dots (b) K with 1 dot (c) N with 5 dots (one pair + three singles) (d) I with 7 dots (three pairs + one single).
3 (2nd). Write the valence shell configuration of (a) an element in period 3, Group VA (b) an element in period 2, Group VIA.
   Answer: (a) 3s² 3p³ (phosphorus) (b) 2s² 2p⁴ (oxygen).
4 (2nd). Copy and complete the table of atomic number, mass number, protons, neutrons and electrons.
   Answer: 
13. Give block, group and period: (a) 1s² 2s¹ (b) 1s² 2s² 2p⁵ (c) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² (d) 1s²
   Answer: (a) Li – s-block, Group 1, Period 2 (b) F – p-block, Group 17, Period 2 (c) Mg – s-block, Group 2, Period 3 (d) He – s-block configuration, placed in Group 18, Period 1.
14. What types of elements have the highest and lowest ionisation energies? Argue.
   Answer: Highest: noble gases (and halogens) at the top-right – full or nearly full shells, small atoms, high nuclear charge, little shielding. Lowest: alkali metals at the bottom-left (Cs, Fr) – one electron in a large outer shell, far from the nucleus and strongly shielded.
15(i). Two atoms have configurations 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ and 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. Their IEs are 2080 and 496 kJ/mol. Match them and give reason.
   Answer: 2080 kJ/mol → 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ (neon): complete octet, very stable, electron close to nucleus. 496 kJ/mol → 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ (sodium): single 3s electron in a new shell, far and well shielded, easily removed to give a stable Na⁺.
15(ii). Use the second member of Groups IA, IIA and VIIA to show that the number of valence electrons equals the group number.
   Answer: Na (IA): 2,8,1 → 1 valence electron. Mg (IIA): 2,8,2 → 2. Cl (VIIA): 2,8,7 → 7. Each equals its group number.
15(iii). Letters A–F mark elements in the given periodic-table figure. Answer a–l.
   Answer: Positions read from the figure: A = period 3, Group 1 (Na); B = period 3, Group 14 (Si); C = period 2, Group 16 (O); D = period 4, Group 2 (Ca); E = period 4, Group 15 (As); F = period 5, Group 17 (I).
a. Same period: A and B (period 3); D and E (period 4).
b. Valence configuration of D: 4s².
c. Metals: A and D.
d. Can lose two electrons: D.
e. E is in Group 15 (VA).
f. Halogen: F.
g. Forms a dipositive (2+) cation: D (Ca²⁺).
h. Configuration of E (Z = 33): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d¹⁰ 4p³.
i. Ionic bond: A and F (NaI) or D and C (CaO).
j. Yes, C (oxygen) forms C₂ = O₂ by sharing two pairs of electrons (double covalent bond).

16. Configurations: (a) 1s² 2s¹ (b) 1s² 2s² 2p⁵ (c) 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² (d) 1s². Which is (i) an alkali metal (ii) an alkaline earth metal (iii) a noble gas (iv) a halogen?

17. In what region of the periodic table will you find elements with relatively (a) high (b) low ionisation energies?
