chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Justify: (a) fluorine has a smaller shielding effect than chlorine (b) fluorine has a higher ionisation energy than chlorine.
   Answer: (a) F (2,7) has only one inner shell; Cl (2,8,7) has two, so Cl’s valence electrons are more shielded. (b) F’s valence electrons are closer to the nucleus and less shielded, so they are held more strongly and need more energy to remove.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Briefly state the trend of metallic character along (down) a group. Give reason.
   Answer: Metallic character increases down a group because atomic size and shielding increase, so valence electrons are held less tightly and are lost more easily.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] State the general trends down Group 1 for (a) density (b) reactivity.
   Answer: (a) Density generally increases down the group (K is an exception). (b) Reactivity increases – the outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] State the trend in melting point and density of Group IA elements down the group.
   Answer: Melting point decreases (Li 181 °C → Cs 28 °C) because metallic bonding weakens as atoms get bigger; density generally increases because mass increases faster than volume.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] An element has electronic configuration 2,8,7 (Z = 17). Identify its period, group and number of valence electrons.
   Answer: Period 3, Group VIIA (17), 7 valence electrons – chlorine.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Complete the displacement reactions if possible: (a) Br₂ + 2KI → (b) F₂ + 2KCl → (c) I₂ + 2KBr →
   Answer: (a) Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂ (b) F₂ + 2KCl → 2KF + Cl₂ (c) No reaction – iodine is less reactive than bromine.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Complete if possible: (a) Cl₂ + 2KF → (b) F₂ + 2KI → (c) Cl₂ + 2KBr →
   Answer: (a) No reaction (Cl less reactive than F) (b) F₂ + 2KI → 2KF + I₂ (c) Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] What is the periodic table? On what basis are elements arranged in the modern periodic table?
   Answer: A table arranging elements in periods and groups so that elements with similar properties fall in the same group. Basis: increasing atomic number (proton number) – periodic law.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] What is meant by thermal stability of hydrogen halides? Arrange HF, HCl, HBr, HI in increasing thermal stability.
   Answer: Thermal stability is the resistance of a compound to decomposition on heating. HI < HBr < HCl < HF – the H–X bond gets weaker from HF to HI (bond energies 567, 431, 366, 299 kJ/mol).

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] Why do elements in the same group show similar chemical properties? Relate your answer to electronic configuration.
   Answer: Chemical properties depend on valence electrons. Elements in a group have the same valence-shell configuration (e.g. all Group 1 have ns¹), so they lose/gain/share electrons in the same way and form similar compounds.

11. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22); Annual 2025] Write any three properties of transition elements.
   Answer: High density and melting point; variable oxidation states; coloured compounds; act as catalysts (any three).

12. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] Why can fluorine oxidise and displace all other halide ions? Give one example.
   Answer: Fluorine is the most electronegative and strongest oxidising agent among halogens, so it takes electrons from Cl⁻, Br⁻ and I⁻. Example: F₂ + 2KCl → 2KF + Cl₂.

13. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22); 2nd Annual 2025] Give any three differences between metals and non-metals.
   Answer: Metals conduct heat and electricity, are malleable/ductile and usually have high melting points; non-metals are poor conductors, brittle and usually have low melting points.

14. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] What are halogens? State the general trends in density and reactivity down the group.
   Answer: Group 17 diatomic non-metals (F, Cl, Br, I). Down the group density increases and reactivity decreases.

15. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] How many electrons are in the valence shell of Group I and Group VII elements? What kind of ions do they form? Give one example each.
   Answer: Group I: 1 → lose it → +1 ions (Na⁺). Group VII: 7 → gain one → −1 ions (Cl⁻).

16. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Give any two displacement reactions of halogens.
   Answer: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂; Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂.

17. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Identify the group of ³⁹₁₉K, ¹⁶_8O and ^4₂He (Ne) by electronic configuration.
   Answer: K 2,8,8,1 → Group IA; O 2,6 → Group VIA; Ne 2,8 (or He 2) → Group VIIIA (18).

18. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Identify the period of ^6₃Li, ¹¹_5B and ²¹₁₀Ne by electronic configuration.
   Answer: Li 2,1; B 2,3; Ne 2,8 – all have two shells → all in period 2.

19. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Predict the reactions of Cl₂ with (a) Br⁻ (b) I⁻.
   Answer: (a) Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂ (b) Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂. Chlorine is more reactive, so it oxidises both halide ions.

20. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Give three examples of transition metals that act as catalysts.
   Answer: Iron – Haber process; nickel – hydrogenation of oils (margarine); platinum – catalytic converters / Contact process.

21. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Identify the group and period of (a) ¹²_6A (b) ³⁹₁₉B (c) ¹⁹_9C.
   Answer: (a) 2,4 → Group IVA (14), period 2 (b) 2,8,8,1 → Group IA, period 4 (c) 2,7 → Group VIIA (17), period 2.

22. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Write the names of Group VII elements and describe the trend in physical state and density down the group.
   Answer: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine. State changes from gas (F₂, Cl₂) → liquid (Br₂) → solid (I₂, At); density increases down the group.

23. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Compare the variation in reactivity of metals and non-metals using electron behaviour.
   Answer: Metals react by losing electrons, so they become more reactive down a group (electrons easier to lose). Non-metals react by gaining electrons, so they become less reactive down a group (harder to attract an extra electron) and more reactive across a period.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Element Z is below magnesium in Group IIA. (a) Predict its reactivity compared with Mg (b) compare its metallic character (c) compare its ionisation energy.
   Answer: Z is calcium (2,8,8,2).
(a) More reactive than Mg: larger atom, outer electrons more shielded and easier to lose (Ca reacts with cold water; Mg only with steam).
(b) Greater metallic character: loses electrons more easily.
(c) Lower ionisation energy: valence electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Explain how (a) atomic radius (b) reactivity change down Group IA. Give reasons.
   Answer: (a) Atomic radius increases (Li < Na < K < Rb < Cs) because each element has one extra electron shell.
(b) Reactivity increases because the single valence electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so less energy (lower IE) is needed to remove it. Li reacts steadily with water, Na vigorously, K bursts into flame, Rb and Cs explode.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Compare metals and non-metals in terms of (a) thermal conductivity (b) electrical conductivity (c) malleability and ductility.
   Answer: (a) Metals: high thermal conductivity – free electrons and closely packed ions transfer heat. Non-metals: poor conductors (insulators).
(b) Metals: good electrical conductors – delocalised electrons move through the lattice. Non-metals: poor conductors (except graphite).
(c) Metals: malleable and ductile – layers of ions slide without breaking the metallic bond. Non-metals: brittle – break when hammered.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] An element belongs to Group IA and is below sodium. (a) Predict its reactivity with water with reasons. (b) Predict its melting point and density compared to sodium.
   Answer: It is potassium.
(a) More reactive: reacts very vigorously with water, catching fire with a lilac flame: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂. Reason: larger atom, lower IE.
(b) Lower melting point (63 °C vs 98 °C, weaker metallic bonding). Density: generally increases down the group, but K (0.86) is an exception, slightly less dense than Na (0.97).

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Briefly describe ionisation energy and electron affinity with their trends in groups and periods.
   Answer: Ionisation energy: minimum energy to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom. Increases across a period (higher nuclear charge, smaller atom); decreases down a group (larger atom, more shielding).
Electron affinity: energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron to form X⁻. Generally increases across a period (halogens highest) and decreases down a group.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Compare metals and non-metals for thermal conductivity, ductility and melting point.
   Answer: Metals: high thermal conductivity, ductile, mostly high melting points. Non-metals: low thermal conductivity, brittle (not ductile), mostly low melting points.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Predict the trend of atomic size, ionisation energy and electronegativity of Group IIA using chemical periodicity.
   Answer: Down Group IIA (Be → Ba): atomic size increases (new shells); ionisation energy decreases (electrons farther, more shielded); electronegativity decreases (weaker pull on bonding electrons).

8. Describe the properties of transition elements with examples of their use as industrial catalysts.
   Answer: d-block metals (Groups 3–12):
1. High density (Fe 7.87, W 19.3 g cm⁻³).
2. High melting points (W 3422 °C).
3. Variable oxidation states (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Cu⁺/Cu²⁺).
4. Coloured compounds (CuSO₄ blue, FeCl₃ yellow-brown).
5. Catalysts: Fe – Haber process; Pt/Pd/Rh – catalytic converters; Ni – margarine; Pt or V₂O₅ – Contact process.

9. Describe the halogens: physical states and colours, trends in density and reactivity, displacement reactions and thermal stability of hydrogen halides.
   Answer: States/colours: F₂ pale yellow gas, Cl₂ yellow-green gas, Br₂ red-brown liquid, I₂ grey-black solid.
Trends down the group: density and boiling point increase; reactivity, electronegativity and oxidising power decrease (F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂).
Displacement: a halogen displaces those below it: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂; Br₂ + 2KI → 2KBr + I₂; I₂ + KBr → no reaction.
HX stability: HF > HCl > HBr > HI because H–X bond strength decreases as the halogen gets larger.
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 4 in one page
- Periodic law: properties repeat when elements are arranged by increasing Z. 7 periods (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32), 18 groups.
- Position from configuration: block = last sub-shell; period = highest n; group = valence e⁻ (s-block) or valence e⁻ + 10 (p-block).
- Ion charge: Groups 1, 2, 13 → +1, +2, +3; Groups 15, 16, 17 → −3, −2, −1; noble gases none.
- Trends → (across): radius ↓, IE ↑, EA ↑, EN ↑, metallic ↓, shielding constant. ↓ (down): radius ↑, shielding ↑, IE ↓, EA ↓, EN ↓, metallic ↑, density ↑.
- Group 1: ns¹; soft, low density, low m.p. (↓ down), reactivity ↑ down; metal + water → MOH + H₂.
- Group 17: diatomic; F₂ pale yellow gas, Cl₂ yellow-green gas, Br₂ red-brown liquid, I₂ grey-black solid; density ↑, reactivity ↓; displacement: higher displaces lower; HF > HCl > HBr > HI stability.
- Transition metals: high density and m.p., variable oxidation states, coloured compounds, catalysts (Fe Haber; Ni margarine; Pt converters/Contact).
- Noble gases: monatomic, unreactive, full shells.
- Metals vs non-metals: conductivity, malleability/ductility, m.p./b.p.

chapters.title: Chemical Bonding
chapters.introduction:
Why is salt a hard, high-melting solid while water is a liquid and methane a gas? The answer is chemical bonding. This unit explains the octet and duplet rules, how metals and non-metals become stable by forming ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent and metallic bonds, how to draw dot-and-cross and Lewis structures, what intermolecular forces (dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding) do, and how bonding explains melting points, electrical conductivity and the uses of graphite, diamond and metals.

Exam focus (12 summative SLOs): dot-and-cross diagrams (NaF, CaCl₂, MgO, H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, NH₃, N₂, HCN, C₂H₄), ionic vs covalent properties, conductivity of ionic compounds (solid vs molten), metallic bonding, uses of graphite/diamond. A long dot-and-cross question appears in almost every paper.
chapters.urduIntroduction: نمک سخت ٹھوس، پانی مائع اور میتھین گیس کیوں ہے؟ اس کا جواب کیمیائی بندھن میں ہے۔ اس باب میں اوکٹیٹ اور ڈوپلیٹ اصول، آئنی، شریکی، کوآرڈینیٹ اور دھاتی بندھن، ڈاٹ اینڈ کراس ڈایاگرام، بین سالماتی قوتیں اور مرکبات کی خصوصیات پڑھیں گے۔
learningObjectives: Describe how noble gas electronic configuration and the octet and duplet rules help predict the chemical properties of main group elements.
Compare the formation of cations and anions.
Account for the electropositive nature of metals and electronegative nature of non-metals.
Define ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent and metallic bonds.

Differentiate between ionic and covalent compounds (ionic bond = electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions; covalent bond = attraction between shared electrons and two nuclei; metallic bond = attraction between a sea of delocalised electrons and cations).

══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
Exam focus (12 summative SLOs): dot-and-cross diagrams (NaF, CaCl₂, MgO, H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, NH₃, N₂, HCN, C₂H₄), ionic vs covalent properties, conductivity of ionic compounds (solid vs molten), metallic bonding, uses of graphite/diamond. A long dot-and-cross question appears in almost every paper.
Note: Review Q1(i) prints oxygen’s mass number as 8 (it is 16). Review Q1(iv) asks which atom obeys the duplet rule but lists O₂, F₂, F₂, N₂ – none obey the duplet rule (they all follow the octet rule); hydrogen, helium, lithium and beryllium are duplet examples.

══ 5.1 Noble gas configuration: octet and duplet rules (pp. 74–75) ══
Noble gases (Group 18) have completely filled valence shells: ns² np⁶ (8 electrons, an octet), or 1s² for helium (a duplet). That is why they are stable and unreactive.
In 1916 G. N. Lewis used this idea to explain bonding:
- Octet rule: atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons so that they have eight electrons in their valence shell, like the nearest noble gas. It applies to main-group elements (only s and p electrons involved). Example: Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8) like Ne; Cl (2,8,7) → Cl⁻ (2,8,8) like Ar.
- Duplet rule: atoms close to helium (H, Li, Be) tend to reach two electrons in their outer shell, like He. Example: Li (1s² 2s¹) → Li⁺ (1s²); Be → Be²⁺ (1s²); H shares one electron in H₂ to get 2.
These rules let us predict chemical behaviour: how many electrons an atom loses or gains, what ion it forms and how many bonds it makes.
Key Point: Octet = 8 valence electrons (Ne, Ar …). Duplet = 2 (He). Atoms react to reach these stable arrangements.
نوبل گیسوں کا بیرونی شیل مکمل ہوتا ہے (8 الیکٹران یعنی اوکٹیٹ، ہیلیم میں 2 یعنی ڈوپلیٹ)۔ دوسرے ایٹم الیکٹران کھو کر، لے کر یا شریک کر کے یہی مستحکم ترتیب حاصل کرنا چاہتے ہیں۔ ہائیڈروجن، لیتھیم اور بیریلیم ڈوپلیٹ اصول پر چلتے ہیں۔

══ 5.2 Chemical bonds; electropositive metals and electronegative non-metals (pp. 75–78) ══
A chemical bond is the force of attraction that holds atoms together in a substance. The forces are electrical in nature. Atoms bond to become more stable (lower energy) by reaching a noble-gas configuration.
- Metals are electropositive: they have low ionisation energy and low electronegativity, so they lose valence electrons easily to form cations. Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻.
- Non-metals are electronegative: they have high electronegativity and electron affinity, so they gain electrons to form anions. F + e⁻ → F⁻; O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻.
- Atoms can also reach the octet by sharing electrons (covalent bonding).
Cation vs anion formation: cations form by loss of electrons (metals, Groups 1–3; charge = group number); anions form by gain of electrons (non-metals, Groups 15–17; charge = 8 − group number). A cation is smaller than its atom; an anion is larger.
[Table: Formation of cations and anions]
 | Cation | Anion
• Process | Loss of electrons | Gain of electrons
• Formed by | Metals (electropositive) | Non-metals (electronegative)
• Energy idea | Needs ionisation energy | Releases electron affinity
• Number of electrons | Group number (1, 2, 3) | 8 − group number (3, 2, 1)
• Size vs atom | Smaller | Larger
• Examples | Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ | Cl⁻, O²⁻, N³⁻
کیمیائی بندھن وہ کشش کی قوت ہے جو ایٹموں کو جوڑے رکھتی ہے۔ دھاتیں الیکٹرو پازیٹو ہیں: آسانی سے الیکٹران کھو کر مثبت آئن بناتی ہیں۔ غیر دھاتیں الیکٹرونیگیٹو ہیں: الیکٹران لے کر منفی آئن بناتی ہیں۔

══ 5.3 Ionic bonds and ionic compounds (pp. 78–80) ══
An ionic bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (a metal cation and a non-metal anion). It forms when a metal atom transfers electrons to a non-metal atom. Compounds held by ionic bonds are ionic compounds; overall they are neutral, so total positive charge = total negative charge.
Steps to show formation (dot-and-cross):
1. Write the metal’s valence electrons as dots and the non-metal’s as crosses.
2. Move the metal’s electrons to the non-metal until both have octets.
3. Write the ions in brackets with charges; balance the charges to get the formula.
- NaCl: Na• + ×Cl (7×) → [Na]⁺ [Cl (8)]⁻ ; 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
- NaF, NaBr: same 1 : 1 pattern.
- MgF₂: Mg loses 2e⁻ → Mg²⁺; each F gains 1e⁻ → 2F⁻. Mg + F₂ → MgF₂.
- CaCl₂: Ca (2,8,8,2) → Ca²⁺; two Cl atoms each gain 1 → 2Cl⁻.
- MgO: Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻; O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻; ratio 1 : 1.
- AlCl₃: Al → Al³⁺; 3 Cl⁻.
- Na₂S: each of two Na loses 1e⁻; S gains 2e⁻ → S²⁻.
Recognising ionic compounds: a metal (Groups 1, 2, 13) combined with a non-metal (Groups 15–17): KCl, AlCl₃, MgF₂, NaF, NaBr, MgO, CaO.
Exam Tip: In dot-and-cross diagrams for ionic compounds always draw square brackets around each ion, show the full outer shell of the anion (dots + the transferred cross), and write the charge at the top right of the bracket.
آئنی بندھن مخالف چارج والے آئنوں (دھاتی مثبت اور غیر دھاتی منفی) کے درمیان مضبوط برقی کشش ہے۔ یہ اس وقت بنتا ہے جب دھات اپنے الیکٹران غیر دھات کو منتقل کر دیتی ہے، جیسے سوڈیم اپنا ایک الیکٹران کلورین کو دے کر NaCl بناتا ہے۔

══ 5.4 Covalent bonds: single, double and triple (pp. 80–83) ══
A covalent bond is formed by the mutual sharing of a pair of electrons between two atoms (usually two non-metals). The bond is the strong electrostatic attraction between the shared electron pair and the two nuclei.
- Single bond (−): one shared pair. H₂ (H–H), F₂, Cl₂, HCl, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄, C₂H₆, CH₃OH.
- Double bond (=): two shared pairs. O₂ (O=O), CO₂ (O=C=O), C₂H₄ (H₂C=CH₂), CS₂.
- Triple bond (≡): three shared pairs. N₂ (N≡N), HCN (H–C≡N), C₂H₂.
Lone pairs: valence electron pairs that are not shared. F₂ has 3 lone pairs on each F; H₂O has 2 lone pairs on O; NH₃ has 1 lone pair on N.
How to draw dot-and-cross structures:
1. Pick the central atom – the one that needs to share most electrons (C in CH₄, CO₂, HCN; O in H₂O; N in NH₃).
2. Put its valence electrons as dots; put the other atoms’ electrons as crosses.
3. Share pairs until every atom has an octet (H only 2).
4. Check total electrons and that each atom obeys the octet/duplet rule.
Examples:
- CH₄: C (4) shares one electron with each of 4 H → 4 single bonds, no lone pairs.
- H₂O: O (6) shares with 2 H → 2 single bonds + 2 lone pairs on O.
- NH₃: N (5) shares with 3 H → 3 single bonds + 1 lone pair.
- CO₂: C shares 2 pairs with each O → O=C=O; each O has 2 lone pairs.
- N₂: each N shares 3 electrons → N≡N; one lone pair on each N.
- HCN: H–C single bond; C≡N triple bond; one lone pair on N.
- C₂H₄: C=C double bond; each C also bonds to 2 H.
- CH₃OH: C bonded to 3 H and O; O bonded to H; 2 lone pairs on O.
[Table: Common molecules]
Molecule | Bonds | Lone pairs on central atom | Lewis structure
• H₂ | 1 single | — | H–H
• Cl₂ | 1 single | 3 on each Cl | Cl–Cl
• HCl | 1 single | 3 on Cl | H–Cl
• H₂O | 2 single | 2 on O | H–O–H
• NH₃ | 3 single | 1 on N | N bonded to 3 H
• CH₄ | 4 single | 0 | C bonded to 4 H
• O₂ | 1 double | 2 on each O | O=O
• CO₂ | 2 double | 0 on C (2 on each O) | O=C=O
• C₂H₄ | 1 double + 4 single | 0 | H₂C=CH₂
• N₂ | 1 triple | 1 on each N | N≡N
• HCN | 1 single + 1 triple | 1 on N | H–C≡N
شریکی (کوویلنٹ) بندھن دو ایٹموں کے درمیان الیکٹران کے ایک جوڑے کی باہمی شراکت سے بنتا ہے، عموماً دو غیر دھاتوں میں۔ ایک جوڑا = سنگل، دو جوڑے = ڈبل، تین جوڑے = ٹرپل بندھن۔ جو جوڑے شریک نہ ہوں انہیں لون پیئر کہتے ہیں۔

══ 5.5 Polar and non-polar covalent bonds; coordinate covalent bonds (pp. 84–85) ══
Non-polar covalent bond: between identical atoms (or atoms of equal electronegativity); the shared pair is shared equally. H–H, Cl–Cl, O=O, N≡N.
Polar covalent bond: between different atoms; the more electronegative atom pulls the shared pair towards itself and gets a partial negative charge (δ−), the other a partial positive charge (δ+). Hδ⁺–Clδ⁻, H–O in water, H–N in ammonia.
Coordinate covalent (dative) bond: a covalent bond in which both shared electrons come from one atom (the donor, which has a lone pair) and the other atom (the acceptor) has an empty orbital. Once formed it is identical to an ordinary covalent bond. Shown by an arrow (→) from donor to acceptor.
- Ammonium ion, NH₄^+: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄^+. The lone pair on N bonds to H⁺ (from HCl).
- Hydronium ion, H₃O⁺: H₂O + H⁺ → H₃O⁺ (when HCl dissolves in water). A lone pair on O bonds to H⁺.
- NH₃·BF₃: B in BF₃ has only 6 valence electrons (electron deficient); N of NH₃ donates its lone pair: H₃N→BF₃.
[Table: Ordinary covalent vs coordinate covalent bond]
Covalent bond | Coordinate covalent bond
• Each atom contributes one electron to the shared pair | Both electrons come from one atom (donor)
• Shown by a line (–) | Shown by an arrow (→) from donor to acceptor
• e.g. H–H, H–Cl | e.g. NH₄^+, H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃
ایک جیسے ایٹموں میں الیکٹرانوں کی برابر شراکت غیر قطبی بندھن ہے۔ مختلف ایٹموں میں زیادہ الیکٹرونیگیٹو ایٹم الیکٹران اپنی طرف کھینچتا ہے اور قطبی بندھن بنتا ہے۔ کوآرڈینیٹ بندھن میں دونوں الیکٹران ایک ہی ایٹم دیتا ہے، جیسے NH₄^+ اور H₃O⁺۔

══ 5.6 Intermolecular forces: dipole–dipole and hydrogen bonding (pp. 85–86) ══
Intermolecular forces are attractive forces between molecules (much weaker than covalent bonds within molecules).
- Dipole–dipole forces: between polar molecules; the δ+ end of one molecule attracts the δ− end of another (e.g. HCl molecules).
- Hydrogen bonding: a special, stronger dipole–dipole attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to a very electronegative atom (N, O or F) and a lone pair on an N, O or F atom of a nearby molecule. Example: water, where Hδ⁺ of one molecule is attracted to O of another.
Importance: hydrogen bonds give water its high boiling point; they hold together proteins and DNA; the adhesive action of paints, dyes and glues comes from hydrogen bonding and dipole–dipole interactions with the surface. Epoxy resins (O–H groups) form strong hydrogen bonds and are used as adhesives in aircraft, cars and boats.
بین سالماتی قوتیں سالموں کے درمیان کشش کی کمزور قوتیں ہیں۔ قطبی سالموں میں ڈائی پول ڈائی پول کشش ہوتی ہے۔ جب ہائیڈروجن N، O یا F سے جڑی ہو اور قریبی سالمے کے N، O یا F کے لون پیئر کی طرف کھنچے تو اسے ہائیڈروجن بانڈ کہتے ہیں۔ پینٹ، رنگ اور گوند کی چپکنے کی صلاحیت اسی کی وجہ سے ہے۔

══ 5.7 Properties of ionic and covalent compounds (pp. 86–88) ══
Properties depend on (1) the type of particles (atoms, ions, molecules), (2) how strongly they are held, and (3) their arrangement.
Ionic compounds (e.g. NaCl, MgO): giant lattice of ions held by strong electrostatic forces →
- High melting and boiling points (NaCl 801/1465 °C, NaF 996/1695 °C, MgCl₂ 714/1412 °C).
- Hard and brittle crystalline solids.
- Do not conduct electricity when solid (ions fixed in place) but conduct when molten or dissolved in water (ions free to move).
- Usually soluble in water, insoluble in organic solvents.
Simple covalent (molecular) compounds (e.g. H₂O, CH₄, CO₂, ethanol): strong bonds inside molecules but weak intermolecular forces →
- Low melting and boiling points (water 0/100 °C, methane −183/−162 °C, ethanol −117/78 °C) – melting only breaks weak forces between molecules.
- Often gases or liquids; do not conduct electricity (no ions or free electrons).
- Some covalent compounds ionise in water: acids such as HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃ form H⁺ and anions in solution, so their aqueous solutions conduct electricity.
Giant covalent structures (diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide SiO₂/quartz): every atom covalently bonded to its neighbours in a huge network → very high melting points, very hard (except graphite), used as abrasives and refractories.
Metals: conduct because of free delocalised electrons.
[Table: Ionic vs covalent compounds]
Property | Ionic compounds | Covalent (molecular) compounds
• Particles | Ions | Molecules
• Bond formation | Electron transfer | Electron sharing
• Forces between particles | Strong electrostatic | Weak intermolecular
• State at room temperature | Crystalline solids | Gases, liquids or soft solids
• Melting/boiling points | High | Low
• Conductivity | Molten or aqueous: yes; solid: no | No (except acids in water)
• Solubility | Usually soluble in water | Usually soluble in organic solvents
• Examples | NaCl, MgO, KF | H₂O, CH₄, CO₂
Exam Tip: “Why does molten NaCl conduct but solid NaCl does not?” – In the solid the ions are locked in the lattice; when molten (or dissolved) the ions are free to move and carry charge.
آئنی مرکبات کا نقطہ پگھلاؤ زیادہ ہوتا ہے کیونکہ آئنوں کے درمیان مضبوط برقی قوت ہے؛ ٹھوس حالت میں بجلی نہیں گزارتے مگر پگھلنے یا پانی میں گھلنے پر گزارتے ہیں کیونکہ آئن آزاد ہو جاتے ہیں۔ سادہ شریکی مرکبات کا نقطہ پگھلاؤ کم ہوتا ہے کیونکہ سالموں کے درمیان قوتیں کمزور ہیں، اور یہ بجلی نہیں گزارتے۔ تیزاب پانی میں آئن بنا کر بجلی گزارتے ہیں۔

══ 5.8 Graphite and diamond: structure and industrial uses (pp. 88–90) ══
Graphite (Greek graphein = to write; “black lead”): each C bonded to 3 others in flat hexagonal layers; weak van der Waals forces between layers; one delocalised electron per C.
Uses justified by structure:
- Lubricant – layers slide over one another.
- Pencils – layers rub off on paper.
- Electrodes in electrolysis and electric furnaces, carbon brushes in motors – conducts electricity.
- Refractory bricks, crucibles – stable at high temperature, chemically inert.
- Moderator rods in nuclear reactors; bearings, piston rings.
Diamond: each C bonded to 4 others tetrahedrally (C–C 1.544 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, bond angle 109.5°) in a rigid 3-D network; hardest natural substance; density 3.514 g cm⁻³; no free electrons → electrical insulator; high refractive index (sparkle).
Uses: cutting, drilling and grinding tools (glass cutters, rock drills) because it is extremely hard; jewellery because it sparkles.
گریفائٹ: تہوں میں ترتیب، ہر کاربن تین سے جڑا، تہیں پھسلتی ہیں (چکنائی، پنسل) اور آزاد الیکٹران کی وجہ سے بجلی گزارتا ہے (الیکٹروڈ)۔ ہیرا: ہر کاربن چار سے مضبوطی سے جڑا، سب سے سخت مادہ، اس لیے کاٹنے اور ڈرل کرنے کے اوزاروں میں استعمال۔

══ 5.9 Metallic bonding and properties of metals (pp. 90–91) ══
In a metal, atoms lose their valence electrons, which become delocalised (free to move through the whole structure) – a “sea” of electrons. The positive metal ions (cations) are arranged in regular layers.
Metallic bond: the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive metal ions and the sea of delocalised electrons.
Properties explained:
- High melting and boiling points – strong metallic bonding in a giant structure.
- Good electrical conductivity – delocalised electrons move when a voltage is applied → metals used for wires (Cu, Al).
- Good thermal conductivity – free electrons carry heat → cooking pots.
- Malleable and ductile – layers of ions can slide over each other without breaking the bond (the electron sea holds them) → sheets and wires.
- Lustre – free electrons reflect light.
[Table: Material choice and bonding]
Use | Material | Property due to bonding
• Electrical wires | Copper, aluminium (metallic) | Free electrons conduct; ductile
• Cooking pots, sheets | Aluminium, steel | Conduct heat; malleable
• Lubricant, electrodes | Graphite (giant covalent, layers) | Layers slide; delocalised electrons
• Cutting tools | Diamond (giant covalent, 3-D) | Extremely hard
• Electrolyte in batteries/cells | Ionic compounds in solution or molten | Mobile ions conduct
• Abrasives, refractories | SiO₂, silicon carbide | Very hard, very high melting point
دھاتوں میں مثبت آئن آزاد الیکٹرانوں کے “سمندر” میں ڈوبے ہوتے ہیں؛ ان کے درمیان مضبوط برقی کشش دھاتی بندھن ہے۔ اسی وجہ سے دھاتیں بجلی اور حرارت کی اچھی موصل، چادر و تار پذیر اور زیادہ نقطہ پگھلاؤ والی ہوتی ہیں۔

══ Chapter 5 in one page
- Octet/duplet rules: atoms lose, gain or share electrons to reach 8 (or 2 for H, Li, Be) valence electrons like noble gases.
- Metals electropositive → cations; non-metals electronegative → anions.
- Ionic bond: electron transfer; electrostatic attraction between ions (NaCl, MgO, CaCl₂, MgF₂, AlCl₃, Na₂S). Draw brackets and charges.
- Covalent bond: shared pair attracted by two nuclei. Single (H₂, HCl, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄), double (O₂, CO₂, C₂H₄), triple (N₂, HCN). Lone pairs: H₂O 2, NH₃ 1.
- Polar (unequal sharing, δ+/δ−) vs non-polar (equal). Coordinate bond: both electrons from one atom (NH₄^+, H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃).
- Intermolecular forces: dipole–dipole; hydrogen bonding (H on N/O/F) – adhesives, water’s high b.p.
- Properties: ionic – high m.p., conduct when molten/aqueous; covalent – low m.p., non-conductors (acids ionise in water); giant covalent (diamond, SiO₂) – very high m.p.
- Graphite: layers → lubricant, pencils; delocalised electrons → electrodes. Diamond: 3-D, 109.5° → cutting tools.
- Metallic bond: cations + sea of electrons → conduct heat and electricity, malleable, ductile, high m.p.

ایٹم اوکٹیٹ یا ڈوپلیٹ حاصل کرنے کے لیے بندھن بناتے ہیں۔ آئنی بندھن: الیکٹران کی منتقلی (NaCl)۔ شریکی بندھن: الیکٹران کی شراکت (H₂O، CH₄)۔ کوآرڈینیٹ بندھن: دونوں الیکٹران ایک ایٹم سے (NH₄^+)۔ دھاتی بندھن: مثبت آئن اور آزاد الیکٹرانوں کا سمندر۔ آئنی مرکبات کا نقطہ پگھلاؤ زیادہ اور شریکی کا کم ہوتا ہے۔

Exam Focus: Exam focus (12 summative SLOs): dot-and-cross diagrams (NaF, CaCl₂, MgO, H₂O, CO₂, CH₄, NH₃, N₂, HCN, C₂H₄), ionic vs covalent properties, conductivity of ionic compounds (solid vs molten), metallic bonding, uses of graphite/diamond. A long dot-and-cross question appears in almost every paper.
chapters.definitions:
• Octet rule (اوکٹیٹ اصول) [p. 75]: Atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons to have eight electrons in their valence shell.
• Duplet rule (ڈوپلیٹ اصول) [p. 75]: Atoms close to helium tend to attain two electrons in their outermost shell.
• Chemical bond (کیمیائی بندھن) [p. 75]: The force of attraction that holds atoms together in a substance.
• Electropositivity (برقی مثبتیت) [p. 75]: The tendency of (metal) atoms to lose electrons and form positive ions.
• Ionic bond (آئنی بندھن) [p. 78]: The strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by transfer of electrons.
• Ionic compound (آئنی مرکب) [p. 78]: A compound made of ions held together by electrostatic forces.
• Covalent bond (شریکی بندھن) [p. 80]: A bond formed by mutual sharing of a pair of electrons between two atoms; the attraction between the shared pair and both nuclei.
• Single, double, triple covalent bond (سنگل، ڈبل، ٹرپل بندھن) [p. 81]: Covalent bonds formed by sharing one, two and three electron pairs respectively.
• Lone pair (لون پیئر) [p. 81]: A pair of valence electrons not shared with another atom.
• Non-polar covalent bond (غیر قطبی بندھن) [p. 84]: A covalent bond in which electrons are shared equally, e.g. between identical atoms.
• Polar covalent bond (قطبی بندھن) [p. 84]: A covalent bond in which the shared pair is pulled towards the more electronegative atom, giving partial charges.
• Coordinate covalent (dative) bond (کوآرڈینیٹ بندھن) [p. 84]: A covalent bond in which both shared electrons are donated by one atom.
• Intermolecular forces (بین سالماتی قوتیں) [p. 85]: Attractive forces between molecules.
• Dipole–dipole forces (ڈائی پول ڈائی پول قوتیں) [p. 85]: Attractions between the oppositely charged ends of polar molecules.
• Hydrogen bonding (ہائیڈروجن بندھن) [p. 86]: Attraction between a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on a nearby N, O or F atom.
• Metallic bond (دھاتی بندھن) [p. 90]: The strong electrostatic attraction between positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
• Delocalised electrons (آزاد الیکٹران) [p. 90]: Electrons not attached to any one atom and free to move through a structure.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Chemical bond (کیمیائی بندھن): Force holding atoms together
• Ionic bond (آئنی بندھن): Attraction between ions
• Covalent bond (شریکی بندھن): Shared electron pair
• Lone pair (غیر شریک جوڑا): Unshared electron pair
• Polar (قطبی): Having partial charges
• Coordinate bond (ہم آہنگ بندھن): Both electrons from one atom
• Donor (دینے والا): Atom giving the lone pair
• Acceptor (لینے والا): Atom receiving the pair
• Intermolecular (بین سالماتی): Between molecules
• Hydrogen bond (ہائیڈروجن بندھن): H attracted to N/O/F lone pair
• Lattice (جالی): Regular 3-D arrangement
• Delocalised (آزاد / غیر مقامی): Free to move
• Malleable (چادر پذیر): Can be hammered into sheets
• Brittle (بھربھرا): Breaks easily
• Conductor (موصل): Allows current/heat to flow
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Electrons lost by metal (Groups 1–3): = group number (Na 1, Mg 2, Al 3)
• Electrons gained by non-metal: = 8 − group number (O: 8 − 6 = 2; Cl: 8 − 7 = 1)
• Sodium chloride: NaCl (1 : 1)
• Magnesium fluoride: MgF₂ (Mg²⁺ + 2F⁻)
• Calcium chloride: CaCl₂ (Ca²⁺ + 2Cl⁻)
• Aluminium chloride: AlCl₃ (Al³⁺ + 3Cl⁻)
• Sodium sulphide: Na₂S (2Na⁺ + S²⁻)
• Ammonium ion: NH₄^+ (Contains a coordinate bond)
• Hydronium ion: H₃O⁺ (Contains a coordinate bond)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) -> 2NaCl(s) — Ionic bond formation by electron transfer.
• Mg(s) + F₂(g) -> MgF₂(s) — Each Mg gives 2 electrons, one to each F.
• 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) -> 2MgO(s) — Mg²⁺O²⁻.
• 2Al(s) + 3Cl₂(g) -> 2AlCl₃(s)
• NH₃ + HCl -> NH₄^+ + Cl⁻ — Coordinate bond: N lone pair to H⁺.
• H₂O + HCl -> H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ — Coordinate bond: O lone pair to H⁺.
• NH₃ + BF₃ -> H₃N→BF₃ — Coordinate bond to electron-deficient boron.
• HCl(g) --water--> H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) — Covalent acid ionises in water, so the solution conducts.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why do noble gases not form bonds under normal conditions?
   Answer: They already have a stable octet (or duplet), so they have no tendency to lose, gain or share electrons.
2. Diamond and graphite are both carbon. Why is one an insulator and the other a conductor?
   Answer: In diamond all four valence electrons are in bonds; in graphite one electron per carbon is delocalised and can move.
3. Why are ionic compounds brittle while metals are malleable?
   Answer: When layers of an ionic crystal shift, ions of the same charge come next to each other and repel, cracking the crystal. In metals the electron sea keeps holding the shifted layers.
4. Methane (CH₄) has strong C–H bonds but boils at −162 °C. Explain.
   Answer: Boiling only overcomes the weak intermolecular forces between CH₄ molecules, not the strong covalent bonds inside them.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Why are electrical wires made of copper but coated with plastic?
   Answer: Copper (metallic bonding, free electrons) conducts; plastic (covalent, no free charges) insulates for safety.
2. Why is graphite used as an electrode in electrolysis instead of diamond?
   Answer: Graphite conducts electricity (delocalised electrons) and is inert; diamond does not conduct.
3. Epoxy glue is used to join aircraft parts. Which forces make it stick?
   Answer: Hydrogen bonding and dipole–dipole attractions between the polar O–H groups of the resin and the surfaces.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Use dot-and-cross structures to write the formation of an ionic compound from (a) Na and Cl (b) Mg and F. (Example 5.3)
   Solution: (a) Na (2,8,1) loses its 1 electron → Na⁺; Cl (2,8,7) gains it → Cl⁻. Ratio 1:1. 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
(b) Mg (2,8,2) loses 2 electrons → Mg²⁺; each F (2,7) gains 1 → F⁻. Two F⁻ needed per Mg²⁺. Mg + F₂ → MgF₂.

2. Concept Assessment 5.3: write the formation of ionic compounds from (a) Mg and O (b) Al and Cl.
   Solution: (a) Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻; O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻; MgO (1:1). 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
(b) Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻; each Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻; three Cl⁻ per Al³⁺: AlCl₃. 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃.

3. Draw dot-and-cross structures for CO₂ and HCN. (Example 5.6)
   Solution: CO₂: C (4 valence) is central. Each O (6) needs 2. C shares 2 of its electrons with each O and each O shares 2 with C → two double bonds, O=C=O; each O keeps 2 lone pairs; C has no lone pair. Every atom has 8.
HCN: H (1), C (4), N (5). C shares 1 electron with H (single bond) and 3 with N (triple bond): H–C≡N; N keeps one lone pair. C and N have octets, H has 2.

4. Concept Assessment 5.4/5.5: draw dot-and-cross for NH₃, HCl, CH₃OH, CS₂, N₂ and C₂H₆.
   Solution: - NH₃: N shares one electron with each of 3 H; 1 lone pair on N.
- HCl: H and Cl share one pair; Cl has 3 lone pairs.
- CH₃OH: C bonded to 3 H and to O by single bonds; O bonded to H; O has 2 lone pairs.
- CS₂: like CO₂: S=C=S, 2 lone pairs on each S.
- N₂: N≡N, one lone pair on each N.
- C₂H₆: C–C single bond; each C bonded to 3 H; all single bonds.
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 5 Exercises (92–95):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. Which of the following atoms will form an ion of charge −2? (a) Z 12, A 24 (b) Z 14, A 28 (c) Z 8, A 8 (d) Z 10, A 20 → C (Z = 8) | Z = 8 is oxygen (2,6); it gains 2 electrons to form O²⁻.
ii. Which of the following atoms will not form a cation or anion? → C (Atomic No. 18) | Z = 18 is argon, a noble gas with a full octet.
iii. Which of the following atoms will form a cation? → A (Atomic number 20) | Z = 20 is calcium (2,8,8,2), a metal that loses 2 electrons.
iv. Which of the following atoms obey duplet rule? → 
v. Silicon belongs to Group IVA. It has ___ electrons in the valence shell. → C (4) | Group IVA: 4 valence electrons (2,8,4).
vi. Phosphorus belongs to the third period of Group VA. How many electrons does it need to complete its valence shell? → B (3) | 5 valence electrons; 8 − 5 = 3.
vii. In the formation of AlF₃, the aluminium atom loses ___ electrons. → C (3) | Al (2,8,3) → Al³⁺.
viii. Which of the following is not true about the formation of Na₂S? → D (Each sulphur atom gains one electron) | Sulphur gains two electrons to form S²⁻.
ix. Identify the covalent compound: → C (H₂O) | H₂O is formed by sharing electrons between non-metals.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) State octet and duplet rules.
   Answer: Octet rule: atoms gain, lose or share electrons to get eight electrons in their valence shell (noble-gas configuration). Duplet rule: atoms close to helium (H, Li, Be) tend to get two electrons in their outermost shell, like He.
(ii) Explain the formation of a covalent bond between two nitrogen atoms.
   Answer: Each N (2,5) has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more. The two atoms share three pairs of electrons (each contributes 3), forming a triple bond N≡N. Each N then has an octet (6 shared + 1 lone pair).
(iii) How does Al form a cation?
   Answer: Al (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p¹; 2,8,3) loses its 3 valence electrons: Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻. Al³⁺ has the neon configuration (2,8).
(iv) How does O form an anion?
   Answer: O (2,6) gains 2 electrons: O + 2e⁻ → O²⁻, which has the neon configuration (2,8).
(v) Draw electron cross and dot structure for the H₂O molecule.
   Answer: O in the centre with 6 dots; each H contributes one cross. Two shared pairs (•×) form two O–H single bonds; the remaining four dots on O form two lone pairs. O has 8 electrons, each H has 2. (See the diagram in Tables & Diagrams.)

— Q3–Q14. Descriptive questions —
3. Describe the importance of noble gas electronic configuration.
   Answer: Noble gases have full valence shells (ns² np⁶; He 1s²), so they are stable and unreactive. Other atoms react to achieve the same configuration:
- metals lose electrons → cations with noble-gas configuration (Na⁺ like Ne);
- non-metals gain electrons → anions (Cl⁻ like Ar);
- non-metals share electrons → covalent molecules where each atom has an octet.
So the noble-gas configuration explains why atoms bond, which ions they form, the formulas of compounds and the number of bonds an atom makes (octet and duplet rules).
4. Explain how elements attain stability.
   Answer: Elements attain stability by reaching a noble-gas (octet or duplet) configuration through (1) losing electrons – metals form cations (ionic bonding), (2) gaining electrons – non-metals form anions (ionic bonding), (3) sharing electrons – non-metals form covalent bonds (single, double, triple), including coordinate bonds where one atom donates both electrons, and (4) in metals, by releasing electrons into a delocalised sea (metallic bonding).
5. Describe the ways in which bonds may be formed.
   Answer: 1. Ionic bond – complete transfer of electrons from metal to non-metal; attraction between ions (NaCl).
2. Covalent bond – mutual sharing of electron pairs between non-metals: single (H₂), double (O₂), triple (N₂); polar (HCl) or non-polar (Cl₂).
3. Coordinate covalent bond – both shared electrons from one atom (NH₄^+, H₃O⁺).
4. Metallic bond – attraction between cations and a sea of delocalised electrons (Cu, Fe).
6. Describe the formation of a covalent bond between two non-metallic elements.
   Answer: Two non-metal atoms each need electrons, so neither gives up electrons; instead each contributes electron(s) to a shared pair located between the nuclei. Both nuclei attract the shared pair, holding the atoms together. Example: H (1 e) + Cl (7 e) → H–Cl; the shared pair gives H a duplet and Cl an octet. Because Cl is more electronegative the bond is polar (Hδ⁺–Clδ⁻).
7. Explain with examples single, double and triple covalent bonds.
   Answer: - Single (one shared pair, –): H₂ (H–H), Cl₂, HCl, CH₄, H₂O.
- Double (two shared pairs, =): O₂ (O=O), CO₂ (O=C=O), C₂H₄ (H₂C=CH₂).
- Triple (three shared pairs, ≡): N₂ (N≡N), HCN (H–C≡N), C₂H₂ (HC≡CH).
More shared pairs make the bond shorter and stronger.
8. Find the number of valence electrons in (a) boron (b) neon (c) rubidium (d) barium (e) arsenic using the periodic table.
   Answer: (a) B, Group IIIA: 3 (b) Ne, Group VIIIA: 8 (c) Rb, Group IA: 1 (d) Ba, Group IIA: 2 (e) As, Group VA: 5.
9. Represent the formation of cations of (a) Al (b) Sr (c) Ba using electron dot structures.
   Answer: (a) Al with 3 dots → [Al]³⁺ + 3e⁻ (b) Sr with 2 dots → [Sr]²⁺ + 2e⁻ (c) Ba with 2 dots → [Ba]²⁺ + 2e⁻. The cations are written without dots because the outer shell has been emptied.
10. A sample of sulphur from a volcano has isotopes S-32 (95.0%), S-33 (0.76%), S-34 (4.22%). (a) Define isotope (b) define relative atomic mass (c) calculate Aᵣ of sulphur (d) complete p/n/e for S-32 and S-34 (e) place S in the periodic table (f) how many electrons does S lose or gain? (g) how many atoms in 0.3 mole of sulphur?
   Answer: (a) Atoms of the same element with the same Z but different mass numbers.
(b) Average mass of an element’s atoms compared with 1/12 of a C-12 atom.
(c) Aᵣ = (32 × 95.0 + 33 × 0.76 + 34 × 4.22) ÷ 100 = (3040 + 25.08 + 143.48) ÷ 100 = 32.09.
(d) S-32: 16 p, 16 n, 16 e. S-34: 16 p, 18 n, 16 e.
(e) 2,8,6 → Group VIA (16), Period 3.
(f) Gains 2 electrons → S²⁻ (2,8,8).
(g) atoms = 0.3 × 6.02 × 10²³ = 1.81 × 10²³ atoms.
11. An atom has atomic number 9 and mass number 19. (a) protons and neutrons (b) electrons (c) show ion formation by dot-and-cross (d) electronic configuration (e) group (f) period.
   Answer: It is fluorine.
(a) 9 protons, 19 − 9 = 10 neutrons. (b) 9 electrons.
(c) F with 7 crosses gains one electron (dot) → [F]⁻ with 8 electrons.
(d) 1s² 2s² 2p⁵ (2,7). (e) Group VIIA (17). (f) Period 2.
12. Magnesium oxide is made of magnesium ions and oxide ions. (a) What is the charge on these ions? (b) How do these ions get these charges? (c) Show the formation of these ions with dot-and-cross diagrams.
   Answer: (a) Mg²⁺ and O²⁻.
(b) Mg (2,8,2) loses its 2 valence electrons; O (2,6) gains those 2 electrons; both reach the neon configuration.
(c) Mg with 2 dots, O with 6 crosses → [Mg]²⁺ [O with 6 × + 2 •]²⁻.
13. Diagrams show the electronic structures of an atom of calcium and an atom of oxygen. Draw the structures of the ions formed when these atoms react.
   Answer: Ca (2,8,8,2) loses 2 electrons → [Ca]²⁺ with shells 2,8,8. O (2,6) gains 2 → [O]²⁻ with shells 2,8 (draw 6 crosses + 2 dots in the outer shell). Compound: CaO.
14. Four substances A–D: A high m.p., no conduction solid or molten; B high m.p., conducts only when molten; C low m.p., no conduction; D high m.p., conducts solid and molten. Which is (a) a metal (b) an ionic compound (c) a covalent compound (d) a non-metal?
   Answer: (a) D – metal (free electrons conduct in both states). (b) B – ionic (ions mobile only when molten). (c) C – simple covalent (low m.p., no ions). (d) A – non-metal with a giant covalent structure, e.g. diamond (high m.p., no free charges).
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] How is an ionic bond formed? Give one example of a compound having an ionic bond.
   Answer: An ionic bond forms when a metal transfers its valence electron(s) to a non-metal; the resulting cation and anion are held by strong electrostatic attraction. Example: NaCl (Na → Na⁺ + e⁻; Cl + e⁻ → Cl⁻).

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] Show the formation of NaF and NaBr using electron dot-and-cross structures and identify the positive and negative ions.
   Answer: Na (1 dot) transfers its electron to F (7 crosses) → [Na]⁺ [F]⁻. Similarly Na → Na⁺ and Br + e⁻ → Br⁻ giving [Na]⁺[Br]⁻. Positive ion: Na⁺. Negative ions: F⁻ and Br⁻.

3. What type of bond is formed when two atoms share one or more pairs of electrons?
   Answer: A covalent bond.

4. Why does solid NaCl not conduct electricity while molten NaCl does?
   Answer: In solid NaCl the ions are fixed in the lattice; in molten NaCl the ions are free to move and carry charge.

5. Why do aqueous solutions of acids such as HCl conduct electricity although HCl is covalent?
   Answer: HCl ionises in water: HCl → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). The mobile ions carry current.

6. Give two uses each of graphite and diamond and relate them to structure.
   Answer: Graphite: lubricant (layers slide), electrodes (delocalised electrons). Diamond: cutting tools and drill bits (rigid 3-D network, hardest), jewellery (sparkle).

7. Differentiate between polar and non-polar covalent bonds.
   Answer: Non-polar: electrons shared equally between identical atoms (H–H, Cl–Cl). Polar: shared pair pulled towards the more electronegative atom, giving δ+ and δ− ends (H–Cl, O–H).

8. How is a coordinate covalent bond different from an ordinary covalent bond? Give an example.
   Answer: In a coordinate bond both shared electrons come from one atom (donor); in an ordinary covalent bond each atom gives one. Example: NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄^+ (N donates its lone pair).

9. What is hydrogen bonding? Why does water have a high boiling point?
   Answer: Attraction between H (bonded to N, O or F) and a lone pair on a nearby N, O or F. Water molecules are held together by many hydrogen bonds, so more energy is needed to separate them.

10. Explain why metals are malleable and ductile.
   Answer: Layers of metal cations can slide over each other while the sea of delocalised electrons keeps holding them, so the metal changes shape without breaking.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Show covalent bond formation using dot-and-cross structures in (a) CO₂ (b) H₂O (c) CH₄.
   Answer: (a) CO₂: C (4 dots) central; each O (6 crosses) shares two pairs with C → two double bonds O=C=O; 2 lone pairs on each O.
(b) H₂O: O (6 dots) shares one pair with each H (1 cross) → two single bonds; 2 lone pairs on O.
(c) CH₄: C (4 dots) shares one pair with each of 4 H (crosses) → four single bonds; no lone pairs. Every atom except H has an octet; H has a duplet.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Show the ionic bond formation of (a) NaF (b) CaCl₂ using electron dot-and-cross structures.
   Answer: (a) NaF: Na (2,8,1; 1 dot) → [Na]⁺ ; F (2,7; 7 crosses) + • → [F]⁻ with 8 electrons. Formula NaF (1:1).
(b) CaCl₂: Ca (2,8,8,2; 2 dots) loses both → [Ca]²⁺; each of two Cl (2,8,7; 7 crosses) gains one dot → 2[Cl]⁻. Formula CaCl₂. Equation: Ca + Cl₂ → CaCl₂.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Describe the metallic bond in terms of electrostatic attraction. Write any two properties of metals which make them different from non-metals.
   Answer: Metallic bond: metal atoms release their valence electrons, forming positive ions arranged in layers and a “sea” of delocalised electrons. The strong electrostatic attraction between the cations and the delocalised electrons is the metallic bond.
Properties: (1) good conductors of electricity and heat (free electrons); (2) malleable and ductile (layers slide). Also high melting points and lustre. Non-metals lack free electrons, so they are poor conductors and brittle.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Draw dot-and-cross structures to show the formation of (i) sodium fluoride (NaF) (ii) water (H₂O). Also identify the type of bonding.
   Answer: (i) NaF – ionic bond: Na transfers 1 electron to F → [Na]⁺[F]⁻. (ii) H₂O – covalent (polar) bonds: O shares one pair with each H; 2 lone pairs on O.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Draw electron dot-and-cross structures for (a) NH₃ (b) N₂ (c) CH₄.
   Answer: (a) NH₃: N shares one pair with each of 3 H; 1 lone pair on N. (b) N₂: three shared pairs (N≡N); 1 lone pair on each N. (c) CH₄: four C–H single bonds; no lone pairs.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Draw electron dot-and-cross structures for (a) HCN (b) Cl₂ (c) CO₂.
   Answer: (a) HCN: H–C single bond, C≡N triple bond, lone pair on N. (b) Cl₂: one shared pair, 3 lone pairs on each Cl. (c) CO₂: O=C=O, two double bonds, 2 lone pairs on each O.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Draw the dot-and-cross diagrams and Lewis dot structures of HCN, MgO and C₂H₄.
   Answer: HCN: H–C≡N (Lewis: H–C≡N: with lone pair on N). MgO: [Mg]²⁺[O]²⁻ (ionic; O with 8 electrons). C₂H₄: H₂C=CH₂ – two C atoms share two pairs; each C shares one pair with each of two H.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] An unknown solid is hard and crystalline with a very high melting point; it does not conduct electricity when solid but conducts when melted. Explain the type of bonding, how it forms, and relate it to the melting point and conductivity.
   Answer: The substance is ionic (e.g. NaCl).
Formation: a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal; the cations and anions attract strongly and arrange in a giant lattice.
High melting point: many strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions must be broken.
Conductivity: in the solid the ions are fixed and cannot move, so no current; when melted the ions become mobile and carry charge.

9. Differentiate between ionic and covalent compounds. Explain their properties in terms of bonding and structure.
   Answer: See the comparison table in topic 5.7: ionic – ions, transfer, strong electrostatic forces, high m.p., conduct when molten/aqueous, soluble in water; covalent – molecules, sharing, weak intermolecular forces, low m.p., non-conductors (except acids in water), soluble in organic solvents.
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 5 in one page
- Octet/duplet rules: atoms lose, gain or share electrons to reach 8 (or 2 for H, Li, Be) valence electrons like noble gases.
- Metals electropositive → cations; non-metals electronegative → anions.
- Ionic bond: electron transfer; electrostatic attraction between ions (NaCl, MgO, CaCl₂, MgF₂, AlCl₃, Na₂S). Draw brackets and charges.
- Covalent bond: shared pair attracted by two nuclei. Single (H₂, HCl, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄), double (O₂, CO₂, C₂H₄), triple (N₂, HCN). Lone pairs: H₂O 2, NH₃ 1.
- Polar (unequal sharing, δ+/δ−) vs non-polar (equal). Coordinate bond: both electrons from one atom (NH₄^+, H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃).
- Intermolecular forces: dipole–dipole; hydrogen bonding (H on N/O/F) – adhesives, water’s high b.p.
- Properties: ionic – high m.p., conduct when molten/aqueous; covalent – low m.p., non-conductors (acids ionise in water); giant covalent (diamond, SiO₂) – very high m.p.
- Graphite: layers → lubricant, pencils; delocalised electrons → electrodes. Diamond: 3-D, 109.5° → cutting tools.
- Metallic bond: cations + sea of electrons → conduct heat and electricity, malleable, ductile, high m.p.

ایٹم اوکٹیٹ یا ڈوپلیٹ حاصل کرنے کے لیے بندھن بناتے ہیں۔ آئنی بندھن: الیکٹران کی منتقلی (NaCl)۔ شریکی بندھن: الیکٹران کی شراکت (H₂O، CH₄)۔ کوآرڈینیٹ بندھن: دونوں الیکٹران ایک ایٹم سے (NH₄^+)۔ دھاتی بندھن: مثبت آئن اور آزاد الیکٹرانوں کا سمندر۔ آئنی مرکبات کا نقطہ پگھلاؤ زیادہ اور شریکی کا کم ہوتا ہے۔

chapters.title: Stoichiometry
chapters.introduction:
Stoichiometry is the arithmetic of chemistry. In this unit you learn the formulae of common substances, empirical and molecular formulae, how to name and write formulae of binary ionic compounds, how to calculate molecular and formula masses, and the mole and Avogadro’s number. You will do mole–mass and mole–particle calculations, write and balance chemical equations with state symbols, and write ionic equations.

Exam focus (10 summative SLOs, many Application-level): mole calculations (moles ↔ mass ↔ particles), formulae from ions, empirical vs molecular formula, balancing equations and ionic equations. Every recent paper has at least one numerical from this chapter.

══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
Exam focus (10 summative SLOs, many Application-level): mole calculations (moles ↔ mass ↔ particles), formulae from ions, empirical vs molecular formula, balancing equations and ionic equations. Every recent paper has at least one numerical from this chapter.

══ 6.1 Chemical formulae: empirical and molecular (pp. 97–98) ══
A chemical formula shows which elements a substance contains and the whole-number ratio of their atoms.
- Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element. Hydrogen peroxide H₂O₂ → HO; glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ → CH₂O; benzene C₆H₆ → CH.
- Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule: H₂O₂, C₆H₁₂O₆, C₆H₆.
- Molecular formula = n × empirical formula (n = 1, 2, 3 …). For many compounds n = 1, so both are the same: H₂O, CO₂, NH₃, CH₄, SO₂.
Formulae of common substances: H₂, O₂, N₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂ (diatomic elements); water H₂O, carbon dioxide CO₂, hydrochloric acid HCl, sodium hydroxide NaOH, copper(II) sulphate CuSO₄, glucose C₆H₁₂O₆, ammonia NH₃, methane CH₄, sulphuric acid H₂SO₄.
Writing a molecular formula from a structural formula: identify the elements, count the atoms of each in the structure, and write them as subscripts. n-butane CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃ → C₄H₁₀.
[Table: Empirical vs molecular formula]
Compound | Molecular formula | Empirical formula
• Hydrogen peroxide | H₂O₂ | HO
• Glucose | C₆H₁₂O₆ | CH₂O
• Benzene | C₆H₆ | CH
• Ethane | C₂H₆ | CH₃
• Acetic acid | C₂H₄O₂ | CH₂O
• Aspirin | C₉H₈O₄ | C₉H₈O₄
• Caffeine | C₈H₁₀N₄O₂ | C₄H₅N₂O
• Phosphorus(V) oxide | P₄O₁₀ | P₂O₅
• Water | H₂O | H₂O
Exam Tip: To find an empirical formula from a molecular formula, divide all subscripts by their highest common factor. If they have no common factor the two formulae are the same.
ایمپیریکل فارمولا ایٹموں کا سادہ ترین مکمل عددی تناسب بتاتا ہے، جیسے گلوکوز کا CH₂O۔ مالیکیولر فارمولا ایک سالمے میں ہر عنصر کے اصل ایٹم بتاتا ہے، جیسے C₆H₁₂O₆۔ پانی اور CO₂ میں دونوں ایک ہی ہیں۔

══ 6.2 Molecular mass and formula mass (pp. 98–100) ══
- Molecular mass: the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in one molecule (for molecular/covalent substances). H₂O = 2(1.008) + 16 = 18.016 amu; glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ = 6(12) + 12(1.008) + 6(16) = 180.1 amu; naphthalene C₁₀H₈ = 128 amu.
- Formula unit: the simplest ratio of ions in an ionic compound (NaCl, MgCl₂), because ionic compounds have no separate molecules.
- Formula mass: the sum of atomic masses of all atoms in one formula unit. NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 amu; Mg(OH)₂ = 24 + 2(16) + 2(1) = 58 amu.
Useful atomic masses (amu): H 1, C 12, N 14, O 16, Na 23, Mg 24, Al 27, S 32, Cl 35.5, K 39, Ca 40, Fe 56, Cu 63.5, Zn 65, Br 80, I 127, Ba 137.
[Table: Worked masses]
Substance | Calculation | Mass (amu)
• KClO₃ | 39 + 35.5 + 3(16) | 122.5
• NaHCO₃ | 23 + 1 + 12 + 3(16) | 84
• CO₂ | 12 + 2(16) | 44
• Urea (NH₂)₂CO | 2(14) + 4(1) + 12 + 16 | 60
• NH₄NO₃ | 2(14) + 4(1) + 3(16) | 80
• CuSO₄·5H₂O | 63.5 + 32 + 64 + 5(18) | 249.5
• BaSO₄ | 137 + 32 + 64 | 233
• H₂SO₄ | 2 + 32 + 64 | 98
مالیکیولر ماس کسی سالمے کے تمام ایٹموں کی ایٹمی کمیتوں کا مجموعہ ہے (H₂O = 18)۔ آئنی مرکبات میں سالمے نہیں ہوتے، اس لیے ہم فارمولا یونٹ اور فارمولا ماس استعمال کرتے ہیں (NaCl = 58.5)۔

══ 6.3 Names and formulae of binary ionic compounds (pp. 100–101) ══
A binary ionic compound contains a mono-atomic metal cation and a mono-atomic non-metal anion.
Naming: cation first (same name as the metal), then the anion with the ending -ide: sodium chloride, magnesium oxide, aluminium nitride, calcium fluoride. Metals with more than one charge use Roman numerals: iron(II) chloride FeCl₂, iron(III) chloride FeCl₃, copper(II) oxide CuO.
Writing the formula (criss-cross / balancing charges):
1. Write the cation and anion with their charges: Al³⁺ O²⁻.
2. Find the smallest numbers that make total positive = total negative: 2 × (+3) = 3 × (−2) = 6.
3. Write these numbers as subscripts: Al₂O₃.
4. Leave out charges and the subscript 1.
Examples: Na⁺ + Cl⁻ → NaCl; Mg²⁺ + Cl⁻ → MgCl₂; Ca²⁺ + NO₃^- → Ca(NO₃)₂ (brackets around polyatomic ions); Al³⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → Al₂(SO₄)₃; NH₄^+ + Cl⁻ → NH₄Cl.
[Table: Common ions]
Cations | Charge | Anions | Charge
• Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Ag⁺ | +1 | F⁻, Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻ | −1
• NH₄^+ (ammonium) | +1 | OH⁻ (hydroxide), NO₃^- (nitrate), NO₂^- (nitrite), HCO₃^- | −1
• Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺, Zn²⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺ | +2 | O²⁻, S²⁻, SO₄²⁻, CO₃²⁻ | −2
• Al³⁺, Fe³⁺ | +3 | N³⁻, PO₄³⁻ (phosphate) | −3
آئنی مرکب کا نام لکھتے وقت پہلے دھات اور پھر غیر دھات کا نام “آئیڈ” کے ساتھ (سوڈیم کلورائیڈ)۔ فارمولا لکھنے کے لیے مثبت اور منفی چارج برابر کریں: Al³⁺ اور O²⁻ سے Al₂O₃۔

══ 6.4 The mole and Avogadro’s number (pp. 101–103) ══
Chemists count tiny particles in a large “bundle” called the mole (like a dozen = 12, a ream = 500).
- Mole: the amount of substance that contains 6.022 × 10²³ representative particles (atoms, molecules, ions or formula units). It is also the amount containing as many particles as there are atoms in exactly 12 g of carbon-12.
- Avogadro’s number (N_A) = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. One mole of anything contains N_A particles. 1 mol C = 6.022 × 10²³ atoms; 1 mol H₂O = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules; 1 mol NaCl = 6.022 × 10²³ formula units.
- Molar mass: the mass of one mole, in g mol⁻¹; numerically equal to the atomic, molecular or formula mass:
- Gram atomic mass – atomic mass in grams (1 mol of atoms): C 12 g, Na 23 g, Zn 63.54 g.
- Gram molecular mass – molecular mass in grams (1 mol of molecules): H₂O 18.016 g, glucose 180.1 g, N₂ 28 g.
- Gram formula mass – formula mass in grams (1 mol of formula units): NaCl 58.5 g, KCl 74.5 g.
One mole of different substances has the same number of particles but different masses (1 mol C = 12 g; 1 mol S = 32 g), just as a dozen eggs and a dozen bananas weigh differently.
Note: 1 mol of H₂ molecules (2.016 g) contains 2 mol of H atoms; 1 mol of H atoms has mass 1.008 g.
Exam Tip: Avogadro’s number is so large that counting one mole of coins would take the whole world’s population about a million years.
مول کسی مادے کی وہ مقدار ہے جس میں 6.022 × 10²³ ذرات ہوں؛ اس عدد کو ایووگیڈرو نمبر کہتے ہیں۔ ایک مول کی کمیت (گرام میں) مولر ماس کہلاتی ہے، جیسے کاربن 12 گرام، پانی 18 گرام۔ ہر مادے کے ایک مول میں ذرات برابر مگر کمیت مختلف ہوتی ہے۔

══ 6.5 Mole calculations: mass ↔ moles ↔ particles (pp. 104–108) ══
Two key relationships:
- moles (n) = mass (m) ÷ molar mass (M), so m = n × M.
- number of particles (N) = moles × N_A, so n = N ÷ N_A.
Combine them: mass → moles → particles, or particles → moles → mass.
Mole–mass examples:
- Mass of 9.05 mol O₃: M = 48 g mol⁻¹; m = 9.05 × 48 = 434.4 g.
- Mass of 0.25 mol CO₂: 0.25 × 44 = 11 g.
- Moles in 5 g H₂: 5 ÷ 2.016 = 2.48 mol. Moles in 100 g H₂O: 100 ÷ 18.016 = 5.55 mol.
Mole–particle examples:
- Atoms in 1.25 mol Zn: 1.25 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 7.53 × 10²³.
- Atoms in 0.2 mol Al: 1.20 × 10²³.
- Molecules in 0.5 mol CH₄: 3.011 × 10²³; in 0.25 mol SO₂: 1.506 × 10²³.
- Moles in 3.011 × 10²³ Ti atoms: 0.5 mol; in 3.011 × 10²² CH₂O molecules: 0.05 mol.
Atoms vs molecules: in 2 mol of O₂ there are 2 × N_A = 1.204 × 10²⁴ molecules but 4 × N_A = 2.409 × 10²⁴ atoms (each molecule has 2 atoms). Always check which particle the question asks for.
Exam Tip: Use the Given → Required → Formula → Substitution → Calculation → Answer (with unit) layout for every numerical; examiners award marks for each step.
مول = کمیت ÷ مولر ماس، اور ذرات = مول × 6.022 × 10²³۔ مثال: 0.25 مول CO₂ کی کمیت = 0.25 × 44 = 11 گرام۔ دھیان رکھیں کہ سوال ایٹموں کا پوچھ رہا ہے یا سالموں کا۔

══ 6.6 Chemical equations, balancing and state symbols (pp. 108–109) ══
A chemical equation is the symbolic representation of a chemical reaction: reactants → products.
Writing an equation:
1. Write a word equation: coal + oxygen → carbon dioxide.
2. Write formulae and state symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) aqueous solution. C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g).
3. Balance it: atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so each element must have the same number of atoms on both sides. Change only the coefficients (numbers in front), never the subscripts.
Balancing CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O:
- C: 1 = 1 ✓. H: 4 on left, 2 on right → put 2 before H₂O.
- O: now 2 + 2 = 4 on right → put 2 before O₂.
- CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) ✓
More examples:
- 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)
- 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)
- 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)
- 2NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3H₂(g)
- 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 4H₂O + 2NO
کیمیائی مساوات کسی تعامل کو علامتوں سے ظاہر کرتی ہے۔ حالت کی علامات: (s) ٹھوس، (l) مائع، (g) گیس، (aq) آبی محلول۔ مساوات متوازن کرنے کے لیے صرف آگے کے عددی ضریب بدلیں، چھوٹے نمبر (سب اسکرپٹ) نہیں۔

══ 6.7 Ionic equations and spectator ions (pp. 109–110) ══
An ionic equation shows substances that are dissolved in water (and are ionic) as separate ions.
Steps:
1. Write the balanced equation with state symbols.
2. Split all aqueous ionic substances (strong acids, soluble salts, alkalis) into ions. Keep solids, liquids, gases and covalent molecules (H₂O, H₂) as formulae.
3. Cancel ions that appear unchanged on both sides – the spectator ions.
4. What remains is the net ionic equation.
Example 1: Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) + H₂(g)
Spectator: SO₄²⁻. Net: Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g)
Example 2: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s) + NaNO₃(aq)
Spectators: Na⁺, NO₃^-. Net: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) (white precipitate).
Example 3: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Net: Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g).
Example 4 (neutralisation): HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l). Net: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).
Example 5: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Net: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s).
آئنی مساوات میں پانی میں گھلے آئنی مادے الگ الگ آئنوں کی صورت میں لکھے جاتے ہیں۔ جو آئن دونوں طرف بغیر تبدیلی کے موجود ہوں (تماشائی آئن) انہیں ہٹا کر خالص آئنی مساوات حاصل ہوتی ہے، جیسے Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. The mole “bridge”: Divide to go towards moles, multiply to go away from moles.

- Empirical formula = simplest ratio (CH₂O); molecular formula = actual atoms (C₆H₁₂O₆) = n × empirical.
- Molecular mass (molecules) and formula mass (ionic formula units) = sum of atomic masses.

ایمپیریکل فارمولا سادہ ترین تناسب، مالیکیولر فارمولا اصل تعداد۔ مول = 6.022 × 10²³ ذرات۔ مول = کمیت ÷ مولر ماس، ذرات = مول × N_A۔ مساوات صرف ضریب بدل کر متوازن کریں۔ آئنی مساوات میں تماشائی آئن ہٹا دیں۔

chapters.definitions:
• Empirical formula (ایمپیریکل فارمولا) [p. 97]: The chemical formula giving the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
• Molecular formula (مالیکیولر فارمولا) [p. 97]: The formula showing the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.
• Structural formula (ساختی فارمولا) [p. 110]: A formula showing how the atoms in a molecule are arranged and bonded.
• Molecular mass (مالیکیولر ماس) [p. 98]: The sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in one molecule.
• Formula unit (فارمولا یونٹ) [p. 99]: The simplest ratio of cations to anions in an ionic compound.
• Formula mass (فارمولا ماس) [p. 99]: The sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in one formula unit of a substance.
• Binary ionic compound (دوہرا آئنی مرکب) [p. 100]: An ionic compound of a mono-atomic metal cation and a mono-atomic non-metal anion.
• Mole (مول) [p. 101]: The amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ representative particles; equal to the atomic, molecular or formula mass expressed in grams.
• Avogadro’s number (ایووگیڈرو نمبر) [p. 101]: The number of particles in one mole of a substance, 6.022 × 10²³.
• Molar mass (مولر ماس) [p. 101]: The mass of one mole of a substance, in g mol⁻¹.
• Gram atomic mass (گرام ایٹمی ماس) [p. 102]: The atomic mass of an element expressed in grams; it contains one mole of atoms.
• Gram molecular mass (گرام مالیکیولر ماس) [p. 103]: The molecular mass of a substance expressed in grams; it contains one mole of molecules.
• Gram formula mass (گرام فارمولا ماس) [p. 103]: The formula mass of an ionic compound expressed in grams; it contains one mole of formula units.
• Chemical equation (کیمیائی مساوات) [p. 108]: The symbolic representation of a chemical reaction using formulae of reactants and products.
• Balanced equation (متوازن مساوات) [p. 109]: A chemical equation with equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides.
• Ionic equation (آئنی مساوات) [p. 109]: A chemical equation in which dissolved ionic substances are written as separate ions.
• Spectator ions (تماشائی آئن) [p. 109]: Ions present in the reaction mixture that do not take part in the reaction and appear unchanged on both sides.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Stoichiometry (مقداری کیمیا): Calculations with reacting amounts
• Empirical formula (تجرباتی فارمولا): Simplest ratio
• Molecular formula (سالماتی فارمولا): Actual number of atoms
• Mole (مول): 6.022 × 10²³ particles
• Molar mass (مولر کمیت): Mass of one mole
• Coefficient (ضریب): Number in front of a formula
• Subscript (زیریں عدد): Small number in a formula
• Reactant (متعامل): Starting substance
• Product (حاصل): Substance formed
• Precipitate (تلچھٹ / رسوب): Insoluble solid formed in solution
• Spectator ion (تماشائی آئن): Ion not taking part
• Aqueous (آبی): Dissolved in water
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Number of moles: n = m ÷ M (m in g; M in g mol⁻¹)
• Mass: m = n × M
• Molar mass: M = m ÷ n
• Number of particles: N = n × N_A (N_A = 6.022 × 10²³)
• Moles from particles: n = N ÷ N_A
• Mass from particles: m = (N ÷ N_A) × M
• Atoms in a molecular sample: atoms = molecules × atoms per molecule (O₂: × 2; H₂O: × 3)
• Molecular formula: = n × empirical formula (n = whole number)
• Avogadro’s constant: N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• C(s) + O₂(g) -> CO₂(g) — Burning of coal.
• CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) -> CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l) — Balanced combustion of methane.
• 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) -> 2H₂O(l) — Burning of hydrogen.
• 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) -> 2MgO(s) — Burning of magnesium.
• 2NH₃(g) -> N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) — Balanced decomposition (review Q15b).
• Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) -> Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g) — Net ionic equation (SO₄²⁻ spectator).
• Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) -> AgCl(s) — Net ionic equation for forming silver chloride.
• H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) -> H₂O(l) — Net ionic equation for neutralisation.
• Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) -> Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s) — Net ionic equation, zinc + copper(II) sulphate.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Do 1 mol of O₂ and 1 mol of CO₂ have the same mass? The same number of molecules?
   Answer: Different masses (32 g vs 44 g) but the same number of molecules (6.022 × 10²³).
2. Why do we use “formula mass” for NaCl but “molecular mass” for H₂O?
   Answer: NaCl is ionic: no discrete molecules, only formula units. H₂O exists as separate molecules.
3. Which has more atoms: 1 g of H₂ or 1 g of O₂?
   Answer: 1 g H₂ = 0.496 mol molecules = 0.992 mol atoms; 1 g O₂ = 0.031 mol molecules = 0.0625 mol atoms. Hydrogen has many more atoms.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. A spoon of table salt contains 12.5 g NaCl. How many moles is that?
   Answer: 12.5 ÷ 58.5 = 0.214 mol.
2. Before an X-ray of the digestive system a patient swallows BaSO₄. Find the mass of 1 mole.
   Answer: 137 + 32 + 64 = 233 g.
3. An aspirin tablet contains 1.25 × 10²¹ molecules (C₉H₈O₄). How many moles and what mass is that?
   Answer: n = 1.25 × 10²¹ ÷ 6.022 × 10²³ = 2.08 × 10⁻³ mol; M = 180 g mol⁻¹; mass = 0.374 g.

1. Determine the molecular mass of glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ and of naphthalene C₁₀H₈. (Example 6.1)
   Given: C = 12, H = 1.008, O = 16

   Given: n = 9.05 mol; M(O₃) = 3 × 16 = 48 g mol⁻¹
   Required: Mass m
   Formula: m = n × M
   Substitution: m = 9.05 × 48
   Calculation: = 434.4
   Final Answer: 434.4 g of ozone

3. How many moles are in (a) 5 g of hydrogen gas (b) 100 g of ice? (Example 6.6)
   Given: M(H₂) = 2.016; M(H₂O) = 18.016 g mol⁻¹
   Required: Moles
   Formula: n = m ÷ M
   Substitution: (a) 5 ÷ 2.016 (b) 100 ÷ 18.016
   Calculation: (a) 2.48 (b) 5.55
   Final Answer: (a) 2.48 mol H₂ (b) 5.55 mol H₂O

4. How many atoms are in 1.25 moles of zinc? (Example 6.7)
   Given: n = 1.25 mol
   Required: Number of atoms
   Formula: N = n × N_A
   Substitution: N = 1.25 × 6.022 × 10²³
   Calculation: = 7.53 × 10²³
   Final Answer: 7.53 × 10²³ Zn atoms

5. How many moles are in a sample containing 3.011 × 10²³ Ti atoms? (Example 6.9)
   Given: N = 3.011 × 10²³
   Required: n
   Formula: n = N ÷ N_A
   Substitution: = 3.011 × 10²³ ÷ 6.022 × 10²³
   Calculation: = 0.5
   Final Answer: 0.5 mol Ti

6. Write the formulae of (a) sodium chloride (b) aluminium oxide using charges.
   Solution: (a) Na⁺ and Cl⁻: charges already balance → NaCl. (b) Al³⁺ and O²⁻: LCM of 3 and 2 is 6 → 2 Al³⁺ (+6) and 3 O²⁻ (−6) → Al₂O₃.

7. Transform into ionic equations: (1) AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃ (2) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂. (Concept Assessment)
   Solution: (1) Ag⁺(aq) + NO₃^-(aq) + Na⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s) + Na⁺(aq) + NO₃^-(aq). Net: Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
(2) Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq) + H₂(g). Net: Zn(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + H₂(g).

1. How many molecules are in 4.4 g of CO₂?
   Given: m = 4.4 g; M = 44
   Required: N
   Formula: N = (m ÷ M) × N_A
   Substitution: = (4.4 ÷ 44) × 6.022 × 10²³
   Calculation: = 0.1 × 6.022 × 10²³
   Final Answer: 6.022 × 10²² molecules

2. Find the mass of 1.5 × 10²³ molecules of H₂O.
   Given: N = 1.5 × 10²³; M = 18
   Required: m
   Formula: m = (N ÷ N_A) × M
   Substitution: = (1.5 × 10²³ ÷ 6.022 × 10²³) × 18

   Final Answer: 4.48 g

3. How many oxygen atoms are in 0.5 mol of H₂SO₄?
   Given: n = 0.5 mol; 4 O per formula

chapters.title: Electrochemistry
chapters.introduction:
Rusting iron, burning fuel, a car battery and the bleach in your house all involve redox reactions – reactions in which oxidation and reduction happen together. This unit defines oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen, hydrogen, electrons and oxidation number, gives rules for finding oxidation states, shows how to identify oxidising and reducing agents (including colour tests with acidified KMnO₄ and KI), how Roman numerals name compounds, and explains corrosion and how to prevent it.

Exam focus (10 summative SLOs): identify oxidising/reducing agents using oxidation numbers (WO₃ + H₂, H₂S + Cl₂, Fe₂O₃ + CO, KI + Cl₂), oxidation number of an element in a compound or ion (H₃BO₃, NH₄^+, CO₃²⁻, K₂Cr₂O₇), corrosion prevention (galvanising, sacrificial protection, electroplating).
