══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
Exam focus (10 summative SLOs): identify oxidising/reducing agents using oxidation numbers (WO₃ + H₂, H₂S + Cl₂, Fe₂O₃ + CO, KI + Cl₂), oxidation number of an element in a compound or ion (H₃BO₃, NH₄^+, CO₃²⁻, K₂Cr₂O₇), corrosion prevention (galvanising, sacrificial protection, electroplating).
Note: Review Q6(a) prints “N₂ + 3H₂ → NH₃”; the balanced equation is N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.

══ 7.1 Oxidation and reduction: oxygen, hydrogen and electrons (pp. 115–117) ══
Redox reactions are reactions in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously: whenever one substance is oxidised, another is reduced.
1. In terms of oxygen: oxidation = gain of oxygen; reduction = loss of oxygen.
In the blast furnace: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. CO gains oxygen (oxidised); Fe₂O₃ loses oxygen (reduced).
2. In terms of hydrogen: oxidation = loss of hydrogen; reduction = gain of hydrogen.
Oxy-acetylene flame: 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ → 4CO₂ + 2H₂O. C₂H₂ loses H (oxidised); O₂ gains H (reduced).
3. In terms of electrons: oxidation = loss of electrons; reduction = gain of electrons. Memory aid: OIL RIG – Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.
CuO + Zn → Cu + ZnO; ionic: Cu²⁺ + Zn → Cu + Zn²⁺. Zn loses 2e⁻ (oxidised); Cu²⁺ gains 2e⁻ (reduced).
2Ca + O₂ → 2CaO: 2Ca → 2Ca²⁺ + 4e⁻ (oxidation); O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻ (reduction).
4. In terms of oxidation number: oxidation = increase in oxidation number; reduction = decrease.
Everyday redox: rusting, burning fuel, respiration (oxidation of glucose), photosynthesis, batteries, bleaching, photography (AgBr reduced to black silver by the developer hydroquinone), extraction of metals.
[Table: Table 7.1 – Oxidation and reduction]
Oxidation | Reduction
• Gain of oxygen | Loss of oxygen
• Loss of hydrogen | Gain of hydrogen
• Loss of electrons | Gain of electrons
• Increase in oxidation number | Decrease in oxidation number
Key Point: OIL RIG. Oxidation and reduction always happen together – that is why the reaction is called redox.
آکسیڈیشن: آکسیجن کا ملنا، ہائیڈروجن کا نکلنا، الیکٹران کا کھونا یا آکسیڈیشن نمبر کا بڑھنا۔ ریڈکشن: اس کے الٹ۔ یہ دونوں ہمیشہ ساتھ ہوتے ہیں، اس لیے ریڈوکس کہلاتے ہیں۔ یاد رکھنے کے لیے: OIL RIG (آکسیڈیشن = کھونا، ریڈکشن = لینا)۔

══ 7.2 Oxidation states (numbers) and the rules (pp. 117–120) ══
Oxidation state (oxidation number) is the apparent charge an atom has in a molecule or compound (as if all bonds were ionic).
Rules:
1. An uncombined (free) element has oxidation number 0: Na, Fe, H₂, O₂, Cl₂, S₈.
2. A monatomic ion: oxidation number = its charge. Na⁺ = +1, Mg²⁺ = +2, Cl⁻ = −1, O²⁻ = −2.
3. In a neutral compound the oxidation numbers add up to zero. In CO₂: C + 2(−2) = 0 → C = +4.
4. In a polyatomic ion they add up to the charge on the ion. In CO₃²⁻: C + 3(−2) = −2 → C = +4; in NH₄^+: N + 4(+1) = +1 → N = −3.
Fixed values (Table 7.2): Group IA +1; Group IIA +2; Al +3; H +1 (−1 in metal hydrides like NaH); F always −1; O −2 (except peroxides, e.g. H₂O₂, where O = −1); Group VIIA usually −1 in binary compounds with metals.
Worked examples:
- K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 → 2x = 12 → Cr = +6.
- H₃BO₃: 3(+1) + x + 3(−2) = 0 → B = +3.
- SO₄²⁻: x + 4(−2) = −2 → S = +6. PO₄³⁻: x − 8 = −3 → P = +5.
- NO₂: N = +4; HNO₃: 1 + x − 6 = 0 → N = +5; SO₂: S = +4; H₂SO₄: S = +6.
- H₂CrO₄: 2 + x − 8 = 0 → Cr = +6.
Exam Tip: Write the oxidation number of each atom above the symbol before deciding what is oxidised or reduced. Multiply by the number of atoms of that element.
آکسیڈیشن نمبر وہ ظاہری چارج ہے جو کسی ایٹم کا مرکب میں ہوتا ہے۔ اصول: آزاد عنصر کا صفر، یک ایٹمی آئن کا اس کے چارج کے برابر، غیر جانبدار مرکب میں مجموعہ صفر، اور کثیر ایٹمی آئن میں مجموعہ آئن کے چارج کے برابر۔ آکسیجن عموماً −2 اور ہائیڈروجن +1۔

══ 7.3 Formulae from ionic charges; Roman numerals (pp. 121) ══
Ionic compounds are neutral: total positive charge = total negative charge.
1. Identify the ions and charges. 2. Find the ratio that balances the charges. 3. Write the formula, using brackets for more than one polyatomic ion.
- Ca²⁺ + Cl⁻ → CaCl₂
- Mg²⁺ + O²⁻ → MgO
- Al³⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → Al₂(SO₄)₃
Roman numerals show the oxidation number of a metal that has variable oxidation states (mostly transition metals):
- CuSO₄ – copper(II) sulphate; Cu₂O – copper(I) oxide
- FeCl₂ – iron(II) chloride; FeCl₃ – iron(III) chloride
- KMnO₄ – potassium manganate(VII) (Mn = +7); K₂Cr₂O₇ – potassium dichromate(VI); WO₃ – tungsten(VI) oxide.
آئنی مرکب کا فارمولا مثبت اور منفی چارج برابر کر کے لکھا جاتا ہے۔ جن دھاتوں کی ایک سے زیادہ آکسیڈیشن حالتیں ہوں، ان کے نام میں رومن عدد لکھا جاتا ہے، جیسے آئرن (II) کلورائیڈ FeCl₂ اور آئرن (III) کلورائیڈ FeCl₃۔

══ 7.4 Oxidising and reducing agents (pp. 121–123) ══
- Oxidising agent: a substance that oxidises another by taking electrons from it (electron acceptor). It is itself reduced (its oxidation number decreases). Examples: O₂, Cl₂, H₂O₂, KMnO₄, K₂Cr₂O₇, concentrated HNO₃.
- Reducing agent: a substance that reduces another by giving electrons to it (electron donor). It is itself oxidised (its oxidation number increases). Examples: H₂, C, CO, metals (Zn, Al, Mg), H₂S, KI, NaBH₄.
How to identify them:
1. Write oxidation numbers of all atoms.
2. The element whose number increases is oxidised → the reactant containing it is the reducing agent.
3. The element whose number decreases is reduced → the reactant containing it is the oxidising agent.
(The agent is the whole molecule or formula unit, not just the atom.)
Examples:
- Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂: Fe +3 → 0 (reduced), C +2 → +4 (oxidised). Oxidising agent Fe₂O₃; reducing agent CO.
- WO₃ + 3H₂ → W + 3H₂O: W +6 → 0 (reduced); H 0 → +1 (oxidised). OA WO₃; RA H₂.
- 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl: Na 0 → +1 (RA Na); Cl 0 → −1 (OA Cl₂).
- H₂S + Cl₂ → 2HCl + S: S −2 → 0 (RA H₂S); Cl 0 → −1 (OA Cl₂).
Colour tests for redox:
- Acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄ is an oxidising agent used to test for reducing agents: its colour changes from purple to colourless as MnO₄^- (Mn +7) is reduced to Mn²⁺ (+2). E.g. with acidified FeSO₄ (Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺) or SO₂.
- Aqueous potassium iodide, KI is a reducing agent used to test for oxidising agents: the solution turns from colourless to (reddish-)brown as I⁻ is oxidised to I₂. E.g. with acidified H₂O₂ or Cl₂.
[Table: Oxidising vs reducing agent]
Oxidising agent | Reducing agent
• Accepts electrons | Donates electrons
• Is itself reduced | Is itself oxidised
• Oxidation number of its element decreases | Oxidation number of its element increases
• e.g. O₂, Cl₂, KMnO₄, H₂O₂ | e.g. H₂, CO, C, Zn, Mg, KI
• Test with KI: colourless → brown | Test with acidified KMnO₄: purple → colourless
Exam Tip: In a two-mark answer always state BOTH: which element’s oxidation number changes (with numbers) and which reactant is the agent.
آکسیڈائزنگ ایجنٹ دوسرے سے الیکٹران لے کر اسے آکسیڈائز کرتا ہے اور خود ریڈیوس ہوتا ہے (جیسے O₂، Cl₂، KMnO₄)۔ ریڈیوسنگ ایجنٹ الیکٹران دے کر دوسرے کو ریڈیوس کرتا ہے اور خود آکسیڈائز ہوتا ہے (جیسے H₂، CO، Zn)۔ تیزابی KMnO₄ کا جامنی رنگ ریڈیوسنگ ایجنٹ کی موجودگی میں غائب ہو جاتا ہے، اور KI کا محلول آکسیڈائزنگ ایجنٹ سے بھورا ہو جاتا ہے۔

══ 7.5 Corrosion and rusting (pp. 124) ══
Corrosion is the gradual destruction of a metal by its reaction with the environment (oxygen and moisture, and pollutants) – an electrochemical redox process that changes refined metals into more stable oxides. It damages bridges, cars, ships and pipes.
Rusting of iron needs both oxygen and water:
- At a drier region of the surface (anode), iron is oxidised: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻.
- At a wetter region (cathode), the electrons reduce oxygen: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻.
- Fe²⁺ ions move through the moisture and are further oxidised by oxygen to form rust, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O (hydrated iron(III) oxide).
Salt water and acid rain speed up rusting. Silver tarnishes (turns black) by forming silver sulphide with H₂S or SO₂ in air or sulphur-rich foods like eggs.
کوروژن دھات کا ماحول (آکسیجن اور نمی) سے آہستہ آہستہ تعامل کر کے خراب ہونا ہے۔ لوہے کو زنگ لگنے کے لیے آکسیجن اور پانی دونوں ضروری ہیں۔ زنگ دراصل ہائیڈریٹڈ آئرن (III) آکسائیڈ Fe₂O₃·xH₂O ہے۔

══ 7.6 Prevention of corrosion (pp. 124–125) ══
1. Barrier methods: cover the metal so air and water cannot reach it – painting (cars, bridges, trains), greasing/oiling (machine parts), plastic coating (garden furniture, wires), epoxy coatings.
2. Alloying: mixing iron with chromium and nickel gives stainless steel, which resists corrosion (cutlery, food-processing equipment).
3. Coating with another metal:
- Tinning (tin plating): clean iron sheet dipped in molten tin and rolled. Tin is unreactive and non-toxic, so tin-plated steel is used for food cans. (If scratched, the exposed iron rusts faster.)
- Galvanising: coating iron with zinc by dipping in molten zinc. Zinc protects even when scratched because it is more reactive and corrodes first. Used for roofing sheets, buckets, pipes.
- Electroplating: using electrolysis to deposit a thin layer of a protective metal (chromium, nickel, silver, tin) on another metal. The object is the cathode, the plating metal is the anode, and the electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal (e.g. CuSO₄ for copper plating). Used for taps, car parts, cutlery and jewellery.
4. Cathodic (sacrificial) protection: the iron object is connected to a block of a more reactive metal (magnesium or zinc/aluminium). The more reactive metal is oxidised instead of iron – it is sacrificed – so the iron acts as the cathode and does not rust. Used for ships’ hulls, underground pipelines, oil rigs and storage tanks.
Food and beverage industry: tin-plated steel or lacquered aluminium cans, stainless-steel tanks and pipes, plastic linings, and keeping equipment clean and dry.
[Table: Corrosion prevention summary]
Method | How it works | Example use
• Painting / greasing / plastic | Barrier keeps out air and water | Cars, bridges, tools
• Alloying | Cr, Ni form a protective oxide layer | Stainless-steel cutlery
• Tinning | Unreactive tin barrier | Food cans
• Galvanising | Zinc barrier + sacrificial | Roof sheets, buckets
• Electroplating | Electrolysis deposits Cr, Ni, Ag | Taps, car bumpers, jewellery
• Sacrificial protection | More reactive Mg/Zn corrodes instead | Ships, pipelines, oil rigs
زنگ سے بچاؤ کے طریقے: رنگ، تیل یا پلاسٹک کی تہہ (رکاوٹ)، اسٹین لیس اسٹیل بنانا (الائے)، ٹن کی تہہ (کھانے کے ڈبے)، زنک کی تہہ یعنی گیلوانائزنگ، الیکٹروپلیٹنگ (بجلی کے ذریعے دھات کی تہہ چڑھانا)، اور قربانی والا تحفظ جس میں میگنیشیم جیسی زیادہ فعال دھات لوہے کی جگہ خود زنگ آلود ہوتی ہے۔

chapters.definitions:
• Redox reaction (ریڈوکس تعامل) [p. 115]: A reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
• Oxidation (آکسیڈیشن) [p. 116]: Gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen, loss of electrons or increase in oxidation number.
• Reduction (ریڈکشن) [p. 116]: Loss of oxygen, gain of hydrogen, gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation number.
• Oxidation state (number) (آکسیڈیشن نمبر) [p. 117]: The apparent charge that an atom has in a molecule or compound.
• Oxidising agent (آکسیڈائزنگ ایجنٹ) [p. 121]: A substance that oxidises another substance by accepting electrons; it is itself reduced.
• Reducing agent (ریڈیوسنگ ایجنٹ) [p. 122]: A substance that reduces another substance by donating electrons; it is itself oxidised.
• Corrosion (کوروژن / زنگ لگنا) [p. 124]: The slow destruction of a metal by reaction with oxygen and moisture in its environment.
• Rust (زنگ) [p. 124]: Hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, formed when iron corrodes.
• Galvanising (گیلوانائزنگ) [p. 125]: Coating iron or steel with a layer of zinc to prevent corrosion.
• Tinning (قلعی کرنا) [p. 125]: Coating iron with a thin layer of tin by dipping it in molten tin.
• Electroplating (برقی ملمع کاری) [p. 125]: Using electrolysis to deposit a thin layer of one metal on another metal.
• Cathodic (sacrificial) protection (قربانی والا تحفظ) [p. 125]: Protecting a metal by connecting it to a more reactive metal (Mg, Zn, Al) that corrodes instead.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Oxidation (تکسید): Loss of electrons
• Reduction (تخفیف): Gain of electrons
• Redox (ریڈوکس): Oxidation + reduction
• Oxidation number (تکسیدی عدد): Apparent charge
• Oxidising agent (تکسیدی عامل): Electron acceptor
• Reducing agent (تخفیفی عامل): Electron donor
• Corrosion (زنگ / فرسودگی): Destruction of metal
• Rust (زنگ): Hydrated iron oxide
• Galvanising (جستی کاری): Zinc coating
• Electroplating (برقی ملمع کاری): Plating by electrolysis
• Anode (مثبت برقیرہ (اینوڈ)): Electrode where oxidation occurs
• Cathode (منفی برقیرہ (کیتھوڈ)): Electrode where reduction occurs
• Tarnish (ماند پڑنا): Dull layer on a metal
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Free element: oxidation number = 0 (Na, O₂, Cl₂)
• Monatomic ion: oxidation number = charge (Mg²⁺ = +2)
• Neutral compound: Σ oxidation numbers = 0
• Polyatomic ion: Σ oxidation numbers = charge on ion
• Usual values: H = +1, O = −2, F = −1, Group I = +1, Group II = +2 (O = −1 in peroxides; H = −1 in metal hydrides)
• Potassium manganate(VII): KMnO₄ (Mn = +7) (Purple; reduced to Mn²⁺ (colourless))
• Potassium dichromate(VI): K₂Cr₂O₇ (Cr = +6) (Orange; breathalyser)
• Rust: Fe₂O₃·xH₂O

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• Fe₂O₃ + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO₂ — Blast furnace: CO oxidised (reducing agent), Fe₂O₃ reduced (oxidising agent).
• 2C₂H₂ + 5O₂ -> 4CO₂ + 2H₂O — Oxy-acetylene flame: C₂H₂ loses hydrogen (oxidised).
• CuO + Zn -> Cu + ZnO ; Cu²⁺ + Zn -> Cu + Zn²⁺ — Electron transfer: Zn oxidised, Cu²⁺ reduced.
• CH₄ + 2O₂ -> CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat — Burning Sui gas: C oxidised, O reduced.
• 2Ca + O₂ -> 2CaO — Ca → Ca²⁺ + 2e⁻ ; O₂ + 4e⁻ → 2O²⁻.
• WO₃ + 3H₂ -> W + 3H₂O — Tungsten extraction: WO₃ oxidising agent, H₂ reducing agent.
• 2Na + Cl₂ -> 2NaCl — Na reducing agent, Cl₂ oxidising agent.
• MnO₄^- (purple) + reducing agent -> Mn²⁺ (colourless) — Test for reducing agents with acidified KMnO₄ (e.g. Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺).
• 2I⁻ (colourless) -> I₂ (brown) + 2e⁻ — Test for oxidising agents with KI (e.g. H₂O₂, Cl₂).
• Fe -> Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ ; O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ -> 4OH⁻ — Rusting: anode and cathode reactions.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Can oxidation take place without reduction?
   Answer: No. Electrons lost by one substance must be gained by another, so they always occur together.
2. Why is the oxidising agent itself reduced?
   Answer: Because it takes electrons from the other substance; gaining electrons is reduction.
3. Why is O = −1 in H₂O₂ and not −2?
   Answer: H₂O₂ is a peroxide (O–O bond). With H = +1: 2(+1) + 2x = 0 → x = −1.
4. Why do cars rust faster near the sea?
   Answer: Salt water conducts better and speeds up the electrochemical corrosion reactions.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. A farmer’s iron gate is rusting. Suggest two cheap ways to protect it.
   Answer: Paint it (barrier) or oil/grease it; for longer life use galvanised iron.
2. Underground water pipes are connected by wires to magnesium blocks. Explain.
   Answer: Sacrificial protection: Mg is more reactive, so it corrodes instead of the iron pipes.
3. Silver jewellery turns black after eating eggs. What happened and what type of reaction is it?
   Answer: Silver reacted with sulphur compounds to form black silver sulphide (tarnish); a redox reaction where silver is oxidised.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. In Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, which substance is oxidised and which is reduced in terms of oxygen?
   Solution: CO gains oxygen → oxidised to CO₂. Fe₂O₃ loses oxygen → reduced to Fe.

2. Determine the oxidation state of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ (breathalyser). (Example 7.3)
   Given: K = +1, O = −2; compound neutral
   Required: Oxidation number of Cr (x)
   Formula: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0
   Substitution: 2 + 2x − 14 = 0
   Calculation: 2x = 12 → x = +6
   Final Answer: Cr = +6

3. What is the oxidation state of B in boric acid H₃BO₃? (Example 7.4)
   Given: H = +1, O = −2
   Required: B (x)
   Formula: 3(+1) + x + 3(−2) = 0
   Substitution: 3 + x − 6 = 0
   Calculation: x = +3
   Final Answer: B = +3

4. What is the oxidation number of C in the carbonate ion CO₃²⁻? (Example 7.5)
   Given: O = −2; ion charge −2
   Required: C (x)
   Formula: x + 3(−2) = −2
   Substitution: x − 6 = −2
   Calculation: x = +4
   Final Answer: C = +4

5. Find the oxidation states of S in SO₄²⁻, P in PO₄³⁻ and N in NH₄^+.
   Solution: S: x − 8 = −2 → +6. P: x − 8 = −3 → +5. N: x + 4 = +1 → −3.

6. Identify the oxidising and reducing agents in WO₃ + 3H₂ → W + 3H₂O. (Example 7.6) [also FBISE Annual 2026]
   Solution: Oxidation numbers: W +6 → 0 (decrease, reduced); H 0 → +1 (increase, oxidised); O stays −2. Oxidising agent: WO₃. Reducing agent: H₂.

NBF Chapter 7 Exercises (126–128):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. In which of the following changes is the nitrogen atom reduced? → C (N₂ to NH₃) | N: 0 → −3 (decrease). In the others N increases.
ii. Which of the following changes is an example of oxidation? → B (Silver atoms to silver(I) ion) | Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻ (loss of electron).
iii. Which element in ZnO + H₂ → Zn + H₂O is reduced? → C (Zn) | Zinc goes from +2 to 0. (ZnO is the substance reduced; the element is Zn.)
iv. In H₂S + Cl₂ → 2HCl + S, H₂S behaves as: → A (Reducing agent) | S: −2 → 0, so H₂S is oxidised and reduces Cl₂.
v. The oxidation state of Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ is: → B (+6) | 2 + 2x − 14 = 0.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) What is oxidation state?
   Answer: The apparent charge an atom has in a molecule, compound or ion, worked out with the oxidation-number rules (free element 0; sum zero in a compound; sum = charge in an ion).
(ii) What is the oxidation number of Cr in chromic acid (H₂CrO₄)?
   Answer: 
(iii–iv) Identify the reducing agent in CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O.
   Answer: H: 0 → +1 (oxidised), Cu: +2 → 0 (reduced). Reducing agent: H₂ (oxidising agent: CuO).
(v) Why is tin-plated steel used to make food cans?
   Answer: Tin is unreactive and non-toxic; it forms a barrier that stops air and moisture reaching the iron, so the can does not rust and the food is not contaminated. Steel gives strength cheaply.
(vi) Explain one example from daily life that involves an oxidation–reduction reaction.
   Answer: Burning of natural gas (Sui gas): CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Carbon gains oxygen/loses hydrogen (oxidised) while oxygen is reduced. Other examples: rusting of iron, respiration, batteries, bleaching.

— Q3–Q10. Descriptive questions —
3. Compare and contrast oxidation and reduction.
   Answer: Contrast: see Table 7.1 – oxidation is gain of O / loss of H / loss of e⁻ / increase in oxidation number; reduction is the opposite. Compare (similarity): both always happen together in a redox reaction; the electrons lost in oxidation equal those gained in reduction; both are shown by changes in oxidation number.
4. Define oxidation and reduction in terms of loss or gain of electrons.
   Answer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons by an atom or ion (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻). Reduction is the gain of electrons (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). (OIL RIG.)
5. Explain how food and beverage industries deal with corrosion.
   Answer: They use tin-plated steel cans (tin is unreactive and non-toxic), aluminium cans with lacquer/polymer linings, stainless steel tanks, pipes and machines (Cr/Ni alloy resists rust), plastic or glass containers, and keep equipment clean and dry. These stop metal reacting with acids in food and drinks and prevent contamination.
6. State the substances which are oxidised or reduced, with reasons: (a) N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃ (b) CO₂ + 2Mg → 2MgO + C (c) Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂ (d) H₂S + Cl₂ → 2HCl + S (e) 2NH₃ + 3CuO → 3Cu + N₂ + 3H₂O
   Answer: (a) N: 0 → −3 reduced (N₂ gains H); H: 0 → +1 oxidised.
(b) Mg: 0 → +2 oxidised (gains O); C: +4 → 0 reduced (CO₂ loses O).
(c) Mg: 0 → +2 oxidised; H: +1 → 0 reduced (H₂O loses O).
(d) S: −2 → 0 oxidised (H₂S loses H); Cl: 0 → −1 reduced.
(e) N: −3 → 0 oxidised (NH₃ loses H); Cu: +2 → 0 reduced (CuO loses O).
7. (a) Define oxidation number. (b) Find the oxidation state of nitrogen in (i) NO₂ (ii) N₂O (iii) N₂O₃ (iv) HNO₃.
   Answer: (a) The apparent charge on an atom in a compound or ion. (b) (i) x + 2(−2) = 0 → +4 (ii) 2x − 2 = 0 → +1 (iii) 2x − 6 = 0 → +3 (iv) 1 + x − 6 = 0 → +5.
8. Find the oxidation state of S in (a) H₂S (b) H₂SO₃ (c) Na₂S₂O₃.
   Answer: (a) 2 + x = 0 → −2 (b) 2 + x − 6 = 0 → +4 (c) 2 + 2x − 6 = 0 → +2.
9. (a) Define oxidising and reducing agents. (b) Identify them in: (i) H₂S + Cl₂ → 2HCl + S (ii) 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃ (iii) 2KI + Cl₂ → 2KCl + I₂ (iv) Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
   Answer: (a) Oxidising agent: accepts electrons and is reduced. Reducing agent: donates electrons and is oxidised.
(b) (i) OA Cl₂, RA H₂S (S −2 → 0)
(ii) OA Cl₂, RA FeCl₂ (Fe +2 → +3)
(iii) OA Cl₂, RA KI (I −1 → 0)
(iv) OA HCl (H +1 → 0), RA Mg (0 → +2)
10. Hydrogen peroxide reacts as follows: (i) H₂O₂ + Ag₂O → 2Ag + H₂O + O₂ (ii) 4H₂O₂ + PbS → PbSO₄ + 4H₂O. Is H₂O₂ an oxidising or reducing agent in each? Argue.
   Answer: In H₂O₂ oxygen has oxidation number −1.
(i) Ag: +1 → 0 (reduced). Some O in H₂O₂: −1 → 0 in O₂ (oxidised). So H₂O₂ gives electrons → reducing agent.
(ii) S in PbS: −2 → +6 in PbSO₄ (oxidised). O in H₂O₂: −1 → −2 in H₂O (reduced). So H₂O₂ accepts electrons → oxidising agent.
H₂O₂ can act both ways because O = −1 lies between 0 and −2.
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Sum of oxidation numbers in sulphate ion: explain how the sum of oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion equals its charge. Calculate for (a) NH₄^+ (b) CO₃²⁻.
   Answer: The rule: Σ oxidation numbers = charge on the ion. (a) N + 4(+1) = +1 → N = −3; check: −3 + 4 = +1 ✓ (b) C + 3(−2) = −2 → C = +4; check: +4 − 6 = −2 ✓.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] Determine the oxidation number of B in H₃BO₃.
   Answer: 

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Identify the oxidising and reducing agents in H₂S + Cl₂ → S + 2HCl.
   Answer: S: −2 → 0 (oxidised) so H₂S is the reducing agent; Cl: 0 → −1 (reduced) so Cl₂ is the oxidising agent.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Identify the oxidising and reducing agents in 2KI + Cl₂ → 2KCl + I₂.
   Answer: I: −1 → 0 (oxidised): KI reducing agent. Cl: 0 → −1 (reduced): Cl₂ oxidising agent.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Identify oxidising agents in (a) 2NH₃ + 3CuO → 3Cu + N₂ + 3H₂O (b) 2FeCl₂ + Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃.
   Answer: (a) Cu: +2 → 0, so CuO is the oxidising agent (NH₃ is the reducing agent). (b) Cl: 0 → −1, so Cl₂ is the oxidising agent (FeCl₂ is the reducing agent).

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Give in detail the process of electroplating to prevent metals from corrosion.
   Answer: Electroplating uses electrolysis to coat an object with a thin protective metal layer.
- The object to be plated (e.g. a steel spoon) is made the cathode (−).
- A bar of the plating metal (e.g. nickel, chromium, silver) is the anode (+).
- The electrolyte is a solution of a salt of the plating metal (e.g. NiSO₄).
- On passing current, metal ions move to the cathode and deposit as metal (Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Ni), while the anode dissolves to replace them (Ni → Ni²⁺ + 2e⁻).
The layer stops air and moisture reaching the base metal and also gives a shiny finish.

7. What is OIL RIG?
   Answer: A memory aid: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

8. Why does acidified KMnO₄ become colourless when FeSO₄ is added?
   Answer: Fe²⁺ is a reducing agent; it reduces purple MnO₄^- (Mn +7) to colourless Mn²⁺ (+2) and is itself oxidised to Fe³⁺.

9. Why does KI solution turn brown with hydrogen peroxide?
   Answer: H₂O₂ is an oxidising agent; it oxidises colourless I⁻ to I₂, which is brown in solution.

10. State two conditions necessary for rusting.
   Answer: Presence of both oxygen (air) and water (moisture).

11. Why does galvanised iron not rust even when scratched?
   Answer: Zinc is more reactive than iron; it is oxidised in preference (sacrificial protection), so the exposed iron is protected.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Identify the oxidising and reducing agents by assigning oxidation states (H = +1, O = −2): (a) WO₃ + 3H₂ → W + 3H₂O (b) H₂S + Cl₂ → 2HCl + S.
   Answer: (a) W: +6 → 0 (decrease, reduced); H: 0 → +1 (increase, oxidised). OA: WO₃; RA: H₂.
(b) S: −2 → 0 (oxidised); Cl: 0 → −1 (reduced); H stays +1. OA: Cl₂; RA: H₂S.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Identify the oxidising and reducing agents by showing changes in oxidation states: (a) 2S + Cl₂ → S₂Cl₂ (b) WO₃ + 3H₂ → W + 3H₂O.
   Answer: (a) S: 0 → +1 (oxidised), Cl: 0 → −1 (reduced). RA: S; OA: Cl₂. (b) OA: WO₃; RA: H₂ (W +6 → 0; H 0 → +1).

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] What is a redox reaction? How do oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously? Explain with an example.
   Answer: A redox reaction is one in which oxidation and reduction take place together. Electrons lost by one species must be gained by another, so one cannot happen without the other.
Example: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Ionic: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidation) and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduction). Zn is the reducing agent; Cu²⁺ is the oxidising agent. The blue colour fades and red-brown copper deposits.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What is corrosion? Write its chemical reaction. Describe one method to prevent corrosion.
   Answer: Corrosion is the slow destruction of a metal by reaction with oxygen and moisture. Rusting: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ (anode); O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ (cathode); overall rust Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.
Prevention (galvanising): iron is dipped in molten zinc; zinc forms a barrier and, being more reactive, corrodes first even if scratched.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Explain the following methods of prevention of corrosion: (a) sacrificial protection (b) galvanising.
   Answer: (a) Sacrificial (cathodic) protection: iron/steel is connected to a block of a more reactive metal (Mg, Zn, Al). The reactive metal is oxidised (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻) and supplies electrons to the iron, which becomes the cathode and is not oxidised. Used for ships, pipelines and oil rigs; blocks are replaced when used up.
(b) Galvanising: a clean iron sheet is dipped in molten zinc to form a zinc coating. Zinc protects as a barrier and also sacrificially when scratched. Used for roofing sheets, buckets, fences.

6. Describe the colour tests used to identify redox reactions with acidified KMnO₄ and aqueous KI.
   Answer: Acidified KMnO₄ (oxidising agent, purple MnO₄^-): add a few drops to a solution containing a reducing agent (e.g. acidified FeSO₄ or SO₂). The purple colour disappears as MnO₄^- (+7) is reduced to Mn²⁺ (+2, colourless): shows the solution contains a reducing agent.
Aqueous KI (reducing agent, colourless I⁻): add to an oxidising agent (e.g. acidified H₂O₂ or Cl₂). The solution turns reddish-brown as I⁻ is oxidised to I₂: shows an oxidising agent is present.

══ Chapter 7 in one page
- Redox: oxidation and reduction together. Oxidation = +O, −H, −e⁻, ↑ oxidation number. Reduction = opposite. OIL RIG.
- Oxidation number rules: free element 0; monatomic ion = charge; Σ = 0 in compounds; Σ = charge in ions. H +1, O −2 (−1 in peroxides), F −1, Group I +1, Group II +2.
- Key values: Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ +6; B in H₃BO₃ +3; C in CO₃²⁻ +4; N in NH₄^+ −3, NO₂ +4, HNO₃ +5; S in SO₄²⁻ +6, H₂S −2; Mn in KMnO₄ +7.
- Roman numerals: iron(II) FeCl₂, iron(III) FeCl₃, copper(II) CuSO₄.
- Oxidising agent = electron acceptor, itself reduced (O₂, Cl₂, KMnO₄, H₂O₂). Reducing agent = electron donor, itself oxidised (H₂, CO, C, Zn, Mg, KI, H₂S).
- Tests: acidified KMnO₄ purple → colourless (reducing agent present); KI colourless → brown (oxidising agent present).
- Corrosion/rusting: needs O₂ + H₂O; Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻; rust Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.
- Prevention: paint/grease/plastic; alloying (stainless steel); tinning (food cans); galvanising (Zn); electroplating (object = cathode); sacrificial protection (Mg/Zn blocks on ships, pipelines).

chapters.title: Energetics
chapters.introduction:
Every chemical reaction involves an energy change. This unit (chemical energetics) introduces the system and surroundings, exothermic and endothermic reactions, enthalpy change (ΔH) and its sign, bond breaking and bond making, calculating ΔH from bond energies, activation energy, the effect of a catalyst on reaction pathway diagrams, and how respiration releases energy in living things.

Exam focus (10 summative SLOs): ΔH from bond energies (H₂ + Cl₂, H₂ + I₂, H₂ + F₂ appear every year), labelled energy-profile diagrams with and without catalyst, exothermic vs endothermic with examples, activation energy, respiration.

══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
Exam focus (10 summative SLOs): ΔH from bond energies (H₂ + Cl₂, H₂ + I₂, H₂ + F₂ appear every year), labelled energy-profile diagrams with and without catalyst, exothermic vs endothermic with examples, activation energy, respiration.
Note: The textbook lists H₂(g) + I₂(s) → 2HI(g), ΔH = +53.8 kJ (iodine starts as a solid, which must first be vaporised). With gaseous iodine and bond energies the same reaction gives ΔH ≈ −11 kJ mol⁻¹, as worked on p. 132. Both are correct for their conditions.

══ 8.1 System, surroundings and thermochemistry (pp. 130) ══
Chemical energetics is the study of energy changes in chemical reactions. In a reaction old bonds break (energy absorbed) and new bonds form (energy released), so energy is exchanged with the surroundings.
- System: the part of the universe we focus on – the reacting substances. E.g. limestone + hydrochloric acid in a test tube.
- Surroundings: everything else – the test tube, the air, the thermometer, your hand.
- Energy is transferred between the system and surroundings as heat, light or work. A thermometer in the surroundings shows a temperature rise (heat given out) or fall (heat taken in).
- Thermochemistry: the branch of chemistry dealing with heat changes in reactions. A thermochemical equation is a balanced equation that also shows the heat change (ΔH), e.g. C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹.
نظام وہ حصہ ہے جس کا ہم مطالعہ کر رہے ہیں (تعامل کرنے والے مادے)، اور باقی سب ماحول ہے۔ تعامل کے دوران نظام اور ماحول کے درمیان حرارت کا تبادلہ ہوتا ہے۔

══ 8.2 Exothermic and endothermic reactions; enthalpy change (pp. 130–131) ══
Exothermic reaction: gives out heat to the surroundings; the surroundings get hotter. Products have less energy than reactants. ΔH is negative.
Examples: burning of fuels (C + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −393.5 kJ; CH₄ combustion), respiration, neutralisation (acid + alkali), H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl, rusting, freezing of water, condensation of steam.
Endothermic reaction: takes in heat from the surroundings; the surroundings get colder. Products have more energy than reactants. ΔH is positive.
Examples: thermal decomposition of limestone (CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂), photosynthesis, N₂ + O₂ → 2NO (in lightning or car engines), dissolving ammonium nitrate in water (feels cold), melting ice, evaporation, sublimation of dry ice, cooking an egg.
Enthalpy change (ΔH): the heat evolved or absorbed in a reaction at constant pressure. Standard enthalpy change (ΔH°) is measured at 25 °C (298 K) and 1 atm. Unit: kJ mol⁻¹.
[Table: Exothermic vs endothermic]
 | Exothermic | Endothermic
• Heat | Given out to surroundings | Taken in from surroundings
• Temperature of surroundings | Rises | Falls
• Sign of ΔH | Negative (−) | Positive (+)
• Energy of products vs reactants | Lower | Higher
• Bond energies | Energy released in making bonds > energy absorbed in breaking | Energy absorbed in breaking > energy released in making
• Examples | Combustion, respiration, neutralisation | Photosynthesis, decomposition of CaCO₃, dissolving NH₄NO₃
Exam Tip: Classification exercise: freezing of water – exothermic; combustion of methane – exothermic; sublimation of dry ice – endothermic; H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) – endothermic; decomposition of limestone – endothermic.
ایگزوتھرمک تعامل ماحول کو حرارت دیتا ہے، درجہ حرارت بڑھتا ہے اور ΔH منفی ہوتا ہے (جیسے ایندھن کا جلنا، تنفس)۔ اینڈوتھرمک تعامل ماحول سے حرارت لیتا ہے، درجہ حرارت گھٹتا ہے اور ΔH مثبت ہوتا ہے (جیسے ضیائی تالیف، چونے کے پتھر کا ٹوٹنا، امونیم نائٹریٹ کا پانی میں گھلنا)۔

══ 8.3 Bond breaking, bond making and ΔH from bond energies (pp. 131–132) ══
- Bond breaking is always endothermic (energy must be supplied to pull atoms apart).
- Bond making is always exothermic (energy is released when atoms join).
- Bond dissociation energy: energy required to break one mole of a particular bond to give separate gaseous atoms. Bond energy: energy released when one mole of that bond forms (same size).
ΔH = Σ(bond energies of bonds broken in reactants) − Σ(bond energies of bonds formed in products)
If more energy is released in making bonds than is absorbed in breaking them, ΔH is negative (exothermic); otherwise positive.
Method: (1) write the balanced equation with all species as gases; (2) list bonds broken and formed, counting how many of each; (3) substitute bond energies; (4) subtract and give the sign and unit.
Example – H₂ + I₂ → 2HI (H–H 436, I–I 151, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹):
Broken = 436 + 151 = 587; formed = 2 × 299 = 598; ΔH = 587 − 598 = −11 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic).
Example – H₂ + F₂ → 2HF (H–H 436, F–F 155, H–F 567):
Broken = 591; formed = 1134; ΔH = −543 kJ mol⁻¹.
Example – H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl (H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432):
Broken = 679; formed = 864; ΔH = −185 kJ mol⁻¹.
Values from bond energies are averages and can differ slightly from experimental values.
[Table: Bond energies used in exams (kJ mol⁻¹)]
Bond | Energy | Bond | Energy
• H–H | 436 | H–F | 567
• F–F | 155 | H–Cl | 431–432
• Cl–Cl | 242–243 | H–Br | 366
• Br–Br | 193 | H–I | 299
• I–I | 151 | C–H | 413
• O=O | 498 | O–H | 463
• C=O (in CO₂) | 805 | N≡N | 945
Exam Tip: Always multiply by the number of bonds: 2HCl means TWO H–Cl bonds formed. Write the final answer with sign and unit, e.g. −185 kJ mol⁻¹.
بانڈ توڑنے میں ہمیشہ توانائی جذب ہوتی ہے (اینڈوتھرمک) اور بانڈ بنانے میں خارج ہوتی ہے (ایگزوتھرمک)۔ ΔH = ٹوٹنے والے بانڈز کی توانائی کا مجموعہ − بننے والے بانڈز کی توانائی کا مجموعہ۔ جواب منفی ہو تو تعامل ایگزوتھرمک ہے۔

══ 8.4 Activation energy, effective collisions and catalysts (pp. 132–133) ══
Collision theory: particles must collide to react. A collision is effective (successful) only if the particles have enough energy and the correct orientation.
Activation energy (Eₐ): the minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a successful collision – the energy “hill” between reactants and products. Higher Eₐ → slower reaction. Eₐ is always greater than the average kinetic energy of the molecules; only the fastest molecules can react.
Catalyst: a substance that increases the rate of a reaction but remains chemically unchanged at the end. It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions succeed.
- A catalyst does not change ΔH (reactant and product energies stay the same), and it does not change the products.
- Enzymes are biological catalysts (proteins) that speed up reactions in living organisms at body temperature, e.g. amylase digests starch.
- Industrial catalysts: Fe (Haber), V₂O₅/Pt (Contact), Ni (hydrogenation), Pt/Pd/Rh (catalytic converters).
ایکٹیویشن انرجی وہ کم از کم توانائی ہے جو ٹکرانے والے ذرات کے پاس کامیاب ٹکر کے لیے ہونی چاہیے۔ عمل انگیز (کیٹالسٹ) ایک متبادل راستہ دیتا ہے جس کی ایکٹیویشن انرجی کم ہوتی ہے، اس لیے تعامل تیز ہو جاتا ہے، مگر ΔH نہیں بدلتا۔ جانداروں میں انزائمز عمل انگیز کا کام کرتے ہیں۔

══ 8.5 Reaction pathway (energy profile) diagrams (pp. 132–133) ══
A reaction pathway diagram plots energy (y-axis) against progress of reaction (x-axis).
Exothermic: reactants line higher, products line lower; a hump between them. Label: reactants, products, Eₐ (arrow from reactants up to the peak), ΔH (arrow from reactants down to products, negative), and a lower dashed hump labelled Eₐ (catalysed).
Endothermic: reactants line lower, products line higher. Eₐ arrow from reactants to peak; ΔH arrow from reactants up to products (positive). Catalysed pathway: lower dashed hump.
Key differences: in an exothermic diagram the products are below the reactants (ΔH  0). A catalyst lowers only the peak.
Exam Tip: Marks are given for: labelled axes, reactant and product levels at correct heights, Eₐ arrow starting at the reactants and ending at the peak, ΔH arrow between reactant and product levels with sign, and a lower catalysed hump.
توانائی کا خاکہ: عمودی محور پر توانائی اور افقی پر تعامل کی پیش رفت۔ ایگزوتھرمک میں حاصلات نیچے اور اینڈوتھرمک میں اوپر ہوتے ہیں۔ Eₐ کا تیر متعاملات سے چوٹی تک اور ΔH کا تیر متعاملات سے حاصلات تک۔ عمل انگیز صرف چوٹی کو نیچا کرتا ہے۔

══ 8.6 Respiration: energy for living things (pp. 133–134) ══
Respiration is the biochemical process in which glucose is oxidised in cells to release energy. It is exothermic.
- Aerobic respiration (needs oxygen): C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (about 2800 kJ per mole of glucose). Products: carbon dioxide, water and a large amount of energy.
- Anaerobic respiration (without oxygen, e.g. in muscles during hard exercise): C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ (lactic acid) + a small amount of energy. Lactic acid build-up causes muscle tiredness and cramps.
- Aerobic releases much more energy than anaerobic.
Lipids (fats and oils) are reserve stores of energy: they store a lot of energy per gram (about 37 kJ g⁻¹, compared with about 17 kJ g⁻¹ for carbohydrates). During long, intense exercise when glucose runs short, lipids are oxidised for energy.
Respiration is crucial: it provides energy for muscle contraction, heartbeat, brain activity, growth, active transport and keeping body temperature at 37 °C.
[Table: Aerobic vs anaerobic respiration]
Aerobic | Anaerobic
• Needs oxygen | No oxygen needed
• Glucose → CO₂ + H₂O + energy | Glucose → lactic acid + energy (in muscles)
• Large amount of energy | Small amount of energy
• Complete oxidation of glucose | Incomplete breakdown of glucose
• Normal activity | Intense exercise, oxygen shortage
تنفس میں خلیوں کے اندر گلوکوز کی آکسیڈیشن سے توانائی نکلتی ہے، اس لیے یہ ایگزوتھرمک عمل ہے۔ ہوائی تنفس آکسیجن کے ساتھ ہوتا ہے اور زیادہ توانائی دیتا ہے (CO₂ + پانی)۔ غیر ہوائی تنفس آکسیجن کے بغیر ہوتا ہے، کم توانائی اور لیکٹک ایسڈ بناتا ہے۔ چربی (لپڈز) توانائی کا محفوظ ذخیرہ ہے۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Energy profile: exothermic reaction (with and without catalyst): Products below reactants: ΔH negative. The dashed curve is the catalysed pathway with lower Eₐ.
2. Energy profile: endothermic reaction: Products above reactants: ΔH positive.
chapters.shortNotes:
══ Chapter 8 in one page
- System (reacting substances) vs surroundings (everything else); energy flows between them.
- Exothermic: heat out, surroundings warm, ΔH − (combustion, respiration, neutralisation, freezing). Endothermic: heat in, surroundings cool, ΔH + (photosynthesis, CaCO₃ decomposition, N₂ + O₂ → 2NO, dissolving NH₄NO₃, melting, evaporation).
- ΔH° at 25 °C and 1 atm, kJ mol⁻¹.
- Bond breaking endothermic; bond making exothermic. ΔH = Σ broken − Σ formed. H₂ + I₂: −11; H₂ + Cl₂: −185 (or −184); H₂ + F₂: −543 kJ mol⁻¹.
- Activation energy: minimum energy for a successful collision (energy + orientation). Higher Eₐ → slower.
- Catalyst: alternative pathway, lower Eₐ, faster, unchanged ΔH; enzymes are biological catalysts.
- Energy profiles: label axes, reactants, products, Eₐ (from reactants to peak), ΔH (sign), catalysed dashed hump.
- Respiration: aerobic C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (large); anaerobic → lactic acid + little energy. Lipids = reserve energy store.

chapters.definitions:
• Chemical energetics (کیمیائی توانائیات) [p. 130]: The study of energy changes that take place in chemical reactions.
• System (نظام) [p. 130]: The part of the universe under study, usually the reacting substances.
• Surroundings (ماحول) [p. 130]: Everything outside the system.
• Thermochemical equation (حراری کیمیائی مساوات) [p. 130]: A balanced chemical equation that also shows the heat change of the reaction.
• Exothermic reaction (حرارت خارج کرنے والا تعامل) [p. 130]: A reaction that gives out heat to the surroundings; ΔH is negative.
• Endothermic reaction (حرارت جذب کرنے والا تعامل) [p. 131]: A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings; ΔH is positive.
• Enthalpy of reaction (ΔH) (اینتھالپی) [p. 131]: The amount of heat evolved or absorbed in a chemical reaction.
• Standard enthalpy change (ΔH°) (معیاری اینتھالپی) [p. 131]: Enthalpy change measured at 25 °C (298 K) and 1 atmosphere pressure.
• Bond dissociation energy (بانڈ توڑنے کی توانائی) [p. 131]: The energy required to break one mole of a particular bond to form neutral gaseous atoms.
• Activation energy (ایکٹیویشن انرجی) [p. 132]: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a successful (effective) collision.
• Effective collision (مؤثر ٹکر) [p. 132]: A collision with enough energy and correct orientation to produce a reaction.
• Catalyst (عمل انگیز) [p. 133]: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing a pathway of lower activation energy and remains chemically unchanged at the end.
• Enzyme (خامرہ / انزائم) [p. 133]: A biological catalyst (protein) that speeds up reactions in living organisms.
• Aerobic respiration (ہوائی تنفس) [p. 134]: Respiration that uses oxygen to break down glucose, releasing energy, CO₂ and water.
• Anaerobic respiration (غیر ہوائی تنفس) [p. 134]: Respiration without oxygen, breaking glucose into lactic acid with less energy.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Energetics (توانائیات): Study of energy changes
• Exothermic (حرارت زا): Gives out heat
• Endothermic (حرارت گیر): Takes in heat
• Enthalpy (اینتھالپی): Heat content change
• Bond energy (بانڈ توانائی): Energy of a bond
• Activation energy (عاملی توانائی): Energy barrier
• Catalyst (عمل انگیز): Speeds up a reaction
• Enzyme (خامرہ): Biological catalyst
• Collision (ٹکر): Particles hitting each other
• Respiration (تنفس): Release of energy from food
• Aerobic (ہوائی): With oxygen
• Anaerobic (غیر ہوائی): Without oxygen
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Enthalpy from bond energies: ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) (kJ mol⁻¹)
• Exothermic: ΔH < 0 (Products lower in energy)
• Endothermic: ΔH > 0 (Products higher in energy)
• Standard conditions: 298 K (25 °C), 1 atm (ΔH°)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• C(s) + O₂(g) -> CO₂(g)  ΔH = −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹ — Exothermic combustion.
• CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) -> CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)  ΔH = −890 kJ mol⁻¹ — Burning natural gas.
• HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)  ΔH = −57 kJ mol⁻¹ — Neutralisation is exothermic.
• CaCO₃(s) -> CaO(s) + CO₂(g)  ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ — Endothermic decomposition of limestone.
• N₂(g) + O₂(g) -> 2NO(g)  ΔH = +180 kJ mol⁻¹ — Endothermic; happens in lightning and car engines.
• H₂(g) + I₂(s) -> 2HI(g)  ΔH = +53.8 kJ — Endothermic (textbook) when iodine starts as a solid.
• 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy -> C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — Photosynthesis is endothermic.
• C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ -> 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy — Aerobic respiration (exothermic).
• C₆H₁₂O₆ -> 2C₃H₆O₃ (lactic acid) + energy — Anaerobic respiration in muscles.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why does a reaction mixture feel cold when ammonium nitrate dissolves?
   Answer: Dissolving is endothermic: it takes heat from the surroundings (your hand and the water), so they cool.
2. Does a catalyst make an endothermic reaction exothermic?
   Answer: No. A catalyst only lowers activation energy; ΔH and its sign stay the same.
3. Why does a mixture of petrol and air not burn until a spark is applied?
   Answer: The reaction has a high activation energy; the spark supplies it to start the exothermic reaction, which then provides energy to continue.
4. Why do lipids make good energy stores?
   Answer: They release about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates when oxidised.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Why do athletes feel cramps after a 400 m sprint?
   Answer: Muscles respire anaerobically when oxygen is short, producing lactic acid that causes fatigue and cramps.
2. Why are enzymes added to washing powders?
   Answer: Enzymes catalyse the breakdown of food stains (proteins, fats) at low temperatures, saving energy.
3. Instant cold packs contain ammonium nitrate and water in separate bags. Explain how they work.
   Answer: When the inner bag breaks, NH₄NO₃ dissolves endothermically, absorbing heat so the pack becomes cold.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Calculate ΔH for H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g). Bond energies: H–H 436, I–I 151, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹. (Textbook p. 132; FBISE Annual 2025, Annual 2026 Old-22)
   Given: H–H 436, I–I 151, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹
   Required: ΔH
   Formula: ΔH = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed)
   Substitution: = (436 + 151) − (2 × 299)
   Calculation: = 587 − 598
   Final Answer: ΔH = −11 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic)

2. Calculate ΔH for H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2HF(g). H–H 436, F–F 155, H–F 567 kJ mol⁻¹. (Textbook p. 132; FBISE Annual 2026)
   Given: H–H 436, F–F 155, H–F 567
   Required: ΔH
   Formula: ΔH = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed)
   Substitution: = (436 + 155) − (2 × 567)
   Calculation: = 591 − 1134
   Final Answer: ΔH = −543 kJ mol⁻¹ (exothermic)

3. Classify as exothermic or endothermic: (a) freezing of water (b) combustion of methane (c) sublimation of dry ice (d) H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) (e) decomposition of limestone.
   Solution: (a) Exothermic (heat released when liquid becomes solid). (b) Exothermic. (c) Endothermic (heat needed to turn solid into gas). (d) Endothermic (evaporation). (e) Endothermic (CaCO₃ must be heated strongly).


══ ADDITIONAL SLO NUMERICAL PRACTICE ══

1. Calculate ΔH for H₂ + Br₂ → 2HBr. H–H 436, Br–Br 193, H–Br 366 kJ mol⁻¹.
   Given: H–H 436, Br–Br 193, H–Br 366
   Required: ΔH
   Formula: ΔH = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed)
   Substitution: = (436 + 193) − 2(366)
   Calculation: = 629 − 732
   Final Answer: ΔH = −103 kJ mol⁻¹

2. Calculate ΔH for N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391 kJ mol⁻¹.
   Given: N≡N 945, H–H 436, N–H 391
   Required: ΔH
   Formula: ΔH = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed)
   Substitution: = (945 + 3 × 436) − (6 × 391)
   Calculation: = 2253 − 2346
   Final Answer: ΔH = −93 kJ mol⁻¹

3. Calculate ΔH for CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 463 kJ mol⁻¹.
   Given: C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O 805, O–H 463
   Required: ΔH
   Formula: ΔH = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed)
   Substitution: = (4 × 413 + 2 × 498) − (2 × 805 + 4 × 463)
   Calculation: = 2648 − 3462
   Final Answer: ΔH = −814 kJ mol⁻¹

NBF Chapter 8 Exercises (135–136):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. If the ΔH value is negative then the reaction will be: → A (Exothermic) | Negative ΔH = heat released.
ii. All chemical reactions involve: → C (Energy changes) | Bonds break and form in every reaction.
iii. Which is not released in aerobic respiration? → D (Lactic acid) | Lactic acid forms in anaerobic respiration.
iv. A catalyst increases the rate of a chemical reaction by: → D (None of these) | It LOWERS the activation energy, which is not among options (a)–(c). ΔH is unchanged.
v. Activation energy of a chemical reaction must be ____ the average kinetic energy of reacting molecules. → B (Greater than) | Only molecules with energy above average can react.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) Define exothermic and endothermic reactions.
   Answer: Exothermic: a reaction that gives out heat to the surroundings (ΔH negative), e.g. burning of fuels. Endothermic: a reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings (ΔH positive), e.g. decomposition of limestone.
(ii) Define enthalpy of a chemical reaction.
   Answer: The amount of heat evolved or absorbed when a reaction takes place (at constant pressure), shown as ΔH in kJ mol⁻¹; negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions.
(iii) What is anaerobic respiration?
   Answer: Breakdown of glucose without oxygen to release a small amount of energy, producing lactic acid in muscles: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₃H₆O₃ + energy.
(iv) Define activation energy.
   Answer: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a successful (effective) collision that leads to a reaction.
(v) What is the role of a catalyst in a chemical reaction?
   Answer: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful and the reaction is faster. It is not used up and does not change ΔH or the products.
(vi) Differentiate between aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
   Answer: 

— Q3–Q7. Descriptive questions —
3. How can you determine the enthalpy of a chemical reaction?
   Answer: Using bond energies:
1. Write the balanced equation with all substances as gases.
2. Identify all bonds broken in the reactants and all bonds formed in the products, counting each.
3. Add up the energy absorbed to break bonds (Σ broken) and the energy released when forming bonds (Σ formed).
4. ΔH = Σ(broken) − Σ(formed). A negative result means exothermic; positive means endothermic.
(ΔH can also be measured experimentally with a calorimeter from the temperature change of the surroundings.)
4. Explain how the process of respiration provides us energy.
   Answer: In our cells, glucose from digested food is oxidised by oxygen in aerobic respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy. This reaction is exothermic; the energy released is stored in ATP and used for muscle movement, heartbeat, brain function, growth and keeping the body at 37 °C. During intense exercise, when oxygen is short, anaerobic respiration gives a little extra energy and lactic acid. When glucose runs low, stored lipids are oxidised as reserve energy.
5. Draw a labelled reaction pathway diagram for an exothermic and an endothermic reaction.
   Answer: See the two diagrams in Tables & Diagrams. Exothermic: reactants high, products low, ΔH arrow pointing down (negative). Endothermic: reactants low, products high, ΔH arrow pointing up (positive). In both, label energy and progress axes, Eₐ from reactants to the peak, and a lower dashed catalysed curve.
6. Calculate the enthalpy of reaction between hydrogen and chlorine to form hydrogen chloride. H–H 436, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 432 kJ mol⁻¹.
   Answer: 
7. Justify the statement that the process of respiration is crucial for us.
   Answer: Every life process needs energy: muscle contraction, heartbeat, breathing, nerve impulses, digestion, making new cells and keeping body temperature constant. Respiration is the only process that releases this energy from food (glucose and lipids) inside our cells. Without it, cells would stop working within minutes – which is why we die quickly without oxygen.

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Briefly describe how a catalyst affects (a) the reaction rate (b) the activation energy.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Using bond energies, calculate ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl. H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431 kJ mol⁻¹.
   Answer: 

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Which type of reaction has a positive sign of enthalpy change? Give one example.
   Answer: Endothermic reactions. Example: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ (or photosynthesis).

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] What is meant by activation energy? How does a catalyst affect it?
   Answer: Minimum energy colliding particles need for a successful collision. A catalyst lowers it by providing a different reaction pathway.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] What is activation energy? What is meant by a successful collision?
   Answer: Activation energy: minimum energy for a successful collision. Successful (effective) collision: a collision with energy ≥ Eₐ and the correct orientation, so that bonds break and new bonds form.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] Differentiate exothermic and endothermic reactions with one example each.
   Answer: Exothermic: heat released, ΔH −, e.g. C + O₂ → CO₂. Endothermic: heat absorbed, ΔH +, e.g. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22); Annual 2025] Find ΔH for H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g); H–H 436, I–I 151, H–I 299 kJ mol⁻¹.
   Answer: 

8. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Draw and label a reaction pathway diagram of an exothermic or endothermic reaction showing activation energy, reactants and products.
   Answer: See the labelled diagrams in Tables & Diagrams.

9. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] What kind of reaction occurs in respiration? Give its reaction.
   Answer: An exothermic (redox/oxidation) reaction: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy.

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What are exothermic reactions? Give an example.
   Answer: Reactions that release heat to the surroundings (ΔH negative), e.g. CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

11. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Draw a labelled pathway sketch of an uncatalysed exothermic reaction.
   Answer: Reactants high on the left, hump (Eₐ) in the middle, products lower on the right; ΔH arrow down between reactant and product levels (negative).

12. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What are endothermic reactions? Give an example with chemical equation.
   Answer: Reactions absorbing heat (ΔH positive), e.g. N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH = +180 kJ mol⁻¹.

13. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] (a) What type of energy change occurs during bond breaking? Name the process. (b) Write one difference between bond breaking and bond making in terms of energy change.
   Answer: (a) Energy is absorbed; bond breaking is endothermic. (b) Bond breaking absorbs energy (endothermic) whereas bond making releases energy (exothermic).

14. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] How does the energy profile diagram for an endothermic reaction differ from that of an exothermic reaction in terms of activation energy and enthalpy change?
   Answer: Endothermic: products above reactants, ΔH positive, and Eₐ is larger than ΔH (peak above products). Exothermic: products below reactants, ΔH negative; Eₐ measured from the higher reactant level is relatively smaller.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] (a) What is meant by exothermic and endothermic reactions? (b) Calculate ΔH for H₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2HF(g). H–H 436, F–F 155, H–F 567 kJ mol⁻¹.
   Answer: (a) Exothermic: releases heat, ΔH negative (combustion). Endothermic: absorbs heat, ΔH positive (photosynthesis).
(b) Bonds broken = 436 + 155 = 591 kJ; bonds formed = 2 × 567 = 1134 kJ. ΔH = 591 − 1134 = −543 kJ mol⁻¹ (strongly exothermic).

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Draw a well-labelled reaction pathway diagram for an exothermic and an endothermic reaction showing reactants, products, activation energy and enthalpy change. Interpret how a catalyst affects the energy profile.
   Answer: Draw both diagrams (see Tables & Diagrams). Interpretation: a catalyst gives a lower dashed hump – the activation energy is lowered for both forward and reverse reactions; the energies of reactants and products, and therefore ΔH, stay the same; more collisions succeed so the rate increases.

3. Explain why bond breaking is endothermic and bond making is exothermic. Use this idea to explain why burning methane is exothermic.
   Answer: Breaking a bond requires energy to overcome the attraction between the atoms; forming a bond lets atoms reach a lower-energy, more stable arrangement and the extra energy is released. In CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, the energy released in forming 2 C=O and 4 O–H bonds (≈ 3462 kJ) is greater than the energy absorbed to break 4 C–H and 2 O=O bonds (≈ 2648 kJ), so overall ≈ −814 kJ: exothermic.

chapters.title: Chemical Equilibrium
chapters.introduction:
Some reactions never finish: the products react to give back the reactants. These are reversible reactions, shown with the ⇌ sign. In a closed system a reversible reaction reaches chemical equilibrium, a dynamic state where the forward and reverse rates are equal. This short unit also shows how changing conditions (heating, adding water) shifts the equilibrium, using hydrated copper(II) sulphate and cobalt(II) chloride as examples.

Exam focus (3 summative SLOs but asked every year): ⇌ symbol, why a closed system is needed, conditions for equilibrium, effect of heating and adding water on CuSO₄·5H₂O and CoCl₂·6H₂O equilibria.

══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
Exam focus (3 summative SLOs but asked every year): ⇌ symbol, why a closed system is needed, conditions for equilibrium, effect of heating and adding water on CuSO₄·5H₂O and CoCl₂·6H₂O equilibria.

══ 9.1 Irreversible and reversible reactions (pp. 138) ══
A complete (irreversible) reaction goes in one direction only until the reactants are used up, e.g. burning of fuel: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O. Shown with a single arrow (→).
A reversible reaction is one in which the products can react together to re-form the original reactants under the same conditions. It proceeds in both directions at the same time and does not go to completion – a mixture of reactants and products remains. Shown with a double arrow ⇌.
- Forward reaction: reactants → products (left to right).
- Reverse (backward) reaction: products → reactants (right to left).
Examples:
- 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g) (Contact process, 450 °C, 200 atm)
- N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) (Haber process, 400 °C, 200 atm)
- N₂(g) + 2O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO₂(g) (electric spark)
- H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g)
- Physical: liquid ⇌ vapour in a closed bottle; CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) in fizzy drinks.
[Table: Irreversible vs reversible reactions]
Irreversible | Reversible
• Goes in one direction only | Goes in both directions
• Goes to completion | Does not go to completion
• Shown by → | Shown by ⇌
• Products cannot re-form reactants | Products react to re-form reactants
• No equilibrium | Reaches equilibrium in a closed system
• e.g. burning of fuel | e.g. N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
ناقابلِ رجعت تعامل صرف ایک سمت میں مکمل ہوتا ہے (→)۔ قابلِ رجعت تعامل دونوں سمتوں میں ایک ساتھ چلتا ہے اور مکمل نہیں ہوتا (⇌)، جیسے امونیا کا بننا N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃۔

══ 9.2 Chemical equilibrium: a dynamic state (pp. 138–140) ══
Imagine SO₂ and O₂ sealed in a container:
1. At first only reactants are present: the forward rate is highest and the reverse rate is zero.
2. As SO₃ forms, reactant concentrations fall, so the forward rate decreases.
3. SO₃ starts to decompose: the reverse rate increases as [SO₃] rises.
4. Eventually forward rate = reverse rate. From now on the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant: the system is at chemical equilibrium.
Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant.
It is dynamic: the reactions do not stop; molecules keep reacting in both directions, but there is no overall change. (A physical example: in a closed bottle of liquid, evaporation and condensation happen at the same rate.)
Conditions needed (and to keep it unchanged):
1. A closed system – nothing can enter or escape. In an open system a gaseous product escapes and the reverse reaction cannot happen, so equilibrium is never reached.
2. Constant temperature.
3. Constant pressure/volume.
4. No change in concentration of any reactant or product (nothing added or removed).
Equilibrium can be reached starting from pure reactants, pure products or a mixture.
Key Point: - Equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate.
- Dynamic, not static: both reactions continue.
- Concentrations constant (not necessarily equal).
- Needs a closed system.
Exam Tip: Common mistake: at equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are CONSTANT, not EQUAL.
کیمیائی توازن وہ حالت ہے جب آگے اور پیچھے کے تعاملات کی رفتار برابر ہو جائے اور متعاملات و حاصلات کی مقدار مستقل رہے۔ یہ حرکی توازن ہے: تعاملات رکتے نہیں، دونوں طرف جاری رہتے ہیں۔ اس کے لیے بند نظام، مستقل درجہ حرارت، دباؤ اور مقدار ضروری ہیں۔

══ 9.3 Changing conditions: hydrated salts, heat and water (pp. 140) ══
Changing a condition (temperature, adding/removing a substance) disturbs the equilibrium and the reaction shifts in the direction that tends to reduce the change.
Copper(II) sulphate:
CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) (blue) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) (white) + 5H₂O(g)
- Heating blue hydrated crystals drives off water → equilibrium shifts forward (right): white anhydrous CuSO₄ forms. The forward reaction is endothermic, so heat favours it.
- Adding water to white anhydrous CuSO₄ → shifts backward (left): it turns blue again (and becomes warm – the reverse reaction is exothermic). This is the test for water.
Cobalt(II) chloride:
CoCl₂·6H₂O(s) (pink) ⇌ CoCl₂(s) (blue) + 6H₂O
- Heating → shifts right: pink turns blue (water removed).
- Adding water (or cooling in moist air) → shifts left: blue turns pink. Cobalt chloride paper is used to test for water.
Fizzy drinks: CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq). Under pressure in the sealed bottle CO₂ dissolves (forward). Opening the bottle releases pressure and CO₂ escapes, so the equilibrium shifts back and bubbles appear. Closing the lid stops the bubbling.
Activity (textbook): heat 5 g of blue hydrated CuSO₄ – it turns white; cool and add a few drops of water – it turns blue again. (CuSO₄ is harmful; work with your teacher.)
[Table: Colour changes]
Substance | Hydrated | Anhydrous | Heating | Adding water
• Copper(II) sulphate | CuSO₄·5H₂O blue | CuSO₄ white | Blue → white (shift right) | White → blue (shift left)
• Cobalt(II) chloride | CoCl₂·6H₂O pink | CoCl₂ blue | Pink → blue (shift right) | Blue → pink (shift left)

1. Rates approaching equilibrium: The forward rate falls and the reverse rate rises until they become equal at equilibrium.

chapters.definitions:
• Irreversible (complete) reaction (ناقابلِ رجعت تعامل) [p. 138]: A reaction in which all reactants are converted into products and the products cannot re-form the reactants.
• Reversible reaction (قابلِ رجعت تعامل) [p. 138]: A reaction in which the products can react together to re-form the original reactants; it proceeds in both directions under the same conditions.
• Forward reaction (آگے کا تعامل) [p. 139]: The reaction from reactants to products (left to right).
• Reverse (backward) reaction (پیچھے کا تعامل) [p. 139]: The reaction from products back to reactants (right to left).
• Chemical equilibrium (کیمیائی توازن) [p. 139]: The state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so concentrations remain constant.
• Dynamic equilibrium (حرکی توازن) [p. 139]: An equilibrium in which both forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates, so there is no net change.
• Closed system (بند نظام) [p. 140]: A system from which no substance can escape and into which none can enter.
• Hydrated salt (آبیدہ نمک) [p. 140]: A salt containing water of crystallisation, e.g. CuSO₄·5H₂O.
• Anhydrous salt (بے آب نمک) [p. 140]: A salt without water of crystallisation, e.g. white CuSO₄.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Reversible (قابلِ رجعت): Can go both ways
• Irreversible (ناقابلِ رجعت): One way only
• Equilibrium (توازن): Balanced state
• Dynamic (حرکی): Always moving
• Closed system (بند نظام): Nothing enters or leaves
• Forward reaction (پیش رو تعامل): Reactants to products
• Reverse reaction (الٹا تعامل): Products to reactants
• Hydrated (آبیدہ): Contains water of crystallisation
• Anhydrous (بے آب): Without water
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Reversible reaction sign: ⇌ (Double half-arrows)
• Condition for equilibrium: rate (forward) = rate (reverse)
• Hydrated copper(II) sulphate: CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue) (Anhydrous: CuSO₄ (white))
• Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride: CoCl₂·6H₂O (pink) (Anhydrous: CoCl₂ (blue))

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g)  2SO₃(g) — Contact process (450 °C, 200 atm).
• N₂(g) + 3H₂(g)  2NH₃(g) — Haber process (400 °C, 200 atm).
• N₂(g) + 2O₂(g)  2NO₂(g) — In an electric spark.
• H₂(g) + I₂(g)  2HI(g) — At equilibrium H₂, I₂ and HI are all present.
• CuSO₄·5H₂O(s)  CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(g) — Blue ⇌ white. Heat shifts right; water shifts left.
• CoCl₂·6H₂O(s)  CoCl₂(s) + 6H₂O — Pink ⇌ blue. Heat shifts right; water shifts left.
• CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)  H₂CO₃(aq) — Fizzy drinks: opening the bottle shifts it left.
• C(s) + H₂O(g)  CO(g) + H₂(g) — Coal with steam (review Q3).
• CO(g) + 3H₂(g)  CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) — Methane formation with a catalyst (review Q3).
• 2BrCl(g)  Br₂(g) + Cl₂(g) — Decomposition of bromine chloride (Think Tank).

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. At equilibrium, are the concentrations of reactants and products equal?
   Answer: Not necessarily. They are constant, but can have any values.
2. Can equilibrium be reached by starting with only products?
   Answer: Yes. The reverse reaction starts first and the forward reaction builds up until rates are equal.
3. Why does burning a candle in open air not reach equilibrium?
   Answer: The products (CO₂, H₂O) escape and the reaction is irreversible.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. How can anhydrous copper(II) sulphate be used to test whether a liquid contains water?
   Answer: Add a few drops of the liquid: if the white powder turns blue, water is present.
2. Silica gel in shoe boxes contains a little cobalt chloride. Why does it change colour?
   Answer: Blue anhydrous CoCl₂ turns pink as it absorbs moisture, showing the gel is saturated with water.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue) ⇌ CuSO₄ (white) + 5H₂O. How will heating affect the equilibrium? [FBISE Annual 2026]
   Solution: Heating supplies energy for the endothermic forward reaction and drives off water vapour, so the equilibrium shifts to the right: blue hydrated crystals turn into white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate.

2. CoCl₂·6H₂O (pink) ⇌ CoCl₂ (blue) + 6H₂O. Describe the effect of adding water. [FBISE Annual 2026]
   Solution: Adding water increases the amount of product, so the equilibrium shifts to the left (reverse): blue anhydrous cobalt chloride absorbs water and turns pink (hydrated).

3. When H₂ and I₂ are sealed in a flask at 25 °C, which substances are present at equilibrium?
   Solution: H₂, I₂ and HI – a reversible reaction never goes to completion, so reactants and products are all present.
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 9 Exercises (141–142):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. Which is true about the equilibrium state? → D (Both forward and reverse reactions continue at the same rate) | Equilibrium is dynamic.
ii. H₂ and I₂ are sealed in a flask at 25 °C: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). Which substances will be present in the equilibrium mixture? → D (H₂, I₂ and HI) | All reactants and products remain.
iii. Concentrations of reactants and products at equilibrium remain unchanged if: → D (all of the above are observed) | All three conditions are needed.
iv. Which of the following does not happen when a system is at equilibrium? → A (Forward and reverse reactions stop) | They never stop – equilibrium is dynamic.
v. In an irreversible reaction equilibrium is: → C (never established) | Only reversible reactions reach equilibrium.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) Differentiate between forward and reverse reactions.
   Answer: The forward reaction converts reactants into products (left → right), e.g. N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. The reverse reaction converts products back into reactants (right → left), e.g. 2NH₃ → N₂ + 3H₂. In a reversible reaction both occur at the same time.
(ii) What is chemical equilibrium?
   Answer: The state of a reversible reaction in a closed system where the forward and reverse reactions take place at the same rate, so the concentrations of reactants and products remain constant. It is dynamic.
(iii) Write two chemical equations of reversible reactions.
   Answer: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g); 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g). (Also CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O.)
(iv) Write down the conditions for equilibrium.
   Answer: (1) Closed system (2) constant temperature (3) constant pressure/volume (4) concentrations of reactants and products not changed by adding or removing substances.

— Q3–Q4 and Think Tank —
3. Coal reacts with hot steam to form CO and H₂. These react further in the presence of a catalyst to give methane and water vapour. Write forward and reverse reactions.
   Answer: Step 1: forward C(s) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + H₂(g); reverse CO(g) + H₂(g) → C(s) + H₂O(g). Overall: C(s) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂(g).
Step 2: forward CO(g) + 3H₂(g) → CH₄(g) + H₂O(g); reverse CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) → CO(g) + 3H₂(g). Overall: CO(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ CH₄(g) + H₂O(g) (catalyst: Ni).
4. How does temperature affect the cobalt chloride equilibrium?
   Answer: CoCl₂·6H₂O (pink) ⇌ CoCl₂ (blue) + 6H₂O. The forward reaction (losing water) is endothermic. Raising the temperature shifts the equilibrium to the right: pink turns blue. Lowering the temperature (in moist air) or adding water shifts it to the left: blue turns pink.
TT1. Bromine chloride (BrCl) decomposes to form chlorine and bromine. Write the reversible chemical equation.
   Answer: 2BrCl(g) ⇌ Br₂(g) + Cl₂(g)
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] What is meant by a reversible chemical reaction? Does it ever go to completion? Give reason.
   Answer: A reaction in which products react to re-form reactants, so it goes both ways at once. It never goes to completion, because as soon as products form, some of them change back into reactants; a mixture always remains.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] CoCl₂·6H₂O (pink) ⇌ CoCl₂ (blue) + 6H₂O. Describe the effect of addition of water on the equilibrium.
   Answer: Adding water (a product) shifts the equilibrium backward (left); blue CoCl₂ absorbs water and turns pink CoCl₂·6H₂O.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue) ⇌ CuSO₄ (white) + 5H₂O. How will heating affect the equilibrium?
   Answer: Heating drives the endothermic forward reaction: equilibrium shifts right, blue crystals turn white.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22); Annual 2025] Why is a closed system necessary for a reversible reaction to achieve equilibrium?
   Answer: In an open system, products (especially gases) escape, so they cannot react back to form reactants; the reverse reaction cannot keep pace and the forward reaction runs towards completion. In a closed system all substances stay, so the reverse rate can rise until it equals the forward rate.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] What happens when water is added to anhydrous copper(II) sulphate? How does this change in physical condition redirect the reversible reaction?
   Answer: White anhydrous CuSO₄ turns blue (and warms up) as it forms CuSO₄·5H₂O. Adding water increases the product side, so the equilibrium CuSO₄·5H₂O ⇌ CuSO₄ + 5H₂O shifts backward (left).

6. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] State the physical change observed by adding water to CuSO₄. Also write its reversible balanced equation.
   Answer: White powder turns blue. CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) ⇌ CuSO₄·5H₂O(s).

7. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] What is chemical equilibrium? State the conditions for a reversible reaction to reach equilibrium in a closed system.
   Answer: Equilibrium: forward rate = reverse rate; concentrations constant. Conditions: closed system, constant temperature, constant pressure/volume, no addition or removal of substances.

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Write three conditions required for chemical equilibrium.
   Answer: Closed system; constant temperature; constant pressure (and no change in concentrations).

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What is a reversible reaction? Give one example.
   Answer: A reaction that proceeds in both directions, products re-forming reactants: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃.

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Consider CoCl₂·2H₂O(s) + heat ⇌ CoCl₂(s) + 2H₂O(g). Predict the direction when (a) the system is heated (b) water is added (c) water is removed.
   Answer: (a) Forward (right) – heat favours the endothermic forward reaction. (b) Reverse (left) – more product. (c) Forward (right) – removing a product.

11. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Give the ways a closed system contributes to the establishment of equilibrium in reversible reactions.
   Answer: It prevents products from escaping, so they can react back; it keeps the total amount of matter constant; it allows the reverse rate to increase until it equals the forward rate; it keeps pressure constant for gaseous systems.

12. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] Define a reversible reaction and explain the conditions under which it reaches equilibrium.
   Answer: A reaction in which products can re-form reactants (⇌). It reaches equilibrium in a closed system at constant temperature and pressure when the forward and reverse rates become equal.

13. Why is chemical equilibrium called dynamic?
   Answer: Because the forward and reverse reactions do not stop; they continue at equal rates, so there is no net change.

14. Why do bubbles appear when a cold-drink bottle is opened and stop when it is closed?
   Answer: CO₂(g) + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃. Opening lowers pressure; CO₂ escapes and the equilibrium shifts left (bubbles). Closing lets pressure build so the equilibrium is re-established.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. Describe how the establishment of equilibrium occurs when SO₂ and O₂ are sealed in a container. Why is it called dynamic equilibrium?
   Answer: At the start only SO₂ and O₂ are present: the forward rate is maximum and the reverse rate is zero. As SO₃ forms, [SO₂] and [O₂] fall so the forward rate decreases; [SO₃] rises so the reverse reaction (2SO₃ → 2SO₂ + O₂) speeds up. Eventually the two rates become equal: 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ is at equilibrium and all concentrations remain constant. It is dynamic because molecules continue to react in both directions; only the net amounts stop changing.

2. Describe an experiment to show the reversible reaction of copper(II) sulphate. Write the equation and explain the colour changes in terms of equilibrium.
   Answer: Put about 5 g of blue hydrated copper(II) sulphate in a dry test tube and heat gently: water vapour condenses at the mouth and the solid turns white – CuSO₄·5H₂O → CuSO₄ + 5H₂O (forward, endothermic; heat shifts equilibrium right). Let it cool, then add a few drops of water with a dropper: the white powder turns blue and becomes warm – CuSO₄ + 5H₂O → CuSO₄·5H₂O (reverse, exothermic; adding a product shifts equilibrium left). Overall: CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) ⇌ CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O. Safety: CuSO₄ is harmful – wear goggles and work under teacher supervision.

chapters.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
chapters.introduction:
Vinegar, lemon juice and toilet cleaners contain acids; soap, antacids and drain cleaners contain bases. This unit compares the Arrhenius and Brønsted–Lowry theories, strong and weak acids and bases with their dissociation equations, the difference between bases and alkalis, the characteristic reactions of acids (with metals, bases and carbonates) and bases (with acids and ammonium salts), amphoteric substances, and acid rain.

Exam focus (9 summative SLOs): Brønsted–Lowry acid/base identification (NH₃ + H₂O, HCl + NH₃), strong vs weak with dissociation equations (HCl, H₂SO₄, HNO₃, CH₃COOH, NaOH), reactions of HCl with Zn/Mg, NaOH, Na₂CO₃/CaCO₃, NaOH with NH₄Cl. A long question on acid or base reactions appears in nearly every paper.

══ 10.1 Properties of acids and bases; Arrhenius theory (pp. 144–145) ══
Everyday acids: vinegar (acetic acid), lemon/oranges (citric acid), aspirin, cola drinks, tomatoes, toilet cleaners. Everyday bases: drain cleaner (NaOH), antacids (Mg(OH)₂), baking soda, soap, toothpaste.
Arrhenius theory (1887, Svante Arrhenius):
- An acid ionises in water to produce H⁺ ions: HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃^-; H₂SO₄ → 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻.
- A base ionises in water to produce OH⁻ ions: NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq); KOH → K⁺ + OH⁻.
Limitations: it applies only to aqueous solutions, and cannot explain why CO₂ or SO₂ (no H) are acidic or why NH₃ (no OH) is basic.
[Table: Table 10.1 – Properties of acids and bases]
Property | Acids | Bases
• Taste | Sour | Bitter
• Blue litmus | Turns red | No effect
• Red litmus | No effect | Turns blue
• Effect on skin | Corrosive | Corrosive (slippery feel)
• Aqueous solution | Conducts electricity | Conducts electricity
• Ions in water | H⁺ (H₃O⁺) | OH⁻
• pH | Less than 7 | More than 7
