Name | Formula | Common use
• Hydrochloric acid | HCl | Cleaning metals and bricks, removing scale from boilers
• Nitric acid | HNO₃ | Fertilizers, explosives
• Sulphuric acid | H₂SO₄ | Chemicals, drugs, dyes, paints, explosives, batteries
• Phosphoric acid | H₃PO₄ | Fertilizers, acidulant in food
• Sodium hydroxide | NaOH | Soap making, drain cleaners
• Potassium hydroxide | KOH | Liquid soap, shaving cream
• Calcium hydroxide | Ca(OH)₂ | Mortar, plaster, cement
• Magnesium hydroxide | Mg(OH)₂ | Antacid, laxative
ارہینیس نظریہ: تیزاب وہ ہے جو پانی میں H⁺ آئن دے اور اساس وہ ہے جو OH⁻ آئن دے۔ یہ نظریہ صرف پانی والے محلول پر لاگو ہوتا ہے اور CO₂ کی تیزابیت یا NH₃ کی اساسیت کی وضاحت نہیں کرتا۔

══ 10.2 Brønsted–Lowry theory; amphoteric water (pp. 145–147) ══
Brønsted–Lowry theory (1923, J. N. Brønsted and T. M. Lowry):
- An acid is a proton (H⁺) donor.
- A base is a proton acceptor.
Examples:
- HCl(g) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq): HCl donates H⁺ → acid; H₂O accepts H⁺ → base (forms hydronium ion H₃O⁺).
- NH₃(g) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄^+(aq) + OH⁻(aq): H₂O donates H⁺ → acid; NH₃ accepts → base. This explains where OH⁻ comes from in ammonia solution.
- HCl + NH₃ → NH₄^+ + Cl⁻ (NH₄Cl): HCl acid, NH₃ base – no water needed.
Water is amphoteric: it acts as a base with HCl and as an acid with NH₃. Amphoteric substances react as both acids and bases.
Self-ionisation of water: H₂O + H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻ (or H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻).
All Arrhenius acids are Brønsted–Lowry acids, but the Brønsted–Lowry definition of base is much wider (NH₃, CO₃²⁻, HCO₃^- are bases).
Spotting them: the acid loses an H⁺ and becomes more negative (HCl → Cl⁻); the base gains H⁺ and becomes more positive (H₂O → H₃O⁺; NH₃ → NH₄^+).
[Table: Arrhenius vs Brønsted–Lowry]
 | Arrhenius | Brønsted–Lowry
• Acid | Gives H⁺ in water | Proton donor
• Base | Gives OH⁻ in water | Proton acceptor
• Solvent | Water only | Any (or none)
• NH₃ | Not explained | Base (accepts H⁺)
• Example | HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻ | HCl + NH₃ → NH₄^+ + Cl⁻
Exam Tip: In every Brønsted–Lowry reaction, find the species that loses H⁺ (acid) and the one that gains it (base). Water can be either.
برونسٹڈ لوری نظریہ: تیزاب پروٹون دینے والا اور اساس پروٹون لینے والا ہے۔ HCl پانی کو پروٹون دیتا ہے (HCl تیزاب، پانی اساس)؛ NH₃ پانی سے پروٹون لیتا ہے (NH₃ اساس، پانی تیزاب)۔ اس طرح پانی دونوں کام کرتا ہے، اسے ایمفوٹیرک کہتے ہیں۔

══ 10.3 Strong and weak acids and bases; dissociation equations (pp. 147) ══
Acids and bases ionise (dissociate) in water to different extents.
- Strong acid: ionises completely (100%) in water. Single arrow →.
- HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
- HNO₃(aq) → H⁺(aq) + NO₃^-(aq)
- H₂SO₄(aq) → 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq)
- HI(aq) → H⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq)
- Weak acid: ionises partially; most molecules stay un-ionised. Equilibrium arrow ⇌.
- CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) (ethanoic/acetic acid in vinegar, only about 5% ionised)
- HNO₂ ⇌ H⁺ + NO₂^-; H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃^-
- Strong base: ionises completely: NaOH(aq) → Na⁺ + OH⁻; KOH → K⁺ + OH⁻; Ca(OH)₂ → Ca²⁺ + 2OH⁻.
- Weak base: ionises slightly, producing few OH⁻ ions: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄^+ + OH⁻; Al(OH)₃.
Strength ≠ concentration: a strong acid can be dilute, and a weak acid can be concentrated. Strength is about the degree of ionisation.
[Table: Strong vs weak acids]
Strong acid | Weak acid
• Ionises completely in water | Ionises partially
• Many H⁺ ions | Few H⁺ ions
• Shown with → | Shown with ⇌
• Reacts vigorously with Mg, conducts well | Reacts slowly, conducts poorly
• HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄ | CH₃COOH, H₂CO₃, citric acid
طاقتور تیزاب پانی میں مکمل طور پر آئنوں میں ٹوٹ جاتا ہے (HCl، HNO₃، H₂SO₄)، جبکہ کمزور تیزاب صرف جزوی طور پر (ایسیٹک ایسڈ صرف تقریباً 5%)۔ اسی طرح NaOH طاقتور اور NH₃ کمزور اساس ہے۔

══ 10.4 Bases, alkalis and metal oxides; amphoteric oxides (pp. 148–149) ══
- Bases are oxides or hydroxides of metals: Na₂O, MgO, CaO, NaOH, Cu(OH)₂, Fe(OH)₃.
- Alkalis are water-soluble bases: NaOH, KOH, Ca(OH)₂ (slightly), NH₄OH/NH₃(aq). All alkalis are bases, but not all bases are alkalis – Cu(OH)₂, Al(OH)₃, Fe(OH)₃ are insoluble bases.
- Metal oxides form when metals burn in oxygen: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O; 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
- Soluble metal oxides react with water to form hydroxides (alkalis): Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH; CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂. The oxide ion O²⁻ accepts a proton from water: O²⁻ + H₂O → 2OH⁻.
- Amphoteric oxides and hydroxides react with both acids and bases: Al₂O₃, Al(OH)₃, ZnO, Zn(OH)₂.
- Non-metal oxides (CO₂, SO₂, NO₂) are acidic: they dissolve in water to form acids.
دھاتوں کے آکسائیڈ اور ہائیڈرو آکسائیڈ اساس ہیں؛ جو پانی میں گھل جائیں وہ الکلی ہیں (NaOH، KOH)۔ ہر الکلی اساس ہے مگر ہر اساس الکلی نہیں۔ Al₂O₃ اور ZnO ایمفوٹیرک ہیں جو تیزاب اور اساس دونوں سے تعامل کرتے ہیں۔

══ 10.5 Reactions of acids (pp. 148) ══
1. Acid + reactive metal → salt + hydrogen (bubbles of H₂; burns with a pop):
- Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
- Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)
- Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
(Copper, silver and gold do not react with dilute acids.)
2. Acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide (effervescence; CO₂ turns limewater milky):
- Na₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
- CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
- CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂
- NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂
3. Acid + base → salt + water (neutralisation, exothermic):
- HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l)
- H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O
- 2HCl + Mg(OH)₂ → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O (antacid)
- H₂SO₄ + Mg(OH)₂ → MgSO₄ + 2H₂O
- HNO₃ + NH₄OH → NH₄NO₃ + H₂O
- 2HCl + CuO → CuCl₂ + H₂O (metal oxide)
- Ionic equation for all neutralisations: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l)
Other properties: sour taste; turn blue litmus red; corrode metals.
Exam Tip: For “describe reactions of HCl with Zn, NaOH and Na₂CO₃” give one balanced equation for each AND one observation: bubbles of H₂; warming (no visible change) / neutral solution; fizzing CO₂ that turns limewater milky.
تیزاب کے تعاملات: (1) دھات + تیزاب ← نمک + ہائیڈروجن (Zn + 2HCl ← ZnCl₂ + H₂)۔ (2) کاربونیٹ + تیزاب ← نمک + پانی + CO₂ (جھاگ بنتا ہے)۔ (3) تیزاب + اساس ← نمک + پانی (تعدیل)۔

══ 10.6 Reactions of bases (pp. 149) ══
1. Base + acid → salt + water (neutralisation): NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O; 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.
2. Base (alkali) + ammonium salt, warmed → salt + ammonia + water. Ammonia gas (pungent smell) turns damp red litmus blue. This is the test for ammonium ions.
- NaOH(aq) + NH₄Cl(s) → NaCl(aq) + NH₃(g) + H₂O(l)
- Ca(OH)₂ + 2NH₄Cl → CaCl₂ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O (laboratory preparation of ammonia)
- 2NaOH + (NH₄)₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2NH₃ + 2H₂O
Other properties: bitter taste; soapy, slippery feel; turn red litmus blue; aqueous solutions conduct electricity.
اساس کے تعاملات: (1) تیزاب کے ساتھ نمک اور پانی۔ (2) امونیم نمک کے ساتھ گرم کرنے پر امونیا گیس نکلتی ہے جو گیلے سرخ لٹمس کو نیلا کر دیتی ہے: NaOH + NH₄Cl ← NaCl + NH₃ + H₂O۔

══ 10.7 Acid rain (pp. 148–149) ══
Normal rain is slightly acidic (pH about 5.6) because CO₂ dissolves in it to form carbonic acid.
Acid rain is rain (or snow, fog) with a pH below about 5.6, made more acidic by sulphuric and nitric acids formed from SO₂ and nitrogen oxides (NO, NO₂) released by burning fossil fuels, power stations, factories and vehicle engines.
- SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃; 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄
- 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃
Effects (linked to properties of acids):
- Acids react with carbonates: marble and limestone buildings and statues are eaten away: CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂; CaCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂.
- Acids react with metals: bridges, railings, cars and pipelines corrode faster.
- Acidity: lakes and rivers become acidic, killing fish and aquatic life; soil nutrients (Ca, Mg, K) are leached away and toxic aluminium is released, damaging forests and crops.
- Health: SO₂ and acid mist irritate lungs.
(Details in Chapter 11.)
تیزابی بارش وہ بارش ہے جس کا pH تقریباً 5.6 سے کم ہو، جس میں SO₂ اور نائٹروجن کے آکسائیڈز سے بننے والے سلفیورک اور نائٹرک ایسڈ ملے ہوں۔ یہ سنگِ مرمر کی عمارتوں کو کھا جاتی ہے، دھاتوں کو زنگ لگاتی ہے، جھیلوں کی مچھلیاں مار دیتی ہے اور جنگلات و فصلوں کو نقصان پہنچاتی ہے۔
chapters.shortNotes:
══ Chapter 10 in one page

- Arrhenius: acid gives H⁺, base gives OH⁻ (water only). Brønsted–Lowry: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor. Water is amphoteric. H₃O⁺ = hydronium.

- Base + NH₄^+ salt (warm) → salt + NH₃ + H₂O (NH₃ turns damp red litmus blue).
- Acid rain: pH < 5.6; H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ from SO₂ and NOₓ; dissolves marble (CaCO₃), corrodes metals, kills fish, damages forests.

تیزاب پروٹون دیتا ہے اور اساس لیتی ہے (برونسٹڈ لوری)۔ طاقتور تیزاب مکمل اور کمزور جزوی آئنائز ہوتا ہے۔ تیزاب + دھات ← نمک + ہائیڈروجن؛ تیزاب + کاربونیٹ ← نمک + پانی + CO₂؛ تیزاب + اساس ← نمک + پانی۔ اساس + امونیم نمک ← امونیا۔ تیزابی بارش سنگِ مرمر کو نقصان پہنچاتی ہے۔

chapters.definitions:
• Arrhenius acid (ارہینیس تیزاب) [p. 144]: A substance that ionises in water to produce H⁺ ions.
• Arrhenius base (ارہینیس اساس) [p. 144]: A substance that ionises in water to produce OH⁻ ions.
• Brønsted–Lowry acid (برونسٹڈ لوری تیزاب) [p. 145]: A proton (H⁺) donor.
• Brønsted–Lowry base (برونسٹڈ لوری اساس) [p. 145]: A proton (H⁺) acceptor.
• Amphoteric substance (ایمفوٹیرک مادہ) [p. 146]: A substance that can react both as an acid and as a base, e.g. water, Al₂O₃, ZnO.
• Strong acid (طاقتور تیزاب) [p. 147]: An acid that ionises completely in aqueous solution, e.g. HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄.
• Weak acid (کمزور تیزاب) [p. 147]: An acid that ionises only partially in aqueous solution, e.g. ethanoic acid.
• Strong base (طاقتور اساس) [p. 147]: A base that ionises completely in aqueous solution, e.g. NaOH, KOH.
• Weak base (کمزور اساس) [p. 147]: A base that ionises only slightly in water, producing few OH⁻ ions, e.g. NH₃.
• Base (اساس) [p. 149]: An oxide or hydroxide of a metal that neutralises an acid.
• Alkali (الکلی) [p. 148]: A base that is soluble in water.
• Neutralisation (تعدیل) [p. 148]: The reaction of an acid with a base to form salt and water.
• Salt (نمک) [p. 148]: An ionic compound formed when the H⁺ of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.
• Hydronium ion (ہائیڈرونیم آئن) [p. 146]: H₃O⁺, formed when a water molecule accepts a proton.
• Acid rain (تیزابی بارش) [p. 148]: Rain with pH below about 5.6, containing dissolved sulphuric and nitric acids from SO₂ and oxides of nitrogen.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Acid (تیزاب): Proton donor
• Base (اساس): Proton acceptor
• Alkali (قلی / الکلی): Soluble base
• Neutralisation (تعدیل): Acid + base → salt + water
• Salt (نمک): Ionic product of neutralisation
• Indicator (نشاندہ / انڈیکیٹر): Changes colour with pH
• Litmus (لٹمس): Common indicator
• Amphoteric (دو رخی / ایمفوٹیرک): Acts as acid and base
• Dissociation (تفریق / ٹوٹنا): Splitting into ions
• Effervescence (جھاگ بننا): Fizzing of gas
• Corrosive (کھا جانے والا): Destroys materials
• Acid rain (تیزابی بارش): Acidic rainfall
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Hydronium ion: H₃O⁺
• Self-ionisation of water: H₂O + H₂O  H₃O⁺ + OH⁻
• Acid + metal: salt + H₂
• Acid + carbonate: salt + H₂O + CO₂
• Acid + base: salt + H₂O (Neutralisation)
• Alkali + ammonium salt: salt + NH₃ + H₂O (Warm)
• Acidic solution: [H⁺] > [OH⁻] (pH < 7)
• Neutral solution: [H⁺] = [OH⁻] (pH = 7)
• Basic solution: [OH⁻] > [H⁺] (pH > 7)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• HCl(aq) -> H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) — Strong acid: complete dissociation.
• H₂SO₄(aq) -> 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) — Strong acid (dibasic).
• HNO₃(aq) -> H⁺(aq) + NO₃^-(aq) — Strong acid.
• CH₃COOH(aq)  CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) — Weak acid: partial dissociation.
• NaOH(aq) -> Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) — Strong base.
• NH₃(g) + H₂O(l)  NH₄^+(aq) + OH⁻(aq) — Weak base; NH₃ is a Brønsted base, water an acid.
• HCl(g) + H₂O(l) -> H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) — HCl Brønsted acid, water base.
• HCl + NH₃ -> NH₄^+ + Cl⁻ — Brønsted–Lowry reaction between HCl and NH₃.
• Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) — Acid + metal.
• Na₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) — Acid + carbonate: effervescence.
• HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) — Neutralisation.
• NaOH(aq) + NH₄Cl(s) -> NaCl(aq) + NH₃(g) + H₂O(l) — Base + ammonium salt releases ammonia.
• Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) — Metal oxide + water → alkali.
• CaCO₃(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) -> CaSO₄(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) — Acid rain attacking marble.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. CO₂ contains no hydrogen, yet its solution is acidic. Explain.
   Answer: CO₂ reacts with water to form carbonic acid, H₂CO₃, which donates H⁺: CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃^-.
2. Is a concentrated solution of ethanoic acid a strong acid?
   Answer: No. Strength depends on degree of ionisation, not concentration. Ethanoic acid is weak even when concentrated.
3. Why do we squeeze lemon juice on fried fish?
   Answer: Citric acid neutralises the basic amines that give fish its strong smell, forming odourless salts.
4. Why is Cu(OH)₂ a base but not an alkali?
   Answer: It neutralises acids but is insoluble in water.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. A person with acidity takes an antacid tablet of Mg(OH)₂. Write the equation.
   Answer: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.
2. Farmers add lime (CaO) to acidic soil. Why?
   Answer: Lime is basic; it neutralises the acid in the soil so crops grow better.
3. Why should acids not be stored in metal containers?
   Answer: Acids react with metals, corroding the container and releasing hydrogen.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Identify Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases: (1) HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻ (2) NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄^+ + OH⁻. (Example 10.1)
   Solution: (1) HCl loses H⁺ → acid; H₂O gains H⁺ → base. (2) H₂O loses H⁺ (becomes OH⁻) → acid; NH₃ gains H⁺ (becomes NH₄^+) → base. Water is amphoteric.

2. Explain the Brønsted–Lowry acid and base in NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄^+ + OH⁻. [FBISE Annual 2026]
   Solution: Acid: H₂O (donates a proton and becomes OH⁻). Base: NH₃ (accepts a proton and becomes NH₄^+).
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 10 Exercises (150–152):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. Which of the following cannot be classified as an Arrhenius acid? → C (CO₂) | CO₂ has no hydrogen to give H⁺.
ii. Which of the following is a Brønsted base? → A (NH₃) | NH₃ accepts a proton.
iii. Milk of magnesia contains Mg(OH)₂ and neutralises excess stomach acid. Which salt is formed? → C (MgCl₂) | Stomach acid is HCl: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O.
iv. Ammonia is a base because it: → D (Can accept proton) | Brønsted–Lowry base.
v–vii. In H₂O + HCl ⇌ H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻, which species is the proton acceptor? → A (H₂O) | Water accepts H⁺ to form H₃O⁺.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) Write the equation for the self-ionisation of water.
   Answer: H₂O(l) + H₂O(l) ⇌ H₃O⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) (or H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻). One molecule donates a proton, the other accepts it.
(ii) Define and give examples of Arrhenius acids.
   Answer: An Arrhenius acid ionises in water to give H⁺ ions. Examples: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻; HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃^-; H₂SO₄ → 2H⁺ + SO₄²⁻.
(iii) Why does HCl act as a strong acid?
   Answer: Because it ionises completely (100%) in water: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻, giving a high concentration of H⁺ ions.
(iv) Why does NH₃ act as a Brønsted–Lowry base?
   Answer: Its nitrogen has a lone pair that accepts a proton (from water or an acid): NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄^+.
(v) Why does ammonia act as a weak base?
   Answer: It reacts with water only partially: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄^+ + OH⁻. Most molecules remain as NH₃, so few OH⁻ ions are produced.

— Q3–Q12. Descriptive questions —
3. Ammonium hydroxide and nitric acid react to produce ammonium nitrate and water. Write the balanced equation.
   Answer: NH₄OH(aq) + HNO₃(aq) → NH₄NO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
4. Write balanced equations: (i) sulphuric acid + magnesium hydroxide → magnesium sulphate + water (ii) sulphuric acid + sodium carbonate → … (iii) hydrochloric acid + magnesium → …
   Answer: (i) H₂SO₄ + Mg(OH)₂ → MgSO₄ + 2H₂O
(ii) H₂SO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O + CO₂ (the book leaves out CO₂; carbonates always give CO₂ with acids)
(iii) 2HCl + Mg → MgCl₂ + H₂ (the book says “water”; a metal and an acid give hydrogen)
5. Identify Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases: (i) HNO₃ + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + NO₃^- (ii) NH₃ + HNO₃ → NH₄NO₃
   Answer: (i) Acid HNO₃, base H₂O. (ii) Acid HNO₃, base NH₃.
6. Give the Brønsted–Lowry definition of an acid. Write an equation that illustrates it.
   Answer: An acid is a proton donor. HCl(g) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq): HCl donates H⁺ to water.
7. Identify Brønsted acids and bases; classify water as proton donor or acceptor: (i) CH₃COOH + H₂O ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H₃O⁺ (ii) HCO₃^- + H₂O ⇌ CO₃²⁻ + H₃O⁺ (iii) NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄^+ + OH⁻ (iv) HCl + HCO₃^- ⇌ H₂CO₃ + Cl⁻ (v) HS⁻ + H₂O ⇌ S²⁻ + H₃O⁺
   Answer: (i) Acid CH₃COOH; base H₂O (acceptor).
(ii) Acid HCO₃^-; base H₂O (acceptor).
(iii) Acid H₂O (donor); base NH₃.
(iv) Acid HCl; base HCO₃^- (no water involved).
(v) Acid HS⁻; base H₂O (acceptor).
8–9. Write equations showing the ionisation of (a) HI(aq) (b) HNO₂(aq) as Arrhenius acids.
   Answer: (a) HI(aq) → H⁺(aq) + I⁻(aq) (strong acid). (b) HNO₂(aq) ⇌ H⁺(aq) + NO₂^-(aq) (weak acid).
10. Compare the relative concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻ ions in (a) acidic (b) basic (c) neutral solutions.
   Answer: (a) Acidic: [H⁺] > [OH⁻] (b) Basic: [OH⁻] > [H⁺] (c) Neutral: [H⁺] = [OH⁻].
11. Codeine C₁₈H₂₁NO₃ dissolves in water: C₁₈H₂₁NO₃ + H₂O ⇌ [C₁₈H₂₁HNO₃]⁺ + OH⁻. Identify codeine and water as Brønsted acid or base.
   Answer: Codeine accepts a proton → base. Water donates a proton (becomes OH⁻) → acid.
12. Examine some ways to determine whether a water solution contains an acid or a base.
   Answer: - Litmus: acid turns blue litmus red; base turns red litmus blue.
- Indicators: phenolphthalein turns pink in bases (colourless in acid); methyl orange red in acid, yellow in base.
- Universal indicator / pH paper: pH  7 base.
- Chemical test: add a carbonate – fizzing (CO₂) shows an acid; add magnesium – H₂ bubbles show an acid; warm with an ammonium salt – ammonia smell shows a base.
- Taste and touch are NOT safe methods.
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Write the chemical reaction when an acid reacts with a carbonate. Describe the visible change that may appear.
   Answer: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ (or CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂). Visible change: effervescence (fizzing bubbles) of a colourless gas that turns limewater milky; a solid carbonate dissolves.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Write dissociation equations of sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄) and sodium hydroxide (NaOH) in aqueous solution.
   Answer: H₂SO₄(aq) → 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq); NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). Both are strong, so dissociation is complete.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] State the Brønsted–Lowry acid–base concept. Give an example of the reaction between HCl and NH₃.
   Answer: Acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor. HCl(g) + NH₃(g) → NH₄^+ + Cl⁻ (white NH₄Cl): HCl donates H⁺ (acid), NH₃ accepts it (base).

4. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] A student added HCl to Na₂CO₃ solution and bubbles were observed. Identify the gas evolved and write a balanced equation.
   Answer: The gas is carbon dioxide. Na₂CO₃(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g).

5. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Differentiate between a strong acid and a weak acid by explaining their dissociation in aqueous solution. Give one example each.
   Answer: Strong acid ionises completely: HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻. Weak acid ionises partially: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What is meant by a strong acid? Give one example with equation.
   Answer: An acid that ionises completely in water. HNO₃(aq) → H⁺(aq) + NO₃^-(aq).

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What is a strong base? Write the equation for dissociation of NaOH in water.
   Answer: A base that ionises completely in water. NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Write the reaction of any one metal oxide with water. Identify the nature of the product.
   Answer: Na₂O(s) + H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) (or CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂). The product is an alkali (basic, turns red litmus blue).

9. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What is a Brønsted–Lowry acid? Give one reaction as an example.
   Answer: A proton donor. HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻.

10. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF)] Define Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases with two examples each.
   Answer: Acid (proton donor): HCl, HNO₃ (also CH₃COOH, H₂O with NH₃). Base (proton acceptor): NH₃, H₂O (with HCl) (also OH⁻, CO₃²⁻).

11. What is the difference between a base and an alkali?
   Answer: A base is any metal oxide or hydroxide that neutralises an acid; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water (NaOH). All alkalis are bases, not all bases are alkalis (Cu(OH)₂ is insoluble).

12. Why is water called amphoteric?
   Answer: It acts as a base with HCl (accepts H⁺) and as an acid with NH₃ (donates H⁺).

13. Define acid rain and give its two main causes.
   Answer: Rain with pH below about 5.6 containing H₂SO₄ and HNO₃; caused by SO₂ (burning sulphur-containing fuels) and nitrogen oxides (vehicle engines, power stations).


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Explain the terms acid and base according to the Brønsted–Lowry theory. Identify the acid and base in NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄^+ + OH⁻.
   Answer: Brønsted–Lowry acid: a species that donates a proton (H⁺). Base: a species that accepts a proton. The theory works with or without water and explains bases like NH₃ that have no OH.
In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄^+ + OH⁻: H₂O is the acid (gives H⁺ and becomes OH⁻); NH₃ is the base (accepts H⁺ and becomes NH₄^+). Because water can also act as a base (e.g. with HCl), it is amphoteric.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Write chemical reactions of HCl with (a) Mg (b) CaCO₃ (c) NaOH.
   Answer: (a) Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g) – fizzing, hydrogen burns with a pop.
(b) CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) – effervescence; CO₂ turns limewater milky.
(c) NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) – neutralisation, solution warms; ionic: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Differentiate between a strong acid and a weak acid. Write dissociation equations for HCl and CH₃COOH to support your answer.
   Answer: Strong acid: complete ionisation, many H⁺, good conductor, fast reactions: HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq). Weak acid: partial ionisation, few H⁺, poorer conductor, slower reactions: CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) (about 5% ionised).

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22); Annual 2025] Give complete and balanced chemical reactions of NaOH with HCl, NH₄Cl and H₂SO₄.
   Answer: - NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) (neutralisation)
- NaOH(aq) + NH₄Cl(s) → NaCl(aq) + NH₃(g) + H₂O(l) (on warming; ammonia turns damp red litmus blue)
- 2NaOH(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → Na₂SO₄(aq) + 2H₂O(l) (neutralisation)

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] Give balanced chemical reactions of HCl with (i) Zn (ii) Na₂CO₃ (iii) NaOH.
   Answer: (i) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ (ii) Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ (iii) NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Compare the Arrhenius concept of acids and bases with the Brønsted–Lowry concept. Give one example of each.
   Answer: Arrhenius: acid gives H⁺ in water (HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻); base gives OH⁻ in water (NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻); limited to water; cannot explain NH₃. Brønsted–Lowry: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor; works without water; explains NH₃ as a base (HCl + NH₃ → NH₄Cl) and water as amphoteric.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (AF and 50%)] Describe reactions of HCl with (A) Zn (B) NaOH (C) Na₂CO₃.
   Answer: (A) Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ (bubbles of hydrogen). (B) NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (neutralisation, heat released). (C) Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂ (effervescence).

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] How does acid rain damage marble structures? Write the reactions of sulphuric and nitric acids.
   Answer: Marble and limestone are calcium carbonate. Acids react with carbonates, so acid rain slowly dissolves the stone, roughens carvings and weakens buildings and statues:
- CaCO₃(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CaSO₄(s) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
- CaCO₃(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Ca(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g)
The calcium sulphate formed is crumbly and flakes off, and calcium nitrate is soluble and washes away.
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 10 in one page
- Acids: sour, blue litmus → red, H⁺ in water. Bases: bitter, slippery, red litmus → blue, OH⁻ in water.
- Arrhenius: acid gives H⁺, base gives OH⁻ (water only). Brønsted–Lowry: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor. Water is amphoteric. H₃O⁺ = hydronium.
- Strong (complete, →): HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄; NaOH, KOH. Weak (partial, ⇌): CH₃COOH (5%), H₂CO₃; NH₃.
- Bases = metal oxides/hydroxides; alkalis = soluble bases. Amphoteric: Al₂O₃, ZnO.
- Acid + metal → salt + H₂; acid + carbonate → salt + H₂O + CO₂; acid + base → salt + H₂O (H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O).
- Base + NH₄^+ salt (warm) → salt + NH₃ + H₂O (NH₃ turns damp red litmus blue).
- Acid rain: pH < 5.6; H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ from SO₂ and NOₓ; dissolves marble (CaCO₃), corrodes metals, kills fish, damages forests.

chapters.title: Environmental Chemistry – Air
chapters.introduction:
The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around the Earth. This unit covers the composition of clean, dry air, the main air pollutants (CO₂, CO, particulates, CH₄, NOₓ, SO₂, ground-level ozone), their sources and harmful effects, the greenhouse effect and global warming, acid rain and the role of sulphur and nitrogen oxides, catalytic converters, strategies to reduce pollution, photosynthesis, and how to protect yourself (masks, air quality index, CO detectors).

Exam focus (11 summative SLOs): composition of air (78% N₂, 21% O₂), sources and effects of each pollutant (CO binds haemoglobin; SO₂ → acid rain), greenhouse effect and global warming, catalytic converters (2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂), acid rain chemistry, strategies to reduce pollution. Several MCQs every year (the 50% model paper has 6 from this chapter).

══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
Exam focus (11 summative SLOs): composition of air (78% N₂, 21% O₂), sources and effects of each pollutant (CO binds haemoglobin; SO₂ → acid rain), greenhouse effect and global warming, catalytic converters (2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂), acid rain chemistry, strategies to reduce pollution. Several MCQs every year (the 50% model paper has 6 from this chapter).

══ 11.1 The atmosphere and composition of air (pp. 154–155) ══
The atmosphere is the envelope of gases and water vapour surrounding the Earth.
Composition of clean, dry air (by volume):
- Nitrogen N₂ ≈ 78%
- Oxygen O₂ ≈ 21%
- Argon ≈ 0.93% (the most abundant noble gas in air)
- Carbon dioxide ≈ 0.04%
- Other noble gases (Ne, He, Kr, Xe) and traces of other gases.
Air also contains variable water vapour – almost none over deserts, up to about 4% over tropical rainforests.
Air is a mixture (its composition can vary and its components can be separated by fractional distillation of liquid air).
[Table: Composition of dry air]
Gas | % by volume
• Nitrogen (N₂) | 78.08
• Oxygen (O₂) | 20.95
• Argon (Ar) | 0.93
• Carbon dioxide (CO₂) | ≈ 0.04
• Neon, helium, krypton, xenon, methane, etc. | Traces
صاف خشک ہوا میں تقریباً 78% نائٹروجن، 21% آکسیجن، تقریباً 1% آرگون اور 0.04% کاربن ڈائی آکسائیڈ ہوتی ہے۔ آبی بخارات کی مقدار جگہ کے لحاظ سے بدلتی ہے۔

══ 11.2 Air pollutants: sources and effects (pp. 155–158) ══
A pollutant is anything in air, water or soil that has a harmful effect on part of the environment. Some pollution is natural (volcanoes, forest fires, termites), but most comes from human activities (burning fossil fuels, vehicles, industry, waste incineration, agriculture).
1. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) – from complete combustion of carbon-containing fuels (coal, petrol, natural gas, wood), deforestation and industry. Effect: greenhouse gas → global warming and climate change.
2. Carbon monoxide (CO) – from incomplete combustion (limited oxygen) in vehicles, generators, stoves and heaters. Colourless, odourless and toxic: it combines with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, so blood cannot carry oxygen → headache, dizziness, unconsciousness, brain damage, death.
3. Particulates (particulate matter) – fine particles of soot, smoke, dust from incomplete combustion, diesel engines, construction, brick kilns. Effect: penetrate deep into lungs → respiratory problems (asthma, bronchitis) and cancer; smog and reduced visibility.
4. Methane (CH₄) – from decomposition of vegetation and waste (wetlands, rice fields, landfills) and digestion in animals (cows, goats, sheep). Effect: powerful greenhouse gas → global warming.
5. Oxides of nitrogen (NO, NO₂ = NOₓ) – from car engines, power plants and generators (N₂ and O₂ combine at high temperature). NO₂ is a reddish-brown gas. Effects: acid rain, photochemical smog, eye irritation, headache and respiratory problems.
6. Sulphur dioxide (SO₂) – from burning fossil fuels that contain sulphur (coal, oil) in power plants, industry, vehicles; also volcanoes. Effects: acid rain and haze; irritates lungs, worsens asthma and bronchitis; fades silk and damages buildings.
7. Ground-level ozone (O₃) – a secondary pollutant formed when NOₓ and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) from car exhausts and industry react in sunlight (photochemical reactions): NO₂ → NO + O; O + O₂ → O₃. Effects: main part of smog; irritates respiratory organs and causes asthma; damages crops and forests.
[Table: Pollutants at a glance]
Pollutant | Main source | Harmful effect
• CO₂ | Complete combustion of fuels; deforestation | Global warming, climate change
• CO | Incomplete combustion (vehicles, heaters) | Toxic: binds haemoglobin, death
• Particulates | Incomplete combustion, diesel, dust | Respiratory problems, cancer
• CH₄ | Decaying vegetation, landfills, cattle | Global warming
• NOₓ | Car engines, power plants | Acid rain, smog, breathing problems
• SO₂ | Burning sulphur-containing fossil fuels | Acid rain, haze, lung irritation
• Ground-level O₃ | NOₓ + VOCs + sunlight | Smog, asthma, crop damage
Exam Tip: “Which gas is most dangerous because it binds with haemoglobin?” → CO. “Main source of nitrogen oxides in cities?” → motor vehicles and combustion of fossil fuels.
آلودگی پھیلانے والا مادہ وہ ہے جو ہوا، پانی یا مٹی میں نقصان پہنچائے۔ CO₂ مکمل اور CO و ذرات نامکمل احتراق سے نکلتے ہیں۔ CO خون کے ہیموگلوبن سے جڑ کر آکسیجن کی ترسیل روک دیتی ہے اور جان لیوا ہے۔ میتھین سڑتی ہوئی نباتات اور مویشیوں سے، نائٹروجن آکسائیڈز گاڑیوں کے انجنوں سے اور SO₂ گندھک والے ایندھن جلانے سے نکلتی ہے۔ زمینی سطح کی اوزون دھوپ میں NOₓ اور VOCs کے تعامل سے بنتی ہے۔

══ 11.3 Greenhouse effect and global warming (pp. 158–159) ══
Greenhouse effect: sunlight (mostly visible light) passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface. Some is reflected back. The warm surface emits infrared (thermal) radiation. Greenhouse gases – mainly CO₂, CH₄ and water vapour (also N₂O and CFCs) – absorb this infrared radiation and re-emit it in all directions, including back towards the Earth. This reduces the loss of thermal energy to space and keeps the lower atmosphere warm (like the glass of a greenhouse or a blanket). Without it, Earth would be about −18 °C.
Global warming: human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, livestock farming, industry) have increased the concentration of greenhouse gases, enhancing the natural greenhouse effect so the average global temperature is rising.
Consequences (climate change): melting glaciers and ice caps; rising sea levels and coastal flooding; longer, hotter summers and heatwaves; changes in rainfall – droughts and floods (e.g. Pakistan floods 2022); damage to crops and loss of species.
سورج کی روشنی زمین کو گرم کرتی ہے؛ زمین انفرا ریڈ حرارت خارج کرتی ہے جسے گرین ہاؤس گیسیں (CO₂، میتھین، آبی بخارات) جذب کر کے واپس زمین کی طرف بھیجتی ہیں، یوں حرارت خلا میں کم جاتی ہے۔ یہ گرین ہاؤس اثر ہے۔ انسانی سرگرمیوں سے ان گیسوں میں اضافے کی وجہ سے زمین کا اوسط درجہ حرارت بڑھ رہا ہے، اسے گلوبل وارمنگ کہتے ہیں۔

══ 11.4 Acid rain: role of sulphur and nitrogen oxides (pp. 159–160) ══
Normal rain is slightly acidic (pH ≈ 5.6) because dissolved CO₂ forms weak carbonic acid. Acid rain has pH less than 5.6.
Role of sulphur: fossil fuels contain sulphur; on burning it forms SO₂. SO₂ is oxidised in the air to SO₃, which dissolves in rainwater to form sulphuric acid:
- S + O₂ → SO₂
- 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃
- SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ (also SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃)
Role of NO and NO₂:
- Directly: NO₂ dissolves in rainwater with oxygen to form nitric acid: 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃.
- Catalytically: NO₂ helps oxidise SO₂ to SO₃ and is regenerated: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO; then 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂. So nitrogen oxides speed up the formation of sulphuric acid.
Effects of acid rain:
- Dissolves marble and limestone buildings and statues (CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ → CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂), e.g. damage to the Taj Mahal and old monuments.
- Corrodes metals – bridges, railings, cars.
- Makes lakes and rivers acidic → fish and aquatic life die.
- Leaches nutrients from soil and releases toxic aluminium → forests and crops damaged.
- Irritates eyes and lungs.
عام بارش کا pH تقریباً 5.6 ہوتا ہے؛ تیزابی بارش کا اس سے کم۔ ایندھن میں موجود گندھک جل کر SO₂ بنتی ہے جو SO₃ اور پھر سلفیورک ایسڈ بن جاتی ہے۔ NO₂ خود نائٹرک ایسڈ بناتی ہے اور SO₂ کو SO₃ میں بدلنے میں عمل انگیز کا کام بھی کرتی ہے۔ تیزابی بارش عمارتوں، دھاتوں، جھیلوں، جنگلات اور فصلوں کو نقصان پہنچاتی ہے۔

══ 11.5 Nitrogen oxides in car engines and catalytic converters (pp. 160) ══
Formation in engines: inside a petrol engine the temperature is very high (above 1000 °C) because of the burning fuel and the electric spark. At this temperature nitrogen and oxygen from the air (normally unreactive) combine:
- N₂ + O₂ → 2NO
- 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂
Exhaust gases also contain CO and unburnt hydrocarbons.
Catalytic converter: a device fitted in the exhaust pipe, containing a honeycomb coated with platinum, palladium and rhodium (transition-metal catalysts). It converts harmful gases into less harmful ones:
- 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂
- 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂
- Unburnt hydrocarbons + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O (e.g. C₈H₁₈ + 12½O₂ → 8CO₂ + 9H₂O)
- 2NO → N₂ + O₂
It cannot remove CO₂ (CO₂ is a product). Converters need lead-free petrol (lead poisons the catalyst). The textbook suggests the government should make catalytic converters compulsory in all cars.
گاڑی کے انجن میں بہت زیادہ درجہ حرارت پر ہوا کی نائٹروجن اور آکسیجن مل کر NO اور NO₂ بناتی ہیں۔ کیٹالیٹک کنورٹر میں پلاٹینم، پیلیڈیم اور روڈیم جیسے عمل انگیز ہوتے ہیں جو CO اور NO کو CO₂ اور N₂ میں بدل دیتے ہیں: 2CO + 2NO ← 2CO₂ + N₂۔ یہ CO₂ کو ختم نہیں کر سکتا۔

══ 11.6 Strategies to reduce climate change and acid rain (pp. 161–162) ══
Reducing climate change (greenhouse gases):
- Plant trees (afforestation) and stop deforestation – trees absorb CO₂ by photosynthesis and also prevent soil erosion.
- Reduce livestock farming (less methane).
- Use less fossil fuel: energy efficiency, public transport, electric vehicles.
- Renewable energy: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal.
- Hydrogen economy: hydrogen burns to give only water.
- Circular economy: reduce waste, reuse and recycle; capture methane from landfills.
Reducing acid rain:
- Catalytic converters in vehicles (remove NOₓ).
- Low-sulphur fuels (desulphurise fuels before burning).
- Flue-gas desulphurisation in power stations: waste gases are passed through calcium oxide (lime) or calcium carbonate, which reacts with SO₂: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃ (then oxidised to CaSO₄, gypsum).
- Use renewable energy instead of coal.
These strategies are interrelated and need action by governments, industry and individuals.
گلوبل وارمنگ کم کرنے کے لیے: درخت لگانا، مویشی فارمنگ کم کرنا، فوسل فیول کا استعمال کم کرنا، شمسی اور ہوائی توانائی، ہائیڈروجن ایندھن اور ری سائیکلنگ۔ تیزابی بارش کم کرنے کے لیے: کیٹالیٹک کنورٹر، کم گندھک والا ایندھن، اور بجلی گھروں میں چونے (CaO) سے SO₂ کو جذب کرنا (فلو گیس ڈی سلفرائزیشن)۔

══ 11.7 Photosynthesis (pp. 162) ══
Photosynthesis is the reaction between carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen, in the presence of chlorophyll and using energy from sunlight:
6CO₂ + 6H₂O --(sunlight, chlorophyll)--> C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
It is endothermic (absorbs light energy). Importance: removes CO₂ from the air (reduces global warming), releases the oxygen we breathe, and makes food (glucose) for nearly all life. This is why planting trees improves air quality.
ضیائی تالیف وہ عمل ہے جس میں پودے سورج کی روشنی اور کلوروفل کی مدد سے CO₂ اور پانی سے گلوکوز اور آکسیجن بناتے ہیں۔ یہ فضا سے CO₂ کم کرتا ہے اور ہمیں آکسیجن اور خوراک دیتا ہے۔

══ 11.8 Protecting yourself: masks, AQI, CO detectors and high-risk situations (pp. 162–164) ══
Tools to reduce personal exposure:
- Masks: N95 masks filter fine particles (dust, smoke, PM2.5); gas masks with activated carbon filters absorb some gases and VOCs. Use certified masks that fit properly.
- Air Quality Index (AQI): a number scale showing how polluted the air is (0–50 good … above 300 hazardous). Check it daily (e.g. during winter smog in Lahore) and stay indoors, avoid outdoor exercise and close windows when it is high.
- Carbon monoxide detectors: alarms in homes and offices that warn when CO builds up (e.g. from gas heaters in closed rooms in winter), so people can ventilate and leave.
- Air purifiers, indoor plants, good ventilation.
High-risk situations (long-term exposure → respiratory diseases, shorter and poorer life):
- Living near busy roads, industrial zones, brick kilns or garbage burning.
- Smoking and passive smoking (lung cancer, bronchitis).
- Indoor pollution: cooking on wood/coal stoves, gas heaters in closed rooms.
- Workers in mines, factories, traffic police.
- Smog seasons; allergens; climate-related heatwaves.
Protective habits: reduce exposure, quit smoking, keep good indoor air quality and wear masks.
آلودگی سے بچاؤ کے لیے N95 ماسک، ایئر کوالٹی انڈیکس (AQI) دیکھنا، اور گھروں میں CO ڈیٹیکٹر لگانا۔ زیادہ خطرے کی صورتیں: مصروف سڑکوں یا صنعتی علاقوں کے قریب رہنا، سگریٹ نوشی، بند کمروں میں گیس ہیٹر، اور سموگ کا موسم۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. The greenhouse effect: Sunlight in; infrared out; greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit part of the infrared back to Earth.

chapters.definitions:
• Atmosphere (کرۂ ہوائی / فضا) [p. 155]: The envelope of gases and water vapour surrounding the Earth.
• Pollutant (آلودگی پھیلانے والا مادہ) [p. 155]: Anything in air, water or soil that has a harmful effect on some part of the environment.
• Air pollution (فضائی آلودگی) [p. 164]: The presence in air of harmful particles and gases.
• Particulates (ذراتی مادہ) [p. 156]: Fine solid or liquid particles (soot, smoke, dust) suspended in air.
• Carboxyhaemoglobin (کاربوکسی ہیموگلوبن) [p. 156]: The compound formed when carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin, preventing it from carrying oxygen.
• Ground-level ozone (زمینی سطح کی اوزون) [p. 156]: A secondary pollutant formed by reactions of nitrogen oxides and VOCs in sunlight; part of smog.
• Photochemical smog (ضیائی کیمیائی دھند) [p. 157]: Hazy, polluted air formed when sunlight acts on nitrogen oxides and hydrocarbons, producing ozone.
• Greenhouse effect (گرین ہاؤس اثر) [p. 158]: The trapping of infrared (thermal) energy by greenhouse gases, reducing heat loss from the Earth to space.
• Global warming (عالمی حدت) [p. 158]: The rise in Earth’s average temperature caused by increased greenhouse gases from human activities.
• Acid rain (تیزابی بارش) [p. 159]: Rain having pH less than 5.6, containing sulphuric and nitric acids.
• Catalytic converter (کیٹالیٹک کنورٹر) [p. 160]: A device in a car exhaust containing Pt/Pd/Rh catalysts that converts CO, NO and hydrocarbons into CO₂, N₂ and H₂O.
• Flue-gas desulphurisation (دھوئیں سے گندھک کا اخراج) [p. 161]: Removal of SO₂ from power-station waste gases by reacting it with calcium oxide or calcium carbonate.
• Photosynthesis (ضیائی تالیف) [p. 162]: The reaction of carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen using sunlight energy in the presence of chlorophyll.
• Air Quality Index (AQI) (ہوا کے معیار کا اشاریہ) [p. 163]: A number scale that tells how clean or polluted the air is and the health risk.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Atmosphere (کرۂ ہوائی): Layer of air around Earth
• Pollutant (آلودگی کا سبب): Harmful substance
• Greenhouse gas (گرین ہاؤس گیس): Gas that traps heat
• Global warming (عالمی حدت): Rise in Earth’s temperature
• Acid rain (تیزابی بارش): Rain with pH < 5.6
• Smog (سموگ / دھواں دار دھند): Smoke + fog pollution
• Particulates (ذرات): Tiny suspended particles
• Catalytic converter (کیٹالیٹک کنورٹر): Exhaust-cleaning device
• Combustion (احتراق / جلنا): Burning in oxygen
• Photosynthesis (ضیائی تالیف): Plants making food using light
• Renewable energy (قابلِ تجدید توانائی): Solar, wind, hydro
• Haemoglobin (ہیموگلوبن): Oxygen carrier in blood
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Composition of dry air: N₂ 78%, O₂ 21%, Ar 0.93%, CO₂ 0.04%
• Nitrogen oxides: NOₓ = NO + NO₂ (NO₂ is reddish-brown)
• pH of normal rain: ≈ 5.6 (Acid rain < 5.6)
• Ozone: O₃ (Allotrope of oxygen)
• Dibenzothiophene: C₁₂H₈S (Sulphur compound in coal)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• C + O₂ -> CO₂ — Complete combustion of carbon.
• 2C + O₂ -> 2CO — Incomplete combustion (limited oxygen).
• CH₄ + 2O₂ -> CO₂ + 2H₂O — Complete combustion of methane.
• 2CH₄ + 3O₂ -> 2CO + 4H₂O — Incomplete combustion of methane.
• N₂ + O₂ -> 2NO ; 2NO + O₂ -> 2NO₂ — In hot car engines.
• NO₂ --sunlight--> NO + O ; O + O₂ -> O₃ — Formation of ground-level ozone.
• S + O₂ -> SO₂ ; 2SO₂ + O₂ -> 2SO₃ ; SO₃ + H₂O -> H₂SO₄ — Sulphur to sulphuric acid (acid rain).
• SO₂ + NO₂ -> SO₃ + NO ; 2NO + O₂ -> 2NO₂ — NO₂ catalyses oxidation of SO₂.
• 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O -> 4HNO₃ — Nitric acid in acid rain.
• 2CO + 2NO -> 2CO₂ + N₂ — Catalytic converter (Pt/Pd/Rh).
• CaCO₃ + H₂SO₄ -> CaSO₄ + H₂O + CO₂ — Acid rain dissolving marble.
• CaO + SO₂ -> CaSO₃ — Flue-gas desulphurisation.
• 6CO₂ + 6H₂O --sunlight, chlorophyll--> C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ — Photosynthesis.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why is CO produced in a closed room with a gas heater?
   Answer: Oxygen runs short, so the gas burns incompletely, forming CO instead of CO₂.
2. Why is normal rain slightly acidic?
   Answer: CO₂ dissolves in rainwater to form weak carbonic acid (pH about 5.6).
3. Is ozone always harmful?
   Answer: No. Stratospheric ozone protects us from UV radiation; ground-level ozone is harmful (smog).

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Lahore’s AQI is 350 on a winter morning. What should a student do?
   Answer: Avoid outdoor exercise, stay indoors with windows closed, wear an N95 mask if going out, and keep children and asthma patients indoors.
2. Why are brick kilns being shifted to zig-zag technology in Pakistan?
   Answer: Zig-zag kilns burn fuel more completely, producing less smoke, particulates and CO.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Why is carbon monoxide called a silent killer?
   Solution: It is colourless and odourless, so it cannot be noticed, yet it combines with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, stopping oxygen transport and causing death.

2. Show how a catalytic converter removes CO and NO.
   Solution: Over a Pt/Pd/Rh catalyst: 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂. CO is oxidised and NO is reduced to harmless nitrogen.
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 11 Exercises (164–165):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. Which gas has the highest percentage in the air? → C (N₂) | Nitrogen ≈ 78%.
ii. Which is/are responsible for acid rain? → C (Both NO₂ and SO₂) | Both form strong acids in rainwater.
iii. Which is a reddish-brown gas? → B (NO₂) | NO₂ is reddish-brown.
iv. Most air pollution is caused by: → D (The burning of fossil fuels) | Burning fossil fuels produces most pollutants.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) List two main sources of acid rain.
   Answer: (1) SO₂ from burning sulphur-containing fossil fuels (coal, oil) in power plants and industries. (2) Nitrogen oxides from vehicle engines and power plants.
(ii) List four human activities which contribute to air pollution.
   Answer: Burning fossil fuels in vehicles and power plants; industrial processes and brick kilns; burning garbage/waste incineration; deforestation; livestock farming; smoking.
(iii) What is the importance of catalytic converters?
   Answer: They change harmful exhaust gases into less harmful ones: CO → CO₂, NO → N₂, unburnt hydrocarbons → CO₂ + H₂O (2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂). This reduces smog, acid rain and CO poisoning.
(iv) What is the role of automobiles in air pollution?
   Answer: Vehicle engines release CO and particulates (incomplete combustion), CO₂ (greenhouse gas), nitrogen oxides (acid rain, smog), unburnt hydrocarbons/VOCs (ground-level ozone) and some SO₂. In cities they are the main source of NOₓ.
(v) Define global warming.
   Answer: The increase in the average temperature of the Earth caused by higher concentrations of greenhouse gases (CO₂, CH₄) from human activities, which enhance the natural greenhouse effect.

— Q3–Q8 and Think Tank —
3. Describe sources of air pollutants.
   Answer: Natural: volcanoes (SO₂, ash), forest fires, termites and decaying vegetation (CH₄), lightning (NO). Human: complete combustion of fuels (CO₂); incomplete combustion in vehicles, generators, heaters (CO, soot/particulates); car engines and power plants (NOₓ); burning sulphur-containing coal and oil (SO₂); livestock, rice fields, landfills (CH₄); industry and vehicle VOCs + NOₓ in sunlight (ground-level ozone); waste incineration (CO, NOₓ, SO₂, particulates).
4. Describe acid rain and its effects.
   Answer: Acid rain is rain with pH < 5.6 containing H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ formed from SO₂ and NOₓ (2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄; 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃). Effects: dissolves marble/limestone buildings and statues; corrodes metal bridges and vehicles; acidifies lakes, killing fish; leaches soil nutrients and damages forests and crops; irritates eyes and lungs.
5. Describe global warming.
   Answer: Greenhouse gases absorb infrared radiation from the Earth and re-emit it back, reducing heat loss to space. Burning fossil fuels, deforestation and livestock farming have raised CO₂ and CH₄ levels, so more heat is trapped and the average global temperature rises. Consequences: melting glaciers, rising sea levels, heatwaves, longer summers, floods and droughts, crop failure. Remedies: plant trees, renewable energy, less fossil fuel, less livestock farming.
6. What is ground-level ozone? Explain.
   Answer: Ozone (O₃) near the Earth’s surface is a secondary pollutant. It forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds from vehicles and industry react in sunlight: NO₂ → NO + O; O + O₂ → O₃. It is the main part of photochemical smog, irritates the respiratory system, causes asthma and damages crops and forests. (Ozone high in the stratosphere is useful, protecting us from UV.)
7. Why is global warming often referred to as the greenhouse effect? Justify.
   Answer: Because it is caused by the same process: like the glass of a greenhouse, CO₂ and CH₄ let sunlight in but trap the outgoing infrared heat. Strictly, the greenhouse effect is natural and necessary; global warming is the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by extra greenhouse gases from human activities.
8. Sulphur dioxide is a common pollutant from burning coal. State two effects caused by it.
   Answer: (1) Acid rain – SO₂ forms H₂SO₄ which damages buildings, lakes and forests. (2) Respiratory problems – it irritates the lungs and worsens asthma and bronchitis. (Also haze and fading of fabrics.)
TT1. Dibenzothiophene (C₁₂H₈S) is a common sulphur compound in coal. It is responsible for acid rain. Elaborate.
   Answer: When coal burns, the sulphur in dibenzothiophene is oxidised to SO₂. In the air SO₂ is oxidised to SO₃ (helped by NO₂), which dissolves in rainwater to form sulphuric acid: SO₂ → SO₃ → H₂SO₄. This lowers the pH of rain below 5.6 – acid rain.
TT2. There is a need to remove sulphur from coal before it is burned. Give reason.
   Answer: Removing sulphur (desulphurisation) prevents SO₂ forming during combustion, so less acid rain, haze and lung disease; it is cheaper to prevent emission than to repair damage to buildings, crops and health.
TT3. Examine the ways to reduce pollution caused by cars.
   Answer: Fit catalytic converters; use lead-free, low-sulphur fuel; maintain engines (tuning, air filters); use public transport, car-sharing, cycling or walking; switch to electric, hybrid or hydrogen vehicles; enforce emission testing.
TT4. Certain human activities are responsible for a significant increase in the greenhouse effect. Argue.
   Answer: Burning coal, oil and gas releases CO₂ that was locked underground for millions of years; deforestation removes trees that absorb CO₂; livestock farming, rice paddies and landfills release methane. Measurements show CO₂ has risen from about 0.028% to over 0.04% since industrialisation, matching the rise in global temperature.
TT5. As a global citizen, how can you play a part to reduce air pollution at a personal level?
   Answer: Walk, cycle or use public transport; switch off lights and appliances; avoid burning garbage and leaves; plant and care for trees; use energy-efficient bulbs; avoid smoking; reduce, reuse, recycle; keep family vehicles tuned; raise awareness among friends and family.
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] Increased levels of methane contribute to global warming and climate change. How?
   Answer: Methane is a greenhouse gas (about 25 times stronger than CO₂ per molecule). It absorbs infrared radiation emitted by the Earth and re-emits it back, reducing heat loss to space. More methane (from cattle, rice fields, landfills) traps more heat, raising global temperature and changing climate.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] What is meant by the greenhouse effect? Enlist any two greenhouse gases.
   Answer: Trapping of infrared (heat) radiation from the Earth by gases in the atmosphere, keeping the Earth warm. Greenhouse gases: CO₂ and CH₄ (also water vapour).

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] How do (a) carbon monoxide (b) sulphur dioxide cause harm?
   Answer: (a) CO binds with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, so blood cannot carry oxygen: headache, unconsciousness, death. (b) SO₂ irritates the lungs (asthma, bronchitis) and forms acid rain and haze.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] How do (a) carbon monoxide (b) methane cause harm?
   Answer: (a) CO is toxic: reduces oxygen transport by blood. (b) Methane is a greenhouse gas causing global warming and climate change.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Model Paper (50%)] A city shows a sudden rise in respiratory diseases and reduced visibility. Which pollutant is most likely responsible? Explain how it affects human health and the environment.
   Answer: Particulate matter (fine soot and smoke, often with ground-level ozone in smog). Health: fine particles penetrate deep into the lungs causing asthma, bronchitis and increasing cancer risk. Environment: forms smog/haze that reduces visibility and sunlight, deposits soot on buildings and plants and reduces crop growth.

6. What is the composition of clean, dry air?
   Answer: About 78% N₂, 21% O₂, and the remaining ~1% mainly argon with CO₂ (0.04%) and other noble gases.

7. How do oxides of nitrogen form in car engines?
   Answer: At the very high temperature of the burning fuel and spark, nitrogen and oxygen from the air combine: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO; then 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂.

8. What is flue-gas desulphurisation?
   Answer: Removing SO₂ from power-station exhaust by passing it through calcium oxide/calcium carbonate: CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃.

9. Give three strategies to reduce climate change.
   Answer: Plant trees; use renewable energy (solar, wind); reduce fossil-fuel use and livestock farming; use hydrogen as a clean fuel.

10. How do N95 masks and CO detectors protect people?
   Answer: N95 masks filter fine particles like dust and smoke. CO detectors sound an alarm when carbon monoxide builds up indoors so people can ventilate and leave.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. Describe the strategies to reduce the effects of major environmental issues such as climate change and acid rain.
   Answer: Climate change: plant trees and stop deforestation; reduce livestock farming (methane); use less fossil fuel and more renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal); move to a hydrogen economy; improve energy efficiency; recycle (circular economy).
Acid rain: catalytic converters in vehicles (remove NOₓ); low-sulphur fuels; flue-gas desulphurisation with CaO in power stations (CaO + SO₂ → CaSO₃); replace coal with renewables.

2. Explain how oxides of nitrogen are formed in car engines and how they are removed by catalytic converters. Why can a catalytic converter not remove CO₂?
   Answer: High temperature in the engine makes N₂ and O₂ of air react: N₂ + O₂ → 2NO; 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂. The catalytic converter in the exhaust contains Pt, Pd and Rh on a honeycomb; it catalyses 2CO + 2NO → 2CO₂ + N₂, 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂, and hydrocarbons + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. CO₂ is the final, fully oxidised product of carbon, so it cannot be converted further – the converter actually produces CO₂.

3. Describe the role of sulphur and of NO/NO₂ in the formation of acid rain, with equations.
   Answer: Sulphur in coal and oil burns: S + O₂ → SO₂. SO₂ is oxidised: 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄. NO₂ acts directly – 4NO₂ + O₂ + 2H₂O → 4HNO₃ – and as a catalyst for SO₂ oxidation: SO₂ + NO₂ → SO₃ + NO, then 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ (regenerated).

4. Explain how CO₂ and CH₄ cause global warming in terms of absorption, reflection and emission of thermal energy.
   Answer: 1. Sunlight (short-wave) passes through the atmosphere; some is reflected by clouds and the surface, the rest is absorbed and warms the Earth.
2. The warm surface emits long-wave infrared (thermal) radiation.
3. CO₂ and CH₄ molecules absorb this infrared and re-emit it in all directions, some back to Earth.
4. This reduces thermal energy loss to space. More CO₂ and CH₄ → more energy trapped → global temperature rises.

chapters.title: Environmental Chemistry – Water
chapters.introduction:
Water is essential for life, yet Pakistan faces water scarcity and water-borne diseases. This unit covers the test for water (anhydrous copper(II) sulphate), testing purity by melting and boiling points, distilled vs tap water, the useful and harmful substances found in natural water, treatment of domestic water (sedimentation, filtration, carbon, chlorination), water-borne diseases, water pollution, water scarcity in Pakistan, and fertilizers (urea, ammonium salts, nitrates, NPK).

Exam focus (12 summative SLOs, 3 of them practical/PBA): beneficial vs harmful substances in water (dissolved oxygen, minerals, nitrates, phosphates, sewage, metals), sedimentation and chlorination, water-borne diseases table, water scarcity in Pakistan, NPK and nitrogen fertilizers.

Note: The textbook calls di-ammonium phosphate “superphosphate”. These are different fertilizers: DAP is (NH₄)₂HPO₄, while superphosphate is mainly calcium dihydrogen phosphate. The app keeps both names separate.

══ 12.1 Chemical test for water and testing purity (pp. 167–168) ══
Test for water with anhydrous copper(II) sulphate:
1. Place a little white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate powder in a dry test tube.
2. Add a few drops of the liquid to be tested.
3. If it turns blue, water is present (hydrated copper(II) sulphate forms; the tube also warms).
CuSO₄(s) (white) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) (blue)
This shows water is present, but not that the water is pure. (Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper – blue → pink – is another test.) Copper(II) sulphate is toxic: handle carefully under supervision.
Testing purity with melting and boiling points: pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points.
- Pure water: melts at exactly 0 °C and boils at exactly 100 °C (at 1 atm).
- Impurities lower the melting point (and make it melt over a range) and raise the boiling point (salt water boils above 100 °C).
- So if a sample freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C sharply, it is pure.
[Table: Test for water vs test for purity]
Test | What it shows | Result for water
• Anhydrous CuSO₄ | Presence of water | White → blue
• Cobalt(II) chloride paper | Presence of water | Blue → pink
• Melting point | Purity | Pure water melts sharply at 0 °C
• Boiling point | Purity | Pure water boils at 100 °C (1 atm)
Exam Tip: A chemical test (CuSO₄) shows that water is PRESENT; a physical test (m.p. 0 °C, b.p. 100 °C) shows that water is PURE.
پانی کی شناخت: سفید بے آب کاپر سلفیٹ میں پانی ڈالنے سے یہ نیلا ہو جاتا ہے۔ خالصیت کی جانچ: خالص پانی ٹھیک 0 °C پر جمتا اور 100 °C پر ابلتا ہے؛ ملاوٹ نقطہ انجماد کم اور نقطہ ابال زیادہ کر دیتی ہے۔

══ 12.2 Water as a solvent; distilled water and tap water (pp. 169–171) ══
Water is called the universal solvent because it dissolves a very wide range of substances (salts, gases, many organic compounds). This is why natural water is never pure.
Distilled water: water purified by distillation (boiling water and condensing the steam), leaving dissolved substances behind.
- Free of dissolved salts and microbes; pH 7; very low electrical conductivity.
- Uses in practical chemistry: preparing standard solutions and reagents, rinsing apparatus, calibrating pH meters and sensors, making solutions for titrations (no interfering ions), car batteries and steam irons, medical/pharmaceutical use.
- Not ideal for long-term drinking because it lacks useful minerals.
Tap water: supplied by municipal systems after treatment.
- Contains dissolved minerals (Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻, HCO₃^-), small amounts of chlorine from treatment, sometimes fluoride; may contain traces of impurities.
- pH may be slightly above or below 7; conducts electricity better than distilled water.
- Used for drinking, cooking, washing; in the lab only for rough work and cooling water in condensers – not for preparing accurate solutions.
[Table: Distilled water vs tap water]
Distilled water | Tap water
• Made by distillation | Treated natural water from municipal supply
• No dissolved salts or minerals | Contains dissolved minerals and some chlorine
• pH = 7 | pH about 6.5–8.5
• Very poor conductor of electricity | Conducts electricity (ions present)
• Used for preparing solutions, rinsing apparatus, batteries | Used for drinking, washing, cooling condensers
• Leaves no residue on evaporation | Leaves a residue (scale) on evaporation
کشید شدہ پانی ابال کر بخارات کو ٹھنڈا کرنے سے بنتا ہے؛ اس میں نمکیات نہیں ہوتے، pH 7 ہے اور یہ لیبارٹری میں محلول بنانے اور آلات دھونے میں استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ نلکے کا پانی صاف کیا ہوا قدرتی پانی ہے جس میں معدنیات اور کچھ کلورین ہوتی ہے۔

══ 12.3 Useful and harmful substances in natural water (pp. 169–170) ══
Water from rivers, lakes, wells and rain contains dissolved and suspended substances.
Beneficial substances:
- Dissolved oxygen – essential for fish and other aquatic organisms to breathe; also helps bacteria break down waste.
- Essential minerals (some metal compounds) – calcium and magnesium for bones and teeth; iron for blood; zinc, copper and manganese activate enzymes; small amounts of fluoride protect teeth.
Harmful substances:
- Toxic metal compounds – lead, mercury, arsenic, cadmium from industry, mining, old pipes and batteries: damage kidneys, nervous system and brain; arsenic in groundwater (parts of Punjab and Sindh) causes skin lesions and cancer.
- Plastics – do not decompose; microplastics are eaten by fish and enter food chains; they block drains.
- Sewage – contains harmful microbes (bacteria, viruses, parasites) that cause diarrhoea, cholera, typhoid, dysentery, hepatitis; also uses up oxygen as it decays.
- Nitrates (from fertilizer run-off) – high levels harm infants (“blue-baby syndrome”) and cause eutrophication.
- Phosphates (from fertilizers and detergents) – cause eutrophication: excessive growth of algae; when algae die, bacteria decomposing them use up dissolved oxygen (deoxygenation), so fish die.
- Pesticides, industrial chemicals, oil spills, heat (thermal pollution reduces dissolved oxygen).
[Table: Substances in natural water]
Substance | Source | Effect
• Dissolved oxygen | Air, aquatic plants | Beneficial: needed by aquatic life
• Ca, Mg, Fe, Zn, Cu compounds | Rocks and soil | Beneficial in small amounts: essential minerals
• Pb, Hg, As compounds | Industry, mining, old pipes | Toxic: nerve, kidney damage, cancer
• Plastics | Litter, packaging | Harm aquatic animals; enter food chain
• Sewage | Homes, septic tanks, livestock | Microbes → water-borne diseases; uses up O₂
• Nitrates | Fertilizer run-off | Eutrophication; health risk to infants
• Phosphates | Fertilizers, detergents | Algal bloom → deoxygenation → fish die
مفید مادے: حل شدہ آکسیجن (آبی جانداروں کے لیے) اور کیلشیم، میگنیشیم، آئرن جیسے معدنیات۔ نقصان دہ مادے: سیسہ، پارہ اور آرسینک جیسی زہریلی دھاتیں، پلاسٹک، سیوریج (جراثیم)، کھادوں سے نائٹریٹ اور فاسفیٹ جو الجی بڑھا کر پانی کی آکسیجن ختم کر دیتے ہیں۔

══ 12.4 Treatment of domestic water supply (pp. 170–171) ══
Water from rivers or reservoirs is treated before being supplied to homes:
1. Screening: large objects (leaves, plastic) are removed by screens.
2. Sedimentation (and coagulation): water is left to stand in large tanks so heavy particles settle. Aluminium sulphate (alum) is added; it makes tiny suspended clay particles clump together (coagulate/flocculate) into larger flakes that settle quickly. That is why municipal supplies are treated with aluminium sulphate.
3. Filtration: water passes through beds of sand and gravel that trap remaining small particles.
4. Carbon (activated charcoal) treatment: removes unpleasant tastes, odours and colours by adsorbing organic substances.
5. Chlorination: chlorine is added in the final step to kill harmful microbes (bacteria, viruses) and keep the water safe in the pipes. (Excess chlorine is avoided because it is harmful.)
Sometimes fluoride is added for teeth, and pH is adjusted.
At home: boil water, use filters, or add chlorine tablets when the supply is unsafe.
Exam Tip: FBISE Annual 2026 asked: “Why are sedimentation and chlorination used in water treatment?” Sedimentation removes suspended solids by letting them settle; chlorination kills disease-causing microbes.
گھریلو پانی کی صفائی: (1) جالی سے بڑی چیزیں نکالنا، (2) تہہ نشینی: پانی کو ٹینکوں میں ٹھہرانا اور پھٹکری (ایلومینیم سلفیٹ) ڈالنا تاکہ باریک ذرات اکٹھے ہو کر بیٹھ جائیں، (3) ریت اور بجری سے فلٹریشن، (4) کاربن سے بو اور ذائقہ دور کرنا، (5) کلورینیشن سے جراثیم ختم کرنا۔

══ 12.5 Water pollution and water-borne diseases (pp. 171–173) ══
Water pollution: the contamination of water bodies (rivers, lakes, groundwater, sea) by harmful substances that make it unsafe for drinking and harmful to life.
Sources: household waste and sewage (detergents, food waste, human waste, septic tanks), industrial waste (heavy metals, acids, dyes, oil, hot water), agricultural waste (fertilizers, pesticides, animal waste), plastics, oil spills.
Toxic substances in household waste: detergents (phosphates), bleach and cleaners, paints and solvents, batteries (Hg, Cd, Pb), medicines, pesticides, plastics.
Water-borne diseases are caused by pathogenic microorganisms (disease-causing bacteria, viruses, protozoa, parasites) in contaminated water.
[Table: Common water-borne diseases]
Disease | Cause | Symptoms
• Cholera | Bacterium Vibrio cholerae | Severe watery diarrhoea, vomiting, dehydration
• Typhoid | Bacterium Salmonella typhi | High fever, weakness, stomach pain, headache
• Dysentery | Bacteria (Shigella) or amoeba | Diarrhoea with blood/mucus, stomach cramps, fever
• Hepatitis A/E (jaundice) | Virus | Yellow skin and eyes, loss of appetite, weakness, fatigue
• Diarrhoea | Bacteria, viruses (e.g. rotavirus) | Loose watery stools, dehydration
• Polio | Poliovirus | Fever, paralysis
آبی آلودگی پانی کے ذخائر کا نقصان دہ مادوں سے آلودہ ہونا ہے۔ بیماری پیدا کرنے والے جراثیم (بیکٹیریا، وائرس، پیراسائٹس) آلودہ پانی سے ہیضہ، ٹائیفائیڈ، پیچش، ہیپاٹائٹس (یرقان) اور اسہال جیسی بیماریاں پھیلاتے ہیں۔

══ 12.6 Preventing water-borne diseases and effects of pollutants (pp. 172–173) ══
Steps to avoid water-borne diseases:
- Drink boiled, filtered or chlorinated water.
- Wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before eating – soap removes and kills germs that spread diseases such as diarrhoea, typhoid and hepatitis.
- Keep sewage lines separate from water lines; repair leaking pipes.
- Proper sanitation and toilets; do not dispose of sewage in rivers.
- Cover water tanks and clean them regularly; wash fruit and vegetables.
- Vaccination (typhoid, hepatitis A, polio).
Negative effects of water pollutants on life:
- Humans: diseases, poisoning by heavy metals (kidney and brain damage), cancer from arsenic.
- Aquatic life: low dissolved oxygen (eutrophication, thermal pollution) kills fish; oil spills coat birds and fish; plastics choke animals.
- Agriculture: polluted irrigation water damages soil and crops.
Ways to avoid: treat sewage and industrial waste before release; use fertilizers and pesticides carefully; use phosphate-free detergents; recycle plastics; dispose of batteries and chemicals properly.
Unclean water, poor sanitation and hygiene kill about 2.7 million people worldwide each year (textbook figure).
بچاؤ: ابلا ہوا یا صاف پانی پئیں، بیت الخلا کے بعد صابن سے ہاتھ دھوئیں، سیوریج اور پانی کی لائنیں الگ رکھیں، ٹینک ڈھانپ کر رکھیں اور ویکسین لگوائیں۔ آلودگی سے انسان بیمار ہوتے ہیں، مچھلیاں مرتی ہیں اور فصلیں خراب ہوتی ہیں۔

══ 12.7 Water scarcity in Pakistan (pp. 173–174) ══
Pakistan is one of the most water-stressed countries; available water per person has fallen sharply.
Causes:
1. Population growth – more demand for agriculture, industry and homes.
2. Climate change – irregular rainfall, melting glaciers, droughts and floods.
3. Over-extraction of groundwater – tube-wells lower the water table.
4. Wasteful flood irrigation – large losses by evaporation and seepage; inadequate distribution.
5. Insufficient storage – few dams and reservoirs; pollution makes existing water unusable.
Solutions:
- Effective water management: drip and sprinkler irrigation, lining canals.
- Infrastructure: dams, reservoirs, rainwater harvesting, recharge of aquifers.
- Policy reforms and strict regulation of groundwater extraction and illegal drilling.
- Treat and recycle wastewater; control pollution.
- Public awareness of responsible water use (fix leaks, avoid wastage).
پاکستان میں پانی کی کمی کی وجوہات: آبادی میں اضافہ، موسمیاتی تبدیلی، زیرِ زمین پانی کا بے تحاشا استعمال، سیلابی آبپاشی سے ضیاع اور ڈیموں کی کمی۔ حل: ڈرپ آبپاشی، ڈیم اور بارش کے پانی کا ذخیرہ، قوانین، گندے پانی کی ری سائیکلنگ اور عوامی شعور۔

══ 12.8 Fertilizers: urea, ammonium salts, nitrates and NPK (pp. 174) ══
Fertilizers are substances added to soil to supply essential elements for plant growth and increase crop yield.
Nitrogen fertilizers: urea CO(NH₂)₂ (46% N), ammonium salts – ammonium nitrate NH₄NO₃, ammonium sulphate (NH₄)₂SO₄, di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) (NH₄)₂HPO₄ – and nitrates such as potassium nitrate KNO₃, calcium ammonium nitrate (CAN).
NPK fertilizers supply the three primary nutrients:
- N (nitrogen): growth of leaves and stems; part of proteins and chlorophyll (green colour).
- P (phosphorus): root development, flowering, seeds and fruit; energy transfer.
- K (potassium): healthy growth, disease resistance, fruit quality, water regulation.
Fertilizers are water-soluble, so nutrients are readily available to plants. Applying the right amount at the right time (nutrient management) increases uptake and prevents run-off into rivers, which causes eutrophication.
[Table: Common fertilizers]
Fertilizer | Formula | Main nutrient(s)
• Urea | CO(NH₂)₂ | N (46%)
• Ammonium nitrate | NH₄NO₃ | N
• Ammonium sulphate | (NH₄)₂SO₄ | N, S
• Di-ammonium phosphate (DAP) | (NH₄)₂HPO₄ | N, P
• Potassium nitrate | KNO₃ | K, N
• Superphosphate | Ca(H₂PO₄)₂ (+ CaSO₄) | P
• NPK mixture | — | N, P and K
کھادیں پودوں کو ضروری عناصر مہیا کرتی ہیں۔ یوریا، امونیم نمکیات اور نائٹریٹس نائٹروجن دیتے ہیں۔ NPK کھاد نائٹروجن (پتے اور تنا)، فاسفورس (جڑیں، پھول، بیج) اور پوٹاشیم (بیماری سے بچاؤ، پھل) فراہم کرتی ہے۔ صحیح مقدار اور صحیح وقت پر استعمال سے پانی کی آلودگی کم ہوتی ہے۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Domestic water treatment: Screening → sedimentation (with alum) → sand filtration → carbon → chlorination → storage and supply.

chapters.definitions:
• Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate (بے آب کاپر سلفیٹ) [p. 167]: White CuSO₄ without water of crystallisation; turns blue with water.
• Distilled water (کشید شدہ پانی) [p. 171]: Water purified by distillation; free of dissolved substances, pH 7.
• Tap water (نلکے کا پانی) [p. 171]: Treated water supplied by municipal systems, containing dissolved minerals and a little chlorine.
• Universal solvent (عالمی محلل) [p. 169]: A name for water because it dissolves a very wide range of substances.
• Dissolved oxygen (حل شدہ آکسیجن) [p. 169]: Oxygen dissolved in water, needed by aquatic organisms.
• Eutrophication (غذائی افراط) [p. 170]: Excessive growth of algae caused by nitrates and phosphates, leading to deoxygenation of water when algae decay.
• Sedimentation (تہہ نشینی) [p. 170]: Allowing water to stand so that suspended particles settle to the bottom.
• Coagulation (تکثیف / گچھے بننا) [p. 170]: Making fine suspended particles clump together (e.g. using alum) so they settle.
• Chlorination (کلورینیشن) [p. 171]: Adding chlorine to water to kill harmful microbes.
• Water pollution (آبی آلودگی) [p. 171]: Contamination of water bodies by harmful substances that make the water unsafe for living things.
• Pathogenic microorganisms (بیماری پیدا کرنے والے جراثیم) [p. 172]: Disease-causing bacteria, viruses, protozoa and parasites.
• Water-borne disease (آبی بیماری) [p. 172]: A disease spread by drinking or using water contaminated with pathogens, e.g. cholera, typhoid.
• Water scarcity (پانی کی کمی) [p. 173]: Lack of sufficient clean water to meet the needs of people, agriculture and industry.
• Fertilizer (کھاد) [p. 174]: A substance that provides essential elements for plant growth to increase crop yield.
• NPK fertilizer (این پی کے کھاد) [p. 174]: A fertilizer supplying nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Anhydrous (بے آب): Without water
• Distillation (کشید): Boiling and condensing
• Sedimentation (تہہ نشینی): Settling of particles
• Filtration (چھاننا): Removing solids with a filter
• Chlorination (کلورین ملانا): Disinfecting with chlorine
• Coagulant (جمانے والا مادہ): Makes particles clump
• Pathogen (جرثومہ / مرض زا): Disease-causing microbe
• Eutrophication (غذائی افراط): Algal bloom from nutrients
• Scarcity (قلت): Shortage
• Fertilizer (کھاد): Plant nutrient supply
• Sewage (گندا پانی): Waste water from homes
• Aquifer (زیرِ زمین آبی ذخیرہ): Groundwater layer
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Hydrated copper(II) sulphate: CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue) (Anhydrous CuSO₄ is white)
• Pure water: m.p. 0 °C; b.p. 100 °C; pH 7 (At 1 atm)
• Aluminium sulphate (alum): Al₂(SO₄)₃ (Coagulant)
• Urea: CO(NH₂)₂ (46% nitrogen)
• Ammonium nitrate: NH₄NO₃
• Ammonium sulphate: (NH₄)₂SO₄
• Di-ammonium phosphate: (NH₄)₂HPO₄ (DAP)
• Potassium nitrate: KNO₃

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• CuSO₄(s) (white) + 5H₂O(l) -> CuSO₄·5H₂O(s) (blue) — Chemical test for water.
• CoCl₂(s) (blue) + 6H₂O(l) -> CoCl₂·6H₂O(s) (pink) — Cobalt chloride paper test for water.
• Cl₂ + H₂O -> HCl + HOCl — Chlorine forms hypochlorous acid, which kills microbes.
• Al₂(SO₄)₃ + 3Ca(OH)₂ -> 2Al(OH)₃ + 3CaSO₄ — Alum forms sticky Al(OH)₃ flocs that trap particles (coagulation).
• CO₂ + 2NH₃ -> CO(NH₂)₂ + H₂O — Manufacture of urea.
• NH₃ + HNO₃ -> NH₄NO₃ — Manufacture of ammonium nitrate.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why does a fish die in a pond after lots of fertilizer is washed into it?
   Answer: Nutrients cause an algal bloom; when algae die, bacteria use up dissolved oxygen while decomposing them, so fish suffocate.
2. Why is distilled water preferred for making solutions in the lab?
   Answer: It contains no dissolved ions that could react with or contaminate the solution.
3. Why does boiling make water safe from germs but not from arsenic?
   Answer: Heat kills microbes, but arsenic compounds are not destroyed; they become more concentrated as water evaporates.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. After a flood in a village, what simple steps can a family take to avoid water-borne diseases?
   Answer: Boil water or use chlorine tablets, store it in covered clean containers, wash hands with soap, avoid flood water, and get vaccinated if possible.
2. A farmer wants greener, leafier spinach. Which nutrient should be increased?
   Answer: Nitrogen (e.g. urea or ammonium nitrate).
