chapters.definitions:
• Nutrition (غذائیت) [p. 201]: The process of taking in and using food substances needed for energy, growth, repair and health.
• Balanced diet (متوازن غذا) [p. 201]: A diet providing all nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water, fibre) in suitable amounts and proportions.
• Biochemistry (حیاتیاتی کیمیا) [p. 202]: The study of the chemical molecules and reactions in living organisms.
• Biomolecules (حیاتیاتی مالیکیول) [p. 202]: Molecules produced by living organisms: carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.
• Carbohydrates (کاربوہائیڈریٹس) [p. 202]: Biomolecules of C, H and O whose main function is to supply energy (4 kcal/g).
• Proteins (پروٹین) [p. 203]: Macromolecules made of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; build and repair tissues (4 kcal/g).
• Amino acids (امینو ایسڈز) [p. 204]: The building blocks of proteins.
• Peptide bond (پیپٹائڈ بانڈ) [p. 210]: The bond linking amino acids in a protein.
• Enzymes (خامرے) [p. 203]: Proteins that act as biological catalysts, speeding up reactions in living organisms.
• Lipids (لپڈز) [p. 204]: Fatty acids or their derivatives; insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents; 9 kcal/g.
• Nucleic acids (نیوکلیک ایسڈز) [p. 205]: Large biomolecules made of nucleotides that carry genetic information (DNA, RNA).
• Nucleotide (نیوکلیوٹائڈ) [p. 205]: The basic building block of nucleic acids.
• Calorie (کیلوری) [p. 202]: Energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C.
• Malnutrition (غذائی قلت) [p. 209]: A condition caused by lack (or excess) of nutrients – under- or over-nourishment.
• Marasmus (میراسمس) [p. 209]: Severe undernutrition caused by deficiency of all macronutrients.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Nutrition (غذائیت): Use of food by the body
• Balanced diet (متوازن غذا): All nutrients in proportion
• Carbohydrate (نشاستہ دار غذا): Energy food
• Protein (لحمیات): Body-building food
• Lipid (چکنائی): Fats and oils
• Enzyme (خامرہ): Biological catalyst
• Amino acid (امینو ایسڈ): Unit of protein
• Nucleic acid (مرکزی تیزاب): DNA/RNA
• Calorie (حرارہ): Unit of food energy
• Malnutrition (غذائی قلت): Wrong amount of nutrients
• Deficiency (کمی): Shortage
• Fibre (ریشہ): Indigestible plant material
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Energy from carbohydrate: 1 g → 4 kcal
• Energy from protein: 1 g → 4 kcal
• Energy from lipid: 1 g → 9 kcal (Most energy-dense)
• Glucose: C₆H₁₂O₆ (Monosaccharide)
• Sucrose: C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ (Disaccharide)

══ KEY EQUATIONS & DERIVATIONS ══
• C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ -> 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy — Respiration of glucose in cells.
• Starch + water --enzymes--> glucose — Digestion of carbohydrates.
• Protein + water --enzymes--> amino acids — Digestion of proteins.
• Fat + water --enzymes--> fatty acids + glycerol — Digestion of lipids.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why does the brain suffer quickly when blood glucose is low?
   Answer: The brain cannot easily use fat or protein for energy; glucose is its preferred fuel.
2. Why must we eat some fat even though too much is harmful?
   Answer: Vitamins A, D, E, K need fat to be absorbed; fat is part of cell membranes and hormones.
3. Why do athletes eat pasta the night before a race?
   Answer: To build up glycogen stores for long-lasting energy.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. A student skips breakfast and feels dizzy in class. Which nutrient is low and why?
   Answer: Carbohydrate/glucose – the brain lacks its fuel.
2. Why are vegetable oils considered healthier than ghee?
   Answer: They contain more unsaturated fats and no cholesterol; ghee is rich in saturated fat and cholesterol linked to heart disease.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. A snack contains 20 g carbohydrate, 5 g protein and 10 g fat. How much energy does it provide?
   Given: Carbohydrate 20 g, protein 5 g, fat 10 g; 4, 4 and 9 kcal/g
   Required: Total energy
   Formula: Energy = mass × energy per gram
   Substitution: (20 × 4) + (5 × 4) + (10 × 9)
   Calculation: 80 + 20 + 90 = 190
   Final Answer: 190 kcal
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 15 Exercises (210–211):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. In a small village children frequently suffered from infectious diseases due to weak immune systems. Which major nutrients were lacking in their food? → C (Proteins) | Antibodies are proteins; protein deficiency weakens immunity.
ii. Which of the following food components are rich in fats? → D (Cheese, butter, and oil) | Dairy fats and oils.
iii. Potatoes, cereals, beans, pulses, and oats are rich in: → B (Carbohydrates) | Starchy foods.
iv. What is a bond between amino acids called? → C (Peptide bond) | Peptide bond.
v. The major function of carbohydrates includes: → A (Storage) | Carbohydrates supply and store energy (starch, glycogen).
vi. Which of the following disorders is NOT caused by the deficiency of proteins? → D (Constipation) | Constipation is linked to carbohydrate/fibre deficiency.
vii. Foods containing starch and carbohydrates are important because: → D (They give you energy) | Main energy source.
viii. Meat, fish, and other alternatives provide the following important nutrient: → B (Protein) | Animal protein.
ix. Which nutrient builds, maintains and repairs body tissues and cells? → B (Protein) | Growth and repair.
x. Marium’s doctor told her she has a shortage of blood (anaemia). What nutrient is lacking in her diet? → B (Protein) | Haemoglobin is a protein; the textbook lists anaemia as a protein-deficiency effect.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) Give three reasons why living organisms need food.
   Answer: (1) To get energy for all life activities. (2) For growth – making new cells and tissues. (3) For repair of damaged tissues (and to stay healthy and fight disease).
(ii) What is a balanced diet? What is the importance of a balanced diet?
   Answer: A diet containing all nutrients – carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and fibre – in correct proportions. It provides energy, supports growth and repair, keeps bones and muscles strong, improves immunity, and prevents obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease.
(iii) State four functions of proteins. Give one example to illustrate your answer.
   Answer: Growth and repair of tissues (muscle); enzymes as biological catalysts (amylase digests starch); hormones as messengers (insulin controls blood sugar); antibodies for defence; transport (haemoglobin carries oxygen).
(iv) Suggest two major foods a mother could give to her growing child, and why.
   Answer: Milk – protein for growth and calcium for bones and teeth. Eggs (or pulses/meat) – high-quality protein for building muscles and tissues. (Also cereals/rice for energy.)
(v) Carbohydrates are a major source of energy. Defend the statement.
   Answer: They are quickly digested to glucose; glucose is soluble and easily oxidised in respiration to release energy (4 kcal/g); the brain depends on glucose; they form the largest part of our diet (cereals, rice, potatoes); without them the body has to break down muscle protein for energy.
(vi) Fatima only eats junk food like French fries, burgers and pizza. What will happen? What should she add to her routine food?
   Answer: Junk food is high in fat, salt, sugar and calories but low in vitamins, minerals, fibre and good protein. She may become overweight/obese, develop high cholesterol and blood pressure, constipation, weak immunity and vitamin deficiencies. She should add fruits, vegetables, whole grains, milk, pulses, eggs/fish and plenty of water.

— Q3–Q7. Descriptive questions —
3. What are lipids? How are lipids important to our body?
   Answer: Lipids are fatty, waxy or oily compounds (fatty acids and their derivatives) insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as chloroform; e.g. fats, oils, waxes, steroids. Importance: concentrated energy store (9 kcal/g); part of cell membranes; help absorb vitamins A, D, E, K; make hormones; insulate the body and protect organs. Sources: butter, ghee, cheese, meat, vegetable oils, nuts.
4. How do you maintain a balanced diet?
   Answer: Eat a variety of foods from every food group daily: grains (3–8 bowls), at least 3 servings of vegetables and 2 of fruit, 200–400 g meat/fish/eggs/pulses, 1–2 servings of milk, 6–8 glasses of water; eat the least fat, salt and sugar; prefer whole grains and unsaturated oils; avoid junk food; eat regular meals and match calories to activity.
5. What percentage of fat is required in a balanced diet? Why is the percentage of fat the lowest among major food components? Justify.
   Answer: Roughly 20–35% of daily energy should come from fat (mostly unsaturated), and only a small amount by mass. Fat is kept lowest because it is energy-dense (9 kcal/g, over twice carbohydrates) – a little gives a lot of calories – and excess (especially saturated fat and cholesterol) causes obesity, high cholesterol, blocked arteries and heart disease. Some fat is still essential for vitamins A, D, E, K and cell membranes.
6. What are the sources and functions of nucleic acids?
   Answer: Sources: every living cell; foods such as seeds, grains, fish eggs, meat and fish. Functions: DNA stores all genetic information and passes it to the next generation; RNA copies the genetic code and directs protein synthesis; they control cell growth, division and metabolic regulation.
7. As a nutritionist, design a meal plan for marathon athletes. Explain how carbohydrates affect performance during the marathon.
   Answer: Carbohydrates are stored as glycogen in muscles and liver and are the fastest source of energy. “Carb-loading” (rice, pasta, bread, potatoes, fruits) for 2–3 days before the race fills glycogen stores and delays fatigue (“hitting the wall”). A carbohydrate-rich breakfast 3–4 hours before; sports drinks, bananas or dates during the race keep blood glucose up; after the race carbohydrates plus protein restore glycogen and repair muscles. Plenty of water and electrolytes. Low carbohydrate intake leads to early tiredness, poor concentration and muscle breakdown.
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] What is meant by nutrition? Why is healthy eating important?
   Answer: Nutrition: taking in and using food nutrients for energy, growth, repair and health. Healthy eating gives all nutrients, keeps weight normal, strengthens bones, muscles and immunity, and prevents obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] What is healthy eating? How does it support body functions?
   Answer: Eating a balanced variety of foods in the right amounts (less sugar, salt, fat). It supplies energy (carbohydrates), growth and repair (proteins), energy storage and vitamin absorption (lipids), and regulation (vitamins, minerals, water), supporting brain, heart, bones and immunity.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Name the three main biomolecules and state one food source of each.
   Answer: Carbohydrates – rice/wheat; proteins – eggs/meat/pulses; lipids – butter/oil.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Give two examples of carbohydrate-rich foods and state the role of carbohydrates in the human body.
   Answer: Rice, bread/wheat, potatoes (any two). Role: main source of energy (4 kcal/g) – broken down to glucose for respiration; fuel for the brain; fibre aids digestion.

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] What is nutrition? Why is it essential for proper functioning of the human body?
   Answer: Nutrition is obtaining and using food. It provides energy for all activities, materials for growth and repair, and substances (vitamins, minerals) that regulate body processes and immunity; without it organs cannot work properly.

6. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] Write one source each of carbohydrate, protein and lipid.
   Answer: Carbohydrate: rice; protein: fish/eggs; lipid: butter/cooking oil.

7. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What are carbohydrates? Give two examples.
   Answer: Biomolecules of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen that are the main energy source of the body. Examples: glucose, sucrose, starch (also lactose, glycogen).

8. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What are lipids? Give two sources.
   Answer: Fatty/oily compounds (fatty acids and derivatives) insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. Sources: butter/ghee and vegetable oils (also nuts, cheese).

9. Why do lipids provide more energy per gram than carbohydrates?
   Answer: Lipids are mostly hydrocarbon chains with little oxygen, so more C–H bonds are available for oxidation: 9 kcal/g vs 4 kcal/g.

10. Differentiate between DNA and RNA.
   Answer: DNA: double-stranded, deoxyribose, stores genetic information, mainly in the nucleus. RNA: single-stranded, ribose, uses the information to make proteins.

11. Differentiate between proteins and lipids.
   Answer: Proteins: polymers of amino acids (contain N), build and repair tissues, enzymes, 4 kcal/g; from meat, eggs, pulses. Lipids: fatty acids and glycerol, insoluble in water, energy store, 9 kcal/g; from butter, oils.

12. What is marasmus?
   Answer: A disease of severe undernutrition caused by deficiency of all macronutrients (carbohydrates, proteins and fats), leading to extreme thinness and wasting.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Discuss the functions of carbohydrates and proteins in the human body (any three each).
   Answer: Carbohydrates: (1) main source of energy (4 kcal/g) via glucose; (2) fuel for the brain; (3) stored as glycogen for later energy; fibre aids digestion; spare proteins from being used for energy. Proteins: (1) growth, building and repair of tissues; (2) enzymes as biological catalysts; (3) hormones (insulin), antibodies for immunity, haemoglobin for oxygen transport.

2. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026] Explain the importance of lipids as biomolecules: sources and functions (any three each).
   Answer: Sources: butter/ghee, cheese and milk, meat and eggs, sunflower/olive oil, nuts. Functions: energy store (9 kcal/g), part of cell membranes, absorption of vitamins A, D, E, K, making hormones, insulation and protection of organs.

3. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2026 (Old-22)] Explain the role of carbohydrates in daily activities and how their deficiency affects energy and functioning.
   Answer: Carbohydrates are digested to glucose, which is oxidised in respiration to give energy for walking, studying, playing and keeping the heart and brain working; glucose is the brain’s main fuel; stored glycogen supplies energy between meals. Deficiency: tiredness, weakness, headache, poor concentration, dizziness, constipation (low fibre); the body breaks down muscle protein and fat for energy, causing muscle loss and weight loss.

4. [Verified Official - FBISE 2nd Annual 2025] What are biomolecules? Name three major types and give one function of each.
   Answer: Molecules made by living organisms. Carbohydrates – energy; proteins – growth and repair/enzymes; lipids – energy storage and cell membranes (nucleic acids – genetic information).

5. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What are lipids and proteins? Give two sources of each.
   Answer: Lipids: fatty compounds insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents – butter, vegetable oil. Proteins: macromolecules of amino acids joined by peptide bonds – meat, eggs (also fish, pulses).

6. [Verified Official - FBISE Annual 2025] What are carbohydrates and proteins? Give two sources of each.
   Answer: Carbohydrates: C, H, O compounds giving energy – rice, potatoes. Proteins: amino-acid polymers for growth and repair – fish, pulses.

chapters.introduction:
Chemistry is an experimental science, so measurements must be standard, accurate and precise. This unit covers SI units (base and derived), prefixes (kilo, deci, centi, milli…), unit conversions, why chemists use cm³, g and s in the lab, scientific notation (standard form), accuracy vs precision, reading a meniscus, choosing the right apparatus (stopwatch, thermometer, balances, burette, pipette, measuring cylinder, gas syringe), and the advantages and disadvantages of experimental methods. Lab safety and practical skills (Domain G of the curriculum) are summarised at the end.

Mostly formative and practical (PBA) SLOs: only F-04 (why cm³, g, s) and F-09 (choosing apparatus) are summative, plus several practical-skill SLOs (G-06 to G-20). No question from this unit appears in the 2025–2026 FBISE papers supplied, so all exam-style questions here are AI-generated and labelled as such.

officialSlos: C-09-F-01 [Understanding | Formative]: Explain that units are standardized for better communication and collaboration. (Some examples may include: In the field of chemistry, the International System of Units (SI) is used to measure physical quantities such as mass, volume, and temperature. This standardized system ensures that chemists worldwide can use the same units to measure and communicate their results, facilitating communication and collaboration in the field. -Without standardized units, it would be difficult for chemists to compare their results with one another, and it would be challenging to develop consistent and accurate scientific models. For example, imagine if one chemist measured the mass of a substance in grams, while another used ounces. The two measurements would be difficult to compare and combine, potentially leading to inaccurate or inconsistent results.)

══ 16.1 Why standard units? The SI system (pp. 214–215) ══
Measurement is the comparison of an unknown quantity with a known fixed quantity (a unit). Example: body temperature 102 °F compared with normal 98.6 °F shows a fever.
In the past people used abstract units such as the cubit or hand-span, which varied from person to person – inconvenient and inaccurate.
In 1960 scientists agreed on the International System of Units (SI). Standard units let chemists everywhere measure, compare and communicate results in the same way, which helps collaboration and building consistent scientific models.
A physical quantity is anything that can be measured (mass, length, time, temperature, amount of substance).
Base (fundamental) units – seven independent units. Derived units are made by combining base units, e.g. area m², volume m³, density kg m⁻³, speed m s⁻¹.
[Table: Table 16.1 – The seven SI base units]
Physical quantity | Unit | Symbol
• Mass | kilogram | kg
• Length | metre | m
• Time | second | s
• Temperature | kelvin | K
• Amount of substance | mole | mol
• Electric current | ampere | A
• Luminous intensity | candela | cd
پیمائش نامعلوم مقدار کا معلوم معیاری اکائی سے موازنہ ہے۔ پرانی اکائیاں (ہاتھ، بالشت) ہر شخص کے لیے مختلف تھیں، اس لیے 1960 میں SI نظام اپنایا گیا تاکہ دنیا بھر کے سائنسدان ایک جیسی اکائیوں میں نتائج بیان کر سکیں۔ سات بنیادی اکائیاں: کلوگرام، میٹر، سیکنڈ، کیلون، مول، ایمپیئر اور کینڈیلا۔

══ 16.2 SI prefixes and unit conversions (pp. 215–217) ══
Prefixes are added to units to show multiples or fractions (powers of ten) of the base unit, so very large or small quantities are easy to write.
Converting: larger → smaller unit: multiply; smaller → larger unit: divide.
- 12 kg = 12 × 1000 = 12 000 g = 12 000 × 1000 = 12 000 000 mg.
- 0.2 g = 200 mg (a nurse with 50 mg tablets must give 4 tablets).
- 0.003 kg = 3 g = 3000 mg.
Length: 10 mm = 1 cm; 10 cm = 1 dm; 100 cm = 1 m; 1000 m = 1 km.
Mass: 1000 mg = 1 g; 1000 g = 1 kg.
Time: 60 s = 1 min; 60 min = 1 h; 24 h = 1 day.
Volume: SI unit is m³. 1 L = 1000 mL = 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³; 1 mL = 1 cm³.
Prefixes are also used in naming binary molecular compounds: mono-, di-, tri-, tetra-, penta- (CO carbon monoxide, CO₂ carbon dioxide, CCl₄ carbon tetrachloride, PCl₅ phosphorus pentachloride, N₂O dinitrogen monoxide, S₂Cl₂ disulfur dichloride).
[Table: Table 16.2 – Common SI prefixes]
Prefix | Symbol | Factor | Example
• mega | M | 10⁶ | 1 Mm = 1 000 000 m
• kilo | k | 10³ | 1 km = 1000 m
• hecto | h | 10² | 1 hm = 100 m
• deca | da | 10¹ | 1 dam = 10 m
• — | — | 10⁰ | 1 m
• deci | d | 10⁻¹ | 1 dm = 0.1 m
• centi | c | 10⁻² | 1 cm = 0.01 m
• milli | m | 10⁻³ | 1 mm = 0.001 m
• micro | µ | 10⁻⁶ | 1 µm = 0.000 001 m
• nano | n | 10⁻⁹ | 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m
سابقے (کلو، ڈیسی، سینٹی، ملی وغیرہ) اکائی کے دس کے گنا یا حصے ظاہر کرتے ہیں۔ بڑی سے چھوٹی اکائی میں ضرب اور چھوٹی سے بڑی میں تقسیم کرتے ہیں: 0.003 kg = 3000 mg۔ حجم: 1 لیٹر = 1000 mL = 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³۔

══ 16.3 Why chemists use cm³, g and s in the lab (pp. 217) ══
In school and research labs chemists work with small amounts, so smaller units are more practical than m³, kg and hours:
1. cm³ (volume): easy to measure and calculate small volumes of liquids accurately; matches the scale on burettes, pipettes and measuring cylinders (1 cm³ = 1 mL).
2. g (mass): gives more precise and consistent readings for small samples than kilograms; laboratory balances read in grams (to 0.01 or 0.001 g).
3. s (time): reactions are often fast; seconds allow accurate measurement of reaction rates and times. Hours would be far too coarse (e.g. in a race, results differ by fractions of a second).
4. Compatibility with laboratory equipment and instruments.
5. International standards – recommended within the SI/metric system, so results are easy to share and compare.
لیبارٹری میں تھوڑی مقدار سے کام ہوتا ہے، اس لیے cm³، گرام اور سیکنڈ زیادہ موزوں ہیں: چھوٹے حجم اور کمیت درستگی سے ناپے جا سکتے ہیں، آلات انہی اکائیوں میں نشان زدہ ہوتے ہیں اور تیز تعاملات کا وقت سیکنڈوں میں ناپنا ضروری ہے۔

══ 16.4 Scientific notation (standard form) (pp. 217–219) ══
Scientific notation writes very large or very small numbers as A × 10^n, where 1 ≤ A < 10 and n is a positive or negative integer. It simplifies calculations, comparisons and communication.
Rules:
- Large numbers (≥ 10): move the decimal point left; n is positive. 6000 = 6 × 10³; 650 000 000 = 6.5 × 10⁸; 38 000 000 000 = 3.8 × 10¹⁰.
- Small numbers (< 1): move the decimal point right; n is negative. 0.006 = 6 × 10⁻³; 0.000 000 46 = 4.6 × 10⁻⁷; 0.000 000 000 34 = 3.4 × 10⁻¹⁰.
- 14 × 10³ is not standard form (A must be < 10): write 1.4 × 10⁴.
Calculating in standard form:
- Multiply: multiply the A values and add the powers: (2 × 10³) × (3 × 10⁴) = 6 × 10⁷.
- Divide: divide the A values and subtract the powers: (8 × 10⁶) ÷ (2 × 10²) = 4 × 10⁴.
- Add/subtract: first make the powers the same: 3 × 10⁴ + 5 × 10³ = 3 × 10⁴ + 0.5 × 10⁴ = 3.5 × 10⁴.
Real examples: diameter of Earth 12 800 000 m ≈ 1.28 × 10⁷ m; height of a soldier 1.7 m = 1.7 × 10⁰ m; mosquito 0.01 m = 1 × 10⁻² m; red blood cell 0.000 0075 m = 7.5 × 10⁻⁶ m; Avogadro’s number 6.02 × 10²³.
Exam Tip: Count how many places the decimal point moves: that number is n. Moved left → positive; moved right → negative.
سائنسی ترقیم میں عدد کو A × 10^n لکھتے ہیں جہاں A ایک اور دس کے درمیان ہو۔ بڑے عدد کے لیے اعشاریہ بائیں طرف (n مثبت) اور چھوٹے عدد کے لیے دائیں طرف (n منفی) کھسکاتے ہیں: 6000 = 6 × 10³، 0.006 = 6 × 10⁻³۔

══ 16.5 Accuracy, precision and errors (pp. 220) ══
- Accuracy: how close a measurement is to the true (actual) value. Mostly depends on how well the instrument is calibrated/adjusted.
- Precision: how close repeated measurements are to each other (reproducibility). Mostly depends on the care and technique of the person and the instrument’s scale.
A badly adjusted balance can give very precise but inaccurate results; careless spilling gives imprecise results even with an accurate balance. The dartboard picture: all darts clustered at the centre = accurate and precise; clustered away from the centre = precise but inaccurate; scattered = imprecise.
Calculating accuracy (percentage error):
% error = |measured value − true value| ÷ true value × 100. The smaller the % error, the more accurate the result.
Managing errors:
- Calibrate and zero (tare) instruments before use.
- Read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level to avoid parallax error (reading from above gives a smaller value; from below gives a larger value).
- Repeat readings and take the average; discard anomalous results.
- Choose apparatus with a suitable scale (pipette/burette for accurate volumes).
- Control variables (temperature, draughts on a balance).
درستگی (Accuracy): پیمائش حقیقی قدر کے کتنی قریب ہے۔ یکسانیت (Precision): بار بار کی پیمائشیں ایک دوسرے کے کتنی قریب ہیں۔ غلطی کم کرنے کے لیے آلات کو درست کریں، مینسکس کو آنکھ کی سطح پر پڑھیں، پیمائش دہرا کر اوسط نکالیں۔

══ 16.6 Choosing apparatus for time, temperature, mass and volume (pp. 220–223) ══
Volume:
- Beaker: approximate volumes only; for holding, mixing, heating liquids.
- Measuring cylinder: more accurate than a beaker; 10, 25, 50, 100 cm³ sizes; use when an approximate volume is acceptable.
- Volumetric pipette: delivers one fixed volume (usually 25 cm³) very accurately; always use with a pipette filler.
- Burette: delivers any volume up to 50 cm³; more accurate than a measuring cylinder, less than a pipette; volume = final − initial reading; held in a stand, boss and clamp; used in titrations.
- Gas syringe: collects and measures the volume of a gas; similar accuracy to a measuring cylinder.
Temperature: laboratory thermometer (about −10 °C to 110 °C) for boiling and freezing points and temperature changes.
Mass: analytical balance (very precise, quantitative analysis); beam balance (no electricity needed); electronic balance (quick digital readings; tare before use).
Time: stopwatch/timer – reads to 2 decimal places (precision 0.01 s), measures time intervals in rate experiments.
Liquid in a measuring cylinder forms a U-shaped meniscus: read the bottom of the curve at eye level.
[Table: Apparatus and what it measures]
Quantity | Apparatus | Notes
• Time | Stopwatch | Precision 0.01 s
• Temperature | Thermometer | −10 to 110 °C
• Mass | Electronic / analytical / beam balance | Analytical most precise
• Fixed volume of liquid | Volumetric pipette | Most accurate; e.g. 25.0 cm³
• Variable volume of liquid | Burette | Up to 50 cm³; titrations
• Approximate volume | Measuring cylinder / beaker | Cylinder more accurate
• Volume of gas | Gas syringe | e.g. up to 100 cm³
وقت کے لیے اسٹاپ واچ، درجہ حرارت کے لیے تھرمامیٹر، کمیت کے لیے ترازو (الیکٹرانک، اینالیٹیکل، بیم)، مقررہ حجم کے لیے پپیٹ (سب سے درست)، مختلف حجم کے لیے بیوریٹ (50 cm³ تک)، اندازاً حجم کے لیے ناپنے والا سلنڈر اور گیس کے حجم کے لیے گیس سرنج۔

══ 16.7 Experimental methods; lab safety and practical skills (pp. 223–224) ══
Great chemists (Lavoisier, Boyle, Curie, Rutherford, Pauling) discovered key ideas by experiment; today experiments test new medicines and materials.
Advantages of experimental methods: high level of control over variables; allows many variations to be tested; can give excellent, reliable results; usable in different fields.
Disadvantages: may create artificial situations; can take time and money; can be affected by errors; may not be feasible in some situations (dangerous, unethical).
Lab safety (curriculum Domain G):
- Hazards: flammable/explosive, toxic, corrosive, oxidising, irritant, health hazards. Learn the hazard symbols on bottles.
- PPE: lab coat, safety goggles, gloves; tie back hair; closed shoes.
- Know where the fire extinguisher, emergency shower and eye-wash are; report accidents and spills to the teacher immediately.
Good practical technique: select the most suitable apparatus and justify it; take readings with appropriate precision; repeat measurements; record results in tables with units; plot graphs with best-fit lines; identify anomalous results, sources of error and limitations; suggest improvements; control variables.
[Table: Advantages and disadvantages of experimental methods]
Advantages | Disadvantages
• High level of control | Can lead to artificial situations
• Allows many variations | Can take a lot of time and money
• Can lead to excellent results | Can be affected by errors
• Can be used in different fields | Might not be feasible in some situations
تجرباتی طریقے کے فوائد: متغیرات پر قابو، کئی تبدیلیاں آزمانا، اچھے نتائج۔ نقصانات: مصنوعی حالات، وقت اور خرچ، غلطیاں۔ لیبارٹری میں حفاظتی چشمہ، کوٹ اور دستانے پہنیں، خطرے کی علامات پہچانیں اور آگ بجھانے والے آلے کی جگہ معلوم رکھیں۔

- Measurement = comparing with a standard unit. SI (1960): 7 base units – kg, m, s, K, mol, A, cd. Derived units combine them (m³, g cm⁻³).

chapters.definitions:
• Measurement (پیمائش) [p. 214]: Comparison of an unknown quantity with a known fixed quantity (unit).
• Physical quantity (طبعی مقدار) [p. 215]: A quantity that can be measured, e.g. mass, length, time.
• SI units (بین الاقوامی اکائیاں) [p. 214]: The International System of Units adopted in 1960 for uniform measurement worldwide.
• Base (fundamental) units (بنیادی اکائیاں) [p. 215]: The seven independent SI units: kg, m, s, K, mol, A, cd.
• Derived units (ماخوذ اکائیاں) [p. 215]: Units formed by combining base units, e.g. m³, kg m⁻³.
• Prefix (سابقہ) [p. 215]: A word added to a unit to show a multiple or fraction (power of ten), e.g. kilo, milli.
• Scientific notation (standard form) (سائنسی ترقیم) [p. 217]: Writing a number as A × 10^n with 1 ≤ A < 10 and n an integer.
• Accuracy (درستگی) [p. 220]: How close a measurement is to the true value.
• Precision (یکسانیت) [p. 220]: How close repeated measurements are to each other.
• Meniscus (ہلالی سطح) [p. 220]: The curved surface of a liquid in a narrow tube; read at the bottom for water.
• Parallax error (زاویائی غلطی) [p. 220]: Error from reading a scale with the eye not level with the mark.
• Burette (بیوریٹ) [p. 222]: Graduated tube with a tap delivering any volume up to 50 cm³; used in titrations.
• Volumetric pipette (پپیٹ) [p. 221]: Apparatus that delivers one fixed volume of liquid very accurately.
• Gas syringe (گیس سرنج) [p. 222]: Apparatus to collect and measure the volume of a gas.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Measurement (پیمائش): Comparison with a unit
• Unit (اکائی): Standard quantity
• Prefix (سابقہ): Multiplier word
• Standard form (معیاری صورت): A × 10^n
• Accuracy (درستگی): Close to true value
• Precision (یکسانیت): Repeatability
• Meniscus (ہلالی سطح): Curved liquid surface
• Burette (بیوریٹ): Titration tube
• Pipette (پپیٹ): Fixed-volume transfer
• Balance (ترازو): Measures mass
• Calibrate (درست کرنا / پیمانہ بندی): Adjust to true scale
• Hazard (خطرہ): Source of danger
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Standard form: A × 10^n, 1 ≤ A < 10
• Volume relations: 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1000 mL (1 mL = 1 cm³)
• Mass relations: 1 kg = 1000 g; 1 g = 1000 mg
• Percentage error: % error = |measured − true| ÷ true × 100 (Measures accuracy)
• Burette volume: Volume delivered = final reading − initial reading
• Density: density = mass ÷ volume (g cm⁻³) (Derived quantity)
• Multiplying in standard form: (a × 10^m)(b × 10^n) = ab × 10m⁺ⁿ
• Dividing in standard form: (a × 10^m) ÷ (b × 10^n) = (a/b) × 10m⁻ⁿ

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. A balance always reads 0.20 g too high. Are its readings precise, accurate, both or neither?
   Answer: They can be precise (consistent) but are not accurate (systematic error). Zeroing/calibrating fixes it.
2. Why is 25 × 10³ not in standard form?
   Answer: A must be less than 10; write 2.5 × 10⁴.
3. Why does the SI unit of mass contain a prefix (kilogram)?
   Answer: Historical reason: the base unit was defined as the kilogram; the gram is a derived fraction.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. A pharmacist must give 0.25 g of a medicine using 125 mg tablets. How many tablets?
   Answer: 0.25 g = 250 mg; 250 ÷ 125 = 2 tablets.
2. Why do cricket umpires and athletics officials use electronic timing rather than hand stopwatches?
   Answer: Electronic timing removes human reaction-time error and gives precise readings to 0.01 s or better.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. Convert 0.00000046 into scientific notation.
   Solution: Move the decimal point 7 places to the right to get 4.6; the number is less than 1, so the power is negative: 4.6 × 10⁻⁷.

2. A chemist has 0.003 kg of a sample. Convert it to milligrams.
   Given: Mass = 0.003 kg; 1 kg = 1000 g; 1 g = 1000 mg
   Required: Mass in mg
   Formula: kg → g: × 1000; g → mg: × 1000
   Substitution: 0.003 × 1000 × 1000
   Calculation: 0.003 × 1 000 000 = 3000
   Final Answer: 3000 mg (3 × 10³ mg)

3. A student measures the boiling point of water as 98.5 °C. The true value is 100.0 °C. Calculate the percentage error.
   Given: Measured = 98.5 °C; true = 100.0 °C
   Required: % error
   Formula: % error = |measured − true| ÷ true × 100
   Substitution: |98.5 − 100.0| ÷ 100.0 × 100
   Calculation: 1.5 ÷ 100 × 100 = 1.5
   Final Answer: 1.5 %

4. Calculate (4.0 × 10⁵) × (2.5 × 10⁻³) and give the answer in standard form.
   Given: (4.0 × 10⁵), (2.5 × 10⁻³)
   Required: Product in standard form
   Formula: Multiply A values, add powers
   Substitution: (4.0 × 2.5) × 10⁵⁺⁽⁻³⁾
   Calculation: 10 × 10² = 1.0 × 10³
   Final Answer: 1.0 × 10³
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 16 Exercises (224–226):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. What is the volume of the liquid in the graduated cylinder shown (scale 10–30, 1 cm³ divisions)? → B (24) | The bottom of the meniscus lies about one small division below the 25 mark: 24 cm³.
ii. How many cubic centimetres (cm³) are there in 1 decimetre cube (1 dm³)? → B (1000 cm³) | 1 dm = 10 cm, so 10³ = 1000 cm³.
iii. To change SI units by factors of ten into smaller or bigger units we use: → A (Prefixes) | kilo, milli etc.
iv. A distance of 1 kilometre means: → C (1000 m) | kilo = 1000.
v. One nanometre is equal to: → B (10⁻⁹ m) | nano = 10⁻⁹.
vi. The standard form of 38000000000 is: → C (3.8 × 10¹⁰) | Decimal moves 10 places left.
vii. The property of a measuring instrument to give output very close to the actual value is termed: → B (Accuracy) | Definition of accuracy.
viii. The standard form of 0.00000000034 is: → C (3.4 × 10⁻¹⁰) | Decimal moves 10 places right.
ix. In SI, the unit of mass is: → A (kilogram) | Base unit.
x. In measuring instruments, the degree of conformity and closeness to the true value is known as: → B (Accuracy) | Accuracy.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) What is Système International (SI)? Why are SI units standardised for better communication and collaboration?
   Answer: The International System of Units, agreed in 1960, with seven base units (kg, m, s, K, mol, A, cd). Standard units mean a measurement means the same everywhere, so scientists can compare and repeat each other’s results, share data without confusion, and build consistent models.
(ii) In a race, why is it essential to use seconds or minutes instead of hours for recording time?
   Answer: Race times differ by small amounts (often fractions of a second); hours are too large a unit to show these differences, so results would be imprecise and winners could not be decided.
(iii) Differentiate between accuracy and precision.
   Answer: Accuracy: closeness of a measurement to the true value; depends on calibration. Precision: closeness of repeated measurements to each other; depends on technique and scale. Results can be precise but not accurate.
(iv) A chemist has a sample of mass 0.003 kg. How will he convert this mass to milligrams?
   Answer: Multiply by 1000 to get grams (3 g), then by 1000 again to get milligrams: 0.003 × 10⁶ = 3000 mg.
(v) What is the use of prefixes in measurements?
   Answer: They show multiples or fractions of a unit by powers of ten (kilo = 10³, milli = 10⁻³), so very large or small quantities can be written conveniently and converted easily.
(vi) What are the advantages of using scientific tools like measuring cylinders, stopwatches and thermometers?
   Answer: They give standard, objective, accurate and repeatable readings with known precision; results can be recorded in SI units and compared; they reduce guesswork and human error.

— Q3–Q7. Descriptive questions —
3. How do you calculate the accuracy of measurements?
   Answer: Compare the measured value with the true/accepted value using percentage error = |measured − true| ÷ true × 100. A smaller percentage error means higher accuracy. Example: measured 98.5 °C, true 100 °C → 1.5% error.
4. Evaluate how tools for measurement are helpful in performing scientific techniques.
   Answer: Each tool suits a task: burettes and pipettes give accurate volumes for titrations; balances give precise masses for preparing solutions; thermometers track temperature in m.p./b.p. and energy experiments; stopwatches time reactions for rates; gas syringes measure gas volumes. Correct tools reduce errors, allow repeats and give reliable data for conclusions; limitations (e.g. beakers are only approximate) must be recognised.
5. How does scientific notation enhance the ability to communicate about extremely large and small numbers? Convince.
   Answer: It removes long strings of zeros (6.02 × 10²³ instead of 602 000 000 000 000 000 000 000), making numbers easy to read, write, compare (just compare powers of ten) and calculate with (add/subtract powers); it reduces copying errors and shows significant figures clearly; it is understood worldwide.
6. Why do scientists realise the need for a standardised system of measurement?
   Answer: Old units like the cubit or hand-span varied between people, so results could not be compared or repeated. Science is international and collaborative; trade, medicine and engineering need exact agreed units. A standard system (SI) ensures uniformity, accuracy, easy conversion (powers of ten) and clear communication.
7. Design an experiment to determine the density of a liquid.
   Answer: 1. Find the mass of a clean, dry empty beaker (or measuring cylinder) on an electronic balance: m₁.
2. Using a pipette (or burette), transfer an exact volume, e.g. 25.0 cm³, of the liquid into the beaker.
3. Find the mass again: m₂. Mass of liquid = m₂ − m₁.
4. Density = mass ÷ volume (g cm⁻³).
5. Repeat three times and average; keep the temperature constant; read the meniscus at eye level. Example: 20.0 g ÷ 25.0 cm³ = 0.80 g cm⁻³.
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. Justify why chemists use cm³, g and s as more practical units when working with small amounts in the lab.
   Answer: Lab quantities are small: cm³ matches burette/pipette scales and measures small volumes accurately; grams give precise readings on lab balances; seconds are needed to time fast reactions; these units are compatible with lab equipment and internationally accepted.

2. Identify the most suitable apparatus to measure: (a) exactly 25.0 cm³ of acid (b) the volume of gas given off in a reaction (c) the time for a reaction (d) the volume of alkali added in a titration.
   Answer: (a) Volumetric pipette (b) gas syringe (c) stopwatch (d) burette.

3. Write 0.000 52 and 7 300 000 in standard form.
   Answer: 5.2 × 10⁻⁴; 7.3 × 10⁶.

4. Calculate (6 × 10⁸) ÷ (3 × 10⁻²).
   Answer: 2 × 10¹⁰ (6 ÷ 3 = 2; 8 − (−2) = 10).

5. Why should a measuring cylinder be read at eye level?
   Answer: To avoid parallax error: from above you read too low, from below too high; at eye level the bottom of the meniscus gives the true reading.

6. State two advantages and two disadvantages of experimental methods.
   Answer: Advantages: control of variables; many variations can be tested (excellent results, used in many fields). Disadvantages: artificial situations; costly and time-consuming (errors, not always feasible).

7. Name the seven SI base units.
   Answer: kilogram (mass), metre (length), second (time), kelvin (temperature), mole (amount of substance), ampere (current), candela (luminous intensity).

8. Which is more accurate for measuring volume: a burette or a measuring cylinder? Explain.
   Answer: A burette – it has finer graduations (0.1 cm³) and is read to 0.05 cm³, while a measuring cylinder has wider divisions.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. Explain with examples how different tools and techniques are used to manage accuracy and precision.
   Answer: Accuracy: calibrate balances and thermometers, tare balances, use volumetric pipettes for exact volumes, compare with true values (% error). Precision: use instruments with fine scales (burette 0.1 cm³, stopwatch 0.01 s), read meniscus at eye level, repeat readings and average, careful handling (no spills), control temperature. Example: three titres of 24.10, 24.15, 24.10 cm³ are precise; if the burette was calibrated, they are also accurate.

2. Describe the apparatus used to measure time, temperature, mass and volume in the laboratory, giving one advantage or limitation of each.
   Answer: Stopwatch – precision 0.01 s but human reaction time error. Thermometer – −10 to 110 °C, must be read at eye level. Electronic balance – fast and precise, needs taring and no draughts; beam balance needs no electricity. Pipette – most accurate fixed volume, only one volume. Burette – any volume to 50 cm³, needs stand and careful reading. Measuring cylinder – quick, less accurate. Gas syringe – measures gas volume, plunger may stick.
chapters.chapterSummary:
══ Chapter 16 in one page
- Measurement = comparing with a standard unit. SI (1960): 7 base units – kg, m, s, K, mol, A, cd. Derived units combine them (m³, g cm⁻³).
- Prefixes: k 10³, h 10², da 10, d 10⁻¹, c 10⁻², m 10⁻³, µ 10⁻⁶, n 10⁻⁹. Larger → smaller: multiply; smaller → larger: divide. 1 L = 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³; 1 mL = 1 cm³.
- Lab units cm³, g, s: small amounts, match apparatus scales, precise, fast reactions timed, SI-compatible.
- Standard form: A × 10^n, 1 ≤ A < 10; big numbers +n, small numbers −n. Multiply → add powers; divide → subtract powers.
- Accuracy = close to true value (calibration); precision = repeat readings close together (technique). % error = |measured − true| ÷ true × 100. Read the meniscus bottom at eye level.
- Apparatus: stopwatch (0.01 s), thermometer (−10 to 110 °C), balances (analytical, electronic, beam), pipette (fixed, most accurate), burette (≤ 50 cm³, titrations), measuring cylinder (approximate), gas syringe (gas volume).
- Experimental methods: control, variations, good results vs artificial, costly, errors, not always feasible. Safety: hazard symbols, PPE, know the fire extinguisher and emergency shower.

chapters.title: Separation Techniques
chapters.introduction:
Most materials around us are mixtures. To obtain useful pure substances – drinking water, salt, medicines, petrol – we must separate and purify them using differences in physical properties (particle size, solubility, boiling point). This unit defines the key solution terms (solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution, residue, filtrate) and explains evaporation, filtration, crystallisation, simple and fractional distillation and using a suitable solvent, how to choose a technique, and how melting and boiling points show purity.

All four SLOs (F-11 to F-14) are summative and PBA (practical). They are tested through practical work and short questions on choosing a technique (sand + salt, alcohol + water, salt from sea water) and purity from m.p./b.p. No question from this unit appears in the uploaded 2025–2026 papers, so exam-style questions here are AI-generated.

They are tested through practical work and short questions on choosing a technique (sand + salt, alcohol + water, salt from sea water) and purity from m.p./b.p. Note: Textbook statements corrected: (1) a larger surface area increases evaporation because more molecules are at the surface (not “more molecules per unit volume”); (2) a solute need not be a solid nor the solvent a liquid, though that is the common case; (3) in the gold-panning story the soil is washed away (suspended), not dissolved.

══ 17.1 Mixtures and the language of solutions (pp. 228, 232) ══
A mixture contains two or more substances not chemically combined, present in any proportion, which can be separated by physical methods using differences in size, density, solubility, boiling point, magnetism etc. Separation lets us obtain valuable components (gold from soil, salt from sea water) and study or use pure substances (medicines).
- Heterogeneous mixture: components not evenly distributed (sand in water).
- Homogeneous mixture (solution): components evenly distributed (brine).
Key terms:
- Solvent: the substance that dissolves a solute (usually present in larger amount), e.g. water in salt solution.
- Solute: the substance that dissolves in a solvent (smaller amount), e.g. salt.
- Solution: a mixture of one or more solutes dissolved in a solvent.
- Saturated solution: a solution containing the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in the solvent at a specific temperature; extra solute stays undissolved (dynamic equilibrium between dissolving and crystallising).
- Residue: the substance that remains behind after evaporation, distillation or filtration (e.g. sand on filter paper).
- Filtrate: the liquid or solution that has passed through a filter.
[Table: Solution terms with salt solution example]
Term | Meaning | Example
• Solvent | Dissolves the solute | Water
• Solute | Dissolves in the solvent | Salt
• Solution | Solute + solvent | Brine
• Saturated solution | No more solute dissolves at that temperature | Brine with undissolved salt at the bottom
• Residue | Left behind on the filter / in the dish | Sand on filter paper; salt in evaporating dish
• Filtrate | Liquid passing through the filter | Clear salt water
آمیزہ دو یا زیادہ مادوں کا کیمیائی طور پر غیر ملا ہوا مجموعہ ہے جسے طبعی طریقوں سے الگ کیا جا سکتا ہے۔ محلل (پانی) منحل (نمک) کو حل کرتا ہے اور دونوں مل کر محلول بناتے ہیں۔ سیر شدہ محلول میں کسی خاص درجہ حرارت پر زیادہ سے زیادہ منحل حل ہوتا ہے۔ فلٹر پر رہ جانے والا مادہ باقیات (residue) اور فلٹر سے گزرنے والا مائع فلٹریٹ کہلاتا ہے۔

══ 17.2 Evaporation (pp. 228–230) ══
Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a liquid: the liquid turns into vapour and the non-volatile solid is left behind in an evaporating dish. It works because liquids vaporise easily but solids do not.
Example: heat salt solution in an evaporating dish → water evaporates → salt remains (residue).
Factors affecting the rate of evaporation:
- Temperature: higher temperature → particles have more kinetic energy → faster evaporation.
- Surface area: larger surface → more molecules at the surface able to escape → faster.
- Intermolecular forces: stronger forces → slower evaporation (water evaporates more slowly than acetone).
- Pressure: higher pressure above the liquid → slower evaporation.
- Air flow (wind): moving dry air carries vapour away → faster.
Uses: salt from sea water (salt pans), getting dye from ink, making milk powder and lactose powder, juice concentrates, extracting minerals from mineral water.
Limitation: the liquid is lost, and any soluble impurities stay mixed with the solid; heating to dryness can decompose some solids (e.g. hydrated salts lose water).
تبخیر کے ذریعے حل شدہ ٹھوس کو مائع سے الگ کرتے ہیں: مائع بخارات بن کر اڑ جاتا ہے اور ٹھوس رہ جاتا ہے (سمندری پانی سے نمک)۔ درجہ حرارت، سطحی رقبہ اور ہوا کا بہاؤ بڑھنے سے تبخیر تیز ہوتی ہے؛ زیادہ دباؤ اور مضبوط بین سالمی قوتوں سے سست۔

══ 17.3 Filtration (pp. 231–234) ══
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (heterogeneous mixture) using a filter medium (filter paper, muslin cloth, membrane). The pores let the small liquid particles pass but trap the larger solid particles.
- The solid left on the filter = residue; the liquid that passes through = filtrate.
Gravity filtration: a cone of filter paper in a glass funnel; liquid passes through under gravity. Pore size decides speed.
Vacuum (suction) filtration: a Büchner funnel (flat porcelain funnel with holes) on a side-arm filter flask connected to a vacuum pump; a wetted circular filter paper seals the bottom. Faster, gives drier solids.
Example: sand + water → filter → sand is the residue, water is the filtrate.
Daily-life filtration: coffee and tea bags; kidneys filter blood; HEPA filters in vacuum cleaners and air conditioners; aquarium filters; car and factory air filters; water and sewage treatment; ground (sand and rock) filtering rainwater into aquifers; belt filters in mining.
Limitation: filtration cannot separate a dissolved solid (salt) from a solution – the solute passes through with the filtrate.
فلٹریشن ناحل پذیر ٹھوس کو مائع سے الگ کرتی ہے؛ فلٹر پیپر کے سوراخ مائع کو گزرنے دیتے ہیں مگر ٹھوس ذرات روک لیتے ہیں۔ فلٹر پر بچا مادہ باقیات اور گزرنے والا مائع فلٹریٹ ہے۔ کشش ثقل والی فلٹریشن (قیف اور فلٹر پیپر) اور ویکیوم فلٹریشن (بخنر قیف) دو طریقے ہیں۔ روزمرہ مثالیں: چائے کی پتی، گردے، ایئر کنڈیشنر کے فلٹر۔

══ 17.4 Crystallisation (pp. 234–235) ══
Crystallisation obtains a pure solid (crystals) from its solution. Principle: a solute has limited solubility that decreases as temperature falls; when a hot saturated solution cools, the excess solute separates out as crystals, while soluble impurities stay dissolved in the remaining solution (mother liquor).
Steps:
1. Dissolve the impure solid in the minimum amount of hot solvent (water); filter off any insoluble impurities.
2. Heat the solution to evaporate some solvent until it is saturated – test by dipping a glass rod: crystals form on the rod as the drop cools.
3. Stop heating and let the solution cool slowly.
4. Filter off the crystals.
5. Wash with a little cold solvent and dry (in a warm oven, between filter papers, or in air).
Crystal size: slow cooling → large crystals; rapid cooling → many tiny crystals.
Why crystallisation is better than evaporating to dryness: it removes soluble impurities and does not decompose heat-sensitive or hydrated crystals (e.g. CuSO₄·5H₂O).
Applications: pure salt from sea water; pure alum from impure alum; sugar refining; medicines. Natural crystallisation: ice and snow, honey crystallising, sugar crystals in cooling syrup, stalactites and stalagmites.
قلماؤ سے محلول سے خالص ٹھوس قلمیں حاصل کی جاتی ہیں۔ گرم محلول کو سیر شدہ ہونے تک گرم کرتے ہیں، پھر ٹھنڈا کرتے ہیں؛ حل پذیری کم ہونے سے قلمیں بنتی ہیں اور حل پذیر ملاوٹیں محلول میں رہ جاتی ہیں۔ آہستہ ٹھنڈا کرنے سے بڑی قلمیں بنتی ہیں۔ سمندری پانی سے خالص نمک اور پھٹکری کی صفائی اس کی مثالیں ہیں۔

══ 17.5 Simple and fractional distillation (pp. 230–231) ══
Distillation separates components of a liquid mixture by heating and cooling, using differences in boiling point (volatility). The liquid collected after condensing the vapour is the distillate.
Simple distillation – to get a solvent from a solution (water from salt water) or separate liquids with very different boiling points:
1. Heat the mixture in a round-bottom (distillation) flask; a thermometer at the side arm reads the vapour temperature.
2. The more volatile component (lower b.p.) boils and its vapour enters a water-cooled Liebig condenser (water in at the bottom, out at the top).
3. The vapour condenses and the distillate drips into a receiver/conical flask.
4. The non-volatile solute (salt) stays in the flask.
Fractional distillation – to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points (ethanol 78 °C and water 100 °C; crude oil; liquid air). A fractionating column (packed with glass beads) between flask and condenser creates a temperature gradient – hotter at the bottom, cooler at the top. Vapours repeatedly condense and re-evaporate; the liquid with the lowest boiling point reaches the top first and distils over; the thermometer stays at that b.p. until it is all collected, then rises to the next.
Other types: steam distillation (essential oils from flowers and herbs); vacuum distillation (reduced pressure lowers boiling points – for heat-sensitive substances, saves energy).
Applications: distilled water, desalination of sea water, refining crude oil, purifying alcohol, perfumes and food flavourings, separating air into N₂, O₂ and Ar (cryogenic distillation), purifying industrial liquid products.
[Table: Simple vs fractional distillation]
Simple distillation | Fractional distillation
• Separates a solvent from dissolved solids, or liquids with very different b.p. | Separates miscible liquids with close boiling points
• No fractionating column | Fractionating column gives temperature gradient
• e.g. pure water from salt water | e.g. ethanol from water; crude oil fractions; liquid air
• Simpler apparatus | More efficient separation
کشید میں مائع آمیزے کو گرم کر کے بخارات بنائے جاتے ہیں اور کنڈینسر میں ٹھنڈا کر کے کشید شدہ مائع جمع کیا جاتا ہے۔ سادہ کشید نمکین پانی سے خالص پانی حاصل کرنے کے لیے، اور جزوی کشید (فریکشنیٹنگ کالم کے ساتھ) قریب نقطہ ابال والے مائعات جیسے الکحل اور پانی یا خام تیل کو الگ کرنے کے لیے استعمال ہوتی ہے۔

══ 17.6 Choosing a technique; using a suitable solvent (pp. 235) ══
Choose the method from the properties of the components:
- Insoluble solid + liquid (sand + water, chalk + water): filtration (or decantation/sedimentation for quick, rough separation).
- Dissolved solid + liquid, want the solid: evaporation or (for pure crystals) crystallisation.
- Dissolved solid + liquid, want the liquid: simple distillation (water from sea water).
- Two miscible liquids (alcohol + water): fractional distillation.
- Two immiscible liquids (oil + water): separating funnel.
- Coloured substances in solution (inks, dyes): paper chromatography (Unit 19).
- Magnetic + non-magnetic solids (iron + sulfur): magnet.
- Two solids, one soluble: use a suitable solvent → dissolve, filter, then evaporate/crystallise.
Using a suitable solvent: pick a solvent that dissolves only one component.
- Sand + salt (or sand + sugar): add water and stir (salt/sugar dissolves, sand does not) → filter (sand = residue) → evaporate/crystallise the filtrate to get salt/sugar.
- Salt + iodine: heat – iodine sublimes (or dissolve iodine in an organic solvent).
- Sulfur + salt: sulfur dissolves in carbon disulfide/xylene, salt in water.
- Ethanol is used to extract chlorophyll from leaves; hexane extracts cooking oil from seeds.
[Table: Which technique?]
Mixture | Technique | What you get
• Sand + water | Filtration | Sand (residue), water (filtrate)
• Salt solution (want salt) | Evaporation / crystallisation | Salt crystals
• Sea water (want water) | Simple distillation | Pure water (distillate)
• Ethanol + water | Fractional distillation | Ethanol first (78 °C)
• Sand + salt / sand + sugar | Dissolve in water → filter → evaporate | Sand and salt/sugar
• Inks / food dyes | Paper chromatography | Separated dyes
• Oil + water | Separating funnel | Two layers
• Iron + sulfur | Magnet | Iron filings
طریقہ اجزا کی خصوصیات سے چنا جاتا ہے: ناحل ٹھوس + مائع → فلٹریشن؛ حل شدہ ٹھوس → تبخیر یا قلماؤ؛ محلول سے مائع → سادہ کشید؛ دو ملنے والے مائعات → جزوی کشید؛ ریت اور نمک یا چینی → پانی میں حل کر کے فلٹر کریں، پھر تبخیر کریں۔

══ 17.7 Identifying substances and checking purity by melting and boiling points (pp. 235–236) ══
Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points (at a given pressure); these values are characteristic and help identify a substance by comparison with data tables.
- Pure water: m.p. 0 °C, b.p. 100 °C; pure ethanol b.p. 78 °C.
Impure substances:
- melt at a lower temperature and over a range (not sharp);
- boil at a higher temperature and over a range.
Example: salt water boils above 100 °C (around 101–102 °C) and freezes below 0 °C – this is why salt is spread on icy roads.
Method (melting point): place a little solid in a sealed capillary tube attached to a thermometer, heat slowly in a water/oil bath or melting-point apparatus, and note the temperature range over which it melts. A narrow range at the known value → pure.
Milk chocolate (a mixture with milk fats and sugar) melts more easily in the mouth than 70% dark chocolate.
[Table: Pure vs impure]
 | Pure substance | Impure substance
• Melting point | Sharp, fixed | Lower, over a range
• Boiling point | Sharp, fixed | Higher, over a range
• Example | Water: 0 °C and 100 °C | Salt water:  100 °C
خالص مادوں کے نقطہ پگھلاؤ اور نقطہ ابال مقررہ اور تیز ہوتے ہیں، اس لیے ان سے مادے کی پہچان ہوتی ہے۔ ملاوٹ نقطہ پگھلاؤ کم اور نقطہ ابال زیادہ کر دیتی ہے اور یہ ایک حد میں ہوتا ہے، جیسے نمکین پانی 100 °C سے زیادہ پر ابلتا ہے۔

══ KEY DIAGRAMS & FIGURES ══
1. Simple distillation apparatus: Flask heated → vapour → water-cooled condenser → distillate collected.

chapters.definitions:
• Mixture (آمیزہ) [p. 228]: Two or more substances not chemically combined, separable by physical methods.
• Solvent (محلل) [p. 227]: A substance that dissolves a solute.
• Solute (منحل) [p. 227]: A substance that dissolves in a solvent.
• Solution (محلول) [p. 227]: A mixture of one or more solutes dissolved in a solvent.
• Saturated solution (سیر شدہ محلول) [p. 227]: A solution containing the maximum concentration of solute dissolved in the solvent at a specific temperature.
• Residue (باقیات) [p. 227]: A substance that remains after evaporation, distillation, filtration or a similar process.
• Filtrate (فلٹریٹ) [p. 227]: A liquid or solution that has passed through a filter.
• Evaporation (تبخیر) [p. 228]: Separating a dissolved solid from a liquid by turning the liquid into vapour.
• Filtration (فلٹریشن / چھاننا) [p. 231]: Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using a filter medium.
• Crystallisation (قلماؤ) [p. 234]: Obtaining a pure solid as crystals from a saturated solution by cooling.
• Distillation (کشید) [p. 230]: Separating liquid mixtures by heating and cooling, using differences in boiling point.
• Distillate (کشید شدہ مائع) [p. 230]: The liquid obtained by condensing the vapour in distillation.
• Fractional distillation (جزوی کشید) [p. 231]: Distillation using a fractionating column to separate miscible liquids with close boiling points.
• Vacuum distillation (خلائی کشید) [p. 231]: Distillation under reduced pressure, which lowers boiling points.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Mixture (آمیزہ): Physically combined substances
• Solvent (محلل): Dissolving liquid
• Solute (منحل): Dissolved substance
• Saturated (سیر شدہ): Holds maximum solute
• Residue (باقیات): Solid left behind
• Filtrate (فلٹریٹ): Liquid through the filter
• Evaporation (تبخیر): Liquid to vapour
• Filtration (چھاننا): Separating with a filter
• Crystallisation (قلماؤ): Forming crystals
• Distillation (کشید): Boil and condense
• Condenser (کنڈینسر): Cools vapour
• Purity (خالصیت): Freedom from impurities
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Pure water: m.p. 0 °C, b.p. 100 °C (At 1 atm)
• Ethanol: b.p. 78 °C (Distils before water)
• Effect of impurity: m.p. ↓ (range); b.p. ↑ (range)

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why does a thermometer reading stay constant during the distillation of a pure liquid?
   Answer: At the boiling point, heat energy is used to change state, not to raise temperature.
2. Why do clothes dry faster on a windy day?
   Answer: Moving air removes vapour, keeping the air near the cloth unsaturated, so evaporation is faster.
3. Sugar is not heated to dryness during crystallisation. Why?
   Answer: Strong heat decomposes (chars) sugar; crystallisation gives pure crystals without decomposition.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Why is salt sprinkled on icy roads in cold countries?
   Answer: Impurities lower the melting point of ice, so it melts below 0 °C.
2. Which separation process is used in an oil refinery?
   Answer: Fractional distillation of crude oil into fractions such as petrol, kerosene and diesel.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. How would you obtain pure dry salt from a mixture of sand and salt?
   Solution: 1. Add water and stir – salt dissolves, sand does not. 2. Filter – sand is the residue, salt solution is the filtrate. 3. Evaporate the filtrate until saturated, then cool to crystallise the salt (or evaporate to dryness). 4. Filter off and dry the crystals. (Wash and dry the sand if it is needed too.)

2. A white solid melts between 118 °C and 123 °C. The data book gives 122 °C for pure benzoic acid. Is the sample pure?
   Solution: No. A pure substance melts sharply at a fixed temperature; melting over a range starting below the true value shows impurities are present. Purify it by recrystallisation and test again.
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 17 Exercises (236):

— Q1. Give short answers —
(i) Why is it important to separate materials from a mixture?
   Answer: To obtain useful or valuable components in pure form (gold, salt, drinking water, petrol), to remove harmful or unwanted substances (impurities, germs), and to identify and study the properties of the components (e.g. making medicines).
(ii) What is distillation?
   Answer: A method of separating the components of a liquid mixture by heating it to vapour and cooling the vapour back to liquid (distillate), using differences in boiling points.
(iii) What is filtration?
   Answer: Separating an insoluble solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through a filter medium (filter paper) that lets the liquid (filtrate) through and holds back the solid (residue).
(iv) What is evaporation?
   Answer: The change of a liquid into vapour; as a separation method, heating a solution so the solvent vaporises and the dissolved solid is left behind.

— Q2–Q7. Descriptive questions —
2. What technique would you use to separate sand from water? There are two possibilities. Mention their names.
   Answer: Filtration (sand stays on the filter paper) and sedimentation followed by decantation (let the sand settle, then pour off the water). (Evaporation would also leave sand, but wastes the water.)
3. What technique would you use to separate alcohol from water?
   Answer: Fractional distillation. Alcohol (ethanol, b.p. 78 °C) and water (100 °C) are miscible with fairly close boiling points; the fractionating column lets ethanol vapour reach the condenser first and be collected while water remains.
4. What are mixtures?
   Answer: Materials made of two or more substances (elements or compounds) that are not chemically combined, can be present in any proportion, keep their own properties and can be separated by physical methods. Homogeneous (air, salt solution) or heterogeneous (sand + water).
5. How is a mixture of two or more liquids separated? Name the technique.
   Answer: Miscible liquids (that mix completely) with different boiling points: fractional distillation (or simple distillation if boiling points are far apart). Immiscible liquids (oil and water) form layers and are separated with a separating funnel.
6. How do you separate a mixture of two solids?
   Answer: Use a difference in properties: suitable solvent – dissolve one solid, filter, then evaporate (sand + salt); magnet for magnetic solids (iron + sulfur); sublimation if one sublimes (iodine or ammonium chloride + salt); sieving for different particle sizes.
7. What method will you use to separate a sand and sugar mixture?
   Answer: Add water and stir to dissolve sugar → filter (sand is the residue) → heat the filtrate gently to concentrate and crystallise the sugar (avoid strong heating, which chars sugar) → filter and dry the crystals.
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. Define (a) saturated solution (b) residue (c) filtrate.
   Answer: (a) A solution holding the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at that temperature. (b) The substance left behind after filtration, evaporation or distillation. (c) The liquid that has passed through a filter.

2. Why is crystallisation preferred to evaporation to dryness for purifying copper(II) sulphate?
   Answer: Crystallisation leaves soluble impurities in the mother liquor and keeps the water of crystallisation; evaporating to dryness keeps impurities and can decompose the hydrated crystals into white anhydrous powder.

3. How can you tell that a hot solution is saturated during crystallisation?
   Answer: Dip a glass rod in and lift it out; if crystals form on the rod as the drop cools, the solution is saturated.

4. What is the purpose of the fractionating column?
   Answer: It provides a temperature gradient (hot at the bottom, cool at the top) and a large surface for repeated condensation and evaporation, so only the most volatile component reaches the top and distils over.

5. Why is water passed into the condenser from the bottom?
   Answer: So the condenser jacket fills completely with cold water, giving efficient cooling (counter-current flow).

6. Suggest the method to obtain drinking water from sea water and justify.
   Answer: Simple distillation (desalination): water boils and condenses as pure distillate while the dissolved salts remain in the flask.

7. Give three factors that increase the rate of evaporation.
   Answer: Higher temperature, larger surface area, more air flow (also lower pressure and weaker intermolecular forces).

8. How do melting and boiling points help to check purity?
   Answer: Pure substances melt and boil sharply at fixed values; impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point and make them occur over a range.

9. Give two daily-life examples each of filtration and crystallisation.
   Answer: Filtration: tea bag/coffee filter, kidneys, air-conditioner filters. Crystallisation: salt from sea water, sugar crystals, honey crystallising, ice and snow.

10. Why can’t filtration separate salt from salt water?
   Answer: Dissolved salt particles (ions) are smaller than the filter pores, so they pass through with the water.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. Describe the purification of an impure solid by crystallisation, and explain why slow cooling gives large crystals.
   Answer: Dissolve in minimum hot water, filter hot to remove insoluble impurities, heat to saturation (glass-rod test), cool slowly, filter crystals, wash with a little cold water and dry. Slow cooling lets particles add in an orderly way to a few growing crystals, giving large regular crystals; fast cooling starts many crystals at once, so they stay small.

2. Describe simple and fractional distillation with labelled apparatus and one use of each.
   Answer: Simple: distillation flask with thermometer at the side arm, Liebig condenser (water in at the bottom), receiver; heat – volatile liquid vaporises, condenses and is collected; use – pure water from salt water. Fractional: same plus a fractionating column packed with glass beads between flask and condenser; the component with the lowest b.p. distils first at constant temperature; use – ethanol from water, crude oil refining, liquid air.

3. Suggest, with reasons, suitable techniques to obtain: (a) pure water from ink (b) salt from rock salt (salt + sand) (c) ethanol from fermented sugar solution (d) chalk from chalky water.
   Answer: (a) Simple distillation – water boils off, dye remains. (b) Dissolve in water, filter off sand, evaporate/crystallise the filtrate. (c) Fractional distillation – ethanol (78 °C) distils before water. (d) Filtration – chalk is insoluble (residue).

chapters.title: Qualitative Analysis
chapters.introduction:
Qualitative analysis finds out what substances are present, not how much. This unit describes simple, reliable laboratory tests for gases – ammonia, carbon dioxide, chlorine, hydrogen, oxygen and sulfur dioxide – and the flame test for metal cations (lithium, sodium, potassium, calcium, copper(II), barium and others), with the reasons behind each observation.

Both SLOs (F-15 gas tests, F-16 flame tests) are summative and practical (PBA). They are usually examined in the practical and as short questions (“How is CO₂ identified?”, “What colour does sodium give in a flame test?”). No question from this unit appears in the uploaded 2025–2026 papers, so the exam-style questions here are AI-generated.

══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
Both SLOs (F-15 gas tests, F-16 flame tests) are summative and practical (PBA). They are usually examined in the practical and as short questions (“How is CO₂ identified?”, “What colour does sodium give in a flame test?”). No question from this unit appears in the uploaded 2025–2026 papers, so the exam-style questions here are AI-generated.
Note: Calcium (brick-red) is in the official SLO list but not in the textbook’s colour list; it is added here. The textbook writes the barium flame as “green”; it is usually described as apple-green / pale green.

══ 18.1 Qualitative analysis; test for ammonia (pp. 238) ══
Qualitative analysis tells us the nature (identity) of a substance, not its quantity (that is quantitative analysis). Good tests give a clear, characteristic result; confirmatory tests are the most reliable.
Ammonia, NH₃: a colourless gas with a sharp smell; the only common alkaline (basic) gas; used to make urea fertilizer; made industrially by the Haber process (N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃).
Test:
1. Moisten a piece of red litmus paper with water (gases must dissolve to show acid/base properties).
2. Hold it at the mouth of the test tube containing the gas.
3. Damp red litmus turns blue → ammonia (alkaline gas).
NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄^+ + OH⁻ (the OH⁻ ions turn litmus blue).
(Extra: ammonia gives white fumes of ammonium chloride with HCl gas.)
کیفیتی تجزیہ مادے کی پہچان کرتا ہے۔ امونیا واحد عام قلیائی گیس ہے: نم سرخ لٹمس پیپر کو نیلا کر دیتی ہے کیونکہ پانی میں حل ہو کر OH⁻ آئن بناتی ہے۔

══ 18.2 Test for carbon dioxide (limewater) (pp. 238–239) ══
Preparation: marble chips (CaCO₃) in a conical flask; dilute hydrochloric acid added through a thistle funnel; gas led through a delivery tube.
CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂
Test: bubble the gas through limewater (calcium hydroxide solution, Ca(OH)₂(aq)). Limewater turns milky (cloudy) because insoluble white calcium carbonate forms:
Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l)
This is the confirmatory test for CO₂. (With excess CO₂ the milkiness disappears as soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate forms.)
CO₂ also turns damp blue litmus slightly red (weakly acidic) and puts out a burning splint, but those tests are not specific.
کاربن ڈائی آکسائیڈ کو چونے کے پانی میں سے گزارنے پر یہ دودھیا ہو جاتا ہے کیونکہ ناحل پذیر کیلشیم کاربونیٹ بنتا ہے: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O۔ یہ CO₂ کا تصدیقی ٹیسٹ ہے۔

══ 18.3 Test for chlorine (damp litmus) (pp. 239) ══
Chlorine, Cl₂: greenish-yellow, poisonous gas with a choking smell (test in a fume cupboard).
Test: hold damp blue litmus paper in the gas.
- It first turns red (chlorine dissolves to form acids: Cl₂ + H₂O → HCl + HOCl).
- It is then bleached white (colourless) by hypochlorous acid HOCl, a strong bleaching agent.
Damp red litmus or universal indicator paper is simply bleached.
Why white at the end? HOCl releases oxygen that oxidises the coloured dye of the litmus to a colourless substance.
کلورین سبزی مائل زرد زہریلی گیس ہے۔ نم نیلا لٹمس پیپر پہلے سرخ ہوتا ہے (تیزاب بننے کی وجہ سے) اور پھر سفید ہو جاتا ہے کیونکہ ہائپوکلورس ایسڈ رنگ کاٹ دیتا ہے۔

══ 18.4 Test for hydrogen (lighted splint – “pop”) (pp. 239–240) ══
Preparation: granulated zinc with dilute sulphuric acid in a Woulfe bottle (or flask) fitted with a thistle funnel and delivery tube:
Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂
Hydrogen is very light, so it is collected in a test tube held upside down (mouth downward); it does not escape quickly from an inverted tube.
Test: bring a lighted (burning) splint to the mouth of the tube. The gas burns with a squeaky “pop” sound.
2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
Why the pop? Hydrogen mixed with air explodes rapidly in a tiny controlled explosion when ignited; the sudden expansion of hot gas makes the sound. A little water forms on the cool tube.
ہائیڈروجن زنک اور سلفیورک ایسڈ سے بنتی ہے اور الٹی ٹیسٹ ٹیوب میں جمع کی جاتی ہے۔ جلتی ہوئی تیلی قریب لانے پر یہ پاپ کی آواز کے ساتھ جلتی ہے (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O)۔

══ 18.5 Test for oxygen (glowing splint) (pp. 240–241) ══
Preparation (school lab): decompose hydrogen peroxide using a catalyst (manganese(IV) oxide):
2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂
Test: light a wooden splint, blow it out so it is only glowing at the tip, and insert it into the gas. The glowing splint relights (bursts into flame) → oxygen.
Reason: oxygen supports combustion; the high concentration of O₂ makes the glowing wood burn fiercely.
Compare: a lighted splint is used for hydrogen (pop); a glowing splint is used for oxygen (relights). Work in a well-ventilated area and away from flammable materials.
آکسیجن جلنے میں مدد دیتی ہے۔ سلگتی ہوئی (بجھی مگر دہکتی) تیلی آکسیجن میں ڈالنے پر دوبارہ بھڑک اٹھتی ہے۔

══ 18.6 Test for sulfur dioxide (acidified KMnO₄) (pp. 241) ══
Sulfur dioxide, SO₂: colourless, toxic gas with a choking smell; an acidic gas and a good reducing agent.
Test: pass the gas through (or hold filter paper soaked in) acidified potassium manganate(VII), KMnO₄, which is purple. The solution turns colourless (purple colour is discharged) because SO₂ reduces purple MnO₄^- to almost colourless Mn²⁺.
2KMnO₄ + 5SO₂ + 2H₂O → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 2H₂SO₄
This method is used in analytical chemistry and environmental monitoring of SO₂. (SO₂ also turns damp blue litmus red.)
سلفر ڈائی آکسائیڈ ایک تخفیفی گیس ہے۔ یہ تیزابی پوٹاشیم پرمینگنیٹ کے ارغوانی محلول کو بے رنگ کر دیتی ہے۔

══ 18.7 Flame tests for metal cations (pp. 241–242) ══
Bunsen flame: the outer, hotter, blue part is the oxidising flame (plenty of air/oxygen); the inner part near the burner is the reducing flame (less oxygen, unburnt gas).
Origin of flame colour: the heat of the flame excites electrons in metal atoms/ions to higher energy levels. When they fall back to the ground state, they emit energy as light of particular wavelengths in the visible region – each metal gives its own characteristic colour. Alkali metals have low ionisation energies, so their electrons are excited easily by flame energy.
Procedure:
1. Clean a platinum or nichrome wire loop by dipping in concentrated HCl and heating until it gives no colour.
2. Dip the loop in HCl and then in the sample (salt, solution or paste).
3. Hold it in the hot (non-luminous, blue) part of the Bunsen flame.
4. Observe the colour and compare with a reference chart. Clean the wire between samples.
[Table: Flame test colours]
Cation | Flame colour
• Lithium, Li⁺ | Crimson red
• Sodium, Na⁺ | Golden yellow (persistent)
• Potassium, K⁺ | Lilac / light purple
• Calcium, Ca²⁺ | Brick red (orange-red)
• Copper(II), Cu²⁺ | Bluish-green
• Barium, Ba²⁺ | Apple green (pale green)
• Strontium, Sr²⁺ | Crimson red
• Caesium, Cs⁺ | Blue / violet
Exam Tip: Sodium’s yellow is so strong it can hide other colours; potassium’s lilac is best seen through blue cobalt glass.
شعلہ ٹیسٹ: شعلے کی حرارت سے دھات کے الیکٹران اونچی سطح پر جاتے ہیں اور واپس آتے ہوئے مخصوص رنگ کی روشنی خارج کرتے ہیں۔ لیتھیم – گہرا سرخ، سوڈیم – سنہری زرد، پوٹاشیم – بنفشی، کیلشیم – اینٹ جیسا سرخ، کاپر – نیلگوں سبز، بیریم – ہلکا سبز۔

══ CHAPTER SUMMARY TABLES ══
[Table: Summary of gas tests]
Gas | Test | Positive result
• Ammonia NH₃ | Damp red litmus paper | Turns blue
• Carbon dioxide CO₂ | Bubble through limewater | Limewater turns milky
• Chlorine Cl₂ | Damp blue litmus paper | Turns red, then bleached white
• Hydrogen H₂ | Lighted splint | Burns with a squeaky pop
• Oxygen O₂ | Glowing splint | Splint relights
• Sulfur dioxide SO₂ | Acidified KMnO₄ | Purple → colourless

chapters.definitions:
• Qualitative analysis (کیفیتی تجزیہ) [p. 238]: Analysis that identifies which substances are present, not their amounts.
• Quantitative analysis (مقداری تجزیہ) [p. 238]: Analysis that measures how much of a substance is present.
• Confirmatory test (تصدیقی ٹیسٹ) [p. 238]: A specific, reliable test that confirms the identity of a substance.
• Limewater (چونے کا پانی) [p. 238]: A solution of calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)₂, used to test for CO₂.
• Bleaching agent (رنگ کاٹ مادہ) [p. 239]: A substance that removes colour, e.g. chlorine (as HOCl).
• Flame test (شعلہ ٹیسٹ) [p. 241]: Identifying metal ions by the characteristic colour they give to a flame.
• Oxidising flame (تکسیدی شعلہ) [p. 241]: The outer, hotter part of a Bunsen flame with excess oxygen.
• Reducing flame (تخفیفی شعلہ) [p. 241]: The inner part of a Bunsen flame with less oxygen and unburnt gas.
• Ground state (بنیادی حالت) [p. 241]: The lowest energy arrangement of electrons in an atom.
• Excited state (ہیجان زدہ حالت) [p. 241]: A state in which an electron has absorbed energy and moved to a higher level.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Qualitative (کیفیتی): About identity
• Quantitative (مقداری): About amount
• Litmus (لٹمس): Acid–base indicator paper
• Limewater (چونے کا پانی): Ca(OH)₂ solution
• Splint (لکڑی کی تیلی): Thin wooden stick
• Glowing (سلگتا ہوا): Red-hot without flame
• Bleach (رنگ کاٹنا): Remove colour
• Flame test (شعلہ ٹیسٹ): Identify metals by colour
• Excited (ہیجان زدہ): Raised to higher energy
• Emit (خارج کرنا): Give out light
• Reducing agent (تخفیفی عامل): Gives electrons / removes O
• Confirmatory (تصدیقی): Gives certain identification

• Limewater: Ca(OH)₂(aq)

• NH₃ + H₂O  NH₄^+ + OH⁻ — Why ammonia turns red litmus blue.
• CaCO₃ + 2HCl -> CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂ — Preparation of CO₂.
• Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ -> CaCO₃ + H₂O — Limewater turns milky.

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Why is hydrogen collected in an inverted test tube but oxygen can be collected upright?
   Answer: Hydrogen is much lighter than air and would escape from an upright tube; oxygen is slightly denser than air.
2. Why do different metals give different flame colours?
   Answer: Each element has different electron energy levels, so the energy (wavelength) of light emitted is different.
3. Why is ammonia the only common gas that turns red litmus blue?
   Answer: It is the only common alkaline gas; most other gases are acidic or neutral.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. Fireworks show red, green and yellow colours. Which metal compounds could produce these?
   Answer: Red: strontium or lithium; green: barium (or copper); yellow: sodium.
2. How can you check whether the air you breathe out contains CO₂?
   Answer: Blow through a straw into limewater; it turns milky.
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. A gas turns damp red litmus blue. A second gas relights a glowing splint. A third gives a pop with a lighted splint. Identify them.
   Solution: First: ammonia (alkaline). Second: oxygen. Third: hydrogen.

2. A white solid gives a lilac flame, and when acid is added it releases a gas that turns limewater milky. Identify the solid.
   Solution: Lilac flame → K⁺; gas turning limewater milky → CO₂, so the anion is carbonate: the solid is potassium carbonate, K₂CO₃.
