NBF Chapter 18 Exercises (243):

— Exercise MCQs —
i. Ammonia is a gas which is: → B (Basic) | Turns red litmus blue.
ii. Which gas helps in the combustion process? → A (Oxygen) | Supports burning.
iii. Which gas turns lime water milky? → B (Carbon dioxide) | Forms CaCO₃.
iv. Electrons of alkali metals are excited by absorbing light in the: → A (Visible wavelength) | Low ionisation energy; flame colours are visible.
v. The colour imparted to the flame by sodium is: → C (Golden yellow) | Characteristic Na colour.

— Q2. Give short answers —
(i) How is ammonia detected by litmus paper?
   Answer: Hold damp red litmus paper at the mouth of the tube; ammonia dissolves in the water to form OH⁻ ions and turns the litmus blue.
(ii) How can you identify carbon dioxide?
   Answer: Bubble the gas through limewater; it turns milky due to insoluble calcium carbonate: Ca(OH)₂ + CO₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O.
(iii) How can you detect hydrogen gas?
   Answer: Bring a lighted splint to the mouth of the test tube; hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop sound.
(iv) How can you detect sulphur dioxide?
   Answer: Pass the gas through acidified potassium manganate(VII) solution; the purple colour is discharged (turns colourless) because SO₂ reduces it.
(v) Differentiate between oxidising and reducing flame.
   Answer: Oxidising flame: outer, hottest, non-luminous blue part of the Bunsen flame with excess oxygen (complete combustion). Reducing flame: inner part near the burner with insufficient oxygen and unburnt gas (carbon, CO) that can remove oxygen from compounds.

— Q3–Q6. Descriptive questions —
3. What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative analysis?
   Answer: Qualitative analysis identifies what substances (elements, ions, gases) are present – e.g. flame tests, gas tests. Quantitative analysis measures how much is present – e.g. titration, weighing a precipitate, measuring gas volume.
4. What is the origin of flame colour?
   Answer: Heat from the flame gives energy to electrons of metal atoms/ions, which jump to higher energy levels (excited state). These are unstable, so the electrons fall back to lower levels (ground state), releasing the extra energy as light. The energy gaps are fixed for each element, so each emits light of particular visible wavelengths – a characteristic colour (Na yellow, K lilac, Cu blue-green).
5. Why does hydrogen gas produce a popping sound when exposed to a flame?
   Answer: Hydrogen mixed with air in the tube reacts very rapidly with oxygen when ignited (2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O). This tiny explosion releases heat suddenly, so the hot gases expand very quickly and push the air, producing the “pop”.
6. Why does litmus paper turn white at the end after turning red (in the chlorine test)?
   Answer: Chlorine dissolves in the water on the paper forming HCl and HOCl, which are acidic, so blue litmus turns red. HOCl (hypochlorous acid) is a strong oxidising/bleaching agent that destroys the litmus dye, so the paper becomes white (bleached).

══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. Describe a test for oxygen gas.
   Answer: Insert a glowing splint into the gas; it relights because oxygen supports combustion.

2. How would you distinguish between hydrogen and oxygen using a splint?
   Answer: Hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop. Oxygen: a glowing splint relights.

3. Name the gas that turns damp blue litmus red and then bleaches it.
   Answer: Chlorine.

4. Give the flame colours of Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Cu²⁺.
   Answer: Li⁺ crimson red; Na⁺ golden yellow; K⁺ lilac; Ca²⁺ brick red; Cu²⁺ bluish-green.

5. Why is the platinum/nichrome wire dipped in concentrated HCl before a flame test?
   Answer: To clean it of any previous sample (impurities would give false colours); chlorides are also more volatile, giving clearer colours.

6. Write the equation for the reaction of carbon dioxide with limewater.
   Answer: Ca(OH)₂(aq) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s) + H₂O(l).

7. Why must litmus paper be damp when testing gases?
   Answer: Gases show acidic or alkaline properties only when dissolved in water to form ions (H⁺ or OH⁻).

8. How is sulfur dioxide different from carbon dioxide in its effect on acidified KMnO₄?
   Answer: SO₂ is a reducing agent and decolourises purple KMnO₄; CO₂ does not.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. Describe tests to identify ammonia, carbon dioxide, chlorine, hydrogen, oxygen and sulfur dioxide, giving observations and reasons.
   Answer: NH₃: damp red litmus → blue (alkaline, forms OH⁻). CO₂: limewater → milky (CaCO₃ precipitate). Cl₂: damp blue litmus → red → white (acidic then bleached by HOCl). H₂: lighted splint → squeaky pop (rapid combustion to water). O₂: glowing splint → relights (supports combustion). SO₂: acidified KMnO₄ purple → colourless (SO₂ reduces MnO₄^-).

2. Explain how the flame test is carried out and how it identifies metal cations.
   Answer: Clean a platinum/nichrome loop in conc. HCl until no colour; dip in HCl then the sample; hold in the hot blue flame; note the colour. Heat excites electrons; falling back they emit visible light of fixed wavelengths characteristic of the metal: Li crimson, Na golden yellow, K lilac, Ca brick red, Cu(II) blue-green, Ba apple green.

chapters.title: Chromatography
chapters.introduction:
Chromatography (Greek chroma = colour, graphein = writing) separates the components of a mixture of soluble substances and helps to identify them. This unit explains paper chromatography: the stationary and mobile phases, the practical procedure, locating agents for colourless substances, reading chromatograms to identify unknowns and check purity, and calculating Rf values.

All four SLOs (F-17 to F-20) are summative and practical (PBA): describe paper chromatography, use of locating agents, interpret chromatograms (identify unknowns, pure vs impure) and state and use the Rf equation. No question from this unit appears in the uploaded 2025–2026 papers, so the exam-style questions here are AI-generated.

chapters.completeNotes:
══ FBISE ASSESSMENT & EXAM WEIGHTAGE ══
All four SLOs (F-17 to F-20) are summative and practical (PBA): describe paper chromatography, use of locating agents, interpret chromatograms (identify unknowns, pure vs impure) and state and use the Rf equation. No question from this unit appears in the uploaded 2025–2026 papers, so the exam-style questions here are AI-generated.
Note: The textbook calls Rf both “retardation factor” and “retention factor”; both names are used. The textbook procedure uses a water–ethanol solvent and a strip of filter paper hung from a hook in a measuring cylinder; the more common school method (paper in a beaker) is described too.

══ 19.1 Principle: stationary and mobile phases (pp. 245) ══
Chromatography is a powerful analytical tool used both to separate and to identify compounds (it can be coupled with mass spectrometry in research labs).
Principle (partition): the components of a mixture distribute themselves between two phases:
- Stationary phase: does not move – a solid, or a liquid held on a solid. In paper chromatography it is the water adsorbed on the cellulose fibres of the paper.
- Mobile phase: a liquid (solvent) or gas that moves through or over the stationary phase, e.g. water, ethanol or a mixture of solvents.
As the solvent carries the mixture up the paper, each component interacts differently with the two phases:
- components more soluble in the solvent (more attracted to the mobile phase) travel further and faster;
- components more attracted to the paper (stationary phase) travel less.
So components move at different rates and separate into spots.
Paper chromatography separates inks, dyes, food colours, plant pigments, metal ions and amino acids.
کرومیٹوگرافی کا اصول یہ ہے کہ آمیزے کے اجزا دو فیزز میں تقسیم ہوتے ہیں: ساکن فیز (کاغذ کے ریشوں پر جذب پانی) اور متحرک فیز (محلل جو اوپر چڑھتا ہے)۔ جو جزو محلل میں زیادہ حل ہو وہ زیادہ اوپر جاتا ہے، جو کاغذ سے زیادہ چپکے وہ کم۔ اس طرح اجزا الگ ہو جاتے ہیں۔

══ 19.2 Carrying out paper chromatography (pp. 245–246) ══
Procedure (textbook method for a mixture of inks):
1. Pour a little solvent (water–ethanol mixture) into a tall measuring cylinder (or beaker) and close it so the air becomes saturated with solvent vapour (about 10 minutes).
2. Cut a strip of chromatography/filter paper (Whatman No. 1) to fit.
3. Draw a baseline in pencil about 2 cm from the bottom and mark the starting point. (Pencil, because graphite does not dissolve or move; ink would itself separate.)
4. Use a capillary tube to put a very small, concentrated spot of the mixture on the baseline; let it dry and re-spot if needed. Spot known reference substances alongside for comparison.
5. Hang/stand the paper so the bottom dips into the solvent to a depth of about 5–6 mm – the solvent level must be below the baseline (otherwise the spots dissolve into the solvent).
6. Cover and leave undisturbed while the solvent rises by capillary action.
7. When the solvent is near the top, remove the paper and mark the solvent front in pencil immediately.
8. Dry the paper. The resulting pattern of spots is the chromatogram.
9. Measure distances from the baseline to the centre of each spot and to the solvent front; calculate Rf values.
Choosing a solvent: the substances must be soluble in it; water for water-soluble inks and food dyes, ethanol or other organic solvents for insoluble ones (e.g. permanent marker ink, chlorophyll).
Exam Tip: Two classic exam points: (1) the baseline is drawn in pencil; (2) the solvent level must be below the baseline.
طریقہ: کاغذ پر نیچے سے تقریباً 2 cm اوپر پنسل سے بنیادی لکیر کھینچیں، کیپلری سے آمیزے کا چھوٹا دھبہ لگائیں، کاغذ کو محلل میں اس طرح رکھیں کہ محلل کی سطح لکیر سے نیچے رہے۔ محلل اوپر چڑھ کر اجزا کو الگ کر دیتا ہے۔ محلل کی آخری حد (solvent front) پر نشان لگا کر کاغذ خشک کریں۔

══ 19.3 Locating agents for colourless substances (pp. 246) ══
Some separated components are colourless and cannot be seen on the chromatogram. A locating agent is a substance (solution) sprayed on the dried chromatogram that reacts with the colourless components to form coloured spots, so their positions can be located and Rf values measured.
Example: a mixture of amino acids separated by paper chromatography or thin-layer chromatography (TLC) is invisible; spraying with ninhydrin (and warming) turns the amino-acid spots purple/blue.
Other ways to locate colourless spots: viewing under ultraviolet (UV) light, or exposing to iodine vapour (brown spots).
(Knowledge of specific locating agents is not required by the SLO, but ninhydrin is the textbook example.)
لوکیٹنگ ایجنٹ وہ محلول ہے جو خشک کرومیٹوگرام پر چھڑکا جاتا ہے تاکہ بے رنگ اجزا رنگین دھبوں کی صورت میں نظر آئیں۔ مثال: امینو ایسڈز پر ننہائیڈرن چھڑکنے سے ارغوانی دھبے بنتے ہیں۔

══ 19.4 Rf values (pp. 246–247) ══
The Rf value (retardation/retention factor) measures how far a substance travels compared with the solvent:
Rf = distance travelled by the substance (from baseline to centre of spot) ÷ distance travelled by the solvent (from baseline to solvent front)
- Rf has no units and is always between 0 and 1 (a spot can never move further than the solvent).
- For a given solvent, paper and temperature, each substance has a characteristic Rf.
- A larger Rf → the substance has greater affinity for the mobile phase (more soluble in the solvent). A smaller Rf → greater affinity for the stationary phase.
Textbook example (Figure 19.1): solvent front 10 cm; blue spot 8 cm, purple 6 cm, red 2 cm:
Rf (blue) = 8/10 = 0.8; Rf (purple) = 6/10 = 0.6; Rf (red) = 2/10 = 0.2.
Blue has the greatest affinity for the mobile phase; red has the greatest affinity for the stationary phase.
Rf قدر = مادے کا طے کردہ فاصلہ ÷ محلل کا طے کردہ فاصلہ (دونوں بنیادی لکیر سے)۔ اس کی کوئی اکائی نہیں اور یہ 0 اور 1 کے درمیان ہوتی ہے۔ زیادہ Rf کا مطلب ہے مادہ محلل (متحرک فیز) میں زیادہ حل پذیر ہے۔ مثال: 8 ÷ 10 = 0.8۔

══ 19.5 Interpreting chromatograms: identifying substances and purity (pp. 247) ══
Identifying an unknown: run the unknown alongside known reference substances on the same paper with the same solvent. If a spot from the unknown travels the same distance (same Rf) and has the same colour as a known substance, they are likely the same substance. Rf values can also be compared with data tables of known values.
Pure vs impure:
- A pure substance gives only one spot.
- An impure substance (mixture) gives two or more spots – one for each soluble component.
- If two different substances happen to have the same Rf in one solvent, repeating with a different solvent can separate them.
- A spot that stays on the baseline is insoluble in that solvent.
Uses: checking food colourings (banned dyes), identifying inks in forensic science (forged documents), testing purity of medicines, separating plant pigments, detecting drugs in sport.
نامعلوم مادے کو معلوم مادوں کے ساتھ ایک ہی کاغذ پر چلائیں؛ جس کا دھبہ ایک ہی فاصلے (ایک ہی Rf) تک جائے وہ غالباً ایک ہی مادہ ہے۔ خالص مادہ ایک دھبہ دیتا ہے اور ناخالص مادہ ایک سے زیادہ دھبے۔

══ CHAPTER SUMMARY TABLES ══
[Table: Interpreting a chromatogram]
Observation | Conclusion
• One spot | Pure substance
• Two or more spots | Mixture / impure
• Same Rf and colour as a known substance | Probably the same substance
• Spot stays on the baseline | Insoluble in that solvent
• High Rf | More soluble in solvent (mobile phase)
• Low Rf | More attracted to paper (stationary phase)

1. Paper chromatogram (Figure 19.1 values): Solvent front 10 cm; blue 8 cm (Rf 0.8), purple 6 cm (0.6), red 2 cm (0.2).

chapters.definitions:
• Chromatography (کرومیٹوگرافی) [p. 245]: A technique that separates components of a mixture by their different distribution between a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
• Paper chromatography (کاغذی کرومیٹوگرافی) [p. 245]: Chromatography in which the stationary phase is water held in the cellulose of paper and a solvent moves up the paper.
• Stationary phase (ساکن فیز) [p. 245]: The phase that does not move; in paper chromatography, water adsorbed on the paper.
• Mobile phase (متحرک فیز) [p. 245]: The liquid or gas that moves through or over the stationary phase, carrying the mixture.
• Chromatogram (کرومیٹوگرام) [p. 246]: The pattern of separated spots on the paper after chromatography.
• Baseline (بنیادی لکیر) [p. 245]: The pencil line on which the samples are spotted.
• Solvent front (محلل کی آخری حد) [p. 246]: The furthest point reached by the solvent on the paper.
• Locating agent (نشاندہی کرنے والا مادہ) [p. 246]: A substance sprayed on a chromatogram to make colourless components visible as coloured spots.
• Rf value (آر ایف قدر) [p. 246]: Distance travelled by a substance divided by distance travelled by the solvent.

══ BILINGUAL GLOSSARY ══
• Chromatography (کرومیٹوگرافی): Separation by two phases
• Stationary phase (ساکن فیز): Phase that stays
• Mobile phase (متحرک فیز): Moving solvent
• Chromatogram (کرومیٹوگرام): Paper with spots
• Baseline (بنیادی لکیر): Starting line
• Solvent front (محلل کی حد): Furthest solvent point
• Locating agent (نشاندہی ایجنٹ): Reveals colourless spots
• Rf value (آر ایف قدر): Distance ratio
• Capillary action (شعری عمل): Liquid rising in fine spaces
• Pigment (رنگ دار مادہ): Colouring substance
• Affinity (کشش / رغبت): Attraction
• Forensic (عدالتی سائنس): Crime science
chapters.formulasAndConcepts:
══ KEY FORMULAS & QUANTITIES ══
• Rf value: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent (No units; 0 < Rf < 1)
• Distance moved by substance: = Rf × distance moved by solvent (Rearranged)

══ CONCEPTUAL REASONING (SLO-BASED) ══
1. Two dyes have the same Rf in water. Are they definitely the same?
   Answer: Not necessarily – run again in a different solvent; if Rf values still match, they are very likely the same.
2. Why do different dyes travel different distances?
   Answer: They differ in solubility in the solvent and attraction to the paper.
3. Why must the spot be small and concentrated?
   Answer: Large spots spread and overlap, giving poor separation.

══ APPLIED & REAL-LIFE CONCEPTS ══
1. How could chromatography help detect a forged cheque?
   Answer: Compare the ink on the cheque with the account holder’s pen ink; different dye patterns show different inks.
2. How is chromatography used in sport?
   Answer: Urine samples are tested for banned drugs by comparing with known standards (advanced chromatography).
chapters.solvedExamples:
══ WORKED TEXTBOOK EXAMPLES ══

1. In a chromatogram the solvent front moved 12.0 cm and a red dye moved 4.8 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value.
   Given: Distance moved by dye = 4.8 cm; distance moved by solvent = 12.0 cm
   Required: Rf
   Formula: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent
   Substitution: Rf = 4.8 ÷ 12.0
   Calculation: 4.8 ÷ 12.0 = 0.40
   Final Answer: Rf = 0.40 (no units)

2. A substance has Rf = 0.65. The solvent front travelled 8.0 cm. How far did the spot move?
   Given: Rf = 0.65; solvent distance = 8.0 cm
   Required: Distance moved by substance
   Formula: distance = Rf × solvent distance
   Substitution: 0.65 × 8.0
   Calculation: = 5.2
   Final Answer: 5.2 cm from the baseline

3. A food colouring X gives two spots at the same heights as dyes A and C on the same chromatogram. What can you conclude?
   Solution: X is a mixture (impure) – it gives two spots – and it probably contains dyes A and C, because its spots have the same Rf values as A and C.
chapters.solvedExercises:
NBF Chapter 19 Exercises (247):

— Q1. Give short answers —
(i) Define chromatography.
   Answer: A technique for separating (and identifying) the components of a mixture based on their different distribution between a stationary phase and a mobile phase.
(ii) Define locating agent.
   Answer: A substance sprayed on a chromatogram that reacts with colourless separated components to make them visible as coloured spots, e.g. ninhydrin for amino acids.
(iii) What is the Rf value?
   Answer: The ratio of the distance travelled by a substance to the distance travelled by the solvent front, both measured from the baseline: Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent. It has no units and lies between 0 and 1.
(iv) Define paper chromatography.
   Answer: Chromatography in which the stationary phase is water held in the cellulose fibres of chromatography/filter paper and a solvent (mobile phase) moves up the paper by capillary action, separating soluble substances.
(v) What do you mean by a paper chromatogram?
   Answer: The dried paper showing the pattern of separated spots (and the marked baseline and solvent front) after paper chromatography.

— Q2–Q4. Descriptive questions —
2. Explain paper chromatography in detail.
   Answer: Principle: components distribute between the stationary phase (water on the paper) and the mobile phase (solvent); those more soluble in the solvent move further.
Procedure: draw a pencil baseline 2 cm from the bottom; spot the mixture (and reference substances) with a capillary tube; dip the paper into solvent in a covered container with the solvent below the baseline; let the solvent rise by capillary action; remove the paper, mark the solvent front, dry it.
Results: each component forms a separate spot; colourless spots are revealed with a locating agent (ninhydrin). Calculate Rf = distance of spot ÷ distance of solvent front.
Interpretation: one spot = pure; several = mixture; same Rf as a known = same substance.
Uses: separating inks, dyes, food colours, plant pigments, amino acids, metal ions.
3. How can you identify an unknown substance by chromatography?
   Answer: Spot the unknown and several known substances side by side on the same baseline and run the chromatogram with the same solvent. Compare positions/colours, or calculate Rf values and compare with known Rf data. A spot with the same Rf (and colour) as a known substance is likely the same substance; confirm with a second solvent if needed.
4. Differentiate between stationary and mobile phase.
   Answer: Stationary phase: does not move; solid or liquid held on a solid; in paper chromatography, water adsorbed on cellulose; components attracted strongly to it move slowly. Mobile phase: moves through/over the stationary phase; a liquid solvent or gas; carries the components; components more soluble in it travel further.
chapters.importantQuestions:
══ SHORT RESPONSE QUESTIONS (PAST PAPERS, MODEL PAPERS & SLO PRACTICE) ══

1. Why is the baseline drawn in pencil and not ink?
   Answer: Pencil graphite is insoluble and does not move with the solvent; ink would dissolve and separate, confusing the results.

2. Why must the solvent level be below the baseline?
   Answer: Otherwise the spots would dissolve directly into the solvent in the container instead of travelling up the paper.

3. Why is the container covered during chromatography?
   Answer: To keep the air saturated with solvent vapour so the solvent does not evaporate from the paper and rises evenly.

4. A dye moved 3.6 cm while the solvent moved 9.0 cm. Calculate its Rf.
   Answer: Rf = 3.6 ÷ 9.0 = 0.40.

5. Why can an Rf value never be greater than 1?
   Answer: A substance is carried by the solvent, so it cannot travel further than the solvent front.

6. How does a chromatogram show that a substance is pure?
   Answer: A pure substance gives a single spot.

7. What would you see if a sample contained a component insoluble in the solvent?
   Answer: That component would remain as a spot on the baseline (Rf = 0).

8. State two uses of paper chromatography.
   Answer: Identifying dyes in food colourings or inks (forensics); separating plant pigments or amino acids; checking purity of medicines.


══ EXTENDED / LONG RESPONSE QUESTIONS ══

1. A student tests a brown food colouring with dyes P, Q and R. The brown gives three spots. Explain what this shows and how Rf values would help identify the dyes.
   Answer: Three spots show the brown colouring is a mixture of at least three soluble dyes (not pure). If spots of the brown are at the same heights (same Rf) as P, Q or R, it contains those dyes. Calculating each Rf (spot distance ÷ solvent distance) allows comparison with known values even across different chromatograms run under the same conditions. A spot matching none of P, Q, R is an unknown dye.

2. Describe how colourless amino acids can be separated and identified by paper chromatography.
   Answer: Spot the amino-acid mixture and known amino acids on a pencil baseline; run with a suitable solvent; mark the solvent front and dry. The spots are invisible, so spray with the locating agent ninhydrin and warm – purple spots appear. Measure distances, calculate Rf values and compare with the known amino acids/data tables to identify each one.
